P2-04.title: Denture Bonding and Integration
P2-04.subtitle: From Manufacturing Integration to Long-Term Use and Maintenance
P2-04.thesis: The value of integrated dentures lies in reducing manufacturing errors and improving reliability throughout the entire lifespan. Current evidence has shifted the focus from whether the teeth and denture base can bond securely to assembly deviations, material transition zones, repair structures, and long-term patient use; commercial systems have also entered the regional delivery phase. The next stage of competition will depend on whether manufacturing simplification can continue to translate into fewer adjustments, lower failure rates, and easier maintenance.

questions.question: How to improve the bonding strength between artificial teeth and denture base?
questions.focus: Track combinations of denture teeth, base material, bonding agents and ageing conditions to explain changes in both strength and failure location.

questions.question: Can integrated printing reduce assembly errors?
questions.focus: Separate tooth-socket design, linked-tooth arrangements, continuous material forming and post-processing to establish how each affects tooth position and occlusal relationships.

questions.question: How can denture relining and repair interfaces remain reliable?
questions.focus: Evaluate reline interfaces, fracture-repair structures and subsequent ageing separately, relating each to clinical intervention events.

sections.title: I. Research Questions and Industrial Significance: Placing delivery and maintenance on the same quality chain

blocks.text: This chapter focuses on research published up to November 3, 2026, on tooth-base connections, fabrication integration, and subsequent maintenance. The evaluation focuses on a denture delivered to a patient, designed for continued use and maintenance. Material samples reveal local properties, digital models describe geometric changes, and complete devices and clinical observations link these changes to actual use. The main research thread is to establish a testable chain of evidence connecting initial connection strength, fit location, post-aging load, and patient intervention events.

The connection problem involves both mechanical and geometric dimensions. The connection area needs to transfer loads, while the tooth position determines whether the design relationship can be retained in the finished product. Thickening the binder or changing the positioning method may affect both strength and tooth position simultaneously; therefore, optimizing only one indicator may not improve the final delivery. Existing cyclic loading and tooth position experiments have revealed these two dimensions respectively, and also suggest that subsequent comparisons should incorporate material composition and manufacturing processes into the same design. [R01][R02]

Integrated dentures can be categorized into three levels based on their manufacturing content. The first level consists of a single resin-printed monolithic geometric model, used to answer whether canceling assembly changes position; the second level comprises continuously formed structures of different colors or materials, involving the joint realization of tooth and denture functions; and the third level comprises clinically deliverable commercial dentures, including supporting materials, post-processing, and scope of use. These three levels correspond to geometric, material, and instrumentation issues, respectively, each providing different types of evidence and preserving material differences between different commercial systems. [R02][R03][R04]

The industrial implications of extend to the entire delivery process. Laboratories need to determine if the savings in labor are sufficient to cover equipment, materials, and rework costs; clinics need to assess whether adjustments and repeat visits are reduced; and patients are more concerned with the longevity of their dentures. The interests of these three parties can align, or they can shift: faster initial delivery, but requiring a complete remake after partial damage; fewer manufacturing steps, but more finishing and color treatments. Only by considering both these inputs and results can the total cost change resulting from simplified manufacturing be assessed.

blocks.title: Main evaluation framework
blocks.text: Uses the entire process of each denture, from design to the point where intervention is needed again, as the comparison object. The precision at delivery, failures during use, restoration after repair, and eventual disuse constitute a continuous but distinct hierarchy of outcomes.
N1 | Material combinations and fatigue

A study by Löscher et al., published online in 2024 and included in the 2025 issue, used 11 combinations of artificial teeth with the same tooth shape and connection area, with 8 pieces in each combination. The artificial teeth, denture bases, and connection methods were varied, and then thermomechanical cycles and destructive loads were applied. The duration of cycles and destructive forces differed among the combinations, with some milled, pressed, and prefabricated systems showing better performance. [R01]

This design answers the question of which component in the system becomes the weakest point first. A uniform geometry reduces the interference of tooth shape on stress, while variations in the combination of tooth structure, base, and connector help identify compatibility issues that cannot be detected by evaluating materials individually. Fatigue survival and final failure force serve different purposes: the former observes damage accumulation, while the latter describes the remaining load-bearing capacity. Only by considering both side-by-side can one determine whether a particular combination will detach early or withstand a higher load after cycling.

Failure location and strength must be interpreted together. A stronger interface can shift cracks into a tooth or the base, changing load transfer and subsequent repair options. At the same failure load, a readily replaceable tooth failure and a deep base fracture have different service consequences. Research therefore branches into retaining separate components with better positioning and bonding, or changing manufacturing to reduce assembly. Both approaches should ultimately be compared using common outcomes over the service period.
N2 | Tooth-socket geometry and linked-tooth arrangements define assembly constraints

A 2025 study compared tooth-socket and linked-tooth arrangements in 80 dentures, alongside other manufacturing routes. Three-dimensional tooth-position analysis found the smallest deviations in a semi-conventional flask-and-press group; among relevant separately printed combinations, a full-arch linked dentition with a grooved socket design performed better. [R09]

Tooth sockets accommodate bonding agent and constrain displacement. Larger clearance permits seating but also tooth movement; too little clearance can cause local interference and incomplete seating. Research should therefore examine clearance, depth, locating surfaces and channels for excess bonding agent rather than simply choose a groove or flat socket. A full-arch linked dentition can also convert local displacement into overall deformation, requiring assessment of anterior and posterior regions together.

These interpretations propose a further distinguishable competitive mechanism. If the error originates from assembly gaps, increasing positioning constraints should improve repeatability; if the error mainly stems from the warping of the connecting teeth themselves, excessive constraints may store stress. Scanning at three stages—post-printing, post-trial assembly, and post-bonding—can verify which interpretation aligns with the changed location. The next step, eliminating the assembly stage, forms a mechanism reference, allowing design optimization and manufacturing integration to enter a common geometric evaluation framework.
N3 | Geometric effects of eliminating assembly

A 2026 in vitro study divided 60 dentures into four groups of 15. Two were printed as monolithic units using either model resin or tooth-coloured provisional-crown resin; the other two used separately printed bases and complete or segmented tooth arches bonded afterwards. Three-dimensional matching showed smaller full-arch and regional tooth-position deviations in the monolithic groups. [R02]

The value of a single-piece reference lies in eliminating the manual assembly step, thereby helping to pinpoint the source of finished product deviations. It also alters the material and molding state, so subsequent experiments should control resin shrinkage, support positions, and curing conditions within the same design. Retaining scanned files for each processing node allows observation of whether errors gradually increase or are partially offset during subsequent processing. Preserving data from all six zones provides a better chance of identifying localized anomalies related to occlusal contact than simply reporting the overall arch average.

This research line translates the geometric benefits of integration into testable clinical questions: whether reduced deviations improve initial placement, adjustment time, and occlusal reconstruction. Individual trials of the model or temporary crown resin handle error attribution, while the final material denture handles delivery evaluation. Connected by a common digital design, measurement coordinates, and tooth area definitions, these two levels avoid mixing differences caused by different resins or different cases in comparisons of manufacturing routes.
N4 | Load bearing across continuous material regions

The 2023 study used Stratasys J55 and Vero series materials to print the tooth color and baseplate color areas as continuous units, comparing damage, water absorption, and geometric performance after thermal cycling. The experiment found some favorable load-bearing and shape properties, but also observed high water absorption. [R03]

Continuous forming reduces subsequent assembly while still retaining different functional areas. The teeth need to resist occlusion and wear, while the denture base needs to adapt to tissue surfaces and overall curvature; both have different requirements in terms of thickness, color, and localized loads. Therefore, it is necessary to observe how stress is transferred in material transition areas, whether the dimensions change after environmental water absorption, and from which region the final crack originates. Only by incorporating both geometric and material consistency can it be determined whether the benefits of continuous manufacturing come from reduced interfaces or the material system itself.

The Vero specimen provides the structural concept and testing methodology in this chain. When moving towards deliverable materials, the same loading methods should be maintained, and water absorption, dissolution, and mechanical retention should be remeasured. In this way, the relationship between the preceding and following studies is one of problem-method continuity, while specific properties follow their respective material systems. The next step is to conduct direct experiments on TrueDent to supplement the commercial material's response after surface treatment and environmental aging.
N5 | Surface aging of commercial materials

A 2024 TrueDent material study compared three surface treatments in 90 specimens and included 5,000 thermocycles. Ageing reduced flexural strength, while the glazed group retained strength and surface hardness more favourably. Surface finishing after material jetting was treated as an independent variable. [R04]

Post-treatment can simultaneously alter surface defects, water absorption channels, and outer layer load-bearing capacity, making it suitable for evaluation in conjunction with material formulation. If strength changes only occur under specific surface conditions, the contributions of surface protection and specimen size changes should be further differentiated. Fracture observation, surface roughness, and changes in mass before and after aging can serve as intermediate measurements connecting mechanical results with possible mechanisms. For complete dentures, it is also necessary to consider whether wear or grinding has removed the surface layer, thus altering the initial advantages with use.

This node merges with the geometric branch during the delivery phase. Accurate shape but unstable post-processing, or stable material properties but tooth misalignment, can both increase the need for clinical intervention. Therefore, tooth position, material samples, and surface finish can be recorded simultaneously within the same production batch, using operator and equipment batches as analytical factors. These manufacturing records are then correlated with patient events to examine whether a particular surface or curing step truly shortens or extends the time to no intervention.
N6 | Re-establishing reline interfaces

A 2025 DentaBase study compared mechanical and chemical pretreatments in 90 specimens. Median tensile strength was 25.9 MPa in the intact control, 11.5 MPa in the untreated relined group and 19.7 MPa after sandblasting plus monomer treatment. All relined groups failed at the base–reline-material interface. [R05]

The relining restores tissue surface adaptation, thus the research task differs from the primary tooth-base connection. The original base has already formed a cross-linked network, and the new material needs to establish continuous load transfer on its surface. Roughening increases the contact path, and chemical treatment may improve wetting or surface bonding; the combination of these two deserves further differentiation using surface morphology and chemical characterization. The results of different treatment groups also indicate that a monotonic relationship should not be assumed between the number of complex steps and the connection effect.

Subsequent validation of the complete device can begin with thickness and edges: the same interfacial strength may result in different crack propagation under varying relining thicknesses, baseplate flexibility, and load locations. Edge sealing, localized peeling, and bending loads should be included in the experiments first, followed by recording when patients require a second intervention. This step, along with the repair step, advances manufacturing reliability to post-maintenance reliability and defines relining as an independent event for the clinical registry.
N7 | Repair reinforcement and aging

A 2026 repair experiment compared a complete control, simple resin repair, and metal and thin/thick glass fiber reinforcement. After zero or 10,000 thermal cycles, three-point bending was performed. The thick glass fiber group showed the greatest improvement; the strength after cycling was not significantly different from the complete control, and the failure morphology also changed with the reinforcement method. [R06]

This design evaluates bonding interfaces and reinforcement in the same specimen, separating bonding fractured surfaces from restoring load-bearing capacity. Reinforcement thickness, length and location govern load transfer across the repair; stiffness transitions may shift stress into adjacent regions. Restored flexural strength therefore needs to be interpreted alongside crack location and complete or incomplete fracture. For devices intended to be repaired repeatedly, the structure retained after fracture also affects the feasibility of another repair.

Complete dentures can be further modeled using representative midline, alveolar, and marginal fractures to compare the effects of the same reinforcement method at different locations and record the original material that needs to be removed for repair. Statistical design can pre-define acceptable load-bearing differences and, with a sufficient sample size, evaluate the degree of restoration. Combined with relining studies, clinical follow-up can differentiate between fitting maintenance, structural repair, and complete denture fabrication, avoiding merging interventions of different natures into a single repair rate.
N8 | Patient outcomes test the acceptability of technical workflows

A crossover randomized trial in 2024 enrolled 18 edentulous patients to compare oral health-related quality of life and satisfaction between 3D-printed and traditional complete dentures. The tested printing workflow yielded patient-reported results comparable to traditional dentures. [R08]

A crossover design lets the same patient experience both options, reducing differences in anatomy, prior experience and general expectations, while requiring analysis of wearing order and adaptation. It translates manufacturing measures into experience: are smaller geometric deviations perceptible, and do changes in material or weight affect comfort and willingness to wear the denture? Patient-reported outcomes, adjustment and repair events should be recorded separately because appearance, function and continued use need not change together.

In the chain of evidence, randomized comparisons test early acceptability after delivery, while extended observation tests durability and maintenance. Both can use consistent scales and event definitions, allowing time-varying performance to be interpreted as the same device performing at different stages of use. The option for continued use by follow-up subjects should also be preserved to explain which patients enter long-term observation and whether discontinuation is related to breakage, fit, or personal preference.
N9 | Two-year use and interventions

The prospective study, conducted in 2026, followed 18 patients with 36 printed dentures, of whom 12 patients (24 dentures) completed the two-year observation period. Four maxillary dentures fractured in the first year, and two patients subsequently discontinued use; the reported two-year cumulative success rate and survival rate were 88% and 87%, respectively, with patient-reported outcomes generally stable. [R07]

This study separates the structural event requiring intervention and discontinuation of use into two endpoints, clearly distinguishing between "device malfunction" and "treatment losing its value." Dentures that are continued to be worn after restoration retain their benefits but incur a maintenance burden; discontinuation requires analysis of both device- and patient-level reasons. Since the upper and lower jaws are from the same patient, their correlation should be preserved during analysis, and cumulative indicators should be understood by combining loss to follow-up and different observation periods.

Provides clear feedback to previous nodes through long-term observation: fracture location, critical thickness, material version, and post-treatment records are reconnected to fatigue testing, allowing for the selection of geometry and loads that more closely approximate the event distribution; re-incident events after repair are reconnected to reinforcement and relining experiments. The feedback arrows in the study diagram indicate the next round of experimental tasks accordingly. This allows both integrated and modular approaches to undergo four levels of evaluation: delivery, use, maintenance, and decommissioning, and translates product improvements into specific, repeatable measurable issues.

sections.title: III. Enterprise Evolution: Three Paths Revolving Around Different Process Constraints

blocks.text: Stratasys' strategy centres on multicolour monolithic dentures. TrueDent and its J5 DentaJet workflow were launched in February 2023; TrueDent-D entered Europe as a CE Class I product in January 2025; and TrueDent resin received CE Class IIa certification on 17 March 2026, expanding the corresponding scope of use. Market entry and the later certification-class change represent distinct stages in European development. [R11][R12][R13]

3D Systems' NextDent roadmap comprises a multi-material jetting system consisting of Jet Base, Jet Teeth, and NextDent 300. The company announced a full commercial launch in the US on July 29, 2025; and on April 28, 2026, announced that the portfolio had obtained EU MDR IIa certification, stipulating that it would be available in Europe from May 4th. These milestones record the commercial and certification progress of the specific product portfolio. [R14][R15]

Formlabs retains separate manufacturing and assembly. Its current guide describes bonding Denture Base V2 and Premium Teeth and includes surface repair, fracture repair, tooth replacement, and soft and hard relining. [R16] This approach covers initial manufacture and subsequent local maintenance. Its value can be assessed through the clarity of material and procedural choices and whether laboratories can perform maintenance tasks consistently.

The common goal of the three routes can be stated as reducing uncertainty in delivery, but the control methods differ. Integration places more emphasis on the unified control of materials, equipment, and printing tasks, while modular manufacturing retains component selection while requiring stable connection processes. Therefore, product competition will occur simultaneously at both the process automation and service support levels; which route is more economical will be determined by laboratory output, equipment utilization, and maintenance structure.

The enterprise timeline records the process of a product entering a specific market and workflow, while comparative studies are used to evaluate the performance of each route. After commercial release, the correspondence between material versions, laboratory implementation methods, and patient cohorts is particularly worth tracking. If the resin or post-processing method is subsequently changed, early results correspond to that specific version, and results for the new version need to be accumulated separately. Continuous tracking helps determine whether performance improvements stem from material updates, operator proficiency, or a combination of both.

sections.title: IV. Academic and Industrial Connections: Clarifying Which Results Belong to Which Products

blocks.text: Research–industry relationships include joint participation, direct evaluation of commercial products and parallel work on the same problem. The clinical follow-up series includes co-authors affiliated with Mitsui Chemicals and company participation in fabrication; the evaluated device used the Kulzer separately printed system. [R07] The type of involvement, product identity and study endpoints must be linked to define the specific application supported.

TrueDent has been evaluated in material experiments and in a 2026 case series involving its multicolour monolithic dentures. [R04][R10] These provide controlled material observations and practical examples, respectively; case reports demonstrate implementation but do not establish long-term comparative performance. Match trade names to product versions first, then separately establish manufacturer authorship, support or joint design.

The research platform, material system, and evaluation endpoint jointly determine the scope of the evidence. Vero samples and TrueDent use equipment from the same manufacturer but different materials; monochromatic model studies are used to analyze the relationship between assembly and tooth positions. [R02][R03] Academic achievements are linked to industry routes by defining problems and testing methods, and enterprise products become the specific objects to be tested. Research on the same topic, product evaluation, and joint development thus form different types of academic-industry connections.

Evidence management can utilize a version-updated correspondence table: listing equipment, resin, artificial teeth, binders, post-treatment, research stage, and applicable issues. Each paper only enters the conclusion cell where it was actually measured. This identifies existing direct evidence for the product and also shows that a key issue is only supported by similar materials or adjacent routes, providing a consistent basis for procurement evaluation and research topic selection.

sections.title: V. Challenges and Value in Transformation: Durability, maintenance, and economies of scale need to be realized together.

blocks.text: The primary challenge in durability translation is the incomplete alignment of test conditions with the stress experienced by the actual device. Strip specimens facilitate material and repair method identification, tooth-base specimens facilitate connection comparison, and complete dentures simultaneously incorporate geometry, thickness, and load location. Different layers of research should undertake different tasks: first, use a simplified specimen screening mechanism; then, use device geometry to verify its sustainability; and finally, identify actual events through follow-up. Cross-layer consistency is more important than the highest value of a single indicator. [R01][R03][R06]

Maintenance and translation require a clear understanding of the options available after failure. Relining restores tissue surface fit, tooth replacement involves local tooth position and connection, fracture repair also restores load-bearing capacity, and complete re-fabrication involves re-entering the delivery process. It is recommended to establish decision records based on damage location, remaining thickness, previous repair frequency, and material version, and compare the subsequent use of each branch. Cost accounting should not end at the first charge for inexpensive repairs that repeatedly fail, or quick re-fabrications that require multiple adjustments.

Scale costs should be calculated using the number of qualified deliveries as the denominator. It is recommended to account for costs beyond equipment and materials, including design review, support treatment, cleaning and curing, positioning and connection, finishing and polishing, quality inspection, reprinting of failed products, and maintenance communication. Automation only generates a clear benefit when it reduces total labor or increases qualified output; if the saved assembly time is offset by more quality inspections or complete rework, the value is overestimated by looking at machine uptime alone. High-volume and low-volume labs should be modeled separately, rather than sharing a single average cost.

Quality control should also cover personnel and batch variations. Single operator and single-batch production can reduce experimental noise, but it doesn't directly answer whether reproducibility across different laboratories is possible. The next step could be to include operator, batch, and post-processing equipment as analytical factors, reporting the mean and the percentage of nonconformities. For clinical applications, even small mean deviations accompanied by a few serious deviations can still lead to rework; therefore, stability should be considered a product attribute alongside average performance.

Delivery value also requires patient outcomes. Less chairside adjustment does not necessarily imply greater satisfaction, and structural restoration after repair does not ensure continued wear. Record function, interruptions in use, concern about repeat fracture and time to resume normal use, retaining reasons for loss to follow-up. This separates manufacturing gains, clinical workload and patient experience rather than substituting one satisfaction score for all performance dimensions.

sections.title: VI. Three Scenarios for 2027-2029: Judging Development Direction Based on Observable Conditions

blocks.text: The following scenario is a conditional judgment based on the existing link. The basis for scenario switching comes from the comparison of common endpoints: under the same patient conditions and similar design requirements, whether the initial delivery, usage failure, and maintenance burden have improved synchronously. Commercial expansion can increase observation opportunities, and the traceable delivery and usage records of product versions determine what kind of evidence these opportunities can form.

blocks.title: Scenario 1: Ordered parallelism, product division of labor according to scenario
blocks.text: In 2027, a clearer material combination and delivery standards will be established; in 2028-2029, the integrated system will handle some batch tasks, while the separate system will retain its advantages in local maintenance and equipment compatibility. The prerequisite for this is that both systems have repeatable cost and quality ranges. Observe how the laboratory allocates cases, not just which equipment to purchase; simultaneously track total labor costs, first-time delivery rate, and maintenance methods for each unit.

blocks.title: Scenario 2: Integrated and accelerated expansion, simultaneously improving efficiency and durability
blocks.text: If cross-laboratory results show that fewer assembly errors do indeed reduce grinding and rework, and follow-up and maintenance results do not impose an additional burden, integration may expand its application in 2028-2029. The key condition is that the advantages can be reproduced across batches, across operators, and in specific product versions. Leading indicators should be reduced qualified delivery costs, extended intervention intervals, and increased post-repair reuse rates.

blocks.title: Scenario 3: Scaling slows down, maintenance and consistency become constraints.
blocks.text: If localized damage leads to more complete replacements, post-processing differences result in rework, or clinical adjustments do not decrease with improved geometric parameters, the labor savings from the initial manufacturing may be offset by subsequent costs. In this case, the industry may place greater emphasis on material updates and maintenance agreements, and the modular manufacturing process may continue to have room for improvement. Observe repeated repairs, complete replacements, downtime days, and a few serious deviations, rather than just looking at average strength.

These three scenarios can occur simultaneously in different regions and laboratories. New installations demonstrate the selection process, while continued use and maintenance results validate the rationality of that selection. The focus of annual observation is on how mature the results of the same product version are, which cases and production ranges it is applicable to, and how its implementation has performed after release and certification. Placing speed and performance delivery on the same timeline provides a clearer picture of the development position of each approach.

sections.title: VII. Observational Indicators and Research Priorities: Enabling the Next Round of Evidence to Change Choices

rows: Version, Thickness, Upper and Lower Jaws
Repeat failure and days out of use

blocks.text: The priority research is a design-based error tracking experiment. Split and integrated dentures will be manufactured separately using the same batch clinical design, and scans will be performed at key processing points. The major dental regions, registration methods, and occlusal evaluation methods will be pre-defined, and operator time will be recorded. The research objective should be to explain which steps alter tooth positions and examine the relationship between deviations and adjustments. It is suitable to conduct cross-batch experiments first, followed by clinical delivery comparisons, to avoid attributing differences caused by different designs to the manufacturing process.

The second priority is comparing repairs in complete dentures. Use representative fracture sites and damage severity to compare local repair, structural reinforcement and digital remanufacture, followed by environmental ageing and cyclic loading. Alongside failure load, record changes in failure location, how much original material must be removed and whether another repair remains possible. This can guide maintenance choices and provide clear categories for clinical registries.

Priority Study Three is a multi-center cohort registered by product version. At delivery, resin, equipment, processing procedures, critical thickness, and previous denture status are recorded; during follow-up, damage, relining, repair, re-fabrication, and discontinuation are recorded separately. Analysis is organized at both the patient and device levels to avoid treating the upper and lower jaws of the same individual as completely independent. After product upgrades, the old version cohort is retained, and which issues can be compared across versions are pre-defined.

Clinical comparisons require prior specification of case allocation rules. If more complex cases fall into a particular route, directly comparing rework rates may introduce case differences. Randomization comparisons can be conducted among patients suitable for both approaches, or the factors influencing choice can be recorded and adjusted within the observation cohort. Sample size should be estimated around the difference requiring a change in decision-making, while allowing for loss to follow-up; scan points, independent devices, and independent patients should be processed as different levels of data, ensuring appropriate units of analysis for both geometric precision and clinical outcomes.

Priority Study Four involves cost accounting conducted concurrently with clinical research. For each case, the total cost is calculated by accumulating laboratory and clinic inputs, rework due to failure, and subsequent maintenance, without using material unit prices to represent the total cost. Production volume and equipment utilization can be used as scenario variables to examine when labor savings are sufficient to cover additional inputs. This selection criterion is applicable to large laboratories and also explains why smaller institutions might make different decisions.

Cost studies can simultaneously present costs and effects: first, list the cost of qualified delivery, time to use without intervention, and time to patient discontinuation, then examine whether the choice changes under different weights. If a certain route is only superior under extremely high yield or extremely low maintenance probability, this condition itself is an important result. Publicly disclosing calculation methods, material versions, and event definitions allows other laboratories to recalculate using their own workloads and identify how the benefits of a single institution change in other environments.

Research priorities should follow the principle of "first identifying the locations of errors and failures, then comparing the net benefits of the entire denture." In the short term, the most valuable actions are reproducible assembly and repair protocols; in the medium term, multi-center results for specific product versions; and in the long term, linking design, manufacturing, and maintenance records. Each step should make the next choice clearer: which cases are suitable for which approach, how to restore the denture after damage, and what the total cost is to achieve stable results.

P2-05.title: Clinical Comparisons
P2-05.subtitle: Linking survival, patient experience and maintenance burden through stratified comparisons
P2-05.thesis: Clinical evidence for printed restorations supports specific judgments by material, device use and workflow. Complete dentures, resin single crowns, resin bridges and zirconia crowns have different outcomes. Progress requires distinguishing success, survival and continued use, linking patient experience to intervention costs, and using systematic reviews to identify comparable evidence and subsequent research tasks.

questions.question: What are the differences between printed and traditional dental crowns in terms of clinical survival and complications?
questions.focus: Compare resin and zirconia restorations, single crowns and bridges separately, recording fracture, debonding and biological events while retaining patient- and restoration-level data.

questions.question: What are the differences in patient outcomes between printed dentures and traditional dentures?
questions.focus: Link early patient experience in randomized comparisons to maintenance events during long-term follow-up, assessing function, satisfaction and continued wear.

questions.question: How should systematic reviews assess clinical evidence for digital restorations?
questions.focus: Organize evidence according to the same purpose, control, material version and follow-up length, and examine the impact of bias, heterogeneity and outcome definition on the overall judgment.

sections.title: Research Task and Clinical Comparison Framework

blocks.text: Clinical comparisons first require clarifying what is being chosen. "Printed" and "conventional" are names of manufacturing routes; what patients actually receive is a treatment process comprised of materials, device design, clinical documentation, and post-processing. The main tasks of complete dentures include stability, comfort, and continuous wear; single crowns involve retention, structural and tissue response; and three-unit bridges further increase connectors and span load-bearing capacity. Only by stratifying these tasks can research results be translated into clear selection criteria.

Survival, success and continued patient use are related but distinct outcomes. A recemented restoration may remain in the mouth after requiring intervention; repaired dentures may recover function while adding maintenance costs; and patients may stop using an intact device because of comfort or appearance. Define each outcome level in advance and record event timing and management so that technical problems and patient choices can be interpreted separately.

Clinical comparisons also include resource evaluation. Fewer patient visits, shorter chairside procedures, or less material consumption can reduce the burden on one party; however, if subsequent adjustments are made, the overall investment for the treatment cycle may differ. Therefore, patient experience, device events, and costs should be observed within the same timeframe, clarifying the respective contributions of initial manufacturing, delivery, and maintenance.

Systematic reviews bring together comparable clinical questions and explain differences in findings. They should retain materials, manufacturing versions, case conditions, study designs and follow-up duration rather than group studies only as digital or conventional. Original research provides specific observations, while evidence synthesis examines consistency across conditions; together, they guide subsequent trials.
N1 | Early denture-experience comparisons

A 2022 randomized crossover trial compared conventional and digitally printed dentures, recording satisfaction with speech, cleaning, stability and comfort alongside visits and treatment processes. Conventional dentures performed better on some experience measures, while the digital workflow reduced some visit-related measures. [R01]

The crossover trial allows the same patient to undergo two procedures, reducing discrepancies between individual anatomy and general expectations. The study also explains the need to preserve treatment sequence, adaptation periods, and prior prosthetic experience, as the later approach may be influenced by the initial learning phase. Multidimensional scales help differentiate overall evaluations based on appearance, stability, speech, or treatment convenience, thus linking patient feedback to specific manufacturing and clinical steps.

This node proposes a dual task for subsequent comparisons: firstly, to observe whether the process saves on patient visits; and secondly, to examine whether the wearing experience can be maintained after the savings. The primary outcome most important to patients can be pre-defined, while adjustments and intermediate events are recorded, avoiding simply asking for an overall score at the final follow-up visit. It compares workflow conditions with the next randomized study using a common scale and at the same time points, progressively explaining differences in conclusions.
N2 | Randomized testing of another workflow

2024 18-person crossover randomized trial report, the measured quality of life and satisfaction of printed and traditional complete dentures are comparable. [R02] The study subjects are two denture processes formed by specific design, materials and manufacturing steps.

Places this result alongside earlier studies, and the most valuable question is what conditions changed. Clinical records, fitting methods, materials, tooth position, and operational experience can all influence the experience, and these should be progressively separated through research design. A manufacturing comparison under the same clinical steps can be used, or the complete process can be preserved while detailed records of differences can be kept. The former is more suitable for mechanistic attribution, while the latter is more suitable for treatment selection; the two designs answer different questions and can complement each other.

Short-term patient outcomes also need to be linked to objective retention and long-term events. Similar satisfaction levels may indicate similar function, or patient adaptation may offset different mechanical performances. The next two branches therefore add retention measurements and extended follow-up, respectively, extending early acceptability to reliability during use. Retaining the reasons for selection and withdrawal when the same patients continue observation can indicate the composition of the long-term cohort.
N3 | Measuring retention and experience together

The 2026 crossover trial compared thermo-cured, printed, and injected polyamide complete dentures, while also recording retention and oral quality of life. There were no significant differences in retention between printed and thermo-cured dentures at any observation interval, while the polyamide group differed from both. [R03]

Objective measurements offer mechanistic clues beyond patient perception. Dislodgement-force measurements require standardized loading direction and position, while quality of life captures broader experience. If they change differently, investigate pain, movement at denture borders, saliva and occlusal conditions as additional influences. Longitudinal patient data can establish whether retention and adaptation change at different rates.

Clinical comparisons can thus move from "which is better" to "what explains which outcome." Proposing a hypothesis about the association between fixation and stability in advance, and validating it in independent patients, helps determine which areas should be prioritized for control in manufacturing evaluations. Subsequently, when combined with resource studies, it can also be examined whether reducing steps affects patient experience through some measurable functional change.
N4 | Two-year interventions and continued use

A 2026 prospective cohort followed 18 patients with 36 printed dentures; 12 patients with 24 dentures completed two years of observation. Four maxillary dentures fractured during the first year, and two patients subsequently discontinued use. Success and survival were reported separately, with cumulative estimates of 88% and 87%, respectively. [R04]

Stratifies events to preserve the clinical value of continued use after repair while also presenting the maintenance burden. The initial fracture, repair, recurrence, and discontinuation can form a continuous path; different paths require different resources and affect patient confidence and normal usage time. For maxillary and mandibular dentures from the same patient, the analysis should preserve their association, and follow-up duration and loss to follow-up should be handled using an appropriate time-to-event approach.

This observation extends the early randomized trial into a real-world usage process, but the continued wear choice within the cohort is itself an outcome. Future multicenter designs could include all recipients at initial delivery, continuously recording choice changes and interventions. This would allow for assessment of whether changes in materials, geometry, and clinical manipulation reduced events, and determine appropriate observation periods and primary endpoints for subsequent comparisons.
N5 | A single-crown cohort records survival and success separately

A 2026 study observed 30 VarseoSmile Crown Plus posterior single crowns for two years, reporting a 93% survival rate and an 87% success rate, with some instances of debonding and partial color changes. [R05] The scanning, printing, post-processing, and bonding procedures used have clearly identified materials and equipment.

A single-arm cohort describes which events occur in a defined workflow, when they occur and how they are managed. Debonding, fracture, secondary caries and aesthetic interventions should be separated because they involve different mechanisms. Recemented crowns contribute to restoration survival but also treatment burden; patient satisfaction adds their experience of events and maintenance. Endpoints should therefore extend beyond whether the restoration remains in place.

The next round of controlled studies can allocate treatment within similar preparement heights, periodontal status, and opposing and occlusal conditions, and record cementation materials and treatments. This separates the fabrication route from case conditions. Fixed prosthetic branches are then developed according to pediatric use and zirconia materials, emphasizing that clinical selection is jointly defined by dentition, material, and structural tasks.
N6 | Paediatric split-mouth studies retain differences beyond function

A comparative study of 50 primary molars from 25 children in 2026 showed that printed resin and precast zirconia were similar in retention and multiple functional indicators, but the printed group showed worse results in terms of plaque, gingival indices, wear, and color changes. The observation period was 12 months. [R06]

The contralateral design leverages the shared living environment of the same individual to reduce some differences, while still needing to preserve pairing relationships in statistical analysis. The remaining useful life of deciduous teeth, preparation methods, and gingival margin positions constitute independent application scenarios. Studies can simultaneously record surface condition and cleaning behavior, analyzing whether changes in tissue parameters are consistent with material surface or local geometry. Placing functional retention alongside surface and biological outcomes prevents overall success rates from masking other potential burdens faced by patients.

This node establishes a shared requirement for adult-crown and bridge studies: define multidimensional outcomes and specify clinically decision-relevant differences. Set separate thresholds for wear, colour acceptability and interventions, then examine whether they alter treatment choices. Uses may assign different weights, but clear recording enables later evidence synthesis.
N7 | A randomized zirconia comparison holds material category constant

A randomized trial in 2025 compared NPJ-printed versus milled zirconia single crowns in 48 posterior teeth from 43 participants. At 12 months, the primary aesthetic, functional, and biological parameters were generally similar, with one fracture occurring in each group. [R07]

Comparing manufacturing routes within the same material category helps reduce the interference of material differences on interpretation. Randomization and concealed allocation further reduce the influence of case selection, while standardized evaluation criteria improve endpoint comparability. Studies still need to retain actual forming and heat treatment conditions, as well as adjustments and bonding information at delivery, as these steps can all affect the same clinical outcome. After linking manufacturing data with clinical case numbers, it's possible to further explore which step the discrepancies originate from.

When a between-group difference is not statistically significant, effect estimates and confidence intervals indicate the range of differences still compatible with the data. Demonstrating that a difference is sufficiently small requires prespecified clinically acceptable margins and an appropriate sample size. Longer follow-up with adjustment and resource measures can then compare clinically similar routes in efficiency and maintenance.
N8 | Follow-up of resin three-unit bridges

A 2025 study followed 68 three-unit printed resin-composite posterior bridges in 49 patients for a mean of 22.36 months. Mechanical failures were concentrated at connectors, and estimated cumulative survival accounting for mechanical and biological events was 36.2%. The longest observation exceeded three years. [R08]

This result makes the structural distinction between single crowns and bridges clinically relevant. Connectors, span and multiple supports alter load transfer, so restorations described as resin composites still require use-specific validation. Failure sites linked to connector cross-sections, local thickness and occlusion can generate experimental hypotheses. Because the studies use different materials and cases, comparisons should identify tasks added by bridge use rather than directly infer manufacturing superiority from separate cohorts.

Future bridge studies should distinguish repairable damage, failures requiring remanufacture and events requiring abutment treatment, retaining repeat events and clustering within patients. Changes in both event location and cumulative occurrence after redesign would help explain its clinical effect. This node feeds evidence synthesis by separating printed restorations into specific material–use combinations.
N9 | Clinical outcomes and resources

A retrospective study of 60 participants in 2025 compared traditional, milled, and printed complete dentures. Overall functional outcomes at six months were similar, with the digital group having lower chairside time and laboratory costs. [R09] The study also recorded clinical outcomes and treatment-related inputs.

While reviewing the data can reflect established workflows, it's necessary to explain case selection, staff experience, and cost metrics. Timeframes should be divided into pre-production documentation, trial use, delivery, and subsequent adjustments; costs should retain the components of equipment, materials, and labor, allowing other institutions to incorporate their own resources. Patient travel and downtime can also be listed separately, demonstrating which approach actually benefits in clinically similar cases.

When economic analysis is conducted concurrently with clinical trials, mismatches between different cases and timeframes can be reduced. Pre-defining the observation period and accumulating failures and retakes helps verify whether initial savings can be maintained. This stage provides a resource dimension to the overall system and also reminds subsequent randomized studies to simultaneously measure cost and effect, ensuring that treatment options are not limited to a single satisfaction or retention value.
N10 | Systematic synthesis and stratification

The 2025 review of printed and milled dentures included four studies, showing no significant difference in retention and satisfaction, and exhibiting high heterogeneity. The 2026 review included 25 randomized trials, but no clear advantage of the manufacturing route was shown in the important patient outcomes, and the certainty of the evidence was generally low. [R10][R11]

A comprehensive interpretation of the system requires returning to the study subjects. Different materials, trial procedures, control types, and follow-up times may lead to different treatment protocols; these factors can be stratified before pooling. Crossover and parallel trials require appropriate effect estimates for each, and multiple publications on the same cohort need to be identified to avoid duplication. Prioritizing important patient outcomes helps link statistical differences to actual experience, intervention, and continued use.

The most actionable output of the review is clarifying how to reduce uncertainty in the next round of trials: standardizing the definitions of success and retention, recording by product version, extending observation, incorporating maintenance costs, and selecting differences that can change decisions. The feedback edges in the diagram thus return to the original research design. Adding new trials will only make the overall judgment clearer than simply increasing the number of papers if it complements these specific tasks.

sections.title: Timing of commercial product development and clinical evidence

blocks.text: BEGO released the VarseoSmile Crown plus permanent single crown material in 2020, followed by prospective clinical observations surrounding the material and its associated procedures. [R12][R05] There is a time lag between the proposed use of the product and the maturation of clinical results. Studies should retain the actual version used and the delivery date, distinguishing between information resulting from product updates and extended observation periods.

As of 2026, Formlabs' official permanent-crown guide organizes manufacturing around BEGO VarseoSmile TriniQ and associated equipment such as Form 4B. [R14] This new material–platform combination is a distinct research object that can use established single-crown outcomes. Crown plus observations help identify important endpoints; evidence for the TriniQ workflow must come from its actual clinical use.

Carbon released DB 4000 denture-base resin in 2026, emphasizing work of fracture, printing accuracy and manufacturing economics. [R13] This update shares questions with denture trials and maintenance cohorts: do material or accuracy improvements reduce fracture, adjustment and discontinuation? Release records identify the version's starting point; subsequent case registries establish whether improvements reach actual use.

The enterprise timeline can simultaneously record changes in materials, software, equipment, post-processing, and indications. Clinical evaluation treats each version as a traceable, complete process, which helps explain differences in trials across different years. If multiple stages are updated simultaneously, process controls can be conducted first to identify key contributions, followed by a complete process clinical comparison, avoiding attributing all changes to a single material name.

sections.title: Academic-Enterprise Collaboration and Clinical Translation Value

blocks.text: When commercial materials are directly used in clinical studies, evidence can be grounded in the product, manufacturing process, and intended use. The two-year single crown study and Crown Plus constitute direct product evaluation; randomized and follow-up studies of dentures correspond to their respective actual manufacturing systems. [R05][R02][R04] Product identity and clinical endpoints jointly define the study subjects and provide a reference for comparisons after version updates.

When companies and research institutions develop solutions to the same problems, they can share outcome definitions and measurement methods. For example, the new baseplate resin focuses on toughness, allowing clinical registration to record fracture locations, repairs, and discontinuation; the new rapid process focuses on treatment visits and working hours, while research simultaneously measures patient adaptation and subsequent maintenance. This approach transforms product claims into clear research tasks and enables actual results to, in turn, adjust R&D priorities.

Clinical value should encompass a three-way perspective. Patients are concerned with function, comfort, appearance, and uptime; clinics are concerned with delivery, follow-up visits, and tissue response; and laboratories are concerned with manufacturing consistency, rework, and maintenance. A technology may reduce laboratory time but increase clinic adjustments; therefore, the inputs of all three parties can be reported separately, and the results over the entire treatment cycle can be calculated. This makes it easier to understand why the same technology produces different benefits at different institutions.

Long-term evidence also plays a role in product improvement. When repeated failures occur, linking case design and manufacturing records back to the experiment allows for the selection of more representative geometries, environments, and loads. Companies provide traceable parameters, researchers provide independent measurements and comparisons, and clinicians provide real-world events; these three elements together form the basis for continuous improvement of materials and workflows.

sections.title: Key Design and Interpretation of Clinical Comparisons

blocks.text: Comparisons should first be based on therapeutic purpose. Adult permanent crowns, pediatric deciduous crowns, three-unit bridges, and complete dentures have different service lives and failure mechanisms, and the primary endpoints and follow-up periods need to correspond to these tasks. Material type, support conditions, occlusion, previous restorations, and patient risk, as pre-stratification factors, help explain the variation in mean outcomes across different cases.

Randomized trials can reduce selection bias, single-arm cohorts are suitable for describing events in specific workflows, and retrospective studies supplement implementation and resource information. Different designs should be placed within the same chain of evidence, and the task of each study should be clearly defined. For direct comparisons, standardized reviewer training and blinded interpretation can be used; for long-term registrations, emphasis should be placed on event classification, version tracking, and reasons for loss to follow-up, so that different data can complement each other.

A single patient may have multiple crowns or maxillary/mandibular dentures, and there may be correlations between observations. Studies can employ a two-tiered analysis of patients and devices to avoid treating repeated measurements as new, independent patients. Crossover designs retain pairing, sequence, and stage; long-term outcomes retain time and intermediate events. With clear units of analysis, effect estimation can accurately reflect the clinical choices that truly require change.

Definitions of success and survival should specify how interventions are handled. Record recementation, local repair, relining and complete remanufacture separately; cumulative treatment burden complements the first-event endpoint. Distinguish temporary interruption from permanent discontinuation to calculate time in normal use. These outcomes jointly describe reliability, repairability and treatment experience.

Statistical judgments should be linked to clinical importance. Even when differences are not significant, confidence intervals may still contain meaningful advantages or disadvantages; sample size and primary endpoints should be designed around predefined decision differences. Multiple secondary indicators can help explain mechanisms but should not replace the original primary question. For patient-reported scales, they can indicate scale direction and perceived changes, maintaining a clear link between numbers and user experience.

Evidence synthesis requires indexes of cohorts and product versions. Early satisfaction data and a later two-year cohort may involve the same patients; they can inform distinct endpoints, but the same outcome must not be counted twice. Stratify major material and manufacturing differences before pooling. If conditions alter the question itself, narrative comparisons and ranges of effects may be more informative.

Patient preferences can also be predefined research variables. Some prioritize reducing hospital visits, while others value voice, appearance, or ease of subsequent maintenance; the same overall satisfaction may be composed of different combinations of dimensions. Studies can record these priorities before treatment and then compare whether the actual results meet expectations. This allows for testing under which preferences and resource conditions a manufacturing process is more valuable, while avoiding replacing the patient's complete judgment with a single indicator chosen by the researcher.

Follow-up intervals affect event identification. Longer intervals between follow-up visits may miss mid-term repairs or short periods of inactivity. Studies can maintain event reporting channels in addition to fixed follow-up visits and verify maintenance records. For continuous changes such as color, wear, and fit, standardized photographs, scans, and evaluation scales can be used to distinguish between slow changes and sudden failures in subsequent analyses. Only by combining continuous measurement with event recording can we observe whether a change in a material has occurred before intervention is needed.

Another priority is feasibility. Controlled training and equipment maintenance in clinical trials can establish relatively stable processes; however, scaling up to different institutions will alter operating conditions due to staff turnover, batch sizes, and consumable supply. Studies can use implementation records as process evaluations to analyze deviations related to rework or patient events. This preserves internal consistency in clinical comparisons and progressively demonstrates how results can be replicated in routine services.

In 2027, clinical studies may increasingly revolve around specific materials—workflows and common endpoints. More complete documentation of product versions, maintenance events, and patient outcomes will facilitate new comparisons in systematic synthesis. Observable indicators include pre-registration primary endpoints, complete manufacturing information, multi-center implementation, and clear analysis at the patient and device levels. These determine whether the evidence answers the same question.

In 2028-2029, certain applications may see a clearer division of labor. If resin single crowns, printed zirconia, and digital dentures continue to perform stably under similar patient conditions, and their resource or delivery advantages are reproducible, their suitable applications will become clearer. Expanded conditions should be met by both long-term interventions and important patient outcomes; the focus should be on consistent cumulative events and maintenance burden, rather than the number of individual material tests or device installations.

The development of multi-unit resin bridges is likely to be more driven by structural and fatigue outcomes. If design improvements reduce connection zone failures and do not increase abutment tooth events, clinical studies can further clarify load-bearing and case conditions; if the failure patterns remain the same, the application and material selection will continue to be adjusted. Long-term cohorts can first identify events, and then use controlled studies to validate improvements, forming a continuous R&D pathway.

Different approaches can also lead to differences in workflow even when patient outcomes are similar. A manufacturing method remains valuable if total visit time is reduced, maintenance is easy, and institutional investment is manageable. Conversely, if initial savings are accompanied by more subsequent interventions, redesigning recording, trial fitting, or manufacturing procedures is necessary. Future assessments should consider both effects and costs, ensuring clinical adoption is based on repeatable net benefits.

The primary task is to establish a core outcome set based on usage. For complete dentures, at least quality of life, sub-satisfaction, retention, initial intervention, and discontinuation should be recorded; for fixed restorations, at least fracture, debonding, biological events, aesthetic intervention, and final replacement should be recorded. The timing, severity, and management of each event should be clearly defined, and patient feedback on outcomes should be retained to allow different studies to pool the same endpoint.

Priority Task Two is a clear multicenter comparison of material versions. For applications with early feasibility, assign manufacturing routes under the same case conditions and clinical procedures; if comparing complete workflows, record procedural differences in detail. Estimate sample size based on meaningful clinical differences, account for loss to follow-up, and report effects and intervals. Establish a new hierarchy after product upgrades to avoid misalignment between results from the old and new versions.

The third priority is maintenance and time-to-event cohorts. Preserve design, thickness, connector dimensions and processing at delivery, then link specific damage to its management during follow-up. Record continued use after the first event, repeat events and permanent discontinuation to evaluate the value of repair. Combine retrieved-device examination with experimental failure analysis to identify material and geometric factors most worth improving.

Priority Task Four is concurrent economic research. This involves cumulatively analyzing laboratory, clinic, and patient inputs on a case-by-case basis, presenting total costs, time to no intervention, and patient experience over the same period. Scenario analyses are conducted based on institution size, labor costs, and equipment utilization rates to illustrate under what conditions changes should be made. The results can be used both for treatment procedures and to determine which burdens should be prioritized for reduction in R&D investment.

The hallmark of mature evidence is the reduction of decision-making uncertainty through both primary trials and comprehensive studies. New data can clarify which materials and workflows are suitable for which patient groups, when maintenance is needed, and the total investment required to achieve stable results. By addressing these answerable questions in each round of research, clinical comparisons can shift from name-based debates to concrete treatment choices.
