graph.title: Research Context: Clinical Comparison and Evidence Convergence Stratified by Application
graph.summary: The denture branch extends from crossover trials to retention, maintenance and continued use. Fixed-restoration branches separately assess adult single crowns, paediatric crowns, zirconia and bridges. Efficiency studies and evidence synthesis bring these endpoints together and inform subsequent comparative designs.

nodes.title: Early denture-experience comparisons
nodes.question: How does reducing steps in printed dentures affect experience?
nodes.evidence: A randomized crossover trial assessed multidimensional satisfaction and visits; conventional dentures performed better on some experience measures, while digital workflows reduced some visit measures.

nodes.title: Randomized testing of another workflow
nodes.question: Can quality-of-life outcomes be reproduced across workflows?
nodes.evidence: A randomized crossover comparison in 18 participants found comparable patient-reported outcomes for the specific printed and conventional dentures.

nodes.title: Measuring retention and experience together
nodes.question: Does objective retention explain patient experience?
nodes.evidence: A crossover trial of three material/manufacturing routes found similar retention for printed and heat-cured dentures, with different results in the polyamide group.

nodes.title: Two-year interventions and continued use
nodes.question: Do success and continued wearing coincide?
nodes.evidence: Prospective follow-up of 36 dentures in 18 participants was completed at two years by 12 participants; fractures, repairs and discontinuation were recorded separately.

nodes.title: Adult resin single crowns
nodes.question: What events occur over two years of posterior single-crown use?
nodes.evidence: A prospective cohort of 30 crowns recorded survival, success, debonding and color changes.

nodes.title: Within-child primary molar comparison
nodes.question: How do two crown types differ within the same child?
nodes.evidence: Fifty teeth in 25 participants were followed for 12 months; several functional outcomes were similar, but wear, color and gingival indices were worse in the printed group.

nodes.title: Randomized zirconia trial
nodes.question: Are clinical outcomes similar for the same material made by different processes?
nodes.evidence: NPJ printing and milling were randomly compared in 48 teeth from 43 participants; principal outcomes were similar at 12 months.

nodes.title: Follow-up of resin three-unit bridges
nodes.question: How do span and connectors affect long-term outcomes?
nodes.evidence: Sixty-eight bridges in 49 participants were observed for up to three years; mechanical failures concentrated at connectors, and survival for the combined-event endpoint was estimated at 36.2%.

nodes.title: Clinical outcomes and resources
nodes.question: Can similar clinical outcomes be achieved with fewer treatment resources?
nodes.evidence: A retrospective comparison in 60 participants found lower chairside time and laboratory costs in the digital groups, with similar functional outcomes.

nodes.title: Systematic synthesis and stratification
nodes.question: Which conclusions can be pooled across studies?
nodes.evidence: A synthesis of four printing/milling studies and a synthesis of 25 trials found no clear workflow advantage in patient-important outcomes.

P2-06.title: Prosthetic Sockets
P2-06.subtitle: Digital fitting from residual-limb geometry and interface loading to years of use
P2-06.thesis: The key advance in prosthetic sockets is a closed loop connecting modifiable geometry, validated load bearing and ongoing feedback from wear. Printing accuracy, weight reduction and patient comfort each require appropriate tests for interpretation.

questions.question: How can residual-limb scanning and digital design improve prosthetic socket fit?
questions.focus: How do scanning and clinical shape rectification jointly define the contact surface?

questions.question: How can prosthetic sockets reduce local pressure and improve wearing experience?
questions.focus: How to cross-validate pressure measurement, simulation, and patient experience?

questions.question: How can socket materials and lattice structures provide adequate load-bearing capacity?
questions.focus: How can materials, fibres and lattices form load-bearing designs that can be independently checked?

blocks.text: The socket is the component that provides continuous contact, load transfer, and fixation between the residual limb and the prosthesis. Its digital value depends on whether three issues can be addressed simultaneously: whether the shape of the contact surface is suitable for the specific residual limb, whether the local tissue can withstand the load, and whether the shell and its distal connections can remain intact during repeated use. Scanning, printing, and lattice work each alter a part of these aspects; therefore, the evaluation unit needs to cover the entire fitting process from acquisition to follow-up examination.

This paper treats upper limb and lower limb studies as two related but independent design scenarios. Upper limb sockets need to accommodate hand devices, control components, and grasping activities; lower limb sockets also bear weight transfer, gait cycles, and ground action. Even with the same material grade and similar weight reduction ratios, interpretation needs to be based on the corresponding stress scenarios. Geometric studies focus on contact area errors, structural studies focus on damage and deformation under specific loads, and clinical studies focus on wearability, activity, skin, and maintenance. [R02][R07][R08]

Research has progressed from preserving external shape to recording rectification decisions and testing their effects through pressure measurements and long-term cohorts. The central value of digital sockets is making modifications and their consequences traceable within a fitting episode. Faster delivery, lower local pressure and lighter devices are distinct benefits; linking them in the same user creates knowledge for the next design.
N1 | Testing deep-region errors with smartphone photogrammetry

A 2021 study optimized smartphone photogrammetry using an existing transtibial socket and a printed solid reference, comparing reconstructed volume, surface area, height and internal wall thickness. Overall height and surface area approached the reference, but deep internal surfaces showed substantial distortion. A visually complete reconstruction can therefore still misrepresent the contact surface. [R01]

This node first addresses the issue of digital input fidelity. For the prosthetic socket, the easily accessible surface near the opening and the deeply obscured area have different visibility; a single overall error will average both. Therefore, the design analysis should preserve the spatial location of the error and observe the distal end, bony protrusion area, and rim of the cavity separately. Replicating an existing prosthetic socket also requires distinguishing between the inner and outer surfaces; the wall thickness assumption will translate the shape reconstruction error into actual contact differences.

From this node, the path to digital reshaping begins, and the research variables change accordingly: first, scanning errors are recorded, then the amount of clinically active modifications are recorded, and both are saved separately in the data. When local discomfort occurs in the new prosthetic socket, it can be reviewed whether it is due to input shape deviation or whether the designer intentionally increased or decreased the space. This arrangement also provides a clear quality threshold for remote acquisition, ensuring that the value of low-cost equipment lies in repeatable contact geometry, rather than simply being measured by the number of images or whether the model is closed.
N2 | Linking automated pediatric upper-limb design to materials

The 2021 AutoMedPrint study used a scan of one three-year-old child's upper-limb residual limb to compare PLA and TPE, connection designs and printing parameters. Thirty-six sockets were manufactured and assessed for geometry, roughness and compressive performance. Most met strength requirements, but fit and comfort varied among combinations. [R02]

The methodological contribution lies in breaking down automated modeling into verifiable choices. For the same residual limb contour, using harder and more elastic materials will alter the wearing/removing deformation, edge contact, and connection/fixation methods. Recording both design and material parameters simultaneously can explain why a particular design, while strong enough, is inconvenient to wear. Children also have growth and activity needs; therefore, remanufacturing speed and adjustability should be evaluated along with the initial mechanical results.

This branch provides a transferable experimental organization method for subsequent structural research: first, compare materials under fixed geometry; then, modify the stress path under determined materials; and finally, submit the assembly to actual trial wear. For the upper limb prototype, the strength results correspond to the tested connection and compression scenarios. When moving to lower limb design, it is necessary to redefine the load, fixed end, and cyclic conditions, while retaining the original geometry and contact evaluation, so that load-bearing enhancement does not come at the cost of discomfort.
N3 | Manual versus digital rectification under matched manufacturing

A 2024 feasibility study in nine people with transtibial amputations compared manual casting and rectification with scanning followed by digital rectification; both routes ultimately used printed sockets. Geometry, comfort and workflow time were recorded. Comfort was similar, scanning saved time, and digital rectification took longer. [R03]

The key to this comparison lies in the shared manufacturing process. It focuses clinical questions on "how to determine the contact shape," avoiding attributing all results from simultaneous changes in scanning, software, materials, and printers to digitization. Manual experience, including palpation and assessment of soft tissue deformities, needs to be expressed in software through anatomical marking, local reduction, and spatial addition. Whether these operations are fully recorded determines whether these judgments can be reused among different prosthetists.

At the location shown in the diagram, node represents both the algorithm and interface mechanics. The algorithm needs to learn the modified shape, while the mechanics model needs to understand which contact area has been altered. Subsequent comparisons can retain three surfaces within the same user: the initial residual limb scan, each step of modification, and the final device, while incorporating a unified walking task. This approach not only pinpoints specific differences but also identifies necessary manual adjustments for comfort, thus representing a realistic digital adaptation workload.
N4 | Learning historical shapes for independent-user fitting

A 2025 study developed a transtibial socket-shape algorithm from historical data for 116 patients, then compared algorithm-based and manual routes in 10 participants. Mean predicted-shape deviation was 2.51 mm. Eight algorithm-generated and all 10 manually designed sockets met the criteria for home trials, followed by comfort and professional fit assessments. [R04]

This design allows data learning to bypass model similarity evaluation and move into the selection of practically wearable devices. Historical designs are the result of clinical practice, incorporating prosthetist preferences, patient body types, and specific suspension conditions. Therefore, a small average shape error initially indicates approximation to an existing design distribution; whether the local space meets the needs of a new user still needs to be determined through trial fitting and independent fitting evaluation. The algorithm can be set to provide a starting point, with human modifications then serving as analyzable results.

The next step in the study could be to establish joint endpoints based on the initial protocol acceptance rate, modification location, modification time, and final comfort changes. Protocols that failed to reach home trial settings should still be included in the process evaluation, as the trial and redesign time they consumed impacts actual service efficiency. This would allow for identification of which types of residual geometry the algorithm is stable in, in which situations more professional intervention is needed, and abnormal shapes would be fed back into the data for updates, rather than simply comparing the average scores of those who completed the trial.
N5 | Calibrating interface finite element models with a rollover simulator

The 2025 study integrated a load measurement unit into the outer wall of a printed prosthetic socket, sensing the internal force through the piston interface and comparing it with predictions from finite element methods at seven locations on a rolling simulator. The results show that the accuracy of the geometric description has a crucial impact on the prediction of interface pressure. [R05]

The node places the validity of the computational model within a repeatable experimental context. Simulating residual limbs, prosthetic sockets, and rolling trajectories allows for repeatable load inputs, enabling observation of whether the error originates from material constitutive modeling, contact assumptions, or geometry. The load element measures the normal force at the corresponding location, and the model should output the quantity at the same location, area, and time point. Comparing the maximum stress across the entire field with the local average pressure, even if the numbers are close, fails to verify the prediction mechanism.

This model, along with the scanning nodes, forms a crucial convergence: geometric errors are amplified into pressure errors through contact relationships. Subsequent digital modeling can first predict the direction of change, then compare the before and after modifications using the same device to establish local design rules with clear inputs and results. When transferred to the human body, tissue condition, padding, and suspension conditions must also be recorded. In this way, the pressure model can help interpret the modeling, while patient-reported pain, stability, and activity remain the endpoints of the actual outcome.
N6 | Textile pressure-sensing socks: establish measurement stability before clinical interpretation

A 2026 study integrated textile sensing elements into a prosthetic sock, first testing sensitivity, repeatability and drift, then loading a simulated residual limb made from silicone and printed components. Elements detected changes equivalent to 5% of maximum load and changes in pressure distribution under a 600 N simulated-gait condition. [R06]

This work changes the way measurements enter the prosthetic socket. The sock-like shape more easily covers curved surfaces, but fabric elongation, wrinkles, repeated putting on and taking off, and humidity can also affect the signal. Therefore, even after achieving a stable unit response, the repeatability of the sensing point relative to the anatomical position still needs to be evaluated. The thickness and stiffness of the measurement system itself can also alter the original contact; a comparison before and after inserting the sensing sock can identify this interference effect.

Moving from benchtop use to daily life, the wearing process can be marked for standing, walking on flat ground, walking on slopes, and prolonged sitting, and then correlated with the time of discomfort occurrence. Adaptation decisions may focus on prolonged load in a certain area or the emergence of new focal points throughout the day, rather than the lowest point of a single peak. In the diagram, this node, along with the structural design, ultimately merges into the long-term cohort to determine whether measurable load changes are accompanied by more stable wear and fewer skin problems, and to provide specific locations for the next refit.
N7 | Continuous fibers reinforce load paths

A 2024 study of continuous-fibre-reinforced transfemoral sockets combined material testing, gait finite element analysis and print-path planning to place fibres in load-bearing regions. The tested reinforcement reduced weight by approximately 28% relative to the unreinforced resin design and passed three million loading cycles, illustrating joint design of shape and load bearing. [R07]

The core of this branch is placing reinforcing materials where they can function effectively. The distal connection, local curvature, and rim of the prosthetic socket determine how the load enters the shell, while the fiber orientation affects tensile and bending capacity. Therefore, "fiber addition" needs to be further specified in terms of orientation, continuity, bends, and interlayer connections. Material samples provide basic parameters, and whole-piece cyclic testing verifies whether these parameters remain effective along the actual path and at the connection locations.

The results support staged validation: confirm material-batch properties, verify manufacturing quality along the print path, then test complete sockets in worst-case loading configurations. Weight comparisons should specify whether adapters, liners and outer coverings are included so that system boundaries match. Long-term damage records should return to this node, using actual crack locations to determine whether reinforcement covers the principal failure regions.
N8 | Field-driven upper-limb lattices connect computation and manufacturing

A 2026 field-driven study combined residual-limb reconstruction, elastoplastic homogenization and stress-field mapping to generate spatially varying lattices for upper-limb sockets. Full-size PA12 prototypes were manufactured by Multi Jet Fusion and compared with designs using quasi-static testing and CT. The studied prototype weighed approximately 25% less than the solid design. [R08]

This node extends individualization from external shape to internal material distribution. Local rod diameters and densities are controlled by stress requirements, and the lattice is described using equivalent materials during calculations, then the equivalent results are translated into a manufacturable structure. There are two dimensions that need to be connected here: how the overall shell deforms, and whether the tiny connecting rods can be shaped as designed. CT scans provide an additional physical basis between these two, identifying whether computational performance is built on geometry that doesn't actually exist.

This application targets upper limb devices that connect to wrist components. The research logic can provide a methodological reference for lower limb structures, but the load system needs to be reconfigured according to the task. Further research can compare homogeneous and gradient lattices while maintaining the same shape and suspension, and observe local compliance, clean accessibility, and post-damage propagation. In the figure, it complements fiber branching: the former distributes spatial density, and the latter distributes directional enhancement; the common goal is to bear a defined load with a verifiable structure.
N9 | Rural cohort tracks use and damage

A Sierra Leone cohort study, published online in 2025 and in issue 2026, followed nine lower leg amputees for 2.5 years. Six sockets were damaged during follow-up, and others were replaced due to size issues; the median daily wearing time at the last recorded point was 12.4 hours. The study simultaneously measured activity, function, and quality of life. [R09]

This node adds time to service evaluation. Continued wear shows integration into daily life, while damage and remanufacture reveal the support needed to sustain use. Separate the lifetime of the initial socket, replacement devices, repair waiting time and eventual wear so that high activity after replacement can be interpreted. Activity exposure also matters: the same months of use may represent different step counts and loading cycles.

The two feedback loops in the diagram are thus formed. Size changes are returned to scanning and reshaping, requiring the preservation of the limb's state at each stage; damage location is returned to materials and reinforcement paths, requiring the recording of the fracture area and manufacturing batch. The evaluation of service accessibility further incorporates transportation, remanufacturing, and temporary alternatives. By integrating these records into a single archive and digitizing them, each replacement can become the basis for the next design iteration, and longer effective wear time can be used to verify whether manufacturing efficiency truly improves rehabilitation.

sections.title: Academic Evolution: From Shape Copying to Interpretable Adaptation

blocks.text: Early digital research focused on demonstrating that inputs could become manufacturable three-dimensional surfaces. Subsequent research began separating the roles of shaping and manufacturing, then integrating mechanical simulations, sensing tools, and actual wearable devices into the same object. This shift can be observed at research endpoints: localized pressure emerges after geometric deviations, overall wear cycles after material strength improvements, and damage time and continuous use follow after initial comfort. These new endpoints add different dimensions of information and require older endpoints to retain sufficiently detailed records.

A layer of clinical interpretation is needed between geometry and comfort. The surface of the residual limb is not a static, rigid body; the sampling posture, volumetric state, and padding thickness all alter the contact. Accurately replicating a scan does not equate to creating a space suitable for the load. Digital modification studies therefore play a pivotal role: they receive scans, user feedback, and output practical designs to the load-bearing model. Treating modifications as independent research subjects allows for the accumulation of experience on which areas need to release space and which regions bear support.

Materials and structural studies, particularly those involving, require a unified definition of load. While fiber reinforcement and lattice-based weight reduction seem to share the goal of "lighter and stronger," their actual mechanisms differ: fibers depend on orientation and continuity, while lattices depend on rod diameter, connectivity, and overall distribution. Common endpoints for comparison include cyclic durability, permanent deformation, failure location, and manufacturing dispersion per unit system weight. These endpoints are only suitable for supporting design choices if loads, geometry, and connectivity are identical. [R07][R08]

Future clinical comparisons are better suited to using explicit adaptation strategies as interventions. For example, maintaining the same foot components and suspension methods, comparing conventional and pressure-assisted modifications; or maintaining the same shape, comparing different structural strategies. The learning process for participants using the new device should also be documented, with pre-set adaptation periods and measurement sequences. This makes it easier to attribute differences and corresponds to steps that service providers can actually take to improve.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: Ottobock's iFab organizes scanning, digital modification, and centralized manufacturing into a service process, allowing customer platforms to transfer data and order products. The company also describes a future direction of improving subsequent processes using centralized documentation. Its productization significance lies in expanding "documents can be printed" to "orders that clinical institutions can submit, modify, and reorder," with the service system handling the multiple communications involved in traditional processes. [R10]

Current MyFit TT documentation specifies PA12 Multi Jet Fusion, digital upload and suspension options, and includes stable residual-limb volume among fitting conditions. The page's detailed MyFit TF section describes online geometry adjustments and ordering of diagnostic sockets. [R11] These show different roles for digital tools in definitive load-bearing devices and trial fitting: consistent delivery of a defined device versus rapid assessment of shape changes.

PROTEOR's definitive-socket workflow combines ORTEN software, ICARUS printers and KyronMAX material and explicitly describes printing outside vase mode. [R12] Materials and equipment form a complete process package. The strategy emphasizes in-house manufacturing, shorter order waits and more options for structural paths; actual delivery data can assess these goals.

The differences in enterprise routes also correspond to the choice of service capabilities. Centralized manufacturing is beneficial for aggregating equipment and process control, while in-house manufacturing is beneficial for shortening waiting times after modifications. However, both require clearly defined document versions, qualification criteria, maintenance records, and rework entry points. Optional items in product descriptions should be converted into actual fields in the order, such as suspension type, adapter location, flange shape, and local modifications, rather than simply uploading a mesh file whose origin cannot be explained.

Once the technology platform matures, the focus of competition may shift to the ability to handle abnormal situations. Changes in volume, skin discomfort, localized damage, and equipment downtime may all require rapid redesign. The ability to retain older versions and indicate changes in newer versions facilitates collaboration between prosthetists and manufacturers. When companies publicly disclose clinical usage data, separating statistics by initial delivery, modifications, repairs, and replacements will provide a more accurate picture of service performance than simply showcasing printing speed.

sections.title: Verification Interface Between Research and Product

blocks.text: The first interface is an interpretable geometric profile. A complete case can save the original scan, anatomical landmarks, modification parameters, final internal surface, and post-manufacturing inspection results. Each modification specifies the area and purpose of the change and corresponds to the patient's complaints during the trial fitting. This allows for checking whether the stress model and the patient's experience are inconsistent when first verifying that the same version is being used, before analyzing tissue and padding factors, thus avoiding misinterpreting version differences as model failure.

The second interface is a shared definition of loading. Material suppliers' coupon properties, equipment suppliers' manufacturing capabilities and clinical requirements must be connected through whole-device testing. Beyond maximum load and cycle count, records should include fixture conditions, distal connection, orientation, specimen state and failure location. Research can then supply reproducible product-specification conditions, while manufacturers supply batch variation and production anomalies.

The third interface is the pairing of fit changes with patient outcomes. Pressure-assisted fitting can use a before-and-after comparison of the same user, recording pressure, stability, pain, skin condition, and activity performance under the same task. If pressure decreases in a certain area but the wearing time shortens, further analysis should be conducted to determine if loosening, suspension changes, or new load concentrations have occurred. Multi-endpoint evaluation allows local optimization to serve the overall experience and also establishes practical applications for the sensing system.

The fourth interface,, is long-term maintenance data. Each repair record includes the cause, location, usage duration, and activity exposure, distinguishing between material damage, loose connections, and dimensional inconsistencies. The long-term queue shows that continuous use and maintenance needs can coexist; therefore, evaluating the service system requires statistics on effective wear time and maintenance-related interruptions. [R09] Only after obtaining this structured information can the manufacturing end select to enhance a specific area, change connection details, or adjust the follow-up check schedule.

In institutional collaborations, a standardized medical record can be used while retaining the measurement responsibilities of different roles: prosthetists record fitting and experience, laboratories record support and materials, and manufacturing centers record processes and batches. A common device number connects these three types of data. This interface is suitable for both centralized platforms and local institutional manufacturing, transforming fragmented experience into comparable, adaptable results.

Acceptance can include a within-case check: rescan the manufactured socket against its approved design and preserve any on-site modifications made during fitting. This separates production error from further clinical optimization. For users requiring repeated remanufacture, contact-surface changes form a time series that can be analysed with volume change and activity recovery to guide local adjustment versus renewed shape capture.

sections.title: Conditional Path and Observation Indicators for 2027-2029

blocks.text: If more platforms connect scanning, modification, and follow-up visit data to the same case within the next year, the first visible changes should be more complete version tracking and clearer information on the number of modifications after the initial adaptation. Key indicators include scan redo rate, first-time fitting success rate, time from feedback to new device, and the actual number of patient visits. Only when these aspects improve together will the speed benefits of digital workflow translate into a positive rehabilitation experience.

If pressure-based fittings become routine, the focus in 2027-2028 should be on monitoring sensor repositioning, drift after repeated donning and doffing, and the repeatability of the same modification across different prosthetists. Research can first verify whether "the modification decision has changed," and then verify whether "the change has improved the wearing outcome." This approach separates the engineering performance of the sensing system from its actual clinical use, while maintaining a traceable link between the two.

If fibre or lattice approaches expand to more uses, whole-device durability data stratified by body weight, activity and connection type should emerge in 2028–2029. Track variability in manufacturing quality, permanent deformation, failure locations, repair rates and structural weight. Compare processes using the same shape, connection and loading, including performance after environmental ageing, to establish whether lightweighting preserves load-bearing capacity.

If the algorithm design begins to be used extensively, the evaluation focus should shift to independent institutions and abnormal limb morphology. The proportion of initial plans directly accepted, the time required for manual reshaping, reasons for not conducting home fittings, and the final experience can be recorded. Archiving the model version alongside clinical decisions helps identify whether performance changes stem from training data, software updates, or the experience of the fitting personnel.

Accessibility studies are suitable for continuous observation of the entire service cycle. Beyond material costs, they should include resources needed for printing failures, transportation, repairs, re-manufacturing, and spare equipment, calculated on a per-month effective usage basis or per segment of ongoing rehabilitation. Such results will help determine which regions and populations are best suited for centralized manufacturing, local printing, and hybrid services, and will also provide clear evidence of patient benefit for technology expansion.

The focus of cavity research is shifting from replicating individual body shape to maintaining individual fit within defined stress and life situations. Scans provide recordable input, shaping expresses clinical judgment, pressure measurements examine contact changes, fibers and lattices provide structural choices, and long-term follow-up reveals the persistence of these choices in real life. These nine nodes form a recurring and up-to-date research process.

The most valuable achievement of in this direction is ensuring that each modification leaves an interpretable record, and that these records correspond to actual device versions and usage results. By establishing common data interfaces around geometry, load, structure, and maintenance, academic research can propose more specific design rules, enterprise platforms can implement and correct them more quickly, and users can receive more stable wearable support in continuous service.

P2-07.title: Prostheses and Orthoses
P2-07.subtitle: Organizing personalized devices around tasks, gait and wearing experience
P2-07.thesis: Printing enables individual anatomy to become modifiable structures whose function can be tested through defined tasks. Upper-limb, lower-limb, orthotic and maxillofacial applications have distinct endpoints, while sharing a pathway from user feedback to the next design iteration.

questions.question: How can printed upper limb prostheses improve grasping and daily functions?
questions.focus: Match residual motor ability and grasp configurations to daily tasks.

questions.question: How do printed lower limb prostheses and orthoses affect gait?
questions.focus: Match shape and stiffness to the functional demands of each gait phase.

questions.question: How can patient-specific orthoses combine fit and accessibility?
questions.focus: Evaluate donning and doffing, assisted movements and resources required for complete delivery.

questions.question: How can maxillofacial and ocular prostheses combine appearance with patient-specific fit?
questions.focus: Evaluate geometry, colour, soft-tissue contact and repeat fabrication.

blocks.text: Prostheses, orthotics, and external maxillofacial restorations share the need for personalized manufacturing, but they serve different purposes. Prostheses replace missing parts, orthotics work in conjunction with preserved limbs, and prosthetic eyes and facial prostheses reconstruct shape and contact soft tissue. This article organizes by task: upper limbs focus on grasping, holding, and releasing; lower limbs focus on support and rolling; orthotics focus on positioning or assisting movement; and maxillofacial restorations focus on appearance, wearing, and care.

Personalization includes both form and function. Scanning aligns shells with individual anatomy, while joint orientation, local stiffness, connections, actuation and surface treatment determine their function. Endpoints must therefore be device-specific: grasp success, gait measurements and appearance scores answer different questions. Sustained use additionally requires observation of donning and doffing, training, maintenance and refitting. [R03][R04][R10]

Ten nodes cover the key aspects from structural configuration to clinical experience. The diagram shows both the design progress within similar devices and the connections between different devices sharing evaluation methods. The intersection of academia and industry lies in the fact that design documents can be updated with feedback, manufacturing processes can be executed stably, and users can experience improvements that align with their goals.
N1 | Body-powered fingers in personal tasks

Two finger amputation cases reported in 2022 utilized the open-source Knick Finger design, which assisted flexion and extension by preserving the metacarpophalangeal joint movement and using linkages and traction structures. After one month of training, both participants showed improvement in personal goals such as cooking and computer typing, and reported satisfaction. [R01]

This study focuses on residual motor function as the starting point for structural design. Defects with the same appearance may have different joint ranges of motion, strength, and contact tolerance; therefore, the traction path and fixation method of the device need to be determined in collaboration with the user. Individual goals can also differentiate task requirements: holding cutlery stably, touching a keyboard, and lifting heavy objects all place different demands on fingertip position, movement speed, and contact friction.

Moving from case studies to comparative studies allows for simultaneous recording of standard and personal tasks, observing changes before and after training. Standard tasks facilitate comparison between different devices, while personal tasks explain whether the device alters daily life. It's also important to record which tasks the device is chosen to wear, when it is actively removed, and maintenance needs each day. This ensures the benefits of body-driven design correspond to specific usage scenarios and provides directional feedback for subsequent improvements to joint range of motion, fingertip surfaces, and retainer rings.
N2 | Separating grasp variables through thumb configurations

The 2022 study compared four low-cost prosthetic hand configurations, observing grasping and retention performance using AHAP and simplified SHAP. The combination of thumb opposition, abduction/adduction, and flexion/extension affects the manipulation of different objects; independent control provides more options while increasing the number of control components. [R02]

The node indicates that the number of degrees of freedom needs to be interpreted in conjunction with the motion organization. The thumb's ability to move does not guarantee it will provide adequate counterforce when contacting an object; a fixed thumb, if properly oriented, may stably complete tasks involving large objects. During testing, it should be observed whether the object is grasped, whether the posture matches the target, whether the hand can maintain its position after rotation, and how many repositionings are required. Each failure corresponds to a different design reason.

The design iteration can fix the other fingers and actuators, changing only the thumb's direction, range of motion, or control coupling, and then comparing the results using the same set of objects. This distinguishes configuration effects from surface friction, manufacturing quality, and operator skill. The feedback returned here by subsequent bench comparisons in the diagram precisely transforms certain types of grip failures into modifiable parameters. User training is then arranged after the mechanism's performance stabilizes, ensuring that the added control capabilities ultimately serve to reduce operational burden and achieve more reliable movements.
N3 | A common prosthetic-hand test bench isolates mechanical grasp differences

A 2024 study used a standardized AHAP bench setup to compare three printed and three commercial prosthetic hands, adding published data for four existing printed designs. Printed specimens generally performed worse in cylindrical, diagonal volar, extension and spherical grasps. The results identified targets for improvements in mechanisms or manufacturing quality. [R03]

Bench tests examine hand–object contact while reducing variation from socket fit and myoelectric control. They assess whether a mechanism can hold an object after a grasp pattern is selected and permit repeat testing after component or material changes. Report separate scores for each grasp because an overall mean may conceal weakness in a key daily task.

When conducting user studies, the testing tasks should also include autonomous grip selection, arm positioning, and bimanual coordination. Bench performance forms the structural basis for this type of evaluation, while user outcomes reintegrate control and training. A two-stage comparison can be used, first the bench and then the user, reporting object retention, task time, erroneous actions, and usage preferences on the same version. This provides companies with a concrete list of actionable improvements, and clinical selection can be based on the match between the user's primary tasks and the device's capabilities.
N4 | Scan-customized AFOs in individual gait tests

A 2011 study used laser scanning, computer design, and rapid prototyping to create two individual ankle-foot orthoses, which were then compared with prefabricated polypropylene devices in one subject. The observed gait function was similar, and the digital route enabled adaptation to individual anatomical features. [R04]

This node establishes the basic chain from the body surface to the supporting device. The contact area, edges, and in-shoe space of the ankle-foot orthosis affect whether it can be worn comfortably, while its restriction and support effect on the joint depends on stiffness. When simply replicating the shape, these two layers of effects may be mixed; research designs can compare materials under the same geometry, or change the support range under the same materials, gradually identifying the morphological and mechanical contributions.

Gait assessment should follow the intended treatment goal. For foot drop, assess toe clearance and ankle position during swing; for joint instability, assess weight-bearing phases and asymmetry. Record footwear, walking speed and adaptation time to interpret repeated measurements. Digital records can then guide changes targeted at observed walking problems and support within-person comparisons with the first design.
N5 | Optimizing prosthetic feet for nonlinear toe stiffness

The 2021 prosthetic foot research used finite element analysis to simulate the final support phase, linking the forefoot curve, flexion space, concave structure, and flexion zone to optimize the moment-angle relationship and stress in the toe. The paper resulted in a computational design for a printable structure; physical fabrication and further verification are planned as subsequent steps. [R05]

The question is how one component can provide different responses at different deformation levels. Propulsion demands are not captured by one fixed stiffness; geometry can progressively increase mechanical resistance. A target moment–angle curve shifts design from resembling a foot to producing specified behaviour during a defined gait phase, while a maximum-stress constraint addresses load-bearing capacity.

The model transitions from calculation to actual device implementation, requiring the incorporation of material orientation, interlayer bonding, and printing errors into mechanical verification. This can be achieved by first measuring the actual torque-angle curve, then conducting cyclic and multi-directional load tests, and finally examining the user's rolling propulsion and performance at different speeds. Each stage retains the same design version, allowing simulation, bench testing, and walking to be mutually interpretable. This node, along with the ankle-foot brace, emphasizes that individualized stiffness should be selected according to specific movement goals, and its applicability should be verified through real-world tasks.
N6 | Open-source wrist-driven orthoses: joint iteration by users and fabricators

A 2018 open-source wrist-driven orthosis study incorporated feedback from three people with spinal cord injury and six orthotics students and published dimensions and assembly methods. Material costs were approximately US$15–20 depending on size, and manual assembly took about 1.5 hours. Benefits varied across personal tasks, and feedback informed changes to structure and fasteners. [R06]

This study breaks down accessibility into observable steps. Easy material availability is just the starting point; manufacturers also need to understand sizing modifications, joint assembly, and fitting methods, while users need to be able to put on and take off the garment and maintain stable contact. Modifications to the straps, magnetic connections, and finger supports extend the research from mechanical movements to everyday operations. For individuals with limited hand dexterity, independent wearability is itself an important functional endpoint.

Future evaluation should record the full pathway from measurement to first use, including printing waits, manual assembly, clinical adjustments and remanufacture. Pair reasons for modifications with task outcomes to determine whether simpler assembly affects reliability or easier donning and doffing supports continued use. Versioned open-source documentation enables replication across institutions and feedback from local needs, supporting transition from low-cost prototypes to sustainable rehabilitation services.
N7 | Testing immediate hand function with a myoelectric orthosis

A 2019 study used a printed structure, electromyographic input, and active actuation to construct a hand orthosis, comparing participants with and without the device on the same day in 10 participants with chronic cervical spinal cord injury. Improvements were observed in hand function tests and eating-related performance, while changes in fine object manipulation and other self-care tasks were limited. [R07]

This node shifts evaluation of active assistance from actuator output to the user's ability to complete tasks. Greater grip strength may help lift a cup, but dressing and washing also depend on trunk control, joint movement and bimanual coordination. Report self-care tasks separately, alongside device size, weight, adjustment and wearing requirements, to identify the tasks most directly improved by mechanical assistance.

Longer-term studies can include adaptation before examining whether learning expands task benefits or added control increases fatigue. Hold the device version constant and record myoelectric calibration and daily use to distinguish training from redesign. Feedback to the wrist-driven node represents shared questions of donning and doffing, fit and task matching. Choices between body-powered and active assistance should follow residual abilities and daily-life goals.
N8 | Silicone powder binder jetting: soft prostheses require a complete material process

A study published in a 2022 journal issue used PVB-coated silicone powder for binder jetting, followed by sequential pressure–vacuum infiltration with silicone and solvent to produce final components. Particle size, coating, surface treatment and infiltration conditions jointly influenced the mechanical properties of printed preforms and finished structures. [R08]

Soft facial prostheses must combine shape, thin margins and compliant contact, unlike rigid shells. Conversion of a printed porous preform into an infiltrated component can change dimensions, porosity and material continuity. Printing and post-processing should therefore be assessed as one workflow, with measurements of both the preform and final state to identify sources of appearance or strength deviations.

As this approach is further developed, areas of varying thicknesses can be designed for localized features such as the ear and nose, allowing for comparison of changes after edge tearing, repeated bending, and cleaning. Color and surface detail also need to be evaluated in the final material state, as impregnation and curing alter optical properties. Digital manufacturing provides repeatable geometry, while patient fit determines the suitability of edges, softness, and fixation. The research findings can provide a comparable comparison between mold forming and direct printing.
N9 | OCT and color models generate ocular prostheses

A 2024 study used anterior-segment OCT to capture eye-socket information, a statistical shape model to complete the fitting geometry and calibrated images of the fellow eye to generate appearance. Ocular prostheses were made by multicomponent colour printing and post-processing. Initial clinical applications in 10 patients were presented, with final shapes still fitted and adjusted by an ocularist. [R09]

The individualization here is accomplished through two types of data: geometric description of the spatial relationship between the eyelid and the contact surface, and color description of the appearance of the iris, sclera, and blood vessels. Both need to be consistent across the same coordinate system and production version; otherwise, adjusting the shape may alter the iris position or visible area. The statistical model is responsible for forming a usable initial shape from limited scan information, which is then confirmed by clinical adaptation.

Repeat fabrication is an important endpoint. Appearance data can be retained for the same patient, but eye-socket conditions and preferences may change, so remanufacture should permit colour preservation with independent adjustment of the contact surface. Evaluate automated generation time, manual modifications, fitting attempts and final appearance consistency. Feeding ocularists' adjustments back to the model could improve initial fit and reduce professional work per completed case.
N10 | A randomized ocular-prosthesis comparison separates comfort and microbiological outcomes

A 2023 randomized study randomly assigned 22 participants to either a printed prosthetic eye or a traditional PMMA prosthetic eye, with a three-month follow-up. No significant differences were found in microbiological results between the two groups. The printed group reported better comfort levels, and there were no significant differences between the groups in terms of secretions, tearing, and lubrication frequency. [R10]

This node breaks down the measurement of prosthetic eye performance. Aesthetic acceptance, contact comfort, and microbial colonization can be influenced by various factors, including posterior surface adaptation, polishing, care, and wearing habits. Therefore, the study needs to pre-define the measurement time and methods for each endpoint to avoid using any single factor to represent the entire effect. Actual infection, surface colonization, and subjective discomfort should also be recorded as separate outcomes.

This node provides feedback for automated design: local discomfort informs shape changes, care requirements inform surface and cleaning procedures, and colour changes inform appearance materials. Longer follow-up can record insertion/removal frequency, polishing and replacement reasons. As in hand and gait research, separate endpoints link manufacturing to actual experience and trigger traceable design updates.

sections.title: The Evolution of Academic Approaches and Common Methods

blocks.text: The changes in this research direction are primarily reflected in more specific task descriptions. Hand research has progressed from assessing the flexion and extension capabilities of the mechanism to conducting sub-tests on different grips; gait research has evolved from conforming to the shape to assessing stiffness response during movement; and prosthetic eye research has progressed from aesthetic manufacturing to contact and care. Technological advancements are demonstrated by the new questions that can be answered, rather than by the complexity of the printed parts or the quantity of research conducted.

A second development is preserving shared conditions in comparisons. Prosthetic-hand bench tests reduce effects of control and socket fit to isolate mechanism differences; within-user tests with and without orthoses assess immediate assistance; randomized ocular-prosthesis comparisons place manufacturing routes in a shared follow-up framework. Each addresses part of attribution, together informing the roles of structure, fit and learning. [R03][R07][R10]

Feedback is also becoming stored design information. Open-source wrist-driven orthoses translate users' donning, doffing and grasping difficulties into component changes, while data-driven ocular prostheses retain clinical fitting after automated shape generation. [R06][R09] Recording each modification's location, magnitude and reason creates a comparable version history. Frequent changes can identify parameters suitable for automated adjustment and those still requiring in-person assessment.

Research organizations also need to preserve population differences. Amputation level, residual joint mobility, muscle signals, and trunk control influence device selection; walking ability and footwear affect lower limb support; and orbital morphology and care capabilities affect prosthetic eye use. Stratification is not about increasing reporting complexity, but about ensuring clear applicability of technical conclusions. The same device exhibiting different benefits in different tasks can serve as a basis for design differentiation.

More informative research can use sequential validation: first hold materials and mechanisms constant for bench comparisons, then identify fitting issues through short-term use, and finally assess training, maintenance and long-term choices. Shared version numbers and records of modifications link laboratory and patient results, giving manufacturers specific targets for iteration.

sections.title: The Evolution of Enterprise Products and Digital Services

blocks.text: Naked Prosthetics' PIPDriver is a body-driven finger product that revolves around preserving proximal interphalangeal joints and residual finger conditions. It uses nylon and titanium components and is individually manufactured using advanced printing. The product's positioning shares the idea of "complementing movement with preserved capabilities" with finger case studies, with joint alignment, residual finger length, and contact stability as the core adaptation principles. [R11]

Open Bionics' official timeline states that the Hero Arm was launched in 2018, and in 2020, the early PLA hand and frame were updated to laser-sintered nylon 12, while the inner liner and outer casing connections were improved. This technological evolution encompasses three aspects: structural materials, residual limb interfaces, and user operation, indicating that product updates are gradually revolving around long-term user experience. [R12]

Spentys' current ankle-foot orthosis process incorporates weight, activity level, clinical type, scan source, support shape, local thickness, and manufacturing location into the order. Dynamic models also allow selection of joint configuration and activity requirements. This platform transforms clinical choices into fields that can be passed to both design and manufacturing, enabling individualization beyond physical dimensions and allowing institutions to choose between centralized printing or local manufacturing. [R13]

ActivArmor's provider workflow connects mobile phone scanning, custom design based on clinical positioning and instructions, and in-house manufacturing. Its product service focuses on the delivery of fixation and protection devices, with open structures and adjustable fixation providing operational space for follow-up examinations. [R14] Evaluating this type of platform can focus on observing acquisition success rates, design round trips, initial wear, and adjustments after volume changes to understand how same-day manufacturing goals are achieved within the complete clinical workflow.

Regarding prosthetic eyes, Fraunhofer IGD's 2024 translational data connects Cuttlefish-related technologies, Moorfields clinical applications, and Ocupeye's specialized manufacturing. Software, manufacturing, and clinical fitting are handled by different participants, forming a reusable production chain. [R15] The importance of this organizational approach lies in assigning geometry and color processing, post-printing surface treatment, and final fitting to their respective stages, while connecting them using the same patient data.

These pathways demonstrate how companies are expanding from selling single finished products to providing organizational adaptation services. Body-driven fingers, myoelectric prosthetics, dynamic ankle-foot braces, fixation devices, and prosthetic eyes have different delivery requirements, but all require clearly defined inputs, versions, and subsequent modification entry points. Product comparisons can therefore simultaneously present device capabilities and service capabilities: the former determines what can be done, and the latter determines how quickly usable devices can be restored in case of problems.

sections.title: Research—Industry Connections: From Standard Testing to Individual Benefits

blocks.text: The upper limb device can employ two evaluation systems: a shared object task and a personal goal system. The shared object task records grasping, holding, releasing, time, and failure type, while the personal goal system records the movements the user truly wishes to recover. Manufacturers can use the shared object task to improve mechanisms and controls, while clinicians can use the personal goal system to select devices and training content. Keeping the two types of results separate allows for the explanation of situations where a device's overall score is average but it is very helpful for a specific task.

Lower limb devices require linking design stiffness with gait data. Wall thickness, support range, and joint options in the order should correspond to measurable torque-angle relationships, followed by observation of gait speed, ankle movement, symmetry, and performance on different terrains. Once the footwear and adaptation time are fixed or recorded, the effect of structural changes is easier to assess. Localized pressure and skin feel also need to be considered, as gait stability is built upon the premise of continuous wear.

The accessibility of orthotics should be calculated on a complete service basis. Materials, equipment usage, manual assembly, fitting training, transportation, and remanufacturing are all considered delivery resources. Studies can report the time spent at each stage, while also calculating maintenance inputs during the effective wearing period. This allows for the separate presentation of lower material costs and reduced professional labor, and facilitates the assessment of the suitability of open-source local manufacturing, centralized manufacturing, and enterprise platforms for different institutional conditions.

Maxillofacial and ocular prostheses require parallel records of geometry, appearance and contact. Geometry concerns position and margins; appearance concerns colour and surface detail under different lighting; contact concerns comfort, secretions, skin or conjunctival condition and care. Replacement can retain established parameters while changing only what is necessary. Digital records then support consistent repeat fabrication, with each adjustment confirmed against individual outcomes.

The common interface for collaboration can be the device version, task list, and reason for modification. The research team provides repeatable tests, the clinical team records requirements and usage scenarios, and the manufacturer records materials, processes, and maintenance. By mapping these three together, a functional decline can be traced back to structural wear, control changes, adaptation modifications, or new activity requirements. This type of information is more conducive to developing specific improvements than simply collecting satisfaction data.

sections.title: A verifiable development path from 2027 to 2029

blocks.text: If the product platform further opens up functional parameters, in 2027, the focus should be on observing whether traceable local stiffness, joint movement, and grip configuration appear in orders, and whether these parameters correspond to delivery tests. The visible results for users should be fewer invalid modifications, clearer task matching, and shorter refit time. With the increase in design options, it is also necessary to observe whether clinicians can consistently select appropriate combinations.

If standardized task testing is adopted more widely, in 2027-2028, the results of repeated testing of the same version by different institutions can be compared, and it can be observed whether the improved version truly reduces a certain type of failure. For upper limb devices, the focus is on task completion rate and control burden after autonomous selection of grasp; for lower limb devices, the focus is on different paces and terrains; and for orthotics, the focus is on independent donning and doffing and continuous daily use. Clearly defined tasks will make the benefits of product updates more visible.

If automated design and color manufacturing continue to advance, in 2028-2029, the initial design pass rate, amount of manual modifications, cross-batch color consistency, and surface maintenance for more than one year can be observed in prosthetic eyes and maxillofacial restorations. For soft prostheses, thin edge integrity, post-cleaning performance, and color aging should also be tracked. The effectiveness of automation is measured by the professional labor required for complete delivery and long-term reproducibility.

If local manufacturing becomes a stable service, the evaluation focus will shift to personnel training, equipment maintenance, and raw material replenishment. Different regions can record the total time from initial assessment to available equipment, the number of days of downtime due to maintenance, and the resource input for each effective month of use. Such metrics can illustrate whether digital manufacturing has expanded access to continued rehabilitation services and help arrange the division of labor between centralized production and local adaptation.

In long-term follow-up, the reasons for discontinuation should also be structured and categorized. Task mismatch, difficulty in wearing, control fatigue, appearance preference, and maintenance needs correspond to different directions for improvement. Feeding these results back to specific design milestones will allow future research to gradually lead to product differentiation based on actual user choices, rather than judging value solely based on single laboratory results.

Research in this area has formed multiple executable chains, from individual input and structural design to task evaluation. Upper limb devices focus on residual abilities and grasping mechanisms, lower limb devices focus on staged mechanical responses, orthotics focus on support and independent operation, and maxillofacial restorations focus on appearance and tissue contact. Together, they drive individualization from size matching to designs with clear functional justifications.

The most noteworthy aspect to observe in the next phase is whether each chain can retain complete feedback: task failures return to the mechanism, gait changes return to stiffness, donning and doffing obstacles return to the fixation method, wearing discomfort return to the contact surface, and maintenance issues return to materials and services. By preserving these feedbacks as comparable versions, academic trials and enterprise deliverables can continuously improve around the same user goals.

P3-01.title: Personalized Oral Dosage Forms
P3-01.subtitle: Co-designing dose, release and use
P3-01.thesis: Personalized oral dosage forms align digital geometry, actual drug content and patient use. Geometry and multi-ingredient studies provide design capabilities, pediatric and rare-disease studies define practical constraints, and low-dose comparisons translate capabilities into measurable quality benefits.

questions.question: How can printed tablets achieve personalized doses?
questions.focus: Personalized dosing must match both the prescription and actual drug content. Tablet volume adjusts total quantity, but formulation uniformity, extrusion or sintering, drying and individual-tablet mass all affect the final dose.

questions.question: How do dosage-form shape and internal structure affect administration and release?
questions.focus: Tablet shape, size, porosity and internal cavities alter liquid pathways, diffusion distances and erosion, while affecting handling, swallowing and splitting. The same drug amount can have different structures, and similar appearances can conceal different release mechanisms.

questions.question: What do children and special populations need from personalized dosage forms?
questions.focus: Children may require dose adjustments with weight and disease status and may struggle with swallowing or bitter taste. Some patients need tube feeding, while others take several formulations long term; caregivers also perform preparation and record keeping.

questions.question: How can fast-dissolving oral films and new dosage forms support personalized administration?
questions.focus: Fast-dissolving oral films must be easy to handle, disperse rapidly and retain an accurate drug quantity. Locally adhesive films must remain at a specified site. Both are thin, but their intended uses differ.

questions.question: How can printed capsules and combination formulations support personalized treatment?
questions.focus: Combination formulations must accommodate several active ingredients while addressing dose ratios, compatibility and release. Required combinations may change with treatment, so customization extends beyond placing drugs in one shell.
