blocks.text: This research direction organizes evidence based on specific application tasks, placing formulation design, measurable quality, and actual usage conditions within the same research chain. Geometric adjustments provide design freedom, but each adjustment requires explanation of which physical processes it affects; the usage scenario determines which changes are valuable, and the original questions are addressed accordingly.
How can printed tablets achieve personalized doses?

Personalized dosing must match both the prescription and actual drug content. Tablet volume adjusts total quantity, but formulation uniformity, extrusion or sintering, drying and individual-tablet mass all affect the final dose.
Therefore, the problem has two aspects: how to manufacture multiple dosage strengths, and how to prove that each strength is stable, accurate, and suitable for administration.
How do dosage-form shape and internal structure affect administration and release?

Tablet shape, size, porosity and internal cavities alter liquid pathways, diffusion distances and erosion, while affecting handling, swallowing and splitting. The same drug amount can have different structures, and similar appearances can conceal different release mechanisms.
This question considers structure as part of the formulation's function, focusing on how it affects release and its connection to patient needs.
What do children and special populations need from personalized dosage forms?

Children may require dose adjustments with weight and disease status and may struggle with swallowing or bitter taste. Some patients need tube feeding, while others take several formulations long term; caregivers also perform preparation and record keeping.

Therefore, individualization requires simultaneous consideration of dosage, form, taste, route of administration, and care process. Different populations cannot be distinguished solely by age or tablet size.
How can fast-dissolving oral films and new dosage forms support personalized administration?

Fast-dissolving oral films must be easy to handle, disperse rapidly and retain an accurate drug quantity. Locally adhesive films must remain at a specified site. Both are thin, but their intended uses differ.

The printer allows for adjustable membrane area, thickness, number of layers, and composition distribution. Its practical value lies in adapting dosage or function as needed while maintaining stability in packaging, handling, and drug delivery processes.
How can printed capsules and combination formulations support personalized treatment?

Combination formulations must accommodate several active ingredients while addressing dose ratios, compatibility and release. Required combinations may change with treatment, so customization extends beyond placing drugs in one shell.

This issue includes printing multi-chamber, layered formulations, and printing capsules that synergize with liquid or granule dispensing. They reduce manufacturing limitations between ingredients in different ways.
N1 | Geometry couples dose and release (2015)

A 2015 study printed acetaminophen-containing polyvinyl alcohol filaments into five geometries and found that release correlated with surface-area-to-volume ratio. Dimensional changes can alter both dose and release, so personalized design must control both outcomes. [R01]

Comparing the geometry within the same material system allows for a better separation of compositional and shape changes. Surface area determines the initial interface with the liquid, while volume determines the total amount to be released; therefore, the ratio of the two is closer to the mass transfer task than considering area alone. This conclusion imposes a constraint on individualized dosing: scaling up the volume typically does not increase the interface proportionally, and changing the dosage may simultaneously alter the release rate.

The next step in the research needs to differentiate between external shape, internal structure, and material behavior. If the goal is similar release at different doses, it's advisable to maintain the critical mass transfer length or use a combination of multiple small units, and use measured curves to determine whether this is achieved. N2 and N3 offer two decoupling approaches for the shell and membrane area, respectively, while N9 returns to actual content verification, ultimately linking numerical dimensions to quality evidence.

Causal explanations in geometric studies require a distinction between initial surface area and dynamic surface area that changes with erosion. If the difference in the curves occurs later, the initial shape index may only be a surrogate variable; a time-series characterization of structural evolution can verify whether the model truly captures the controlling process.
N2 | Capsule shells and liquid dispensing (2018)

A 2018 study combined FDM printing of polymer shells with liquid dispensing to load theophylline solution or dipyridamole suspension. Shell material and thickness affected release, while dispensed volume determined drug loading, enabling separate optimization of thermally processed structures and liquid-drug handling. [R02]

Separating shell fabrication from liquid filling allows processing conditions and functions to be optimized for different materials. The shell controls liquid retention and diffusion paths, the dispenser controls the quantity of contents, and their junction provides sealing. Assessing both fill quantity and shell structure shows that personalization need not subject every ingredient to the same thermal or mechanical history.

This modularity raises two new questions: whether the liquid alters the shell properties over time, and whether different filling states change the release. Therefore, validation needs to cover the interaction of fill level, seal integrity, and shelf life, rather than relying solely on fill volume linearity to determine the equivalence of the entire product. N4's hierarchical system further demonstrates that the digital spatial boundaries must also be examined in conjunction with the actual drug distribution.

The capsule system allows for the observation of the independent effect of fill weight on release using controls with different fill levels but identical shells. Conversely, changing the shell while maintaining the fill weight allows for the identification of barrier contributions. This two-way comparison quantifies the advantages of modular manufacturing, rather than remaining solely at the device configuration level.
N3 | Film area linked to drug content (2019)

The 2019 warfarin membrane study used semi-solid extrusion to produce flexible oral membranes with adjustable drug content. The designed dimensions showed a good linear relationship with drug content, making membrane area a dose-adjusting variable. For low-dose formulations, it is crucial to validate this relationship in conjunction with uniform distribution and actual dimensions. [R03]

The oral membrane simplifies a three-dimensional dosage form into a thinner plane, making area a design quantity that is easily adjustable. For changes in area to correspond to changes in dosage, both thickness and drug distribution per unit area must be stable; if different deposition or drying behaviors exist at the membrane edge and center, the overall linear relationship may still mask local inhomogeneities. Therefore, this method selection offers advantages in both manufacturability and testability.

The application tasks of film also include integrity after peeling, handling, and wetting. Thinning facilitates dispersion but may increase operational breakage; increasing the area, while increasing content, may also alter the user experience in the oral cavity. Patient preference studies of N6 provide design feedback suggesting that dosage, strength, and size need to all fall within an acceptable product range, rather than pursuing an extreme value for any one of them.

The area-content relationship requires reporting the prediction interval as well. A high correlation coefficient indicates a consistent trend, but does not directly suggest that the absolute error of each small membrane is sufficiently low; especially in low-drug-loaded units, the proportion of edge loss increases, and both ends of the dose range should be included in independent testing.
N4 | Layering does not ensure ingredient isolation (2019)

In 2019, a six-component photopolymerization study fabricated a multilayer structure, and Raman microscopy was used to examine the distribution. Although independent printed layers were formed, some drugs still diffused across layers, and the differences were related to the drug state. This indicates that the layering in CAD must be confirmed through actual component distribution. [R04]

The choice of Raman microscopy is crucial: ordinary photographs prove the appearance of layers, but cannot prove that each drug remains at the target location. Composition maps link spatial design with chemical distribution, revealing how amorphous or crystalline states and material compatibility can affect migration. Therefore, the focus of research on multi-component formulations shifts from the number of chambers to the actual boundaries of components during manufacturing and storage.

If interlayer migration changes local concentrations, neighboring materials can also influence each ingredient’s release, so simple addition of single-drug results may fail. Comparing single layers, adjacent bilayers and complete combinations can locate interactions at contact interfaces or whole-structure wetting. This converges with patient combination needs in N7: reducing administration frequency requires interpretable, reproducible multi-ingredient quality.

The validation of multi-drug combinations should also consider the selectivity of the detection. Total content or a single spectral peak cannot identify all components; spatial analysis and component-by-component quantification each have their own tasks. Both types of evidence together form the basis for judging the interlayer isolation and the correctness of the combination.
N5 | Validating sustained use in rare disease (2019)

A 2019 isoleucine chewable-formulation study used a single-center prospective crossover design to examine personalized compounding and acceptability in patients with maple syrup urine disease. Evaluation moved from formulation specimens to patients requiring ongoing treatment adjustment, bringing dose, taste and administration together. [R05]

The study uses patients as a comparative context between different formulations, establishing a practical link between continuous dosage needs and manufacturing capabilities. The significance of chewable dosage forms lies not only in changing appearance, but also in changing the patient's action of completing a single dose. Clinical monitoring, taste feedback, and prescription records need to be analyzed in parallel to identify whether observed differences stem from formulation quality, usage behavior, or concurrent disease management.

This small-scale study sets the stage for a reasonable task of further expansion: testing more ingredients, more preferences, and long-term reusability. N7 extends this to six children and a combination amino acid formulation; N9 examines the accuracy of low-dose units at the pharmacy level. The two lines of investigation, one focusing on willingness to use and the other on accurate availability, will ultimately converge in a comprehensive evaluation of the personalized oral product.

The crossover order and time effect in the patient study are also worth observing. Familiarity with the new dosage form may improve later acceptance, and changes in growth and routine management may also alter monitoring indicators; continuous recording can help interpret these factors and provide a basis for designing more targeted comparisons later.
N6 | Children’s preferences alter design constraints (2020)

The 2020 Children's Visual Survey examined the appearance preferences of different printed tablets. It incorporates shape, color, and recognizability into formulation development, but visual preference alone cannot answer questions about actual swallowing or long-term acceptability. [R06]

This survey compares similar sizes and shapes manufactured using different processes to minimize interference from macroscopic geometric differences. Informing children that the formulation is chewable alters their preferences, indicating that children's choices are influenced by both visual perception and expectations of the method of administration. Design decisions that prioritize surface smoothness may overlook usability attributes that make the formulation more acceptable. [R06]

Therefore, preference studies should be designed separately for visual selection, actual user experience, and continuous use. These are at different stages of the behavioral chain and cannot be substituted for one another. For N1 and N3, patient feedback provides the boundaries for shape and size; for N7, it provides the basis for choosing flavor and combination. Future research questions include whether these choices are stable after repeated use and whether caregiver and child evaluations are consistent.

Child studies can further analyze tasks by developmental stage, rather than just by age group. The ability to independently grasp, understand labels, and complete swallowing are different skills; which skill a product needs to be adapted to should be defined in advance. This will change the way acceptance questions are asked and the actual evaluation process.
N7 | Combining multiple ingredients with patient feedback (2024)

The 2024 study developed different amino acid chewable formulations, including two-component combinations, for six children with rare metabolic diseases in a hospital and collected feedback on taste and usage. Target amino acid levels were maintained, and the combination formulations reduced the frequency of administration. Individualization moved from single-dose adjustments to combined adjustments of ingredients, taste, and dosing burden. [R07]

The study expanded from a single manufacturing specification to a portfolio of products catering to multiple patient needs, with ingredient and flavor adjustments incorporated into the actual hospital medication dispensing process. The introduction of mobile phone feedback increased the observation time dimension, allowing receptiveness to go beyond a single interview. Fewer dosing sessions logically reduce preparation steps, but sustained adherence still requires linking feedback to actual usage records.

The benefits and adjustment costs of the combination are intertwined. Whether the entire combination must be remanufactured when one component needs to be changed, whether the release of other components can be maintained, and how to identify different strengths all affect long-term usability. N4 indicates the need to track component distribution, and N9 indicates the need to examine unit content; only by considering both factors and patient burden can it be determined which combination is worth continuing development.

Combination formulations may reduce the identification burden, but they may also increase the complexity of component adjustments. Studies should record the frequency of prescription changes and the number of units replaced to determine whether reducing one administration action is worthwhile by adding an overall preparation task.
N8 | Alternative administration routes redefine disintegration (2024)

An efavirenz study in the same year used laser sintering to prepare porous dispersible tablets for children requiring enteral feeding tubes. Polymer and loading conditions affected dispersion. This development shows that tube-feeding design must consider dispersion volume, residues and blockage risk, beyond simply producing a tablet. [R08]

The tube feeding scenario further refines the concept of "disintegration" into the ability to form a transferable system within a limited liquid and practical apparatus. Porous structures facilitate liquid entry, but matrix dissolution is also constrained by solvent capacity; increasing the polymer content may hinder complete dispersion under certain conditions. The differences observed in this study therefore indicate that porosity and hydrophilicity need to be considered in conjunction with environmental assessments.

Subsequent designs should independently assess device residues, drug-content recovery after dispersion and passage through the device to identify losses in containers or tubing. The task is to establish product tests consistent with intended use. This returns to N1: when the end-use task changes, appropriate geometric metrics also change, and ordinary dissolution tests cannot be extrapolated directly.

Losses in specific pathways are location-dependent. Residues in containers, interfaces, and pipelines reflect different mechanisms; segmented recovery analysis helps distinguish between adsorption, sedimentation, and mechanical retardation, and provides specific feedback for material selection and shape optimization.
N9 | Low-dose comparisons test benefits (2026)

A 2026 metoprolol study compared low-dose units obtained by manual halving, manual quartering and automated printing. Printed formulations met the relevant content-uniformity requirements at two hospital pharmacies and one compounding pharmacy, while manually split units varied more. The study addressed dose quality and established direct comparison with current practice. [R09]

This comparison shifts the value of individualization from design freedom to actual dose error distribution. Manual fracturing relies on fracture behavior, while printing relies on material homogeneity and deposition control; the error mechanisms of the two differ. Using the same content detection framework can identify which mechanism produces greater fluctuations under low-dose conditions and provide a basis for selecting suitable printing tasks.

The next step should be to compare quality benefits with preservation, patient identification, and delivery time in the same way. Personalization can only be transformed from a single-sample service to a repeatable service if stability across different pharmacies is supported by continuous data. This node provides feedback on N1 and N7: the digital dosage range should be defined by validated quality and usage; exceeding this range requires new product studies.

For multi-site comparisons, intra-site and inter-site variability should be estimated separately. The same average content does not necessarily mean that all sites are stable; stratified data by batch, date, and operator can reveal the sources of error that most need to be controlled when scaling up individualized manufacturing.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: How can printed tablets achieve personalized doses?

Aprecia announced the launch of SPRITAM in 2016, using rapidly disintegrating structures formed by powder bonding for industrial pharmaceuticals. It demonstrates that printed formulations can become finished products, but its value lies primarily in dosage form and manufacturing, rather than in the ability for pharmacies to arbitrarily adjust dosages. [R10]

CurifyLabs' dispensing platform and 2026 metoprolol study enable the direct integration of enterprise equipment into small-dose preparation scenarios in hospitals and pharmacies. FABRX offers various printheads, weighing and spectral attachments to support formulation and batch adjustments. [R09] [R11]

The enterprise roadmap has expanded from printing equipment to a combination of prescription execution, formulation, manufacturing, and testing tools. The competitive focus in small-batch, individualized production is shifting towards accurate delivery, not just speed of production.
How do dosage-form shape and internal structure affect administration and release?

Aprecia's SPRITAM combines a porous, rapidly disintegrating structure with high drug loading to create an easily dispersible, industrially viable product. The geometric value chosen by the company is very specific: improved formulation disintegration and administration. [R10]

The FABRX platform supports different printing processes and multiple printheads, providing structural adjustment capabilities for research and small-batch manufacturing. Its quality-control accessories allows for the integration of single-piece weighing and process information into manufacturing. [R11]

These represent different commercial endpoints: one fixes a particular structure into a stable product, while the other provides tools to change structures. Academic principles become reproducible in both settings when incorporated into formulation, process and testing requirements.
What do children and special populations need from personalized dosage forms?

The FABRX equipment and formulation development work has entered into hospital-based individualized research, and its platform supports different extrusion processes, multiple printheads, and quality accessories. This corresponds to the pharmaceutical team's ability to select and execute specific formulation protocols. [R11]

For enterprises, the product value of extends beyond a single printer to include available dosage forms, formulation tools, and consistent workflows. For specific populations, the most meaningful product metrics include applicable dosage range, actual route of administration, and pharmacy processing time.
How can fast-dissolving oral films and new dosage forms support personalized administration?

These enterprise capabilities correspond to formulation and process inspection in the academic chain. For oral films, the real determinants of application also include drying, peeling, single-sheet processing, and packaging, not just the printing path.

If companies can organize the area-dosage relationship, drying conditions, and testing methods of a specific formulation into an executable protocol, they can reduce the workload of developing each item individually. Different drugs still require corresponding formulation validation.
How can printed capsules and combination formulations support personalized treatment?

The expansion of enterprise capabilities is reflected beyond printing: ingredient allocation, process switching, batch recording, and quality inspection together determine whether compound preparations can be remanufactured.

The focus of productization has therefore shifted from "how many drugs can be printed" to "which combinations can be stably executed." Different formulation combinations require corresponding formulation compatibility, content, and release validation.
How can printed tablets achieve personalized doses?

The most direct point of intersection is replacing operations prone to variation. Comparing printing with tablet splitting, powder weighing, or manual filling in the same scenario allows for a clearer understanding of the value brought by the equipment.
How do dosage-form shape and internal structure affect administration and release?
What industry needs is not the most shapes, but a small number of explainable, manufacturable, and patient-friendly designs. Academic research can help converge structural choices into clear rules.
What do children and special populations need from personalized dosage forms?

The real connection is turning patient needs into manufacturing inputs. Research reveals needs and outcomes, businesses provide implementation tools, and healthcare teams complete prescriptions and individual choices.
How can fast-dissolving oral films and new dosage forms support personalized administration?

The cross-value of lies primarily in combining adjustability with quality control. The more flexible the film, the more crucial it is to clearly document every area, formulation, and process modification.
How can printed capsules and combination formulations support personalized treatment?

The clearest approach is to work backward from clinical needs to develop a manufacturing plan, and then evaluate it in conjunction with the quality of each component and patient burden. The complex structure itself is not the final result.
How can printed tablets achieve personalized doses?

The academic focus has shifted from "how many specifications can be produced" to "whether the quality of each specification is maintained." Low-dose treatments requiring gradual adjustments have become clear application scenarios, as these scenarios are most likely to expose the burden of manual tablet splitting or combination.

Research maturity also exhibits stratification: geometric and formulation studies explain manufacturing patterns, comparative formulation studies examine content quality, and patient studies further evaluate acceptability and the usage process. These strata collectively support individualization, but the results they provide differ.
How do dosage-form shape and internal structure affect administration and release?

The academic shift involves moving from comparing external shapes to internal structure and predictive design, and then incorporating user acceptability as a constraint. Geometry is no longer just about free form, but rather a variable that, along with the formulation, determines performance.

For the development process, the most valuable advancement is the identification of transferable patterns: which release changes are explained by the surface area-to-volume ratio, and which require consideration of porosity, material properties, and erosion. This reduces redundant testing and clarifies the applicability of each model.
What do children and special populations need from personalized dosage forms?

The study evolved from "whether children like printed medications" to "how to reliably administer appropriate doses during specific treatments." Actual swallowing, metabolic control of rare diseases, dosing frequency, and tube feeding dispersion became different research pathways.

This change clarifies the boundaries of personalization: the same platform can serve multiple scenarios, but each scenario requires corresponding formulations, dosage forms, and evaluation methods. The success criteria for chewable formulations, dispersible tablets, and regular tablets are not the same.
How can fast-dissolving oral films and new dosage forms support personalized administration?

The academic link moves from geometric tuning to material states, multilayer structures, and local delivery. Meanwhile, spectroscopic and visual methods enable faster quality checks for small-batch film preparations.

The focus of this research direction is shifting from "printing a film" to "defining what function the film should perform." Dosage adjustment, rapid dispersion, treatment of poorly soluble drugs, and local mucosal action can be combined, but the corresponding indicators need to be validated separately.
How can printed capsules and combination formulations support personalized treatment?

The research has shifted from manufacturing multiple components to individually controlling the spatial location, physical state, and release of each component. Subsequently, hospital supply and patient use incorporate these combined regimens into specific treatment procedures.

A noteworthy change is its hybrid manufacturing process: shell printing, semi-solid deposition, and particle distribution can work synergistically. Choosing appropriate processes for each component is often closer to actual pharmaceutical needs than forcing all components to use the same process.

In 2027, continuous quality and acceptability within a limited dose range should be observed; in 2028, the key is the reproducibility of the same regimen in different hospitals and pharmacies; in 2029, if the quality, preservation performance, and patient feedback of multiple specifications can be updated in a coordinated manner, personalized oral formulations can form a transferable product family. These stages depend on the accumulation of evidence, not the number of devices installed.
How can printed tablets achieve personalized doses?
Near term: Low-dose and prescriptions requiring multiple adjustments will be prioritized for application. The quality benefits and workload in these scenarios are easier to quantify.
Mid-term: Dosage ranges may be available in a proven combination of formulations and models. Healthcare institutions choose feasible protocols, not just arbitrary numbers.

Observation indicators: single tablet content, uniformity, release of different specifications, batch changeover time, rework rate and prescription error; patient acceptance and continuous use should also be recorded.
How do dosage-form shape and internal structure affect administration and release?

Near term: Structural design will be developed concurrently with quality control. Modifications to pores, wall thickness, or cavities will more clearly correspond to release, strength, and single-piece quality checks.

Mid-term: Target release and dosage requirements may jointly drive model selection. Children, those with swallowing difficulties, and populations requiring combination doses will impose different design constraints.
Observation indicators: release prediction error, actual porosity and size deviation, transportation damage, disintegration time, swallowing success rate and continuous use experience.
What do children and special populations need from personalized dosage forms?

Near term: Formulations with clearly defined target populations and routes of administration will be prioritized for development. For example, low-dose, chewable, or tube feeding regimens can establish clear quality and usage indicators.
Mid-term: Patient and caregiver feedback may lead to formulation selection. Taste, preparation time, and frequency of administration will influence regimen adjustments along with dosage.

Observation indicators: actual successful administration, refusal and missed administration, preparation time, dose recovery, tube feeding passability, and clinical indicators corresponding to the treatment.
How can fast-dissolving oral films and new dosage forms support personalized administration?
Near term: Dosage customization and rapid testing will be prioritized. Low-dose films are suitable for studying tablet-by-tablet quality and formulation correspondence.

Mid-term: A common substrate and subsequent drug delivery may be modularly manufactured. If the substrate performance is stable, the drug deposition process can be adjusted for different formulations.
Observation indicators: content uniformity, drying and packaging time, mechanical integrity, humidity stability, disintegration or adhesion time, and drug recovery and acceptability in actual use.
How can printed capsules and combination formulations support personalized treatment?

Near term: hybrid manufacturing for defined prescription combinations has room to advance. Suitable dosage forms or particles can be retained for each ingredient, with automated dispensing creating personalized combinations.

Mid-term: Validated combination modules may support more flexible formulation configurations. The key is that when one component is adjusted, other components still maintain their established quality and release.
Observation indicators: content of each component, translayer migration, release independence, switching and cleaning time, storage stability, dosing frequency and actual patient acceptance.

P3-02.title: Drug Release Control
P3-02.subtitle: From geometric adjustment to mechanism-constrained release design
P3-02.thesis: Printed release control requires distinguishing the roles of geometry, drug solid state, material responses and actual exposure conditions. Different mechanisms can produce the same curve; combining structural characterization, independent controls and validation across conditions is necessary for reusable digitally designed release strategies.

questions.question: How can materials and structures enable sustained and controlled release?
questions.focus: Sustained release prolongs release; controlled release also adjusts rate, onset or stages. Printing offers geometric freedom, while water uptake, dissolution, diffusion and structural changes jointly govern release.

questions.question: How can dissolution and immediate release of poorly soluble drugs be improved?
questions.focus: Poorly soluble drugs need improved dissolution; immediate release requires rapid release from the dosage form. Tablet disintegration, drug dissolution and eventual absorption are connected but distinct steps.

questions.question: How can multidrug and layered structures provide staged release?
questions.focus: Staged release includes different ingredients released at different rates, repeated release of one ingredient, or sequential onset of different drugs. Compartments separate space; timing also depends on barrier dissolution, liquid entry and drug-loaded materials.

questions.question: How can gastrointestinal targeting or stimulus responses control release location?
questions.focus: Gastric retention keeps a dosage form in the stomach, whereas intestinal targeting avoids premature release and delivers in a specific segment. Buoyancy, shape change, time barriers and pH responses act through different mechanisms.

blocks.text: This research direction organizes evidence based on specific application tasks, placing formulation design, measurable quality, and actual usage conditions within the same research chain. Geometric adjustments provide design freedom, but each adjustment requires explanation of which physical processes it affects; the usage scenario determines which changes are valuable, and the original questions are addressed accordingly.
How can materials and structures enable sustained and controlled release?

Sustained release prolongs release; controlled release also adjusts rate, onset or stages. Printing offers geometric freedom, while water uptake, dissolution, diffusion and structural changes jointly govern release.
This question focuses on how design variables affect the release mechanism, and which research stages need to be connected when entering product development from the in vitro curve.
How can dissolution and immediate release of poorly soluble drugs be improved?

Poorly soluble drugs need improved dissolution; immediate release requires rapid release from the dosage form. Tablet disintegration, drug dissolution and eventual absorption are connected but distinct steps.
This question focuses on how materials and structure work together to improve release, and how these studies can be incorporated into formulation platforms and actual products.
How can multidrug and layered structures provide staged release?

Staged release includes different ingredients released at different rates, repeated release of one ingredient, or sequential onset of different drugs. Compartments separate space; timing also depends on barrier dissolution, liquid entry and drug-loaded materials.
This problem focuses on analyzing how spatial structure becomes temporal arrangement, and gradually connects in vitro release with in vivo absorption.
How can gastrointestinal targeting or stimulus responses control release location?

Gastric retention keeps a dosage form in the stomach, whereas intestinal targeting avoids premature release and delivers in a specific segment. Buoyancy, shape change, time barriers and pH responses act through different mechanisms.

The positioning of also needs to be combined needs of the drug itself: some drugs require local action, and some active ingredients need to be protected before passing through the gastrointestinal environment. The design needs to specify the location, time, and drug state simultaneously.
N1 | Incorporating geometry into release equations (2015)

A 2015 study of drug-containing tablets of different shapes showed that the surface area to volume ratio could explain the release differences in the studied systems. Geometry therefore became a design variable beyond formulation. [R01]

This method holds material composition constant while changing shape, allowing the independent explanatory value of geometry to be tested. Surface area represents the liquid-contact interface and volume the total quantity to be released, so their ratio provides an initial scale measure. Boundaries move during release, however, and initial geometry cannot replace observations of water uptake and erosion. The node establishes a testable structural hypothesis whose material-specific validity must then be examined.

N2 examines dynamic porosity, and N3 tests whether correlation can lead to prediction. The two branches respectively add mechanism explanation and design applications. More informative comparisons should include samples with the same surface area to volume ratio but different shapes: if the release still differs, curvature, path connectivity, and local mass transfer need to be incorporated into the model.

This approach of controlling variables can also prevent the misconception that smaller tablets release faster because a certain shape is inherently superior. When designing comparisons, it's essential to first define the objective: is it to accelerate early release, prolong overall release, or maintain the curve during dose changes? Different objectives can yield opposing evaluations of the same geometric change.
N2 | Dynamic porosity and matrix changes (2021)

A 2021 study used swellable, erodible polymers to fabricate different porous structures by hot-melt droplet deposition. Porosity was examined in a dynamic material environment: the initially printed structure absorbed water and changed during drug release. [R02]

Printed pores are not static liquid channels. Water absorption can expand the polymer volume and compress the pores, while erosion can open new interfaces; therefore, there is no universal one-to-one correspondence between initial porosity and effective mass transfer area. Choosing swellable and erosive materials allows for proactive testing of the coupling between structure and material response, rather than simply comparing the appearance of dry tablets.

Compared to N1, this study requires incorporating time into the structural description. Subsequently, mass loss, dimensional changes, and release can be recorded simultaneously to determine when diffusion or erosion is dominant. If the geometric predictions of N3 differ across different materials, the reasons should be sought within these processes, and features should be reselected rather than simply increasing regression complexity.

Drug release profiles can be similar but controlled by different mechanisms, and this similarity may disappear after storage or changes in the medium. Therefore, priority should be given to studying perturbations that can distinguish mechanisms, such as changes in medium conditions and structural scale, and observing whether the model parameters remain consistent.
N3 | From correlations to unseen geometries (2021)

The release prediction study of the same year used surface area to volume ratio to organize experimental data and establish a design-release correlation for specified drugs and formulations. The purpose of the prediction is to screen structures that may meet the target, which are then confirmed experimentally. [R03]

The study used previously unprinted geometry for validation, separating the fitting from the prediction. The average dissolution time compresses the curve information, while the complete curve equation preserves the differences between early and late stages; both scales jointly examine whether the geometric features support the design. The juxtaposition of soluble and inert matrices allows for comparison of the applicability of geometric relationships based on the release mechanism. [R03]

The design inversion requires more than just optimal prediction; it also necessitates an acceptable margin of error. Multiple geometric possibilities correspond to approximate release curves, making manufacturing strength, swallowability, and dosage additional conditions for solution selection. This node, combined with the multi-specification instantaneous release of N9, transforms the model from interpreting existing samples to screening candidate products.

The next key validation units are new material batches and new dosage ranges. Successful interpolation within similar shapes alone does not necessarily indicate predictability after scaling down to micro-units or changing drug loading conditions; stratified external validation can clarify at which level the model should be recalibrated.
N4 | Measuring porosity and drug solid state together (2021)

A 2021 lumefantrine study combined water-soluble ingredients with lattice structures. Lower-infill designs achieved rapid release, while higher infill slowed release; micro-CT and Raman analysis linked accessible porosity and drug state to dissolution. [R04]

The release of poorly soluble drugs is influenced by both the openness of the matrix and the drug's own dissolution behavior. Micro-CT observes internal pathways, Raman spectroscopy provides information on drug distribution or state, and dissolution reveals the final outcome; these three types of measurements correspond to different stages, helping to distinguish between "water not being able to enter" and "drug not being able to dissolve." Changing only the filling rate without observing the solid state will incorrectly attribute changes caused by thermal history to porosity.

Therefore, subsequent studies should construct controls with similar structures but different solid states, and similar solid states but different structures. If low filling improves early release but is still limited by dissolution in the later stages, the benefits of simply continuing to increase porosity may be limited. N9's shift to multi-specification and excipient co-design is precisely to put pore research back into the overall formulation task.

Rapid disintegration and rapid dissolution also need to be measured separately. Large particles formed after tablet breakage may still dissolve slowly, especially under incomplete dissolution conditions; this dictates that experiments should report particle formation and eventual dissolution, rather than just the disappearance time.
N5 | Actual chemical boundaries in multilayers (2019)

In a 2019 study of a six-component photocurable compound, Raman microscopy was used to observe the distribution of the drug, revealing that some drugs diffused across layers. The printed independent layers do not automatically form independent drug regions; the material and drug states require joint verification. [R05]

Placing drugs in separate layers is intended to assign distinct release tasks to different materials, but interlayer migration can change that division. Spatial Raman analysis makes digital boundaries observable as chemical distributions, showing that material compatibility and drug state also control structural function. For staged release, both initial positions and positions after storage affect which ingredient contacts liquid first.

The hybrid molding of N8 further materializes the division of labor among different materials. The key issue between the two is maintaining boundaries and ensuring predictable interface behavior, rather than simply increasing the number of layers. Research should compare single-component modules, bi-module contacts, and complete multilayer formulations to identify whether changes in release originate from interfacial migration, overall barriers, or differences in component solubility.

The release curves of each component need to be quantified independently. Even if the total release mass meets the target, it may still mask the offsetting effect of premature release of one component against delayed release of another; the criteria for multi-component systems must be consistent with their respective design objectives.
N6 | Testing enzyme activity and targeting separately (2022)

2022 Alkaline phosphatase research used powder bed printing to print enzyme-containing preparations, employing an intermediate layer and colon-targeting coating. The study examined enzyme activity and simulated gastrointestinal release, ensuring that "activity remained" and "released in the target environment" were integrated into the same validation chain. [R06]

Biomacromolecules add an independent endpoint to release studies: whether the substance remains active upon reaching the medium. Content analysis, enzyme activity assays, and release labeling each answer different questions; none can be used to deduce the whole picture. Studying the formation, coating, and storage as separate observation stages helps pinpoint at which stage activity loss or barrier failure occurs.

This node contrasts with N7: both external coating and dual-material printing attempt to provide an environmental response barrier, but their structural interfaces and defect sources differ. The next step should be to compare pre-response leakage, post-trigger release integrity, and activity recovery to further evaluate which manufacturing organization is more suitable for small-batch variations.

The simulated gastrointestinal system supports a localized release task within a specified environmental sequence. The actual location is also related to transport time, local environment, and pathological state. Studies require linking controllable variables (in vitro) with observable locations (in vivo) to explain inter-individual differences.
N7 | Organizing responsive layers from two materials (2023)

The 2023 dual-nozzle study evaluated the feasibility of colon-oriented delivery using a combination of an HPMCAS outer layer and a PVA internal structure containing 5-aminosalicylic acid. The acid-base responsive layer and drug-containing zone, through printing, reduced the limitations of relying solely on homogeneous formulation designs. [R07]

The dual-nozzle selection allows the barrier and drug delivery zones to use polymers suitable for their respective tasks. External environmental responses alter the degree of pathway opening, while internal structure determines dissolution area and drug diffusion; openings allow for release even in the early stages. Therefore, "colon localization" should be broken down into two aspects: pre-leakage and post-acceleration, rather than a simple binary label.

Compared to the coating method used in N6, the overall printing of increases geometric freedom but introduces problems such as interface adhesion, pinholes, and machining accuracy. Microscopic and tomographic imaging were used to confirm the actual structure before interpreting release differences. The next step in the research should be to incorporate manufacturing deviations into the release model to determine which dimensional errors truly alter the target curve.

Environmental response experiments need to consider changes near the threshold; it's not advisable to select only two conditions with significant differences. Observing the response transition region and its repeatability can estimate the product's sensitivity to physiological fluctuations and provide a basis for robustness across different patient conditions.
N8 | Dividing tasks between printing and injection molding (2024)

2024 bilayer tablet research combines droplet deposition and injection molding to address the rheological and structural requirements of different formulations. The printed portion allows for adjustable porosity, while the overmolded portion forms a denser structure. The combination of these two methods broadens the range of manufacturable formulations and release combinations. [R08]

Combining two forming methods means materials need not suit every manufacturing process. A high-viscosity formulation may be unsuitable for one deposition method yet work in overmolding. Process selection can therefore follow product function rather than allowing one machine to constrain the entire design. Comparing release from porous and dense structures connects manufacturability with performance targets.

A new challenge in hybrid manufacturing of lies at the interface: the two layers have different thermal histories, shrinkage, and wetting behaviors, potentially leading to separation during storage or release. Future research should examine the interface strength in conjunction with single-component release, and use cross-sectional structure analysis to determine whether curve changes originate from delamination or alterations in the diffusion barrier. This node feeds back the manufacturing boundary to N9, aiding in the selection of a scheme capable of stably covering multiple specifications.

Economic considerations also need to be evaluated within the product family framework. Disposable molds and variable printing sections may be suitable for tasks involving repeated changes to local structures, while frequent changes to the entire formulation increase cleaning and validation costs; scientific design and drug delivery organization should jointly determine module division.
N9 | Maintaining immediate release across strengths (2024)

In 2024, the cabozantinib study combined water-soluble polymers, excipients, and geometric design to investigate rheology and establish a calculation method for the required dimensions at different dosages. It advances the problem from the rapid release of a single sample to whether a single formulation can cover multiple strengths. [R09]

This study transforms immediate release from a single-sample attribute to a requirement met by multiple specifications. Dimensional calculations address the geometry corresponding to the target drug dosage, rheological and excipient studies determine whether a stable structure can be formed, and dissolution tests whether the target is retained after dimensional changes. These three factors are interdependent; dose linearity cannot replace release consistency.

N1 to N8 provide design variables such as geometry, dynamic porosity, solid state, interface, and environmental response; N9 consolidates these into a constrained product selection. Subsequent validation of the minimum, maximum, and intermediate specifications is recommended to identify which variable dominates with dimensional variations, and the saved performance should be incorporated into the same judgment.

The final design space should be expressed as conditional relationships: given the material state and manufacturable structure, which dosages maintain the target release, and which changes need to be re-examined. This is how the predictive model is connected to product development, creating a feedback loop from requirements to experimentation and back to digital design.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: How can materials and structures enable sustained and controlled release?

AnelleO uses printing to develop long-acting vaginal rings. Its ANLO102 page targets approximately 28 days of progesterone release and lists studies intended to support subsequent regulatory submissions. The development task combines release duration, local use and device integrity in one program. [R11]

The two approaches target long-term local use and gastrointestinal positioning, respectively, showing that the industrial application of structure-controlled release depends on the clinical setting. Development objectives and completed validation should be shown separately on the timeline.
How can dissolution and immediate release of poorly soluble drugs be improved?

Aprecia's SPRITAM utilizes a porous rapid-disintegration structure to improve dispersion and administration, demonstrating that specific dosage form characteristics can become a core value of industrial products. [R10]

The shared mission of enterprises and academia is to ensure the reproducibility of formulation performance. The maturity of rapidly disintegrating products does not automatically mean that the dissolution problem of any poorly soluble drug has been solved; each active ingredient still has corresponding material and stability requirements.
How can multidrug and layered structures provide staged release?

These enterprise capabilities provide tools for ingredient allocation and batch execution. OPERA's manufacturing tasks primarily focus on composition preparation and quality, while phased release studies further require independent validation of timing controls.

The key to advancing the industry is to incorporate module assembly, formula switching, and the quality of each component into a unified record system. The ability to identify whether other modules maintain their intended release after a change in a module is fundamental to configuration flexibility.
How can gastrointestinal targeting or stimulus responses control release location?

This corporate roadmap connects structural design to specific development projects and human evaluations. The timeline should distinguish between platform construction, research licensing, positioning results, and subsequent efficacy studies, with each node representing a different stage of work.

Academic research can provide material-response and structural mechanisms for this development, while companies’ in vivo localization results help select in vitro evaluations closer to intended-use conditions.
How can materials and structures enable sustained and controlled release?

The main thread of the cross-analysis is from structure to behavior (in vivo). A company's development milestones can help academic research clarify the next validation step, while research models can explain why a product requires specific materials and structures.
How can dissolution and immediate release of poorly soluble drugs be improved?

The link between research and product should be established along clear performance objectives: whether it's improving dispersion, dissolution, or covering multiple dosages. Only after the objectives are clearly defined can the actual contributions of different processes be compared.
How can multidrug and layered structures provide staged release?

The cross-functional value of lies in transforming complex prescriptions into verifiable modular relationships. Enterprise platforms can implement configuration, while academic research needs to explain why each module produces its corresponding temporal behavior.
How can gastrointestinal targeting or stimulus responses control release location?

The cross-analysis should proceed along the path of material mechanism—structural behavior—in vivo location—effect. This approach not only explains the technical connections but also clarifies what each study needs to answer next.
How can materials and structures enable sustained and controlled release?

Academic development has shifted from comparing single variables to a synergistic approach involving structure and materials. Researchers have begun to differentiate between drug-loading regions, control layers, and supporting structures, assigning each component a more clearly defined task.

Another change is the integration of prediction and modularity. The former reduces the workload of structural screening, while the latter allows for changes in load and release configurations on the same shell or manufacturing platform. Both paths require stable material parameters and actual structural measurements as a foundation.
How can dissolution and immediate release of poorly soluble drugs be improved?

The research has evolved from examining whether excipients can be printed to jointly characterizing drug state, internal structure, and release. Non-destructive structural measurements and spectroscopic analysis make the relationship between design and actual formulation easier to interpret.

The development of multi-dose formulations further raises the bar: maintaining target release even after altering volume, porosity, or drug loading. Academic innovation therefore focuses more on the combination of materials, processes, and geometries, rather than simply finding a new printing method.
How can multidrug and layered structures provide staged release?

The research focus has shifted from increasing the number of layers to making drug loading, support, and time control relatively independent. Hybrid manufacturing and modular combination are clear development paths, as different components and structures are not always suitable for the same process.

The evaluation of also shifted from the appearance of the release curve to component distribution, barrier size, and pharmacokinetics of in vivo. The ability to predict initiation time and its fluctuations is closer to product development needs than obtaining a single ideal phased curve.
How can gastrointestinal targeting or stimulus responses control release location?

Research has evolved from simply selecting acid-base sensitive materials to multi-material structures, activity protection, and hybrid manufacturing. Research on gastric retention and intestinal localization is progressing in parallel, but they require different in vivo evaluation methods.

The key transition is from in vitro triggering to observation of in vivo location and absorption. Simulated media support structural comparisons, while imaging and pharmacokinetics establish whether structures undergo the intended gastrointestinal sequence.
How can materials and structures enable sustained and controlled release?

Near term: Measurable control layers and module structures will receive more attention. Compared to complex shapes, film thickness, porosity, and connection quality are more likely to establish a stable relationship with release.

Medium term: in vitro–in vivo relationships will determine whether platforms can expand. Development efficiency will improve sustainably only if the same structural rules are validated repeatedly across doses and use settings.

Observation indicators: release curve variation, structural deviation, post-storage performance, in vivo duration of action, and whether the intended release characteristics can be retained after changing the dosage.
How can dissolution and immediate release of poorly soluble drugs be improved?

Near term: Structural measurements and solid-state analysis will be more frequently used to explain release. Reporting only nominal fill factor is insufficient to explain actual porosity and drug distribution.

Mid-term: Multi-specification platforms will prioritize performance retention after storage and media changes. Achieving a single dissolution target requires printing, followed by demonstrating continued repeatability.

Observation indicators: drug crystallization, dissolution and its variation, actual porosity, storage stability, release consistency between different specifications, and related pharmacokinetic results.
How can multidrug and layered structures provide staged release?
Near term: The combination of printed shells and existing drug units will continue to evolve. This approach allows for the separation of structural design and drug preparation studies.

Mid-term: The core metric for time-series platforms will shift from average latency to individual differences. Gastrointestinal transit, food intake, and barrier changes will all affect actual startup time.

Observation indicators: distribution of each component, barrier thickness, release initiation and duration, in vivo absorption sequence, post-storage performance, and the impact of configuration changes on other modules.
How can gastrointestinal targeting or stimulus responses control release location?

Near term: Human body positioning data will become a crucial differentiator between various platforms. Systems with similar structural designs may exhibit different performance due to variations in transport and material response.

Mid-term: Positioning and activity protection may be more tightly integrated. Proteins and other sensitive ingredients need to address issues related to manufacturing, storage, and passage through the gastrointestinal environment simultaneously.
Observation indicators: target site reach rate, early release, residence time, inter-individual differences, local and systemic exposure, and results corresponding to clinical studies.

sections.title: Observation Indicators and Priority Research Tasks

blocks.text: Release studies for first need to distinguish three time points: the time when the formulation begins to release, the time when the drug is completely released, and the time when the drug reaches the target site or enters circulation. Barrier structure primarily alters the first two, while gastrointestinal transport and the tissue environment also alter the third. Conflating these three factors into a single "sustained-release time" can lead to an overly strong clinical interpretation of identical in vitro curves. Subsequent studies should select appropriate observation methods based on the specific product, ensuring a gradual alignment between structural design and actual targets.

The priority of comparative studies is to establish controls that can distinguish mechanisms, rather than continuing to add uncompared geometries. Keeping drug dosage and materials the same while changing porosity, keeping porosity similar while changing drug solidity, and keeping external geometry the same while changing internal pathways—these address different questions. Only after these independent changes are identified can the synergistic effects in complex multi-material systems have an interpretable reference.

Observable metrics should include curve shape and variability, rather than the average release percentage at a single time point. Early leakage, start-up time distribution, late release integrity, and batch-to-batch variability correspond to different failure mechanisms. For multi-component systems, component-by-component analysis is also required; for sensitive loads, activity recovery should be measured simultaneously; for localized systems, results must be reported under a defined environmental sequence. These metrics constitute the evidence set for the product mission.

The research priorities for digital models are external validation and uncertainty representation. Models can narrow down the range of candidate structures, but manufacturing deviations, material aging, and changes in the medium can cause the input to differ from the actual product. Incorporating these perturbations into model evaluation helps determine whether the prediction error primarily originates from geometric measurements, release experiments, or the model itself. For designers, knowing when retesting is necessary is more valuable than simply obtaining a target dimension accurate to a decimal point.

Commercial development maps to these mechanistic tasks. Aprecia’s rapidly disintegrating products use industrially manufactured porous structures for a defined dosage-form need; AnelleO’s ring platform under development reflects the geometric and barrier requirements of long-term local release. Validation is organized around rapid oral disintegration and sustained local delivery, respectively. Academic papers provide structural principles, while each product requires performance evidence for its materials, use location and manufacturing system. [R10][R11]

In 2027, the focus should be on observing whether multiple specifications can simultaneously maintain content and release. In 2028, the focus should be on whether the structural predictions remain usable in new batches and new equipment. In 2029, it depends on whether the positioning or exposure evidence of in vivo can be linked to the design parameters. If these conditions are met, printing may form a transferable release module; if only in vitro has abundant curves, applications will still mainly rely on product-by-product development and testing.

The most valuable data to prioritize is not the best release curve, but rather the design failure boundaries: what kind of porosity leads to structural brittleness, what interfaces cause early leakage, and what type of dimensional changes turn immediate release into confinement. These failure boundaries can constrain subsequent reverse engineering, reduce repeated exploration of unstable solutions under unmanufacturable or operational conditions, and ensure that feedback from the research graphs truly influences the next round of material and structure selection.

P3-03.title: Printing Quality and Stability
P3-03.subtitle: Jointly validating material compatibility, manufacturing repeatability and storage quality
P3-03.thesis: The quality of printed formulations is determined by materials chemistry, processing history, deposition repeatability, and structural changes during storage. Research is translating printability experience into measurable properties and unit-by-unit evidence; thermal stability, forming accuracy, and content uniformity are measured separately to explain the final release and delivery quality.
