blocks.text: This research direction organizes evidence based on specific application tasks, placing formulation design, measurable quality, and actual usage conditions within the same research chain. Geometric adjustments provide design freedom, but each adjustment requires explanation of which physical processes it affects; the usage scenario determines which changes are valuable, and the original questions are addressed accordingly.
How do printing heat and light affect drug stability?
Printing may involve heating, shear, photoinitiated reactions and drying. Drug content, crystalline state and drug–polymer interactions can change separately, affecting storage and release.
This problem requires distinguishing between chemical degradation and intentional changes in physical state, while also connecting changes during processing with storage before use.
How can printed formulations ensure content uniformity and dose accuracy?

Drug content per tablet depends on dosage-form mass and drug distribution. Consistent mass suggests stable deposition but does not establish consistent drug concentration. These factors require separate testing, particularly for low-dose and multi-ingredient formulations.
This question focuses on the quality chain from ingredient preparation to piece-by-piece output, and how small-batch manufacturing can maintain reliable judgment while reducing destructive sampling.
How do formulation and process parameters affect printability?

Pharmaceutical materials must feed into equipment, flow consistently during deposition, retain structure after forming, and meet drug-quality and release requirements. Filament, semi-solid and photocuring systems impose different material requirements.
This question uses printability as a connection point to analyze how formulation parameters affect the process, and how the process affects the final formulation.
N1 | Material blending meets two functional needs (2016)

2016 polymer blending research attempted to improve the processability of FDM solid dispersions while regulating release. Material composition affects both filament feeding and drug release, shifting formulation optimization from a single mechanical objective to a multi-objective equilibrium. [R01]

Using polymer blends for printability exposes a tension between pharmaceutical materials and mechanical feeding: filaments must resist feeding pressure yet disintegrate after fabrication according to product targets. Comparing whole-matrix disintegration with strip peeling brings interlayer fusion into explanations of release. Printability is therefore a relationship among material, equipment and final performance, rather than a single intrinsic material label. [R01]

Subsequent measurements should cover solid feed, melt flow, and post-cooling interlayer bonding. Optimizing only one stage may transfer defects to another stage; for example, easy-to-feed material may fail to maintain its shape after ejection. N4 translates these empirical judgments into measurable mechanical and rheological variables, while N3 examines the impact of this processing history on chemical stability.

The reference used for material screening should be matched with the target process. The same formulation may perform differently under different gear pressures, nozzles, or paths, so method development should preserve equipment conditions so that the observed material advantages can be accurately reproduced in the next study.
N2 | Photoreactions reveal compatibility limits (2020)

A 2020 four-component photocuring study found a reaction between amlodipine and a diacrylate component, confirmed by infrared spectroscopy and NMR. The issue arose from a specific drug–resin chemical interaction, showing that reduced heat exposure cannot replace formulation-compatibility studies. [R02]

Photocuring can reduce some heat exposure, but it introduces reactive components. The combination of infrared and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) provides evidence of chemical structure, which is more indicative of changes in the original drug than appearance and total peak intensity. The significance of this study lies in using specific functional group interactions as a failure mechanism, demonstrating that "low temperature" cannot encompass the pharmaceutical suitability of the entire process.

This discovery necessitates addressing two issues simultaneously in the screening of N5 resins: whether they can form the target structure, and whether the target chemical composition can be retained after the addition of a specific drug. These two require different experiments and different criteria. When selecting a formulation, it is advisable to compare pure drugs, single resins, and coexisting systems to separate the contributions of light, material contact, and the polymerization reaction.

Compatibility also includes a time dimension. Residual reactive components after printing may continue to come into contact with the drug, therefore immediate content and post-storage impurities should be linked. This node merges with the N3 thermal aging branch, forming an examination of the complete manufacturing history.
N3 | Processing history links to storage changes (2021–2022)

A stability study published online in 2021 simulated heat treatment and storage conditions, finding different drug-polymer combinations yielded different results: some combinations exhibited protective effects, while others showed instability and chemical changes. The study specified process selection as formulation combinations and the conditions they underwent. [R03]

Treating extrusion and reprinting as a continuous thermal history explains why measuring only the thermal decomposition temperature of the raw material is insufficient to determine formulation stability. The molecular environment changes after the drug enters the polymer; interactions may delay these changes or introduce new incompatibilities. Different combinations in the study showed different results, indicating that ranking the heat resistance of pure drugs cannot directly replace formulation-level evaluation.

This method links the process to time, raising shelf-life quality issues with N8. Stability studies should observe different levels of active ingredients, impurities, crystallinity, and functional performance to identify the properties that change first. If chemical content remains stable but releases changes, further examination of moisture, pores, or matrix rearrangement should be conducted, rather than attributing all aging to degradation.

The explanatory power of simulation studies depends on whether they cover the main stresses in the actual process. Besides temperature, residence time distribution, mechanical shear, and humidity may also affect the sample. Subsequent verification of simulation conclusions with real manufactured samples can determine which preliminary screening results have predictive value.
N4 | Mechanical and rheological properties predict quality (2023–2024)

The study, published online in 2023, prepared twenty-three types of filaments and used mechanical and rheological parameters to predict processability and tablet property consistency. Its contribution was transforming the empirical judgment of "too brittle or too soft" into a measurable variable, helping to narrow down the experimental scope. [R04]

Feeding is a solid-state stress problem, while ejection and deposition are melt flow problems; therefore, multiple measurements are closer to the manufacturing process than a single hardness measurement. The study uses multivariate regression to connect material properties and output, and points out that the feeding model is equipment-dependent. This result gives a concrete boundary to the "portable model." With the same material parameters but different equipment forces, the failure threshold may change. [R04]

Subsequent validation should hold out data by equipment and material type to determine where model transfer fails. Feeding failures suggest a mechanical-interface problem; changes in tablet width or release consistency require tracking deposition and cooling. Unit-by-unit weighing in N6 provides production outcome signals that link offline models to actual output.

The regression coefficients should also be understood in conjunction with the correlation between variables. Hardness, elasticity, and viscosity may all change with the formulation simultaneously; the variables selected in the model may not be the sole cause. Targeted changes to a single factor and subsequent analysis of the output are key to advancing statistical prediction into process understanding.
N5 | Systematic screening of photocuring windows (2024)

The study in 2024 screened 156 resin formulations, examining the effects of initiators, polymer molecular size, and liquid fillers on molding. This provided a basis for narrowing down the range of manufacturable formulations; subsequent compatibility and residue evaluations of the selected drugs are also necessary. [R05]

The significance of the system screening lies in simultaneously examining multiple factors, rather than attributing all changes to a single component after repeated substitutions. Photopolymerization rate, viscosity, and network formation jointly determine the molding process, while liquid fillers influence the optical and flow environments. Placing different variables within a common experimental framework allows for the identification of areas requiring joint control and reduces trial-and-error.

N2 reminds users that this formability window must intersect with the drug compatibility window. If a formulation prints optimally but still causes a drug reaction, it is still not within the usable range of the target product. Subsequent considerations include residue, release, and shelf-life performance, and the results should be screened through independent sample testing, rather than using appearance scores as the final quality conclusion.

The window boundary is more suitable for production than a single optimum. Actual materials and equipment fluctuate, and if an optimum is too close to the failure zone, daily operation may be unstable. Studies should report performance changes after perturbations to help select a solution with acceptable tolerances.
N6 | Unit-by-unit weighing captures startup deviations (2024)

The 2024 study integrated an analytical balance into a printer to automatically record the tablet-by-tablet mass of hydrocortisone formulations and compare it with an external balance. The system identified manufacturing deviations in the first tablet, demonstrating that online weighing can capture unit problems that are easily masked by average batch results. [R06]

The tablet-by-tablet record preserves the production sequence, allowing observation of differences during start-up, continuous operation, and termination phases. The output of semi-solid materials can be affected by loading conditions and flow recovery; an abnormal unit may have a small impact on the batch average but a direct significance for the unit's dosage. This explains why quality data must be at the unit level, and not just total yield and average tablet weight.

The weighing feedback, combined with the property prediction of N4, can determine whether a certain type of filament or ink is more prone to temporal drift. However, identical mass does not guarantee identical drug content; N7 further introduces component-sensitive spectroscopy. Only by combining these two methods on the same unit can output quantity deviations be separated from mixing or composition deviations.

When integrating the instrument, vibration, environmental factors, and stabilization time must also be considered. If the measured values are related to the printing action, seemingly realistic process fluctuations may occur. Comparing and verifying measurement repeatability with independent references helps determine whether the anomaly originates from the product or the measurement system.
N7 | Cross-site verification of unit drug content (2025)

A 2025 study applied miniature near-infrared and Raman spectroscopy to tamoxifen formulations produced at Gustave Roussy Hospital. Calibration samples were prepared at the research center, while the hospital collected spectra and validated local products. Material sources were kept consistent, and both open-capsule measurements and measurements through closed shells were examined. [R07]

This design directly addresses the most challenging aspect of knowledge transfer in decentralized manufacturing: the center possesses analytical and development capabilities, while the hospital controls the actual production environment. The outer shell alters the optical path and background, thus closed-shell prediction requires verification that the sampling information represents the internal drug. The complementarity of the two spectra stems from their different physical responses; the choice should not solely rely on goodness of fit but also depend on detection time, packaging interference, maintenance, and the connection to production records.

Compared to N4, N7 is closer to external applications, but the same supply source still constitutes a clear migration condition. The next stage should use raw material batches, operators, and equipment as stratification factors to observe how deviations accumulate; if different institutions are outside the validation set, the central model needs to be updated or partially calibrated. This issue advances the testing research to multi-site comparisons at N9 and reinstates version management requirements to the quality system of the quality validation system.
N8 | Fresh-product conformity and storage performance (2025)

The 2025 furosemide study combined semi-solid extrusion with a near-infrared partial least squares model, and used infrared, diffraction, and surface characterization to explain formulation performance. Fresh samples met the requirements of content uniformity, but the two formulations showed different release characteristics after six months, although the observed drug crystal structures remained intact. [R08]

The results from reveal that quality attributes are not interchangeable. Chemical content and crystalline stability do not guarantee that pores, moisture migration, or matrix wetting conditions remain unchanged; therefore, release changes can occur without clear evidence of chemical degradation. Surface morphology provides candidate interpretations, but still requires confirmation of which process controls dissolution through measurements of water absorption, erosion, and internal structure. Quality studies are shifting from single-point-of-life acceptance to the behavior of products under predetermined storage conditions.

The preservation study provides feedback to N7 regarding model validity: if spectral changes are caused by both content and aging, the model must distinguish between the two sources. It also connects to the comparative design of N9, requiring comparisons between printed and conventional dispensing methods at the same storage stage; directly comparing freshly printed formulations with long-term stored flakes would confound process and time differences.
N9 | Direct comparison with current tablet splitting (2026)

A 2026 metoprolol study compared manual tablet splitting with automated printing at two hospital pharmacies and one compounding pharmacy, using validated liquid chromatography to measure drug content. Printed units had mean content near the target and acceptance values below 15; some manually split low-dose units showed greater variability. [R09]

Direct comparison adds workflow-level explanatory value beyond showing that printed samples meet specifications: improvement occurs in a step already used in practice. Low-dose tablet splitting is particularly sensitive to fracture position and fragment loss, whereas automated dispensing shifts error sources toward mixing uniformity and deposition repeatability. Further work should separate within-site from between-site variation, because a favorable overall mean can conceal one site running high and another running low.

Evidence supports dose-quality benefits for specified formulations and under studied conditions. It provides a manufacturing-level response to the material and performance requirements proposed in N1 and raises maintenance requirements for the quality validation system: does the original comparative advantage still exist after equipment replacement, raw material changes, and software upgrades? Long-term studies should include batch deviations, rework, and pharmacist time to determine whether stable quality is achieved with an manageable workload.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: How do printing heat and light affect drug stability?

The practical value of these capabilities lies in expanding the range of optional processes and preserving process parameters. Whether a formulation can remain stable still depends on the specific drug, temperature, and storage results.

The connection between this direction and industry therefore occurs in process selection and validation services: equipment provides manufacturing conditions, academic research establishes the response laws of drugs and materials, and pharmaceutical development organizes the two into reproducible schemes.
How can printed formulations ensure content uniformity and dose accuracy?

The FABRX platform offers weighing, near-infrared, and pressure accessories, combined with software for batch recording; online balances and hospital spectroscopy studies are directly linked to its related technologies. [R10][R06]

The enterprise roadmap has evolved from "automatically outputting tablets" to "outputting tablets and their manufacturing records." The platform's value depends on its ability to promptly identify anomalies, prevent the delivery of non-conforming units, and retain traceable data.
How do formulation and process parameters affect printability?

The versatility of the enterprise platform means that processes can be selected based on drugs and materials, rather than requiring all formulations to fit the same equipment. Academic models help select process windows, while process sensing helps confirm actual operation.

True product capability lies in delivering the right formula, parameters, and inspection methods together. Adjusting equipment parameters is only the starting point; stable manufacturing requires clearly defined permissible ranges of variation.

In January 2026, CurifyLabs released the PharmaPrinter Aurum, focusing on built-in weighing, cleaning and calibration, ease of loading, and software traceability as key product updates. Its connection to the furosemide study in 2025 and the metoprolol study in 2026 lies in the device's entry into specific formulation validation and multi-site quality comparisons; these studies and product announcements provide quality evidence and product functionality information, respectively. [R08][R09][R11]

The FABRX product configuration aligns with the 2024 balance integration study and the 2025 hospital spectroscopy study, forming a roadmap from deposition to unit-by-unit detection. Enterprise involvement facilitates easier integration of detection and equipment control, while academic evaluation requires continued quantification of detection errors, true anomaly detection, and cross-site migration. The product configuration can support the detection methods, and validated formulations and models determine which products the methods are effective in. [R06][R07][R10]
How do printing heat and light affect drug stability?

The most useful cross-cutting outcome is a set of manufacturing protocols that illustrate applicable drugs, materials, and conditions. This provides greater support for actual formulation development than simply claiming "low temperature" or "thermal-free printing."
How can printed formulations ensure content uniformity and dose accuracy?

The most direct cross-fertilization value is that it transforms the testability in research into an actionable judgment during manufacturing. Only when weight, concentration, and final content are all established can complete dosage evidence be constituted.
How do formulation and process parameters affect printability?

The connection between academia and industry makes these relationships measurable and recordable. By clearly defining which processes and quality changes are affected by material alterations, the platform can support reliable formulation expansion.
How do printing heat and light affect drug stability?

Research is shifting from the general question of whether heat or light damages drugs to the specific mechanisms of action of formulations. Temperature, exposure time, drug state, and excipient combination all contribute to determining the outcome.

A more mature process chain involves continuous performance evaluation throughout the initial screening, actual processing, and post-storage phases. This allows for the identification of unsuitable combinations while also leveraging beneficial dispersion or protection, rather than treating all physical changes as degradation.
How can printed formulations ensure content uniformity and dose accuracy?

The changes in the study are reflected in the shift of granularity from batch to single tablet, the expansion of the scope of inspection from weight to drug signals, and the expansion of the scope of validation from a single location to different actual institutions.

The link improves the interpretability of personalized manufacturing: deposition deviations can be detected by weighing, mixing or concentration issues require content and spectral evidence, and storage changes are further checked by stability and release tests. Different methods each have a clearly defined role.
How do formulation and process parameters affect printability?

Research is moving from empirical screening to understanding the material-process-formulation relationship. Filament mechanics, ink recovery, and photocuring response correspond to different processes, and a single, unified indicator cannot cover all printing methods.

The next phase of change is connecting the model with process data. Early material testing is used to select formulations, while running pressure, mass, or spectral data is used to confirm that the formulation is performing as expected; both work together to reduce failures and rework.
How do printing heat and light affect drug stability?

Near term: Formulation screening will place greater emphasis on processing history. Studies will simultaneously record temperature, residence time, shearing, and post-treatment to explain differences.

Mid-term: The choice between different processes will be based on the compatibility of drugs and excipients. Low-temperature extrusion, room-temperature filling, and hot-melt routes can be developed in parallel to meet different needs.

Observation indicators: stability indicators include content and impurities, crystalline state, residual components, release after storage, and the degree to which the same formula is maintained in different equipment or batches.
How can printed formulations ensure content uniformity and dose accuracy?

Near term: Piece-by-piece recording and automatic anomaly detection will become crucial capabilities for production platforms. Small-batch production, in particular, requires retaining information for each unit.
Mid-term: The transfer and updating of spectral models will be a key focus. Models must maintain their predictive capabilities even after changes in material batches, equipment, and locations.

Observation indicators: mass and drug-content variation, low dose deviation, anomaly identification and missed detection, performance across batches and locations, and actual delivery rate of qualified units.
How do formulation and process parameters affect printability?
Near term: Formulation development will increasingly utilize small-scale material screening and structured parameter recording. This reduces the need for repeated trial and error on whole tablets.
Mid-term: Process feedback will help dynamically identify manufacturing deviations. Pressure, mass and spectra each observe different aspects and need to be correlated with specific failure modes.

Observation indicators: number of formulation screenings, formation success rate, mass and drug content of each tablet, process drift, release consistency, and reproducibility after changing material batches or equipment.

sections.title: Quality Attributes, Level of Evidence, and Research Priorities

blocks.text: Quality assessment requires defining the failure first, followed by instrument selection. Insufficient content, increased related impurities, interlayer delamination, and release shift correspond to different mechanisms and require different reference methods. Even if a spectral model accurately predicts content, it may not be sensitive to low-level impurities; a tablet with intact weight may also have localized delamination compensated for by excessive deposition in other areas. The study design should ensure that each critical failure has at least one directly observable chain of evidence.

The primary priority is to establish a localizable error budget across materials, processes, and products. At the material level, batch composition, moisture content, and flow behavior are observed; at the process level, deposition and energy interactions are recorded; and at the product level, content distribution, mechanical integrity, and release are examined. If a deviation occurs in the final product, the most probable source should be traceable using records from the same unit or batch. This design avoids attributing all anomalies to equipment inaccuracies and helps determine where sensors should be placed for maximum value.

The second priority is to study the non-steady-state phases at the beginning and end of the process. Many screening experiments select samples from continuous, stable phases, easily overlooking deviations at start-up, pauses, replenishment, and restart. Weigh-by-piece studies have shown the value of preserving the production sequence. These phases should be included in the validation scope, and it should be clarified whether the calculated overall pass rate includes the first or last piece manually rejected; otherwise, the quality performance of different studies will lack a common denominator. [R06]

The third priority task is to distinguish between measurement noise and actual product variation. Repeated measurements of the same unit primarily describe instrument repeatability; multiple units within the same batch describe intra-batch variation; multiple batches describe production robustness; and multiple devices and locations describe migration capability. These four types of repetition correspond to different scientific questions. Increasing the number of scans on the same piece can stabilize the signal, but it cannot replace increasing the number of independent batches; resources should be allocated to the layer of variation with the greatest uncertainty during the design phase.

Stability evaluation should consider both chemical and functional aspects. Processing can introduce amorphous states or alter component contact, while storage can lead to rearrangement, hygroscopicity, and interfacial changes. The fact that the drug is still detectable is only part of the chain of evidence. By juxtaposing impurities, crystalline state, content uniformity, and release time series, it's possible to determine whether changes in product performance precede chemical degradation, and to select key variables for packaging and storage studies accordingly. [R03][R08]

For machine learning and regression models, truly reusable outcomes are predictive relationships with applicable scope. Randomly splitting the same batch of data, which often shares materials and environments, can easily underestimate future production uncertainties. Reserving data by batch, date, and location allows for more meaningful validation and makes model update conditions clearly visible. Anomaly identification should also report missed detections and false rejections, not just overall accuracy; these two types of errors affect quality and drug supply differently.

The most likely progress for in 2027 is the combined use of unit weighing and formulation-specific spectroscopy for a limited product range; this is contingent on sufficient reference analysis and outlier samples. In 2028, the key is ensuring calibration remains consistent after batch, machine, and site changes, with key indicators including external prediction bias and model update workload. A strong scenario for 2029 is the integration of material selection, process monitoring, and stability data into a unified change management system, allowing for specification adjustments within clearly defined boundaries.

The relationship between product quality and equipment quality will become clearer. Equipment validation demonstrates that actions and measurements conform to design, while product validation requires demonstrating that specific materials produce predetermined properties after these actions. When software updates change pathways, raw material batches change flow, or detector replacements change signals, the affected layers of evidence differ. Mapping changes to quality attributes allows for focused validation and reduces irrelevant duplication of testing.

Cross-enterprise comparisons should ideally focus on shared product tasks and employ common reference analysis. Equipment resolution, printing speed, and configurable modules each describe different capabilities and cannot individually represent pharmaceutical quality. More comparable endpoints include the percentage of qualified deliveries within a specified specification range, post-storage performance, anomaly traceability, and total verification time. Such comparisons can also help researchers determine whether to prioritize improvements in material compatibility, mechanical stability, or testing information.

Priority shared data should include corresponding records of normal and failed samples, reference analysis results, and material and equipment background. Having only failure labels without root cause analysis makes it difficult to guide the next round of formulation improvements; having only successful samples without perturbation tests also makes it difficult to describe the stability window. Organizing both types of data together allows modeling, mechanism research, and equipment development to focus on the same quality issue.

P3-04.title: Microneedle Delivery
P3-04.subtitle: The chain of evidence from needle tip precision to actual tissue delivery
P3-04.thesis: Microneedle printing connects manufacturable geometry, insertion mechanics and drug disposition. High-resolution molds, direct printing and active infusion provide complementary routes. Translation depends on reproducible tissue delivery and retained function after storage, rather than single-needle appearance or total loading.

blocks.text: This research direction organizes evidence based on specific application tasks, placing formulation design, measurable quality, and actual usage conditions within the same research chain. Geometric adjustments provide design freedom, but each adjustment requires explanation of which physical processes it affects; the usage scenario determines which changes are valuable, and the original questions are addressed accordingly.
How can microneedle structures balance strength and skin insertion?

Microneedles must be sharp enough to enter skin and strong enough to withstand insertion forces. Height, tip geometry, spacing, material and base all contribute; single-needle mechanics differ from whole-array performance.
This question focuses on how geometric design, through manufacturing and mechanical testing, ultimately translates into effective insertion depth and delivery capability.
How can drug-loaded microneedles control transdermal delivery and release?

Microneedle delivery can use surface drug coatings, infusion through hollow channels, or drug loading within dissolving needles. The three routes differ in loading capacity, release mechanism and use.
This question focuses on how drugs cross the skin barrier and what step printing actually plays in the final delivery chain.
How can molds and printing improve microneedle fabrication accuracy?

Key microneedle dimensions include tip geometry, height, channels, spacing and base. Direct printing and replication from printed master molds have different error sources; nominal equipment resolution alone does not represent final geometry.
This question focuses on how digital design maintains critical dimensions through multiple processes and how this precision is linked to puncture, flow, and drug delivery functions.
N1 | Separating needle fabrication and protein coating (2018)

In 2018, research was conducted on printing conical and pyramidal microneedle needles, followed by inkjet coating with insulin and carbohydrate-protective components. Drug structure was examined using spectroscopy, and release was evaluated using a Franz diffusion assay on porcine skin. Printing is responsible for the needle body, while coating is responsible for drug loading and protection; these two steps together determine delivery performance. [R01]

Separating the needle body and drug-loaded layer allows the needle body selection to primarily conform to mechanics and geometry, while the coating selection primarily conforms to drug stability and release. Circular dichroism and Raman spectroscopy are used to observe protein conformation, and porcine skin diffusion assays are used to observe delivery; these two methods correspond to biomolecular states and tissue barrier penetration, respectively. The research design thus breaks down successful manufacturing into two tasks that must be met simultaneously, rather than simply focusing on the integrity of the needle tip.

The coating may alter the needle tip radius, and insertion may leave some load on the skin surface, so the loaded amount needs to be distinguished from the actual amount inserted. The next step should be to connect post-insertion residue, tissue distribution and permeated drug in a mass balance. N2 uses a geometric template for enhanced control, while N3 reduces dependence on surface coating capacity through hollow channels, forming two distinct delivery branches.

The stability of the same drug in different coating materials does not mean that different biomolecules can utilize the same protective relationship. A more suitable approach is a segmented validation method: first confirm the active structure, then confirm shaping and puncture, and finally confirm tissue delivery. Simultaneously, the geometry and load-bearing capacity before and after coating should be compared to determine whether the drug loading step, in turn, weakens the structural function. This creates a two-way feedback loop between pharmaceutics optimization and microstructure optimization.
N2 | Molds isolate geometric variables (2020)

A 2020 two-photon polymerization study fabricated seven master molds with different heights, shapes, base widths and spacing, then replicated them into dissolving and hydrogel microneedles. Needle geometries produced different insertion depths in skin models, broadly corresponding to delivery of a model drug. Molds made geometry a controlled comparison variable. [R02]

The value of the high-precision template lies in making needle formation a repeatable variable. The final material is provided by replication molding, avoiding the need to readjust the high-resolution printing process for each drug-loaded formulation. The study simultaneously compares insertion depth and drug delivery, establishing a relationship between geometric effects and effective intradermal contact, going beyond mere microscopic appearance.

Different geometries result in different insertion depths, which may improve delivery by increasing the drug-load volume entering the tissue; they may also alter the mechanical damage and dissolution environment. To differentiate these explanations, it is necessary to compare the actual needle volume entering the tissue with the delivery amount per unit entry volume. N5 further examines the effect of manufacturing orientation on the needle tip, while N7 and N8 transfer the template capability to different soluble materials.

The repeatability of the template does not mean that the final product will automatically repeat. Negative mold filling, drying shrinkage, and demolding deformation can all alter the needle tip. Quality evaluation should track three stages: the master mold, the negative mold, and the final needle body, to identify at which step the error increases. The center needle and edge needles in each array may bear different loads; spatial distribution is more indicative than average insertion depth of whether some needles have not entered.
N3 | Hollow microneedles with active control (2020–2021)

The hollow-microneedle MEMS study, published online in 2020, combined a printed needle with a control system to observe intradermal fluid distribution in real time and evaluate insulin administration in diabetic animals. The study advanced from passive dissolution and release to a controlled infusion process. [R03]

The hollow structure of the needle separates the drug-load capacity from the needle volume, while the control system makes delivery a time-varying process. The inclusion of real-time imaging is particularly important because not all pumped fluid necessarily reaches the target tissue; channel resistance, contact state, and tissue backpressure can all alter the distribution. Research has shifted from passive release to monitorable infusion, allowing for cross-verification of controlled doses with actual tissue results.

Animal blood glucose monitoring connects the infusion device to the biological response, but drug absorption and distribution remain between the two. Future studies should simultaneously record flow rate, tissue distribution, and drug efficacy time series to identify whether changes in response originate from delivery or physiological processes. The N6 local disease model raises another question: the target of control could be local exposure, rather than a systemic response.

Compared to the soluble microneedle, the active system of adds flow paths, drive components, and connecting parts; therefore, the reliability of the entire device requires a joint evaluation. A single needle's ability to penetrate only indicates that the flow path inlet is adequate; continuous operation also depends on sealing, blockage, and contact stability. The control system's setpoints require independent flow or mass references to rule out situations where commands are executed correctly but actual liquid delivery is insufficient.
N4 | Geometric errors in direct printing (2021)

The 2021 DLP hollow needle microneedle study compared the effects of printing angle on geometry and examined curing and mechanical performance. The actual shape of the needle tip and channel may deviate from the CAD design, thus manufacturing parameters are incorporated into the puncture design, not just production settings. [R04]

The internal channels of the hollow needle complicate manufacturing issues compared to solid needles: over-curing can shrink the opening, and cleaning and residue can alter the actual flow path. The printing orientation affects both stair-stepping, support, and localized exposure; therefore, the actual needle tip and channels should be measured, not just the nominal resolution. Geometric error studies provide interpretable input for subsequent puncture and infusion.

N5 connects this input to the puncture force, demonstrating that manufacturing parameters can become functional variables. For hollow systems, the channel cross-section also needs to be connected to flow resistance; as the orifice size decreases, needles with seemingly identical shapes may exhibit significantly different infusion performance. Studies should combine structural observation and functional measurements to avoid judging structures that do not allow liquids to pass as acceptable solely based on appearance.

Post-curing can also alter material stiffness and residual composition, potentially improving load-bearing capacity while changing brittleness. The quality window should include post-puncture integrity and chemical residue, rather than using maximum hardness as the sole optimization objective. Exposure variations may also exist between different locations within a printing batch; examining a single optimal sample is insufficient to represent the geometric consistency of the entire manufacturing area.
N5 | Build orientation changes insertion (2023)

A 2023 study compared different printing tilt angles, finding that the 45-degree angle required less puncture force than the zero-degree angle in the DLP system used. The results linked process direction, tip formation, and puncture performance, indicating that optimization needs to be based on actual equipment and materials. [R05]

The tilt angle study links digital geometry, printed needle tips, and measured punctures. Its methodological focus is on making the manufacturing orientation a controlled variable, then comparing functions under uniform mechanical conditions. This is more convincing than simply demonstrating the sharpness of a single needle tip, because minute appearance differences only gain practical significance through the response of the tissue or standard model.

The puncture force of the needle is determined by the needle tip, tissue deformation, and array synergy; the advantages of a single needle are not necessarily retained in a dense array. Subsequent observations should be made on multiple skin samples and at different array locations to determine whether the improvement originates from the needle tip rather than overall substrate deformation. The N6's flexible substrate incorporates these array contact issues into its product design.

Different printers have different pixel sizes, optical systems, and material responses, so improvements brought about by manufacturing direction need to be reproduced on a system-by-system basis. A more transferable conclusion is to examine the relationship between the actual needle tip and the puncture, rather than treating a certain angle as a universal process choice. The reduction in puncture force should also be compared with the needle body damage threshold; only by retaining sufficient load-bearing margin can a lower applied load be meaningful for product stability.
N6 | Flexible arrays for localized disease (2023)

In the same year, the flexible hollow microneedle study used a printed master mold and double molding to adjust the needle size and substrate characteristics, and evaluated local delivery in a mouse psoriasis model. The design expanded from a single needle to the overall relationship between the array and skin contact. [R06]

The flexible substrate addresses the fit between the entire array and the skin's curvature, while the needle body handles puncture and delivery; both require different mechanical properties. Dual molding makes it possible to design these two types of requirements separately. Mouse disease models further connect local delivery with tissue response, shifting the evaluation from creating holes to actual effects on specific lesions.

Local application of medication involves a different exposure pathway compared to oral administration; therefore, the results should be interpreted through a combination of local concentration, systemic distribution, and tissue response. The study suggests that delivering the drug to the target location may alter the required overall exposure, rather than directly estimating the dosage for human use. Dynamic distribution imaging of N3 can provide a complementary approach to this, helping to explain the relationship between array adhesion and local exposure.

During the translation process, stability under activity and prolonged contact should also be observed. Flexibility improves adhesion but may also alter the direction of force on the needle; whether skin movement causes local withdrawal or uneven insertion needs to be investigated as part of repeated delivery studies. Tissue response evaluation should separate changes caused by drug action from those caused by the puncture itself; blank arrays and identical material controls help identify their respective contributions.
N7 | Vacuum compression forms drug-loaded needles (2025)

The 2025 rivastigmine study combined DLP and Free-D Molding to examine the finished product's structure, mechanics, and skin permeability. Vacuum compression molding provides another method for drug-loaded materials to enter complex microstructures; accuracy needs to be confirmed on the final needle body. [R07]

This route uses high-precision printing for precursor geometry, followed by vacuum compression of the final material, avoiding the need for the final drug delivery system to be compatible with photopolymerization. Multiple microscopic observations and skin permeability tests are used to examine replication accuracy and functionality, allowing the value of the molding technology to be assessed at the product level. MeltPrep personnel are involved in the research, also establishing a direct link between equipment suppliers and pharmaceutical development. [R07]

The dissolving system requires both dry-state load bearing and wet-state release to occur simultaneously, both of which may be affected by the water content and storage conditions. Insertion, dissolution, and tissue drug recovery at different storage stages should be compared to determine whether the material softens prematurely due to moisture absorption. The N8 PVA/PVP system presents a similar task, but with different material mechanisms; therefore, a shared evaluation framework is more valuable for transfer than replicating individual processes.

The molding cost should also be calculated based on the qualified final array. Reusing the master mold reduces the burden of single-cycle geometry development, but missing needles, air bubbles, and demolding losses may dominate yield; recording these failures can help identify the areas that truly need optimization during manufacturing expansion. Comparisons of ex vivo permeability require maintaining the same skin source and integrity conditions to avoid sample barrier differences overshadowing the influence of the molding method.
N8 | Mechanical support and release in dissolving carriers (2026)

The 2026 pregabalin study involved converting the printed master mold into a PDMS negative mold, followed by the fabrication of a bilayer PVA/PVP microneedle, and examination of morphology, insertion, and release (in vitro). This demonstrates that the accuracy of the master mold and the performance of the final formulation need to be jointly verified; the entire manufacturing chain cannot be evaluated solely based on the master mold image. [R08]

Dissolving microneedles use the carrier material itself as the source of release, tightly coupling mechanics and mass transfer. Dry-state compression and model insertion test load bearing before use; swelling and in vitro release assess behavior after wetting. Linking the two shows whether a structure can enter first and then release its payload. Model insertion provides early evidence for this chain.

The amount of drug in the in vitro release medium is still far from actual intradermal delivery. The next step should be to determine the load destination based on tissue stratification recovery and needle residue after puncture, and to examine whether the two-stage curves originate from matrix dissolution or drug at different locations within the sample. N8 informs the geometric design in N2: if effective delivery primarily occurs at the needle tip entering the skin, additional drug loading in the base may not necessarily improve product efficiency.

This node merges the template, mechanics, and release branches into a material selection problem. Evaluation priorities should shift from total load to the repeatability of actual delivery, while also considering duration of retained activity, humidity sensitivity, and post-use structural integrity, thus defining product boundaries for specific applications. Results from multiple independent preparations and different die locations can supplement single-batch averages, revealing whether the replication route has a basis for stable scaling-up of production.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: How can microneedle structures balance strength and skin insertion?

The core capabilities lie in high-precision geometry manufacturing and template processes. Academic research further provides insertion, material, and delivery verification, enabling the precision structures to be integrated with specific applications.

The choice of product route requires consideration of both accuracy and quantity: direct printing is suitable for exploring complex structures, while master mold replication allows for the transfer of designs to more materials and batch production. The final needle body must be examined for different routes, not just the master mold.
How can drug-loaded microneedles control transdermal delivery and release?

Nanoscribe provides high-precision manufacturing capabilities for complex microneedle models and master molds; MeltPrep's Free-D Molding connects the printing of prototypes, negative molds, and vacuum compression molding, supporting the production of complex dosage form prototypes with small amounts of material. The 2025 rivastigmine research directly adopts this molding route. [R09][R10][R07]

Enterprise capabilities here are divided into manufacturing segments: precision printing determines the geometry, molding allows the target drug and polymer to enter the final needle. Active infusion also requires the joint participation of pumps, flow channels, control, and bonding systems.
The key link between devices and therapeutic products is to combine these components with a defined formulation and usage method, and to validate the final dosage.
How can molds and printing improve microneedle fabrication accuracy?

MeltPrep’s Free-D Molding converts printed engineering-material prototypes into negative molds, then uses vacuum compression to form prototypes in the target material, providing micromolding tools for high-value formulations available in small quantities. [R10]

These two types of companies have complementary capabilities. The choice between direct printing and master mold replication should be based on the final material, required quantity, channel structure, and quality control, rather than simply comparing printing speed.
How can microneedle structures balance strength and skin insertion?

Cross-value translates the geometric capabilities of a device into verifiable puncture performance. Actual insertion and delivery data can, in turn, determine where manufacturing precision should be invested in critical areas.
How can drug-loaded microneedles control transdermal delivery and release?

Cross-analysis should be organized according to the final delivery route, rather than treating all printed microneedle as the same product. This clarifies which problem the enterprise tools address and at which stage the next validation step should be performed.
How can molds and printing improve microneedle fabrication accuracy?

Academic research provides explanations from process errors to functional impacts, while enterprise tools provide recurring manufacturing conditions. Connecting the two helps to focus quality inputs on the areas that most impact puncture and delivery.
How can microneedle structures balance strength and skin insertion?

The research focus has shifted from designing a single needle tip to controlling the combined performance of the actual tip, materials, and array. Printing orientation, curing, and replication errors have all begun to affect the interpretation of results.

Another change is the more clearly defined evaluation hierarchy: mechanical tests observe deformation or fracture, skin models observe insertion, and delivery experiments measure drug entry. Connecting these results layer by layer helps identify whether the problem originates from the structure, the application method, or the drug delivery system.
How can drug-loaded microneedles control transdermal delivery and release?

Research has progressed from changing drug loading alone to coordinating structure, protection, infusion and dissolution. Active hollow systems emphasize flow and control, dissolving microneedles emphasize material and drug distribution, and coated systems emphasize stability and surface release.

Disease models and tissue distribution studies bring delivery evaluation closer to the mechanism of action. A key advance is describing how, where, and when the drug enters tissues, rather than simply reporting drug loading efficiency.
How can molds and printing improve microneedle fabrication accuracy?

The evaluation scope of these research has expanded from single-print results to the entire manufacturing chain. Direct printing requires control of exposure, cleaning, and curing, while the replication route also needs to handle filling, demolding, and material shrinkage.

Another change is the function-oriented precision: the needle tip affects puncture, the lumen affects flow, and the drug distribution between the needle tip and the base affects delivery. Different locations require different examination methods, and uniformly pursuing the smallest size is not always the most effective development strategy.
How can microneedle structures balance strength and skin insertion?
Near term: Final quality checks of the needle tip and channel will be given greater emphasis. Manufacturing errors need to correspond to puncture and flow results.
Mid-term: Array and application device may be jointly optimized. Coordination of structure, substrate, and application method is expected to reduce operator-induced variations.
Observation indicators: effective insertion ratio, depth distribution, needle breakage or deformation, force application window, skin model differences, and actual delivered dose.
How can drug-loaded microneedles control transdermal delivery and release?
Near term: manufacturing and drug-loading routes will have clearer roles. High-resolution master molds followed by molding should continue to support exploration of more formulations.

Mid-term: System reviews will place greater emphasis on actual delivery volume and usage. Active systems will focus on flow rate and control, while soluble systems will focus on needle residue and insertion consistency.

Observation indicators: drug stability, intradermal recovery and distribution, residual amount, release time, blockage or leakage, and corresponding results in disease models and clinical applications.
How can molds and printing improve microneedle fabrication accuracy?

Near term: Finished product geometry and functional checks are more valuable for comparison than equipment resolution. The key is to check the final needle body used, not just the digital design or master mold.

Mid-term: Template libraries and replication processes may improve formulation screening efficiency. Comparing materials under the same geometry allows for a clearer identification of formulation effects.

Observation indicators: needle tip and channel deviation, number of replications and mold life, filling defects, batch consistency, number of effective needles per piece, and puncture and delivery results.

sections.title: Translational Validation and Research Priorities for 2027-2029

blocks.text: A common challenge with and microneedle technologies is connecting five quantities: load capacity, releasable capacity, actual inserted load, tissue recovery, and effective amount reaching the target. These five quantities have different denominators. Coated routes may leave residues on the surface, hollow routes may experience backflow, and soluble routes may leave loads in the substrate that haven't penetrated the skin. Therefore, overall mass balance is more helpful in selecting a product route than simply increasing the loading rate.

Structural comparison requires distinguishing between single-needle and array-based designs. The sharpness of a single needle facilitates localized penetration, while increased array density can cause skin deformation, altering the effective load on each needle. A flexible substrate further affects load distribution. Therefore, the evaluation should simultaneously consider single-needle load-bearing capacity, array puncture, and insertion location distribution to determine whether a particular geometry still holds an advantage in actual array applications.

The model hierarchy should be selected according to the specific problem. Homogeneous membranes facilitate screening and reproducibility, ex vivo skin more closely approximates the stratum corneum and tissue structure, and animal studies allow for observation of local responses and systemic distribution. The evidence provided by different models is complementary in the research chain. Migration from standard membranes to tissues should be compared using the same apparatus and the same evaluation metrics to clearly identify what changes occur with increased biological complexity, rather than directly merging results from different models.

The industrial route can be divided into direct manufacturing of the final needle and replication after mold manufacturing. The former reduces geometry transfer steps, while the latter expands the choice of final materials and facilitates repeated replication. Nanoscribe lists the high-resolution microneedle array and master mold manufacturing as applications, demonstrating the platform's support for geometric research; MeltPrep Free-D connects the printing precursor with vacuum compression forming, emphasizing small-scale prototyping. [R09][R10]

Commercial technology should be tracked by task rather than product counts. Two-photon mold studies in 2020 showed repeatable geometric replication; DLP studies in 2021 and 2023 linked build orientation to function; a 2025 study involving MeltPrep connected replication to specific drug-loaded microneedles. These include both equipment use and company participation; similar processes alone do not establish that all papers belong to one product-development chain. [R02][R04][R05][R07]

For industrial scale-up, the most important metrics are qualified array yield, channel open ratio, needle tip size distribution, drug loading distribution, and final delivery variability. Printing speed only describes one step; if post-processing, duplication, assembly, or inspection becomes a bottleneck, speeding up printing may not improve overall output. Recording failure locations to individual needles or arrays can identify whether investment should be made in printing accuracy, die life, or final inspection capabilities.

The priority study for in 2027 is the consistency of the same product across different skin models and multiple independent batches. For coated, soluble, or hollow systems with clearly defined uses, it is advisable to validate their respective primary dose loss pathways. Evidence triggering further translation should be stable actual delivery rates and that the drug and structure retain their intended function after storage, rather than just a single successful puncture.

A key condition for in 2028 is incorporating application methods and usage scenarios into the design. Skin curvature, movement, different operators, and contact states can affect the number of array entries; device design needs to mitigate the fluctuations caused by these factors. Research can use controlled-change measurements to assess the system's sensitivity to usage differences, feeding the results back to the choice of substrate, needle spacing, or feedback detection.

The stronger scenario for 2029 is the development of an evidence package that can explain actual delivery volume, local tissue response, and long-term product stability, demonstrating its value relative to existing methods in specific drug missions. The weaker scenario involves increasing precision in microstructures, while issues of dose delivery and reusability remain unresolved. The difference between the two depends on whether mechanistic studies can extend to real-world application endpoints.

Research priorities also include a systematic analysis of failed samples. Channel blockage, tip bending, replicated bubbles, and moisture softening each correspond to different improvement directions; if only the most complete array is shown, the manufacturing window will be overestimated. Introducing failed samples into structural, mechanical, and delivery tests can clarify which types of defects have functional significance, thereby determining reasonable inspection priorities.

For cross-route comparisons, a common endpoint consistent with the target should be used. For local skin diseases, priority should be given to the distribution of intratissue exposure and local response; for systemic delivery, the amount entering circulation and changes in time should be considered. This preserves the characteristics of various microneedle types and avoids substituting practical application value with a conveniently measurable in vitro release ratio.

Reusable research findings should also specify the inspection locations of the mold and final product, the background of the tissue sample, and the estimation method for the actual needle insertion. Differences in results obtained by different teams using the same digital model but different tissue or metrological definitions may not necessarily stem from manufacturing level. Establishing common geometric and dosage representations allows subsequent comparisons to focus on genuine material and mechanistic differences and reduces redundant prototype exploration.

P3-05.title: Implantable and Local Delivery
P3-05.subtitle: Local exposure is determined by structure, time, and tissue interface.
P3-05.thesis: The research value of printed local drug delivery lies in transforming shape, reservoir, and barrier into measurable exposure controls. Infection response, tumor rhythm, wound contact, and mucosal retention each impose different constraints, and future competition will depend on whether the design parameters can remain predictable across manufacturing batches and usage environments.
