blocks.text: How do dental implant guides affect placement accuracy?

The implant guide, by fitting itself to the tooth or mucosa, constrains the entry, direction, and depth of the drill hole within a predetermined range. Evaluation requires simultaneous observation of coronal, apical, depth, and angular deviations, taking into account adjacent anatomical structures.
This question distinguishes between the manufacturing error of the surgical guide itself and the actual positional error after implantation.
How do osteotomy guides affect cutting and reconstruction accuracy?

The osteotomy surgical guide delivers the planned cut to the bone tissue and can be used in joint replacement, deformity correction, and tumor resection. It needs to simultaneously meet requirements for fit, accessibility, saw blade movement, and fixation.
The study focuses on the relationship between cutting location, angle, bone volume, and final reconstruction.
How can drill and screw guides improve positioning stability?

The drill and screw surgical guide constrains the entry and direction, and is used in spinal, joint, and multi-ligament reconstruction. Its stability comes from the combined effect of bone surface contact, fixation structure, and guide channel.
The study not only observes whether the screw is within an acceptable range, but also examines how the actual trajectory deviates from the original plan.

These three types of tasks share the "plan-to-patient" transfer chain, but have different error costs. Dental implantation simultaneously serves the restoration location and surrounding bone volume; osteotomy connects bone segments and involves morphology and reconstruction; screws or bone tunnels require maintaining intraosseous access. Research questions should first clearly define the target population, then select measurement tools, and finally determine the threshold that can alter clinical decisions.

The surgical guide is not an operator-independent positioning entity. The contact surfaces, fixation devices, sleeves, and instruments form a set of constraints, and the surgical exposure and loading methods determine whether these constraints function as designed. Rather than abstractly pursuing the highest resolution, a more meaningful task is to identify the most sensitive error directions and ensure they remain under control after manufacturing, sterilization, and intraoperative manipulation.

This direction interprets accuracy as the degree of closeness between the actual result and the target, and repeatability as the degree of dispersion of the results under the same conditions. Both must be reported simultaneously: a stable bias to one side can be improved through correction, while occasional large deviations require identification of contact instability, equipment interference, or process exceptions.
N1 | Mucosal support and measurement references (2021)

A 2021 in vitro edentulous-jaw study used desktop equipment to fabricate mucosa-supported guides and found that mucosal elasticity affected stability and increased implantation deviations. Design must consider how supporting tissue is loaded during use, in addition to static surface geometry. [R01]

The core variable for mucosal support is the shape of the contact surface after loading. The pressure exerted on the guide during scanning may differ from that during drilling, and the fixation pins also alter the pressure distribution. Therefore, evaluation should first determine which surface represents the patient's coordinates before interpreting the relative motion between the guide and the implant. The different registrations observed in the study resulted in varying biases, indicating that the measurement protocol itself is part of the chain of evidence and registration errors should not be inferred from device performance.

Further experiments can be conducted by progressively changing the loading direction and fixing sequence on the same model, repeatedly disassembling and assembling the surgical guide, and simultaneously measuring the rigid body pose of the surgical guide and the borehole axis. If the pose has changed but the borehole axis remains consistent, the measurement reference should be checked; if the surgical guide has not moved but the borehole axis has changed, then the steering sleeve fit and drill bit deflection should be considered. This decomposition delegates the problems to manufacturing spans and clinical workflow nodes.
N2 | Span and manufacturing process (2021–2022)

A commercial-printer study published online in 2021 compared short-span and full-arch guides across five additive manufacturing methods. Short-span guides had higher geometric accuracy in the tested configurations, indicating combined effects of span and equipment parameters. [R02]

The printing accuracy should be interpreted in relation to the relative relationship between the guide channel and the support surface. Even with minimal overall surface deviation, slight warping at the left and right ends of a full dental arch can still cause a seesaw-like contact; single-tooth gap guides may be more constrained by local insertion direction. Therefore, an average surface distance cannot replace mechanical function; the hole shaft, hole diameter, contact area, and connecting arm deformation should be observed simultaneously.

This comparison places the manufacturing process within a specific geometric scale. The next step in designing experiments should fix the material post-processing and scanning methods, then vary the span, wall thickness, and printing orientation to identify truly controllable factors. The most valuable process is not achieving the same error across all surfaces, but rather maintaining stability in clinically hazardous directions while preserving the open space required for cleaning and inspection.
N3 | Separating clinical workflow errors (2024)

A prospective observational study in 2024 analyzed 25 implants, reporting an average origin displacement of approximately 0.71 mm and an angular deviation of approximately 3.34 degrees, and progressively comparing digital design, manufacturing, and surgical outcomes. The study concluded that a significant portion of the deviation stemmed from the surgical procedure, with the learning process also being a contributing factor. [R04]

The significance of this study lies in restoring the final implantation location to a continuous process. The entry point, depth, and angle each correspond to different geometric consequences: translation of the entry point will move the entire implant; angular deviation will amplify with length to the root apex; and depth deviation will alter the relationship between the shoulder and the bone surface. Combining these quantities into a single level of precision will obscure specific areas for improvement.

For finite edentulous spaces where tooth support conditions are relatively clear, it is still necessary to record intraoral scans and image fusion, guide placement checks, and the execution methods for each drilling stage. The study design can plot deviation changes based on the operator's cumulative cases and observe whether adverse outcomes are concentrated under the same support conditions. If manufacturing errors are relatively stable but clinical variability is large, quality improvements should prioritize covering actual procedures.
N4 | Contact location and lateral extensions (2017–2018)

A 2017 online study using a radius model compared different locations with lateral extension designs. The mid-shaft and both ends showed different positioning characteristics; while extension improved some translational errors, it may have increased mid-shaft rotational errors. The relationship between contact area and stability was not a simple linear one. [R06]

The radius, with its near-cylindrical shaft and complexly protruding ends, provides different positioning information. Increasing the contact area is only one way to increase constraint; whether the contact surface has directional characteristics and can prevent axial slippage and rotation around the axis is equally crucial. Lateral extension may also alter the placement path, causing the surgical guide to falsely engage before contacting soft tissue.

Therefore, design optimization should compare both translation and rotation, and should not convert them into a total score without clinical interpretation. The pose distribution obtained from repeated positioning can be projected onto the planning section to predict which rotation is most likely to change the osteotomy thickness. This transformation allows geometric experiments to directly guide the evaluation of knee resection volume and provides a common analytical language for the torsional structure of drill guides.
N5 | Checking resection thickness face by face (2018)

The 2018 knee study compared planned and actual osteotomy thickness in 188 patients and 201 knees. The study translated the geometric effect of the osteotomy guide into an intraoperatively measurable outcome, primarily evaluating osteotomy consistency. [R07]

The osteotomy thickness is the direct endpoint connecting planning and execution, but different sections serve different functions. Distal and posterior condylar resections affect different joint geometry, and similar average thicknesses may arise from local deviations in opposite directions. A reasonable analysis requires retaining signs, absolute values, and large outliers on a section-by-section basis, and specifying whether the measurement includes saw kerf loss or only measures the removed bone fragment.

This node indicates that accuracy evaluation must be closely aligned with the surgical task. Observing the thickness of the removed bone fragment in conjunction with postoperative prosthesis alignment can differentiate between cutting transfer issues and subsequent installation problems. For cases with varying degrees of osteoporosis or residual cartilage, the surgical guide contact model should also match the actual exposed surface during surgery; otherwise, even with correct printing, different cutting heights may still occur.
N6 | Tumor resection-plane errors (2023–2024)

A mandibular-tumor study published online in 2023 included 14 patients and registered preoperative and postoperative models. Mean deviation between planned and actual resection lines was approximately 1.52 mm, bringing resection geometry into evaluation beyond the reconstructed shape. [R09]

In tumor osteotomy, geometric errors are factored into asymmetric consequences: deviation towards the lesion side may alter the resection margin, while deviation towards the normal tissue side increases bone defects and reconstruction difficulty. Therefore, even a one-millimeter deviation cannot be ignored when considering direction, location, and planned safety distance. Preoperative and postoperative registration can show tangential shifts, but it still needs to be considered in conjunction with the pathological resection margin and the length of the reconstructed bone segment.

This node complements the knee joint thickness assessment. The former focuses on joint geometry, while the latter addresses both resection adequacy and reconstructability. In the future, directional deviation maps can be plotted along the entire planned section, simultaneously recording whether the surgical guide is fully fitted, the position of the fixation pins, and the direction of the saw blade entry; this will help identify whether the error occurred during placement, cutting, or bone segment removal.
N7 | Mechanical guidance and navigation (2023)

The 2023 study of condylar osteochondroma compared titanium surgical guides with intraoperative navigation in 21 patients. Both groups were able to approach the planned area relatively well, but the maximum deviations differed, suggesting that the approach method, cutting space, and positioning method all influence the outcome. [R10]

The static surgical guide limits the saw blade movement through a physical surface, while navigation assists the operator in adjustments through a coordinate display; the two serve different informational purposes. The spatial constraints at the condyle make instrument accessibility particularly important: achieving the planned cut and completing a full cut along the planned cut are two issues that need to be verified separately.

Comparative studies should be conducted under conditions of similar lesion morphology, exposure range, and operator experience, while simultaneously observing maximum deviation and operation time. Any need for guide repositioning or navigation re-registration should be included in the workflow. The resulting selection criteria should revolve around whether the fixed plan can be maintained, whether intraoperative adjustments to the cut are necessary, and whether positioning information can be reliably read during critical procedures.
N8 | Iterating drilling structures (2018–2019)

A cervicothoracic study published online in 2018 planned 86 trajectories in five cadavers, iterating from simplified guides to structures with caudal hooks, cross-linked supports and metal inserts. The improved design reduced entry and angular errors, establishing validation from structural modification to actual drilling. [R13]

The drilling surgical guide is not subjected to a single static pressure. Drill bit startup, advance, retraction, and changes in operating angle all generate different torques, and a long guide channel may amplify the inlet force. Hooks and cross-linked structures increase the constraint direction, and the metal sleeve alters the friction and wear-resistant interface; therefore, these changes should be considered as incremental improvements to the mechanical system.

The cadaveric conditions provide a near-realistic scenario for bone surface exposure and instrument manipulation, but further analysis is needed to determine how bone quality, segmental rotation, and adjacent tissues constrain placement. Structural iterations should retain the same trajectory and measurement methods, using repeated loading/unloading and different load directions to interpret outlier trajectories. Subsequently, mature designs should be validated for practical usability in consecutive clinical cases.
N9 | Plan execution and intraoperative conversion (2020–2021)

A clinical study published online in 2020 analyzed 76 guide-assisted trajectories in 15 patients, comparing postoperative CT scans with the planned trajectory. Some originally planned trajectories were not executed as originally intended due to intraoperative decisions or guide design issues, indicating that actual usability is also part of the evaluation. [R14]

The number of planned guide tracks has different meanings from the number of tracks successfully used with the surgical guide. Reducing screws may stem from intraoperative treatment decisions, switching to traditional methods may be related to design or exposure, and bone-related treatments involve patient conditions. Analyzing only completed guide tracks may yield good statistical accuracy, but it cannot answer how many cases were actually used as planned.

Therefore, accuracy and execution rate should be considered as parallel endpoints. Recording the planning, adaptation, drilling, screw placement, and transition status of each trajectory allows for feedback of the causes back to the design team. Case reviews first determine whether modifications to the contact surface or trajectory are needed, and then whether updates to applicable conditions and communication methods are required; this feedback is more helpful for product improvement than repeatedly reporting average errors.
N10 | Collision constraints for multiple tunnels (2026)

A 2026 experimental study on multiple ligaments of the knee compared free hand and patient-specific surgical guides, observing the convergence of multiple femoral tunnels. The surgical guide reduced tunnel conflict during the experiment and improved entry accuracy. The research objective was expanded from a single trajectory to the safety relationship between multiple trajectories. [R15]

Multiligament reconstruction expands the evaluation unit from single-port to the spatial relationship between ports. Even with correct entrances and orientations for each tunnel, they may still intersect within the bone; conversely, to avoid excessive alteration of a tunnel due to impact, it may deviate from the anatomical attachment position that needs to be restored. Therefore, planning should simultaneously maintain the minimum spacing between anatomical targets and channels.

The model control can fix anatomical conditions and observe operator differences, making it suitable for testing the mechanism of combined planning. When transitioning to clinical practice, residual bone volume, fixation methods, and instrument entry sequence should be incorporated. Study endpoints can be divided into four levels: entry deviation, axis deviation, minimum spacing, and actual collision, and then it can be observed whether improvements in these spatial parameters correspond to more reliable fixation and rehabilitation.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: How do dental implant guides affect placement accuracy?

3D Industrial Imaging's DentiqGuide provides dental implant planning and guide design tools. The official manual includes operations such as guide area generation and labeling. The software transforms digital planning into a manufacturable form, representing a design link in the academic error chain. [R05]

The corporate development direction is to connect imaging, intraoral scanning, implant planning, and manufacturing documentation. Clinical studies indicate that these steps still need to be validated together with support and intraoperative procedures; the product's value is ultimately reflected in the reliability of the complete workflow.
A meaningful product comparison should use cases of similar difficulty and similar operating conditions, and document all changes from design to actual implantation.
How do osteotomy guides affect cutting and reconstruction accuracy?

Materialise currently combines osteotomy planning, surgeon confirmation, and Guide Stability Analysis to provide guides for bone deformity correction. Its knee products also incorporate cartilage visualization and different alignment schemes into the planning process. [R11] [R12]

The capabilities have expanded from delivering a printed part to delivering discussed surgical plans and corresponding instruments. Positioning and sectional errors from academic research provide verifiable performance targets for this type of service.

Product differences are more likely to be reflected in the handling of complex cases, design communication, turnaround time, and intraoperative availability, rather than just in the printing materials.
How can drill and screw guides improve positioning stability?

Mighty Oak Medical's FIREFLY pedicle screw-guided product has 510(k) substantial equivalence decisions in the FDA database for 2016 and 2018, demonstrating that patient-specific guided products have entered a clear device pathway. [R16] [R17]

The common foundation of products and research papers from companies is preoperative trajectory planning and patient bone surface localization. Clinical research further answers whether the planning can be practically implemented under complex anatomy and different operational conditions.
Enterprise evaluation needs to combine scope of application, design delivery, and in-process usability, rather than just showing a single success trajectory.

From a product timeline perspective, the FIREFLY regulatory records from 2016 and 2018 provide early patient-specific trajectory guidance nodes; the 2021 DentiqGuide manual showcases the operational interface from digital planning to surgical guide generation; and the current Materialise product documentation places planning confirmation, contact stability, and specialized instruments within the same service. These nodes respectively reflect the product organization methods of dental software, orthopedic planning services, and spinal guidance instruments. [R05][R11][R16][R17]

The essence of an enterprise's delivery capability lies in managing case variability. Dental support, bone surface shape, and surgical exposure cannot be addressed by a uniform guide thickness; designers need to translate these variability into actionable constraints. Product evaluation should therefore simultaneously examine imaging requirements, design communication records, physical acceptance, intraoperative feedback, and version update speed. Only when feedback pinpoints specific design parameters can subsequent improvements be traceable.

sections.title: Key Issues and Validation Methods for translation

blocks.text: How do dental implant guides affect placement accuracy?

The research focus has shifted from the resolution of individual devices to the systemic relationship between support, surgical guide design, and operation. in vitro Manufacturing evaluation and clinical location evaluation have begun to be compared within the same process.

This change means that more precise printing is not the only optimization path. Adaptation checks, fixation methods, sleeve clearance, and personnel training may directly determine whether the preoperative plan can be stably implemented.
How do osteotomy guides affect cutting and reconstruction accuracy?

The academic community is shifting from simple comparisons of "with or without a surgical guide" to analyzing the contact surface, cut surface, and bone fragment location. Different specialties are beginning to use preoperative and postoperative three-dimensional registration, making it easier to track performance deviations.

Another change is that static guides and navigation systems are now being compared in parallel. The research focus is gradually shifting towards which information delivery method is suitable for a particular surgical task, rather than using the same instrument for all scenarios.
How can drill and screw guides improve positioning stability?

The research chain extends from model localization and cadaver drilling to clinical trajectory, and also expands to the relationships between multiple tunnels. Evaluation metrics have also been expanded from screw grading to include entry deviation, 3D angle, and plan execution rate.

This indicates that precision studies are approaching product design: supports, hooks, sleeves, and cross-linking structures are all becoming comparable variables, rather than treating the surgical guide as a single intervention.

The validation can be divided into three consecutive levels. The first level measures the physical errors of the support surface, bore shaft, and groove on a rigid model, fixing manufacturing factors. The second level evaluates the surgical guide pose in repeated positioning and loading tests, incorporating contact and operator factors. The third level compares planned and actual results in clinical settings, while recording unused, repositioned, and converted results. Each level should retain the baseline of the previous level to avoid discovering deviations at the end without being able to pinpoint their source.

Statistically, a hierarchical relationship should be established based on patient, surgical guide, and trajectory. Multiple holes on the same surgical guide are not entirely independent samples, and consecutive operations by the same physician also have experience correlations. The design should report the worst trajectory and the distribution of all trajectories for each patient to avoid a large number of easily completed holes obscuring a few high-risk areas. For navigation or freehand controls, the complexity of the cases should also be comparable to the surgeon's experience.
How do dental implant guides affect placement accuracy?

Near term: In-place verification and process quality control will receive more attention than simply increasing print resolution. This is based on the fact that there are still significant sources of error outside of manufacturing.
Mid-term outlook: Case-condition-driven guide designs may increase. Dental support, bone volume, and intraoral space will play a greater role in design choices.

Observation indicators: repeatability error, coronal and apical deviation, angle and depth, intraoperative modification rate, learning curve, and long-term indicators associated with the repair outcome.
How do osteotomy guides affect cutting and reconstruction accuracy?
Near term: The design of cutting and reconstruction will be expanded. Multiple bone blocks, complex angles, and narrow spaces require more continuous positioning logic.

Interim Stage: The surgical guide may form a task division with navigation. Fixed sections are suitable for mechanical constraints, while steps requiring intraoperative adjustments may utilize more dynamic information.

Observation indicators: cut surface deviation, bone volume error, number of surgical guide repositionings, intraoperative modifications, pathological cut margins or alignment results, and patient functional follow-up.
How can drill and screw guides improve positioning stability?

Near term: Multi-trajectory planning and stability design will be more closely integrated. Especially in surgeries involving small bone volumes, rotational deformities, and multiple tunnels, the relationships between trajectories have direct value.

Interim: Intraoperative adaptation feedback may lead to the next round of design. This is contingent on the continuous recording of conversion reasons and deviations, not just the final successful cases.
Observation indicators: entrance and angle deviation, cortical perforation, tunnel conflict, surgical guide usage rate, reasons for intraoperative conversion and related complications.

A feasible breakthrough by 2027 is to establish in-case, phased error records, enabling companies to obtain execution information beyond the design. This requires hospitals to be able to link postoperative registration results with surgical guide version, fixation method, and reasons for conversion. If only the final image is available without intermediate steps, even with increased data volume, it's difficult to determine whether to improve the printing process or the surgical procedure.

By 2028-2029, joint planning for complex bone surfaces or multi-channel tasks may yield more definite value. Observable indicators include whether reduced multi-track conflicts are accompanied by improved plan execution rates, and whether larger deviations are concentrated and disappear in previously weak scenarios. For simple cases where basic positioning is already stable, research should shift towards delivery efficiency and patient experience, avoiding the direct interpretation of minor geometric improvements as equivalent clinical benefits.

The first priority is to transform clinical failure mechanisms into repeatable trials. Specific scenarios should be selected, focusing on mucosal elasticity, cylindrical bone surfaces, narrow cutting channels, and multiple tunnel intersections, to construct loading and repetitive localization tasks. Experimental results should answer which structural change improved the error in which direction, rather than simply providing a composite score.

The second priority is to compare the clinical interpretability of different error endpoints. Mean deviation, maximum deviation, safety margin encroachment, and plan execution rate are placed in the same consecutive case cohort to observe which indicators best suggest intraoperative modifications or postoperative functional problems. This ensures an acceptance range consistent with the specialty task and reduces apparent inconsistencies between studies due to different endpoints.

The third priority is to study reproducible deliverables. Using the same case data, surgical guides are completed by different designers, production batches, and hospitals to analyze the main sources of discrepancies; subsequently, the effectiveness of standardized validation procedures is assessed. If cross-center reproducibility improves while the mean geometric accuracy remains essentially unchanged, it may still constitute substantial progress, as the clinical value of the product depends on the ability to reliably complete a series of cases.

Prioritize evidence such as reduced error in high-risk areas, improved execution rates in complex cases, and fewer conversion causes. Studies should also simultaneously record additional imaging, design time, and intraoperative preparation to ensure that accuracy improvements are commensurate with resource investment. This leads to task-driven guide engineering: constraining manufacturing and software with specific surgical goals, and continuously refining the design using real-world results.

blocks.text: How do image segmentation and virtual planning affect guide design?

The surgical guide design begins with imaging: tissue segmentation, surface creation, target location selection, and then generation of contact surfaces and guide structures. Each step affects the final relationship between the instrument and the patient's anatomy.
Research focuses on how imagery can become an actionable solution, and how to verify that the digital model does indeed support the required operations.
Where do printing and guide-seating errors arise?

While the surgical guide may closely resemble the CAD design, this does not guarantee that the surgical outcome will perfectly align with the plan. Surface errors, overall translation, rotation, and guide hole orientation all affect different procedures, and the comparison objects should be clearly defined during evaluation.
The study divided errors into three stages: before manufacturing, after manufacturing, and during the procedure, examining how these deviations accumulate or influence each other.
How can guides and navigation systems be combined or compared?

The static surgical guide solidifies the plan into contact surfaces and guide channels, while navigation connects the plan to the real-time positions of the patient and instruments. The former relies on stable positioning, while the latter relies on registration, tracking, and information display.
This research compares the two approaches in fixed cutting, bone-segment repositioning and intraoperative adjustments.

The plan first defines the treatment goal, then encodes the goal as a geometric relationship in the patient's coordinate system. Guides can only execute at clearly defined entry points, directions, sections, or locations; they cannot automatically eliminate the uncertainty of the goal itself. Studies should discuss goal selection, geometric representation, and actual execution separately to avoid considering a precisely executed but poorly chosen plan as a complete success.

Error decomposition requires maintaining a unified coordinate system. When different reference areas are used for image registration, model surface fitting, surgical guide placement, and postoperative measurements, even if the residuals are small, significant deviations may still occur at the target location. Therefore, the report should specify the location and coverage of the reference structure and display the errors near the target separately.

Comparing guides and navigation requires explicit functional boundaries. A workflow may use physical constraints where the plan is fixed and digital information where observation or adjustment is needed. The central questions are which uncertainties can be resolved before surgery, which require intraoperative observation, and how information can pass reliably between them.
N1 | Segmentation and model reconstruction (2021)

The 2021 mandibular reconstruction study established a process around DICOM, CAD, reverse engineering, and printing, and compared model geometry mapping. The study treated data processing as part of manufacturing accuracy, rather than a negligible pre-printing preparation step. [R02]

The boundaries in images are not natural solid surfaces, but rather estimates resulting from the combined effects of resolution, tissue contrast, and segmentation rules. Resampling can improve the continuity of model representation and subsequent processing, but it cannot reconstruct uncollected anatomical information out of thin air. For surgical guides, what is truly sensitive is the local boundary near the contact area and critical structures, rather than whether the entire model appears smooth.

Therefore, original slices and modification records should be retained during the segmentation stage, and local verification should be performed on areas with thin cortex, metal artifacts, and osteophytes. Different personnel can independently generate contact surfaces, and then project the differences onto the surgical guide pose instead of just reporting the model volume. In this way, image processing errors can be directly linked to subsequent positioning and hole axis errors, becoming an assignable design input.
N2 | Soft-tissue surface mapping (2021)

The 2021 breast-conserving surgery study used a breast surface surgical guide created based on MRI tumor extent in a single-center prospective cohort. It demonstrates how imaging lesion information is mapped to the body surface, and also illustrates that intraoperative pathology still contributes to the final resection decision. [R03]

The breast surgical guide reveals difficulties beyond bony localization: the spatial relationship between the outer surface and the internal target changes with body position and tissue stress. Good surface fit only indicates external conformity and cannot guarantee that the internal lesion remains at the same coordinates. Image acquisition posture, arm position, contact pressure, and intraoperative traction should all be incorporated into the same localization model.

This node emphasizes that the planning should be based on the clinical endpoint when selecting validation methods. Lesion boundaries, resection extent, and pathological results serve different purposes; surface geometric measurements cannot replace margin evaluation. Further comparisons of lesion mapping residuals under different patient positions can be made, and it can be examined whether the error changes with breast morphology or lesion depth, thereby determining when additional intraoperative localization information is needed.
N3 | Bone-surface contact and seating (2017–2018)

The radial bone experiment published online in 2017 involved changing the position and lateral extension of the surgical guide on the same bone model. The mid-section surgical guide showed a larger positioning error; extension improved translation but may increase some rotational error. This study indicates that geometrically conformable structures may still exhibit multiple positioning postures. [R08]

The contact surface of the surgical guide determines its rigid body pose in the patient's coordinate system. For approximately axisymmetric bone segments, translation along the axis and rotation about the axis may still have degrees of freedom; complex bone ends, while providing more morphological information, may also require a larger exposure area. A well-designed system should allow unique morphology to participate in positioning while avoiding over-reliance on surfaces that are difficult to expose or easily altered.

If the surgical guide design has only one ideal matching position in the computer, it is still necessary to repeatedly test manually to see if multiple approximately stable positions exist. Measuring the six degrees of freedom deviation of each placement is necessary to determine whether increasing the contact area enhances directional constraints or increases soft tissue interference. This experiment provides a benchmark for subsequent sterilization and storage studies to distinguish between geometric deformation and placement variations.
N4 | Loaded fit after sterilization (2023)

The 2023 study compared the accuracy and positioning of surgical guides before and after steam sterilization. Materials and sterilization processes both affect the results, and the positioning load also alters the fit performance during the experiment. Therefore, the final product quality should reflect its state at the point of preparation for use. [R10]

The gap changes after sterilization are correlated with loading conditions, indicating that "being able to return the model" is not a complete performance endpoint. Larger forces may temporarily reduce the gap or transfer stress to fixed points or weak connections. Evaluation should consider the required positioning force, the post-loading pose, and the recovery after unloading, rather than simply determining whether the model ultimately fits snugly.

From the perspective of error propagation, geometric changes caused by post-processing can be amplified by the support method or absorbed by certain contact areas. surgical guides should be verified under actual use in a fixed state, but batch differences should not be masked by ambiguous manual pressing pressure. Standardized clamping and measurement loads enable repeatable material comparisons and provide a basis for hospital-mandated release checks.
N5 | Coordinate measurements separate deformation sources (2024)

The 2024 study used a coordinate measuring machine to track 22 marker points on a surgical guide, comparing the slicing and resin factors, and repeatedly observing the results during two weeks of storage. End bending primarily reflected deformation caused by printing, with minimal additional displacement during storage. This allowed local orientation errors to be separated from overall surface deviations. [R11]

Using fixed coordinate markers and automatic measurement translates "overall similarity" into the amount of movement of each part in each direction. Global surface fitting may distribute local deformation, making critical hole position errors appear smaller; independent markers help track relative changes in the positions of ends, connection areas, and sleeves. When selecting a coordinate system, its relationship with the actual support area of the surgical guide should be clearly defined.

The storage observations in this study suggest the need to distinguish between the major deformations formed during manufacturing and subsequent minor changes over time. The validation protocol involves repeatedly measuring the same marker after printing, cleaning, post-curing, sterilization, and storage, creating a directed error history. If system warping occurs at a certain stage, adjustments can be made to the support and curing; if the main changes are localized pore size, then compensation and instrumentation should be addressed.
N6 | Tracing errors through clinical stages (2024)

The 2024 dental implant observational study analyzed the design, manufacturing, and surgical results, suggesting that a significant portion of the deviations occurred during the operational phase. Model accuracy needs to be considered in conjunction with placement and instrument usage to determine its practical value. [R05]

The final implantation location can verify the entire system, but it's difficult to automatically pinpoint the key responsible parties. Consistency of the digital model, the quality of the physical surgical guide, and the actual implantation conforming to the plan are three consecutive but not equivalent judgments. Measuring them item by item avoids attributing all deviations to printing and also avoids using operator experience as an unverifiable, general explanation.

Phased retrospective analysis should use corresponding coordinates and error indicators, and retain the case's support type, intraoral space, and sleeve settings. Only when the data before and after are consistently defined can we discuss whether a particular step amplified or mitigated the error. For cases where modifications were made clinically, the plans before and after the modifications should be recorded; otherwise, reasonable treatment adjustments may be misjudged as execution deviations.
N7 | Combining guides and navigation (2019)

The 2019 craniosynostosis study used printed guides and templates to control osteotomy and reshaping in five patients, followed by optical navigation to assist in bone block positioning. The guides and navigation served the functions of mechanical shaping and spatial verification, respectively, demonstrating complementarity rather than simple substitution. [R13]

In skull reconstruction, cutting, shaping, and fixation are not the same positioning task. Guides are suitable for transferring defined cutting lines to the bone, while navigation can continuously display the spatial relationships of bone segments after they have been moved. Both types of tools share a planning model but play a role at different times. The mechanism for their combined use is complementary information transfer, rather than simply adding more equipment.

Research allows for a step-by-step comparison of cut surfaces, bone segment morphology, and final fixation positions to determine the endpoint where each tool contributes. If the error primarily occurs in the final assembly, simply improving the cutting guide's accuracy may have limited effect. Conversely, if the shaping template is inconsistent with the target surface, even correct navigation displaying the correct position cannot eliminate morphological conflicts between bone segments. Process design must respect this division of labor.
N8 | Comparing execution methods for the same task (2023)

The 2023 condylar resection study compared titanium guides with navigation, measuring planned and actual outcomes in 21 patients. Both methods closely approximate the planned outcomes, with differences in maximum three-dimensional deviation. The comparison requires interpretation considering operating space, resection extent, and actual workflow. [R14]

Comparisons of within the same disease and similar surgical approaches are easier to interpret than cross-specialty average accuracy. The mechanical constraints of a guide reduce the need for continuous judgment, while navigation allows for intraoperative path modifications; both rely on accurate registration, but the physical forms and failure modes of registration differ. Comparisons should simultaneously observe planning transfers, repositioning, equipment preparation, and operational accessibility.

If the navigation tracking marker moves, the system display may remain stable while the coordinates have changed; if the surgical guide is padded with soft tissue, its appearance may be close to the design while the cross-section is off. A suitable validation approach is to set independent checkpoints for each technique and compare whether these checks can identify failures. The final choice should be based on whether the task requires adjustments, the exposure conditions, and the team's familiarity with the system.
N9 | Augmented reality verifies seating (2025)

2025 Pelvic Model Study evaluates head-mounted augmented reality-assisted guide placement and osteotomy on ten printed models. Digital displays are used to locate and verify the position, while the solid guide continues to provide cutting constraints. [R15]

In this case, augmented reality provides visual feedback on the surgical guide's positioning, while the mechanical surgical guide continues to provide constraints on the saw blade's direction. This arrangement concentrates digital information on the initial placement step, where deviations are most likely to occur. Research should evaluate the alignment of the virtual overlay, the pose of the physical surgical guide, and the actual osteotomy results separately, avoiding directly equating visual consistency with cut accuracy.

Moving from a printed model to a more surgical environment requires incorporating occlusion, tissue coverage, perspective changes, and operator movement. A practical evaluation of augmented reality should also include the speed of anomaly detection: if the interface can promptly indicate when the guide is not in place, even with limited improvement in average error, it could reduce significant outlier operations. This hypothesis can be verified through pre-set misalignment and blind testing.
N10 | Adjustable guides and real-time feedback (2026)

A 2026 maxillofacial study proposed combining a solid adjustable guide with augmented reality feedback. On a printed mandibular model, anatomical landmarks were registered and HoloLens 2 was used to track and adjust the cut surfaces. The study aimed to alleviate the problem of fixed designs being unable to cope with intraoperative changes. [R16]

The adjustable structure addresses a constraint of static surgical guides: once the plan changes, the original geometry is often difficult to adapt. Combining adjustable joints with digital feedback means that the design goal shifts from replicating a fixed cross-section to reliably setting and locking multiple cross-sections. In this case, the locked stiffness, adjustment resolution, and repeatability error become variables of equal importance to registration.

The validation requires coverage of three states: before adjustment, during adjustment, and after locking, with particular attention to whether loading causes the already aligned surgical guide to shift again. Alignment improvements on the printed model provide a mechanism for validation; subsequent examination of actual reachability can be conducted using cadaver or tissue-covered models. Its development depends on feedback capable of detecting structural drift and adjustment steps that do not introduce time and operational burdens exceeding the surgical benefits.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: How do image segmentation and virtual planning affect guide design?

Materialise's osteotomy service involves discussions between engineers and physicians, protocol confirmation, and stability analysis, creating a collaborative path from image to guide. Its knee platform further provides cartilage visualization and various alignment planning options. [R06][R07]

Early fronto-orbital studies using the product already utilized Materialise SurgiCase-CMF, while current offerings integrate specialty planning and instrument delivery. The observable evolution of the company is an expansion from general-purpose 3D tools to specific surgical workflows.
The software capabilities and clinical judgment are interdependent: automated processing can save operations, but key boundaries, targets and contact areas still need to be clearly identified.
Where do printing and guide-seating errors arise?

Materialise's osteotomy service combines solution confirmation with Guide Stability Analysis, directly addressing placement stability issues. Formlabs' surgical guide material flow integrates printing, cleaning, and post-curing as part of the finished product manufacturing chain. [R06] [R12]

For enterprises, there are two complementary directions: design services reduce in-situ uncertainty, and manufacturing systems reduce material and process variations. Clinical error studies can help both determine where resources should be invested.

Future product comparisons will require more open definition of measurement locations and states to establish a traceable relationship between design accuracy, manufacturing accuracy, and clinical transfer accuracy.
How can guides and navigation systems be combined or compared?

Smith+Nephew also offers the VISIONAIRE patient-matched osteotomy guide and the CORI handheld robotic platform. The former is printed using MRI, X-ray, and physician-engineer planning; the latter emphasizes intraoperative modeling, real-time planning, cutting, and gap assessment. [R17] [R18]

The fact that the same company offers two types of solutions in parallel demonstrates that market demand includes different information processing methods. The surgical guide carries pre-operative decisions into the surgical procedure, while the robot and navigation system add real-time feedback and adjustment capabilities.

The augmented reality hybrid approach in academia proposes the possibility of further combinations, but its model validation and application in existing enterprise products need to be considered separately.

The shift in enterprise roadmaps can be understood through the delivery objects. Planning software initially addresses the organization of models, sections, and instrument geometry; specialized resin workflows incorporate printing, cleaning, and curing into material properties; and interactive surgical systems place some planning decisions intraoperatively. Official documentation from Materialise, Formlabs, and Smith+Nephew presents the interfaces for these three products, respectively. [R06][R12][R18]

For hospitals, clear interfaces determine whether responsibility can be assigned. Design services need to deliver verifiable plans, material flows need to deliver reproducible processing conditions, and navigation or robotic systems need to display interpretable coordinate information on-site. Procurement comparisons should test exceptional scenarios around these interfaces, such as response processes when image updates, surgical guide misalignment, and changes to the original plan are required.

sections.title: Key Issues and Validation Methods for translation

blocks.text: How do image segmentation and virtual planning affect guide design?

Research is progressing from single-case visualization to measurable planning processes. Geometric errors, model processing, and postoperative registration enable the validation of digital designs; soft tissue applications introduce postural and deformation issues.
The development direction is not simply to increase image detail, but to make each step of data processing clearly related to the final surgical task.
Where do printing and guide-seating errors arise?

Research is shifting from single average errors to staged and directional analysis. Coordinate measuring and 3D registration enable the separate discussion of free-end deformation, in-place rotation, and operational deviations.

This also explains why different research results cannot be simply sorted by a single precision number: the comparison objects may be the surgical guide surface, the guide hole position, or the final implantation position, which represent different stages.
How can guides and navigation systems be combined or compared?

Research has moved from asking which technology is more accurate to asking which step needs which constraint or feedback. Combined cranial workflows, augmented-reality-assisted pelvic guide placement and adjustable physical guides illustrate this change.

The evaluation depth has also expanded from geometric deviation to operational flexibility and workflow. Future, more valuable comparisons will be organized by case complexity and task type, rather than grouping all navigation technologies into a single category.

Error budgeting should not simply involve summing the average values of each component. If multiple components shift in the same direction, systemic accumulation may occur; if the error direction is random, the synthesized results will differ. The study can preserve the rigid body transformation matrix and local displacement vectors, estimate the correlation through repeated measurements, and then propagate it to specific hole locations or sections. Ultimately, the spatial distribution should be provided, rather than just a single global value.

The validation protocol should be reviewed in an independent reference system for planning and execution. For example, manufacturing inspection uses calibrated measuring equipment, intraoperative systems use self-registration, and postoperative evaluation uses clearly defined, unaltered bone areas. If planning and acceptance share the same error model, consistency between the two may simply be due to shared biases. The role of an independent reference is to reveal such shared errors and determine whether they affect critical objectives.

In terms of human-computer interaction, blind tasks involving normal, slight, and significant misalignment can be designed to compare the time required for operators to identify errors and the results after correction. Such testing better interprets the value of digital feedback than simply recording the normal process. For adjustable surgical guides, drift after locking should also be measured to ensure that interface prompts correspond to the physical performance.
How do image segmentation and virtual planning affect guide design?

Near term: Planning quality checks will become more task-oriented. Contact surfaces, cutting directions, and avoidance structures will have a more direct impact on design evaluation than the overall model appearance.
Mid-term: Automatic segmentation and manual verification may lead to a clearer division of labor. The condition is that critical errors can be detected, recorded, and passed on to subsequent steps.

Observation indicators: segmentation repeatability, number of planning modifications, design confirmation time, intraoperative fit rate, registration error, and the impact of soft tissue positional changes on positioning.
Where do printing and guide-seating errors arise?
Near term: inspection of critical regions will receive more attention. Guide holes and contact surfaces affect positioning more directly than overall appearance.
Mid-term: Case-level quality documentation could become a service advantage. This is contingent on manufacturing, usage, and post-operative data being continuously stored and used for improvement.

Observation indicators: critical surface deviation, axis error, changes before and after sterilization, repeat placement dispersion, clinical conversion rate, and whether the dominant error has decreased after improvement.
How can guides and navigation systems be combined or compared?

Near term: Combined procedures will be prioritized in complex surgeries that require location verification. They need to demonstrate that the information gained from the additional steps actually improves the procedure.
Mid-term: Adjustable entity constraints may form a new research branch. The key is locking reliability, registration stability, and ease of use during surgery.
Observation indicators: actual section error, registration time, tracking interruption, number of adjustments, personnel learning curve, total process cost, and patient functional outcome.

By 2027, the most actionable advancement will be the integration of local geometry examination into routine case workflows. This requires that design, manufacturing, and clinical processes share symbol definitions and version information; the key performance indicators (KPIs) are whether errors can be identified before reaching the operating room and which processes reduce rework. For data that cannot be accurately mapped to coordinates, increasing the number of cases offers limited value.

The key differentiation in 2028-2029 may lie in adjustability. For complex pelvic and maxillofacial procedures where frequent changes in the slicing plane are required, hybrid guidance methods may be more valuable; for cases with stable plans and clear contact, simple solid guides may continue to be used. The judgment should be based on the success rate of plan modifications, the number of re-registrations, the time spent on key steps, and the actual slicing results, rather than the visual complexity of the interface.

sections.title: Priority Research Tasks and Evaluation Framework

blocks.text: The first task is to create a local error map. Contact areas, guide channels, grooves, and areas adjacent to hazardous structures are selected, and corresponding markers are used in imaging, design, physical models, and postoperative status. The results should indicate at what stage the error occurs, in what direction it propagates, and which parameter adjustment is most likely to be effective.

The second task is to separate soft tissue deformation from rigid body positioning. While bony surfaces can be represented using rigid body pose, tissues such as breast tissue also require consideration of body position and pressure conditions. Studies should select acquisition and placement conditions close to those used in surgery and verify the stability of the relationship between the internal target and the external surface. Different tissue conditions should not be treated with the same surface matching threshold.

The third task is to compare the error recovery capabilities of various guidance methods. Given the same plan, scenarios such as guide misalignment, reference marker movement, or intraoperative target changes are set up to observe whether the team can identify, interpret, and correct the problems. Error recovery quality may be a better differentiator between systems than minute differences in precision under ideal conditions.

The fourth task is to establish a closed loop from research to service. This involves incorporating interim errors, design versions, and reasons for clinical modifications into a traceable record, and regularly analyzing recurring issues. If a product version improves local biases in the model but does not reduce clinical conversions, exposure conditions and workflows should be further examined; if conversions are significantly reduced, cross-personnel and cross-institutional reproducibility should be further validated.

Research priorities should be determined by the magnitude and consequences of uncertainty. Tasks near critical structures, requiring multiple adjustments, or relying on soft tissue morphology should prioritize obtaining independently validated information. For already stable processes, resources should be allocated to weaker interfaces to simultaneously improve overall accuracy and clinical usability.

P4-03.title: Surgical Guide Stability and Safety
P4-03.subtitle: Continuous verification of material handling, geometric preservation, and intraoperative fixation
P4-03.thesis: The stability and safety of the guide plate are determined by the final material handling condition, structural constraints, and patient contact conditions. Manufacturing, cleaning, curing, sterilization, and storage should be validated as a continuous process, and the positioning function should be confirmed under actual loads to ensure that geometric, mechanical, and tissue contact properties correspond to each other.

blocks.text: How do guide materials and structures affect mechanical stability?

Guides experience different loads during seating, fixation, drilling and cutting. Material stiffness governs deformation, span and thickness affect loading, and post-processing changes final performance.
The study links the material properties of standard specimens with the functional stability of actual surgical guides and observes their compatibility with tissue contact requirements.
How do sterilization and storage affect guide dimensions and safety?
From printing to use, surgical guide may undergo cleaning, post-curing, packaging, storage, and sterilization. Each step can affect the geometry, mechanical properties, or surface condition.
The study focuses on how these changes affect adaptation and use, and distinguishes the questions that disinfection, sterilization, and material performance testing each answer.
How do intraoperative fixation and contact surfaces affect guide stability?

Surgical guide stability requires limiting undesirable translation and rotation while maintaining an accessible placement path. Contact area, anatomical features, fixation screws, and intraoperative exposure all contribute to the outcome.
The research focuses on whether the surgical guide can maintain the planned posture from the first positioning to the completion of drilling and cutting.

Stability includes unloaded positioning, retention after fixation, and pose control under drilling loads. Safety involves material contact, treatment effectiveness, and whether geometric failure occurs during operation. These three research questions therefore need to be answered together: materials and structures limit load-bearing capacity; sterilization and storage alter the final state; and intraoperative contact and fixation determine whether these properties can be translated into positioning functionality.

The usability of the surgical guide is limited by several conditions. Too soft a plate may alter tool orientation, while too hard a plate with improper contact may make positioning difficult; excessive coverage may facilitate positioning but hinder exposure and removal. Research should clearly define critical loads, permissible displacements, and necessary operating space, ensuring that material selection and structural design serve the same objective.

This approach uses the final use state as a common benchmark. If geometric scanning, mechanical testing, and cell evaluation occur at different processing stages, the results are difficult to correlate directly. Allocating the same manufacturing batch to different tests and maintaining the same cleaning, curing, sterilization, and storage history allows for a more reliable chain of evidence.
N1 | Post-curing and cellular responses (2017)

A 2017 study compared the effects of Clear and Dental SG resins on cells at different processing stages. Printing and post-curing reduced the impact on cell viability, indicating that the final product state is a better representation of the actual contact material than the raw material name. [R01]

The contact properties of material are gradually formed during printing and post-curing. The study addresses questions at different stages by examining the cellular results obtained from uncured raw materials, initial prints, and final products. Distinguishing these stages helps explain why the same product name cannot substitute for specific cleaning and curing conditions, nor does it represent the same level of treatment for all geometries.

For guides containing narrow channels or varying thicknesses, post-processing accessibility should be incorporated into the design. Evaluation should utilize complete parts that have undergone actual processes or representative hard-to-process areas, combining extraction and direct contact methods to differentiate between releasable components and surface contact effects. The subsequent goal is to link processing conditions, material state, and functional performance, ensuring that biological response and mechanical validation correspond to the same batch of final products.

This logic also aligns material screening with hospital procedures: samples are first prepared using practically feasible post-processing conditions, then cellular and mechanical properties are compared. If cleaning or curing steps need to be changed, the finished product status should be re-examined, and the changes recorded in the corresponding batch. Such comparisons can determine whether the performance stems from the material formulation or from differences in post-manufacturing processing.
N2 | Sterilization and mechanical properties (2022)

A 2022 study tested standard SLA and DLP specimens and complete guides, comparing mechanical properties after disinfection and steam treatment at two temperatures. Heat treatment changed tensile, flexural or load-bearing performance, showing that sterilization is part of the material-processing history. [R03]

Heat treatment can further alter the solidification state and may cause softening, stress release, or dimensional changes, the outcome of which depends on the material and manufacturing process. Therefore, changes in load-bearing capacity cannot be simply summarized as "sterilization damage"; the elastic range, fracture mode, and permanent deformation after loading should be observed separately. The performance of the intact surgical guide is also affected by the geometry of the connecting arm and guide hole.

The standard specimen is suitable for comparing the material itself, while the actual surgical guide reveals the amplification of the load on the structure. Both types of tests should use the same treatment history and be analyzed correspondingly under loads close to the operating direction. If the specimen strength changes little but the surgical guide shifts significantly, geometric deformation and local buckling should be examined; if the shape is maintained but fracture occurs prematurely, attention should be paid to material embrittlement and critical joint areas.
N3 | Loaded fit and deformation (2023)

A 2023 study placed guides on an implant-referenced model before and after sterilization to compare accuracy and fit. Material and sterilization affected results, while seating load also influenced measurements. Free-state scans and actual fit therefore describe different properties. [R09]

This study connects the free form after sterilization with the stress-bearing placement, revealing the significant impact of measurement methods on the conclusions. A larger load reducing the gap does not necessarily mean the surgical guide has returned to its original stress-free shape. The additional load borne by the fixation point and the contact tissue, as well as whether the direction of the guide channel has changed, all need to be examined simultaneously.

For, actual acceptance testing can use displacement curves within the specified loading range, rather than simply measuring whether it is tightly fitted at a single moment. If the surgical guide requires significantly greater force to be in place, it may mean that the deformation has affected the usability window. Using positioning force, post-fixation position, and unloading recovery as a set of indicators can distinguish between acceptable elastic fit and geometric mismatch requiring rework, and prevent operators from habitually masking material differences.
N4 | Local coordinates and storage (2024)

A coordinate measuring machine study conducted in 2024 revealed that the main dimensional deviations of the tested surgical guide were concentrated in the upward bending at the free end. Besides the overall average deviation, localized issues arose with the cantilever and span, requiring evaluation by functional area. [R04]

Local coordinate measurement is suitable for discovering structural problems that are easily hidden by the overall surface average. Upward tilting of the free end indicates that the deformation has direction and spatial distribution, which may change the contact sequence or the sleeve axis. For dental arches or long surgical guides, even end deviations occupying only a small surface area can determine whether wobbling occurs during positioning.

Two-week storage observation of in this experiment mainly showed minor additional changes, which should be distinguished from the initial deviations formed during printing. A more complete design would fix the measurement benchmark, track the same indicators at various time points after processing, and record environmental conditions. If the changes persist over time, further observation should be conducted to see when they stabilize; if they exist from the beginning, priority should be given to optimizing the printing orientation, support, and post-curing.
N5 | Equipment and one-month storage (2025)

2025 SG01 Resin Study: Comparison of three LCD devices, and observation of dimensions after printing, one month of storage, sterilization, and re-storage. Equipment and processing stages both affect the results; even with the same material name, different finished product performances may occur. [R10]

The fact that the same resin yielded different finished products on different equipment illustrates that exposure, light field, support, and post-processing all jointly determine the actual state. Comparing equipment solely based on nominal pixels or layer thickness easily overlooks the degree of polymerization and residual stress. Including a month of storage and sterilization in the same experiment allows for continuous observation of equipment differences throughout the delivery cycle.

For product development, what needs to be defined is the combination of equipment, materials, and processes, rather than a resin name that can be arbitrarily transferred. Results from different geometric specimens should also be interpreted according to functional regions: long spans, pore sizes, and thin walls may have different sensitivities. Validation can be performed by selecting the most unfavorable geometry as representative, and then confirming this representativeness using a real surgical guide, reducing the burden of repeating the entire experiment for each case.
N6 | Hospital workflows and ten materials (2025)

A 2025 study compared the dimensional changes of extruded polymers from ten materials after cleaning, disinfection, and hospital sterilization processes, using a tibial osteotomy guide incorporating freeform surfaces and fine features. The materials' thermal response and hygroscopic properties jointly influenced the results. [R05]

Hospital processing involves continuous chemical contact, humidity, and temperature exposure to the printed material, which may alter the material's quality ranking immediately after printing. The study uses a real osteotomy surgical guide, allowing freeform surfaces and fine features to participate in the evaluation. The local maximum deviation and the overall root mean square error after processing carry different information; both should correspond to the contact and grooving functions.

Material screening should first determine the stable processing conditions that the hospital can perform, and then compare geometric retention and mechanical properties under those conditions. If a material requires additional equipment or special packaging, its delivery cost and process consistency should also be taken into account. Subsequent comparisons of multiple items within the same batch and across batches can be added to determine whether the observed changes are repeatable systematic shifts or unpredictable discrete deformations.
N7 | Bone-surface location and positioning ambiguity (2017–2018)

A 2017 online study using a radius model compared proximal, midshaft, and distal contact and found that positional changes resulted in positioning errors. Lateral extension improved some indicators, but midshaft rotational errors may increase, suggesting that the identification characteristics of the contact surface are more important than the area itself. [R11]

The positioning features provided by the bone surface are directional. Smooth bone shafts may allow rotation, and prominent protrusions can improve identification, but may also cause insertion interference. Increased contact area does not necessarily translate to a proportional increase in stability; the real goal is to constrain key degrees of freedom with exposed structures and make it difficult for erroneous locations to form stable contact.

Design validation should include blinded repeatable positioning, allowing different operators to find a stable position without relying on pre-defined posture cues. After measuring the error distribution, it can be determined which contact structure is most prone to causing directional ambiguity. When connecting to material nodes, it is also necessary to check whether slight warping after sterilization alters the contact sequence, as geometric changes may transform what was originally a unique positioning state into multiple approximately stable positions.
N8 | Supports and metal sleeves (2018–2019)

A spinal cadaver study published online in 2018 improved simplified guides by adding hooks, cross-linked supports and metal inserts. Drilling accuracy improved, directly linking structural support to functional stability.[R02]

In spinal drilling, stability derives from the synergy of bone surface support, connection stiffness, and the tool interface. Cross-linked structures alter the relative motion between the left and right sides, hooks increase anti-slip constraints, and metal sleeves affect wear resistance and instrument fit. These changes correspond to different failure mechanisms, and a comparative design, either item-by-item or in groups, is necessary to determine which factor truly reduces trajectory deviation.

For drilling, the actual drilling process should record the advance, retraction, and eccentric loading processes, not just the position before and after the operation. The surgical guide may experience a brief displacement during operation and then recover; static inspections may miss this change. Connecting the instantaneous pose to the final hole axis allows identification of the roles of flexible deformation, contact slippage, and sleeve clearance, providing a direct target for structural optimization.
N9 | Mucosal support under pressure (2021)

A 2021 in vitro edentulous-jaw study showed that mucosal elasticity affected guide stability. Displacement of soft tissue under pressure created differences between the statically scanned surface and the loaded state.[R12]

Soft tissue support allows for a deformable interface between the surgical guide and the patient. While the surgical guide itself is rigid enough, it cannot guarantee maintaining the same position under varying degrees of pressure. The order of the fixation pins, the operator's pressure direction, and mucosal thickness all affect the contact state; therefore, loading and support conditions need to be clearly defined in stability experiments.

A rigid support model can be paired with a controllably elastic covering layer, keeping the surgical guide geometry unchanged while gradually changing the interface conditions. If the error changes significantly with the elasticity of the microstructure, priority should be given to optimizing the fixation and stress distribution; if similar deviations occur under different interfaces, then the focus should return to manufacturing or sleeve factors. This comparison avoids conflating material stiffness with overall stability.
N10 | Bone support and cochlear receiver beds (2022)

A 2022 cadaveric study of cochlear implantation used nine head specimens and eighteen ears to locate the stimulator's bone bed using a surgical guide with bone support and screw fixation. Different deviations were observed in different directions, suggesting that three-dimensional translation and rotation still need to be checked after fixation. [R13]

The positioning of the bone bed for the cochlear receiver stimulator requires simultaneous control of spatial position and orientation. Deviations in different directions persist even after screw fixation, indicating that while fixation reduces free movement, it cannot eliminate differences between the placement, bone bed preparation, and device installation stages. The surgical guide position, bone bed preparation, and final implant position should be checked sequentially to identify at which step the error occurred.

This study brings the principle of bone support to new anatomical and instrumentation tasks. As we move towards clinical application, flap exposure, bone surface curvature, and implant morphology can all alter the actual procedure. Evaluation should preserve deviations and outliers in all directions and observe whether fixation affects removal and subsequent installation. The ultimate goal is to establish a system that is both stable and easy to perform, rather than simply increasing the number of fixation points.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: How do guide materials and structures affect mechanical stability?

Formlabs' Surgical Guide Resin clearly links compatible printing equipment, cleaning, post-curing, and sterilization processes. The company documentation describes material properties under specified manufacturing conditions, reflecting the complete product form based on the entire process combination. [R06]

Materialise provides stability analysis on the design side and provides an instruction manual entry point for the osteotomy guide. Material processing and patient contact design together constitute the device delivery. [R07] [R08]

Competition among companies therefore involves materials support, manufacturing consistency, and design services. For hospitals or manufacturing partners, repeatable processes are just as important as single-batch material specifications.
How do sterilization and storage affect guide dimensions and safety?

Formlabs provides manufacturing guidelines and usage instructions for surgical guide resins, including connection equipment compatibility, cleaning, post-curing, and applicable sterilization processes. Materialise's osteotomy guide instructions are available in region-specific versions. [R06][R08]

The value of a company's products lies in organizing processing conditions into executable processes, enabling different manufacturing sites to achieve the expected final state. Both hospital production and centralized delivery require the management of processing records and storage cycles.
The market comparison should therefore extend from material prices to process stability, documentation support, and delivery qualification rate.
How do intraoperative fixation and contact surfaces affect guide stability?

Materialise's osteotomy guide service explicitly includes Guide Stability Analysis, designed directly around patient bone surface adaptation. Mighty Oak's FIREFLY regulatory record shows that patient-specific screw-guided devices have formed a product roadmap. [R07] [R16]

The two types of enterprise capabilities respectively highlight patient anatomical design and specialized instrument delivery. Academic research provides interpretations between contact, fixation, and trajectory, enabling products to select structures based on different anatomical sites.
More valuable enterprise data includes duplicate positioning, intraoperative availability, and reasons for design modifications, which reflect true adaptability.

The company roadmap can be observed along three levels: material package, instrument design, and instructions for use. The 2017 resin research brought the then-current Clear and Dental SG materials into cell experiments; the current Formlabs Surgical Guide Resin data connects the materials with specified post-printing processing. Materialise's 2021 instructions for use specifically specify surgical guide adaptation, fixation, sawing fit, and processing requirements; the current product page continues to emphasize contact stability analysis. [R01][R06][R07][R08]

The resulting product capability is the transformation of design freedom into a controlled scope. Which contact areas must be retained, which channels require metal sleeves, and which structures can be adjusted for patient needs should all correspond to validation criteria. For hospital production, equipment availability is only the starting point; cross-batch consistency and delivery records determine whether the same quality guides can be consistently provided.
