sections.title: Key Issues and Validation Methods for translation

blocks.text: How do guide materials and structures affect mechanical stability?

The study is connecting material samples, overall device, and functional outcomes. Early cellular and material testing highlights the importance of the processing phase, while subsequent surgical guide loading and real-world geometric evaluation bring it closer to clinical use.

The development focus has shifted from "which material is the strongest" to "which material-structure-process combination can maintain positioning." Different surgical tasks have different weights for stiffness, transparency, thermal stability, and operability.
How do sterilization and storage affect guide dimensions and safety?

The academic approach has evolved from simple comparisons before and after sterilization to combined analyses of equipment, materials, processes, and time. Actual surgical guide geometry and in-situ measurements further enhance the application value of the results.

The dimensional retention of material needs to be described in conjunction with its specific geometry, handling conditions, and storage life. The next step is to establish a validation scope covering the actual delivery cycle, identifying which structures are most susceptible to change.
How do intraoperative fixation and contact surfaces affect guide stability?

Research focus is shifting from expanding the contact surface to understanding the geometry and stress conditions of the contact area. Bone surfaces, mucosa, and complex, narrow locations present different design challenges.

Meanwhile, clinical studies began to include scenarios where the system was unusable or required conversion. Therefore, stability evaluation extended from experimental error to its feasibility in real-world workflows.

An executable verification sequence is to first establish the geometric baseline, then perform the actual hospital procedure, followed by repeated scanning and load application. Mapping local deviations to the guide shaft and cross-section can convert minor deformations into clinically interpretable spatial errors. If mismatches are found, permanent deformation, elastic indentation, and surface residue should be differentiated, as each requires different corrective measures.

Material validation also needs to cover the most unfavorable geometric conditions. The thickest areas may be more difficult to homogenize, the longest cantilever may be more prone to warping, and the narrowest channels may be more difficult to clean. Representative specimens should come from these structures, rather than simply choosing flat plates that are easy to measure. Fabricating guides of varying difficulty using the same material can verify the reliability of inferences from specimens to real instruments.

The stability measurement increases temporal resolution. It continuously tracks the pose during the drilling process, observing whether instantaneous displacement occurs during load increases, drill retraction, and tool switching. If the surgical guide position eventually recovers but the hole axis has changed, static forward and backward scans may underestimate the problem. Corresponding dynamic displacement to actual machining results allows for a more direct identification of structural components requiring reinforcement.
How do guide materials and structures affect mechanical stability?
Near term: Functional testing of actual surgical guide geometry will increase. Free ends, channels, and thin areas require more targeted evaluation than general-purpose specimens.
Mid-term: Co-design of materials and structure may reduce excessive thickening. The condition is that the predicted stress and deformation match the actual measurements after final processing.
Observation indicators: loading displacement, trajectory change, failure mode, stiffness and size after sterilization, consistency of critical areas, and space required for placement and operation.
How do sterilization and storage affect guide dimensions and safety?
Near term: Post-processing critical dimension acceptance will become more common. This is a direct way to translate materials research into operational reliability.
Mid-term: Delivery time and storage conditions may cause product variations. This is contingent on the ability to jointly verify dimensions, packaging, and handling conditions.

Observation indicators: changes in guide holes and contact surfaces before and after sterilization, mechanical retention, storage time, batch rework rate, placement failure, and completeness of process records.
How do intraoperative fixation and contact surfaces affect guide stability?
Near term: contact-surface design will emphasize distinctive positioning features. Reducing alternative possible poses should improve repeated-seating consistency.
Mid-term: Intraoperative feedback will be used more for design iteration. This is on the premise that the reasons for exposure, fixation, and transformation are structurally documented.

Observation indicators: repeated placement error, displacement under load, number and location of fixation points, soft tissue interference, actual usage rate and number of intraoperative repositionings.

In 2027, validation of the materials and process combination may become the most direct area for improvement in hospital manufacturing. This requires that production and sterilization supplies share a clearly defined version of the processing procedure and that critical dimensions are checked on complete parts. Observable metrics include post-processing rework rate, distribution of in-place forces, and geometric dispersion between different batches.

By 2028-2029, design software is expected to more clearly address contact uniqueness and deformation under load. Its value needs to be verified through repeated placement and dynamic drilling of real surgical guides, rather than simply through simulation diagrams. If predictions can identify existing failure cases and reduce clinical conversions, then the model has captured the key mechanisms; if predictions are out of sync with reality, the assumptions regarding contact and material states should be revised first.

sections.title: Research Priorities and Continuous Evaluation Indicators

blocks.text: The first priority is to establish supporting evidence for the final product. For each combination of materials, equipment, and treatments, local geometry, mechanical function, and contact material evaluations should be simultaneously developed. All tests should use a consistent treatment history so that variations in one stage can be interpreted in other stages, and to clarify which results apply to which guide geometry.

The second priority is quantifying the uniqueness of placement. Different operators repeatedly place the surgical guide within the actual exposed area, recording the position distribution, required pressure, and drift after fixation. The focus is on observing whether multiple seemingly stable positions exist and which structural changes can eliminate this ambiguity. This task directly connects the design software with clinical use.

The third priority is to measure the load throughout the entire process. Drilling, cutting, and continuous traction each have different stress modes and cannot be uniformly replaced by a single static fracture load. Displacement and tool orientation during critical operations should be recorded first, and then the material stiffness, wall thickness, connection method, or sleeve settings should be adjusted accordingly.

The fourth priority is to study the delivery cycle. Incorporate changes in storage time, packaging support, transportation, and surgical scheduling into representative validation, and check whether the surgical guide still meets the original geometry in actual use. For combinations with minor variations, a simple routine acceptance can be established; for time-sensitive combinations, materials or handling strategies should be reselected.

The continuous evaluation should simultaneously include local maximum deviation, repeatability dispersion, in-situ force, post-treatment mechanical changes, and actual conversion causes. This set of indicators connects materials science, structural design, and clinical feedback. If an improvement only increases specimen strength but does not improve positioning under load, interface constraints should be further investigated; if improved stability compromises operating space, structural objectives need to be rebalanced.

P4-04.title: Clinical Workflows and Outcomes
P4-04.subtitle: Stratified Evidence for Efficiency, Precision, and Functional Outcomes: Cross-Specialty Clinical Comparison
P4-04.thesis: Surgical guides can provide three distinct types of benefit: geometric control, operative efficiency and patient outcomes. Comparative studies show that these benefits do not necessarily occur together. Evaluation should combine patient selection, learning, whole-workflow resources and actual utilization to identify the surgical tasks best suited to guides.

blocks.text: Can surgical guides reduce operating and fluoroscopy time?

The surgical guide may reduce intraoperative probing, repeated fluoroscopy, and temporary shaping, but it also increases the steps of positioning, fixation, and verification. The key research focus is on which tasks are eliminated, which are brought forward, and whether the added steps offset the savings.
The duration of surgery, duration of anesthesia, number of fluoroscopy sessions, radiation dose, and preparation time for the entire case are different indicators and should be explained separately.
How do guide-assisted and conventional surgery compare in outcomes?

The surgical guide primarily affects positioning and cutting, and only then can it influence implant placement, tissue damage, healing, and quality of life. Research needs to clarify the causal connections at each step to avoid using a single postoperative angle to represent the overall treatment outcome.
The study focuses on comparisons with conventional surgery, emphasizing the distinction between geometric outcomes, perioperative burden, and long-term patient outcomes.
How do guides perform in actual use across specialties?
Patient-specific guides serve different goals in drilling, bone cutting, sampling and reconstruction. Contact sites, exposure, fixation and soft-tissue interference alter their actual effects.
The study placed real-world applications within specific surgical procedures to observe when the surgical guide could successfully complete its task and when adjustments or replacements were needed.

The three original questions can be organized into a clinical decision chain. First, identify which operational steps the guide alters; then examine whether these changes produce measurable time, imaging, or accuracy benefits; finally, observe whether the benefits are meaningful for patient recovery. Different specialties have different goals, but this mechanism-to-outcome evaluation sequence can be used for all of them.

Surgical time should include clearly defined start and end points. The time from skin incision to suturing, bone manipulation, anesthesia time, and operating room occupancy reflects different resources; the number of fluoroscopy sessions, exposure time, and dosage also carry different information. These definitions must be clearly defined in the study design to ensure the results can be used for hospital scheduling and cost analysis.

Case complexity is an important context for evaluation. Patient-specific devices are more likely to prove effective in tasks where routine positioning is difficult, spatial relationships are complex, or multiple confirmations are required. Therefore, comparisons should define anatomical and procedural characteristics in advance, investigate which patients gain incremental benefits, and whether these benefits change with team experience.
N1 | Complex fractures and incremental value (2021)

The 2021 study of intra-articular radius fractures used patient-specific instruments in 7 patients. Postoperative joint step and space improved, but the researchers believed the benefits were insufficient to offset the additional investment. This suggests that even if individualized localization techniques are feasible, their incremental value relative to conventional methods needs to be demonstrated. [R08]

There is a significant difference between geometric restoration and procedural benefits in complex fractures. While the location of fragments can be described by digital models, the ability to move, reduce, and fix them in the same sequence during surgery depends on soft tissue connections and exposure conditions. Case series are well-suited for uncovering these implementation details, translating "planning feasibility" into "which steps during surgery are challenging."

This study included additional input as part of clinical judgment, suggesting that evaluation should record design and manufacturing wait times, as well as the additional work the surgeon incurs for the adapter. The next step could be to set up comparison groups according to fracture complexity and time requirements, and pre-define the rotational deformities most likely to benefit. If a subgroup shows more significant geometric improvement and the preparation time can be absorbed by surgical scheduling, its application value may differ from the average of all cases.

The study should also include patient waiting time in the outcome. For fractures requiring immediate treatment, the delivery cycle itself influences the choice of treatment plan; for elective orthopedics, there is more opportunity to complete design communication and validation. The value of the same technology can therefore change in the two processes.
N2 | Preoperative organization of maxillofacial reconstruction (2022–2024)

A maxillofacial reconstruction study,, published online in 2022 and in the journal in 2024, compared 13 patients, 8 of whom used virtual planning and printed cutting guides, and 5 of whom used conventional methods. The small-scale series reports reduced surgical time. Its workflow pre-determines fibular segmentation and cutting locations, reducing intraoperative remeasurement and adjustments. [R01]

Fibular flap reconstruction involves donor site cutting, recipient site resection, and multi-segment assembly. Preoperative planning can complete in advance some spatial reasoning and measurements. The time-saving mechanism should be examined through staged recording, such as separately measuring the time spent on cutting, segment positioning, and fixation, to determine which part is truly affected by the surgical guide.

The two groups of cases have relatively small numbers, and comparisons need to retain specific conditions such as defect extent, number of bone segments, and team configuration. A more interpretable subsequent design would be to continuously record cases from the same team and stratify complexity. Intraoperative time, ischemic time, and preoperative time each have different meanings; presenting them separately allows us to determine whether the savings come from work transfer, proficiency in procedures, or substantial improvements in geometric positioning.

For hospital resource evaluation, preoperative tasks can often be completed in parallel, while operating room time is more difficult to extend. Research can use this to calculate the actual input of different positions and observe whether additional procedures, delays, or redundant preparations should be reduced, so that efficiency gains correspond to specific service capabilities.
N3 | Foot osteotomy and imaging frequency (2023)

The 2023 study on rigid clubfoot included 20 patients and 25 feet. The surgical guide group had shorter operation time and fewer radiological examinations, but no significant difference in final functional scores between the groups. This suggests that efficiency gains can precede measurable functional differences. [R02]

Rigid foot deformities involve multiple joints and osteotomy surfaces. The surgical guide transforms the spatial plan into a predetermined operational sequence, potentially reducing repeated measurements and confirmations. Functional recovery is simultaneously influenced by soft tissue condition, fusion, and rehabilitation; therefore, the discrepancies in surgical time and functional scores have an explainable mechanism.

The study design should further break down the number of imaging examinations into exposure time, dosage, and examination purpose. A single image taken to confirm the final correction and a repeated examination due to surgical guide misalignment reflect different procedures. For patients with both feet, the correlation within the same patient should also be considered to ensure that the statistical units are consistent with the actual treatment subjects.

Further validation can be stratified according to the main plane and severity of the deformity to check whether the time benefit is concentrated in multi-planar correction. If conventional methods are already efficient in simpler cases, the incremental value of the surgical guide may mainly appear in cases with more planning difficulties and repeated intraoperative confirmation.
N4 | Prospective high tibial osteotomy comparison (2025)

The 2025 prospective study of high tibial osteotomy randomly assigned 30 patients to different groups. Reports indicated reduced operation time and intraoperative radiographic exposure, but no corresponding advantage in corrective effect or functional outcomes. Time savings and treatment efficacy are two separate outcome chains that need to be validated. [R04]

High tibial osteotomy has a clear corrective goal and a relatively standardized procedure, making it suitable for comparing surgical resources and patient recovery simultaneously. Prospective randomized studies, measuring time and imaging exposure separately from correction and function, suggest that the value of the guide may primarily lie in its efficiency. For resource-constrained day procedures, this benefit needs to be evaluated in conjunction with delivery costs.

Further research should use the same imaging plan, fixation protocol, and rehabilitation pathway to minimize variability beyond the implementation tools. Correction angles should be reported simultaneously with target values, actual values, and outlier distributions; function should be observed at pre-defined time points, and preoperative levels should be recorded. This allows for assessment of whether similar average results mask the reduction in complex cases or poorer outcomes.

The evaluation should also track cancellations, postponements, and temporary conversions. If the saved intraoperative time is offset by production wait times, service capacity may not necessarily improve; however, if production is stable and intraoperative fluctuations are reduced, scheduling may become more predictable, creating another quantifiable benefit.
N5 | Randomized instrument comparison in total knee arthroplasty (2024)

The 2024 randomized trial of total knee replacement enrolled 102 patients, with both groups using AI-assisted preoperative planning. The patient-specific instrument group showed improvements in partial osteotomy and alignment parameters, but the operation time was longer. The surgical guide did not automatically eliminate the time required for learning, placement, and examination. [R03]

Both groups underwent AI-assisted planning, making the comparison closer to the independent contribution of the executing device. Improvements in partial sections and alignment, coupled with increased operation time, suggest that more precise execution may be accompanied by new inspection and placement steps. Pairing these two types of results helps in understanding the actual performance of the product during the learning and process integration phases.

The total time should be broken down into surgical guide exposure, fitting, fixation, cutting, and routine supplementary steps, and adjusted according to the cumulative number of cases observed. If the additional time mainly occurs in the initial learning phase, the benefits for experienced teams may differ; if it comes from necessary steps added by the device itself, then optimization of the structure or process is needed.

Regarding patient outcomes, the role of geometric improvement should be observed through appropriate follow-up. Pain, function, complications, and reoperation each have different mechanisms of formation. Short-term geometric outcomes can serve as intermediate endpoints, and a clearer patient selection rule can only be formed after establishing a link with long-term recovery.
N6 | Unicompartmental replacement and functional signals (2026)

A retrospective study of unicompartmental knee arthroplasty in 2026 compared 22 patients (25 knees) in the surgical guide group with 25 patients (31 knees) in the conventional group, reporting better prosthesis alignment, partial scores, and range of motion. The retrospective comparison suggests areas worthy of further investigation; case selection and team experience still need to be controlled in future prospective designs. [R10]

Unicompartmental knee arthroplasty preserves more of the original joint structure. Its instrument entry space and alignment targets differ from total knee arthroplasty, making it suitable for establishing evidence independently. Retrospective studies showed simultaneous improvement in some geometric and clinical parameters, providing a clear hypothesis for subsequent prospective comparisons: whether improving placement consistency in key directions can reduce poor recovery outcomes.

Validating this hypothesis requires comparable case selection, surgeon experience, and rehabilitation pathways, and pre-defining the primary endpoint. For bilateral knee cases, intra-patient correlations should be addressed; for multiple scoring and imaging parameters, primary and exploratory outcomes should be distinguished. The focus should be on the magnitude and persistence of improvement, and whether it is concentrated in patients who were initially difficult to locate.

This node is compared with a task-based randomized trial of total knee arthroplasty. Both results suggest that the clinical role of surgical guides varies with surgical technique, objective, and implementation method. Product development can use this information to select the scenario with the most mechanistic plausibility and then conduct targeted validation.
N7 | Execution rates of spinal trajectories (2020–2021)

The clinical study, published online in 2020 and in the journal in 2021, used a patient-specific spinal guide in 15 patients, implementing 76 guide tracks. Some planned tracks were modified due to design or other practical conditions. Guide track usage and mid-track switching are important clinical information in addition to accuracy. [R12]

The plan execution rate reveals the actual usage process beyond accuracy statistics. Some trajectories are cancelled due to changes in treatment decisions, and others are changed due to guide design or intraoperative conditions; both should be recorded separately. Reporting the accuracy of actual completed trajectories using the entire plan as the denominator provides a comprehensive answer to both delivery availability and technical performance.

Continuous case registration can retain the design approval, fitting, drilling, and screw placement status for each trajectory, recording the timing and reason for any changes. This allows for determining whether the problem arose during preoperative communication, contact with the design, or on-site. For cases where guides were not used, the final outcome should still be tracked to ensure that selective success does not obscure the entire process.

Data is also suitable for feedback to companies. If the changes are concentrated on the same bone surface or segment, the design team can modify the structure; if they mainly come from changes in the plan, preoperative discussions and backup plans should be improved to make the product more suitable for actual treatment decisions.
N8 | Evaluating mandibular biopsy access (2022)

The 2022 study of jawbone lesion biopsies involved guide-guided procedures in 8 patients, with freehand manipulation compared to corresponding printed jawbone models. Orientation and axis deviations improved, while depth differences were not significant. The study structure included both clinical feasibility and model comparison, with these two types of results addressing the questions of use and localization, respectively. [R13]

The endpoint of a biopsy includes both reaching the intended location and obtaining tissue sufficient for diagnosis. The clinically guided and model-based freehand controls in the study provide real-world operational and geometric comparisons, respectively; the experimental environment of both should be preserved during analysis. Improvements in orientation and axis while the difference in depth is not significant indicate that the constraints on different degrees of freedom are not the same.

Further research could compare sampling adequacy, repeat biopsies, protection of adjacent structures, and operation time, and clarify whether the model includes soft tissue and actual instrument access limitations. For small lesions or access to adjacent tooth roots, directional improvement may be more meaningful; for deep targets, depth control and tissue deformation may become the main variables.

From a cross-disciplinary perspective, this study illustrates that "precision" must be defined according to the task. Screws focus on intraosseous trajectory, while biopsies focus on effective sampling location. Although both share guiding structures, clinical evaluation still needs to be established separately around their ultimate goals.
N9 | Condylar guides and navigation (2023)

A 2023 study of condylar resection in 21 patients compared titanium guides and navigation, measuring the deviation between the actual resection and the planned resection. Both methods closely approximated the planned resection, but the maximum deviations differed, suggesting that tool selection should also consider the operating space and the need for real-time adjustments. [R14]

Both the navigation and physical guides incorporate preoperative planning into the surgery, but rely on real-time coordinate feedback and mechanical constraints, respectively. The spatial limitations of condylar resection make the accessibility, repositioning, and adjustment capabilities of both methods directly significant. Comparisons should include actual incision deviations along with these steps to explain the origins of accuracy differences.

The study could further stratify tasks based on similar lesion extent and surgeon experience. When the plan is stable and clear bone support is available, physical constraints may simplify execution; when adjustments to the cutting plane or guide placement are required, dynamic information may offer greater flexibility. Selection criteria should be based on case conditions and observable execution outcomes.

This node converges on two paths: efficiency and availability. The most suitable technology should enable the team to identify and correct anomalies in a timely manner while maintaining the target profile. Therefore, the endpoint of comparison should also include error recovery time, temporary conversions, and patient outcomes, rather than simply looking for the minimum average deviation under ideal conditions.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: Can surgical guides reduce operating and fluoroscopy time?

Materialise's osteotomy guide service connects preoperative planning with patient-matched instruments, while its knee joint service revolves around standardized surgical preparation procedures. Smith+Nephew VISIONAIRE also utilizes imaging and physician confirmation to generate patient-matched guides. [R05] [R06] [R07]

These products move some work forward in the supply chain. The value of procurement should be judged by case delivery time, number of plan revisions, instrument tray requirements, and actual intraoperative savings, rather than simply by the "individualized" name used to describe efficiency.
How do guide-assisted and conventional surgery compare in outcomes?

VISIONAIRE and Materialise knee joint solutions exemplify a commercial pathway for patient-matched devices; CORI offers another approach through intraoperative mapping and robot-assisted manipulation. [R07] [R06] [R11]

These routes revolve around similar positioning goals, but differ in the required imaging, preoperative preparation, and intraoperative adjustments. Enterprise evaluations should be based on the same surgical procedures and clinical endpoints to further identify which workflow is suitable for which hospital.
How do guides perform in actual use across specialties?

Mighty Oak’s FIREFLY regulatory records show a product pathway for patient-matched spinal guides. Materialise provides osteotomy and knee-planning services, with commercial delivery organized by procedure. [R15][R16][R05][R06]

The common capabilities across different services are image processing, planning communication, and custom manufacturing; the differences lie in access to anatomy, instrument interfaces, and clinical validation. The latter determines whether a capability can be transferred across specialties.

The product evolution manifests in different clinical organizational routes. FIREFLY established patient-specific trajectory-guidance regulatory milestones in 2016 and 2018; Materialise provides preoperative planning and guide delivery; Smith+Nephew simultaneously presents VISIONAIRE preoperative matching instruments and CORI intraoperative interactive planning routes. They respectively configure decisions and constraints preoperatively or intraoperatively. [R05][R07][R11][R15][R16]

The competitive dimensions of enterprises extend from geometric functions to case turnover, plan validation, and field support. For complex reconstructions, delivery stability can reduce ad-hoc adjustments; for standardized joint procedures, instrument preparation and team learning may be more important. Product evaluation should correlate these service links with specific clinical endpoints, enabling hospitals to determine which types of cases are most effective for investment.

sections.title: Specific Connections Between Academia and Enterprise

blocks.text: Can surgical guides reduce operating and fluoroscopy time?

Academic research provides a method for identifying applicable scenarios: if the main bottleneck is complex cutting and positioning, pre-designed constraints are more likely to reduce repetitive operations; if routine procedures are already highly proficient, the placement and verification of new instruments may increase the number of steps.
Companies can organize validation by procedure and experience level, incorporating plan revisions, failed seating and conversion to conventional instruments into workflow improvement.
How do guide-assisted and conventional surgery compare in outcomes?

A key academic contribution is linking commercial technical performance to clinical use: more accurate osteotomy provides mechanistic evidence, whereas patient recovery and reoperation establish therapeutic value.

Comparative studies can also help companies choose their service scope. For routine cases, process costs may be more critical; for complex malformations, control at specific angles or locations may be of greater value.
How do guides perform in actual use across specialties?

Failed seating, conversion to alternative trajectories and functional differences reported in papers directly inform commercial interfaces and service boundaries. Expansion across specialties can reuse manufacturing and quality systems while validating contact geometry, instrument channels and actual loads for new operative goals.

sections.title: Key Issues and Validation Methods for translation

blocks.text: Can surgical guides reduce operating and fluoroscopy time?

The research framework has evolved from "whether surgical guides can speed up a certain step" to "whether efficiency is accompanied by equal or better results." The different outcomes observed in complex reconstructions, foot osteotomies, and knee replacements indicate that the measurement burden of the surgical procedure itself, the team's experience, and the instrumentation process all determine the benefits.
The more valuable change is that it reports time, accuracy, and functionality simultaneously, allowing efficiency to be interpreted as specific process improvements.
How do guide-assisted and conventional surgery compare in outcomes?

Academic evaluation is expanding from "whether it can get closer to the preoperative plan" to "whether this closeness changes the patient outcome." Positive and neutral outcomes from different surgical procedures collectively demonstrate that the advantage of the surgical guide depends on whether the original error has already affected the treatment and whether the improvement is sufficient.
Future explanatory studies will report on the process, geometry, and patient outcomes simultaneously, and retain long-term follow-up.
How do guides perform in actual use across specialties?

The expansion of the surgical guide research is not about replicating a universal device across different organs, but rather about adapting the same digital manufacturing method to different procedures. Research has progressed from model-based localization to patient usage, alternatives, and clinical outcomes.
The most noteworthy aspect of cross-disciplinary growth is whether the validation methods are sound and whether problems encountered in actual use can be incorporated back into the design.

Comparative studies can employ continuous enrollment and predefined complexity stratification, recording surgeon experience, imaging plans, rehabilitation pathways, and guide versions. For randomized trials, the focus is on maintaining common planning conditions and varying the implementation tools; for real-use registers, the focus is on fully recording applicable cases, non-use, and reasons for conversion. Both designs jointly address mechanisms and service performance.

Economic evaluations should record both active working hours and waiting times. Designer work, physician confirmation, and operating room procedures are different resources; some tasks can be completed concurrently, while others may delay treatment. Listing the entire process input by patient, and combining this with reoperation, hospitalization, and follow-up results, can identify at which stage efficiency improvements occurred.

For patient outcomes, indicators that reflect the surgical goals should be selected, while maintaining baseline levels. Statistical significance of different scales cannot be directly compared; more meaningful indicators are the extent of recovery, the proportion of outcomes reaching the goals, and the reduction in poor results. Regarding early precision advantages, continued observation is needed to assess whether they consistently correspond to functional improvement and re-intervention outcomes.
Can surgical guides reduce operating and fluoroscopy time?

Near term: Efficiency advantages will place greater emphasis on specific surgical techniques. Complex osteotomies and multi-segment reconstructions have clear preoperative preparation value, while routine replacements need to demonstrate the benefits of adding these steps.
Mid-term: From operating room time savings to total case cost comparisons. Achieving this change requires standardized recording of design, manufacturing, waiting, and operating hours.

Observation indicators: total preparation period, surgery and anesthesia time, exposure time and dosage, proportion of temporary switching to conventional instruments, postoperative effect and comprehensive cost per case.
How do guide-assisted and conventional surgery compare in outcomes?
Near term: Evidence will be refined towards specific indications and patient subgroups. A uniform claim of improvement across all cases has limited explanatory power.
Mid-term: Competition will increasingly revolve around long-term outcomes and total resource input. Prospective comparisons, clear case selection criteria, and sufficient follow-up are required.
Observation indicators: planning deviation, minimal clinically important difference, complications, reoperation, patient-reported outcomes, loss to follow-up rate, and total cost of cases.
How do guides perform in actual use across specialties?

Near term: The product line will continue to be segmented around specific surgical procedures. The form of the surgical guide and the delivery process will be more closely aligned with actual operations.
Interim: Cross-specialty platforms may reuse design and quality control foundations. Success depends on maintaining independent clinical validation and procedural knowledge.

Observation indicators: new applicable surgical procedures, actual usage rate, reasons for conversion, specialty endpoint, number of preoperative modifications, and consistency of use across hospitals.

In 2027, priority should be given to promoting consistent workflow records across cases, linking preoperative working hours, surgical segment times, imaging exposure, and reasons for conversion to case complexity. The condition is that hospitals can collect data with low workload during normal operations. The most direct observation indicators are whether the fluctuation in surgical time has decreased, and whether temporary adjustments for complex cases have been reduced.

In 2028-2029, patient selection criteria may be more valuable than applying them uniformly to all cases. If prospective studies can identify anatomical or surgical features with clear incremental benefits, product services can be developed into stable processes around these populations. Judgment criteria should simultaneously include geometric goals, patient recovery, and total resource input, and cross-team reproducibility should be tested.

sections.title: Priorities for Clinical Research and Industry Evaluation

blocks.text: The first priority is to standardize the efficiency endpoint. This involves unifying the definitions of the main time period and imaging exposure, retaining the original procedure records for each case, and analyzing the average and dispersion. This allows for the differentiation between stable savings and significant savings in a few cases, and also determines whether the surgical guide makes surgical scheduling more predictable.

The second priority is a comparison with clearly defined design tasks. Select specific scenarios where conventional positioning is difficult, compare different execution tools under common planning conditions, and then interpret clinical outcomes using mechanism-related geometric endpoints. For low-risk scenarios with mature processes, focus on observing additional investment and user experience.

The third priority is to establish a complete plan execution denominator. All cases entering the design process should retain their outcomes, including cancellations, postponements, unused cases, and intraoperative conversions. Categorizing causes into treatment changes, production delivery, adaptation, and operational factors can directly guide companies and hospitals to improve different aspects.

The fourth priority is to incorporate patient experience into long-term observation. Additional imaging, waiting time, preoperative communication, and recovery all affect the practical value of the technique. Studies can record patients' feelings about the preparation process and treatment recovery in addition to functional follow-up and interpret them together with clinical outcomes.

The most compelling progress should be demonstrated by consistent benefits in target cases: reduced key geometric outliers, more predictable processes, patient recovery meeting predefined goals, and clearly explained additional inputs. Such evidence supports product selection and service configuration, and also provides specific questions for the next round of device design.

P4-05.title: Custom Surgical Instruments
P4-05.subtitle: From patient matching to task matching: guidance, retraction and imaging-compatible instruments
P4-05.thesis: Customized surgical instruments like the translate patient geometry, operating space, and surgical sequence into concrete constraints. Orthopedic guidance, cutting in narrow areas, and continuous retraction each require different validations; parametric design and final product processing together determine whether these instruments can evolve from case-specific use to stable delivery.

From local guidance to space maintenance

blocks.text: How do patient-specific instruments assist orthopedic positioning and cutting?

The patient-specific instrument guides drilling, osteotomy, and bone fragment repositioning, and can also be attached to a predetermined implant location. Its function stems from geometric constraints: it uses specific bone surfaces to identify the location and then restricts tool movement.
The study focuses on how this transition process is established, and how design efficiency, surgical operability, and clinical benefits are evaluated together.
How can custom instruments support procedures in complex anatomy?

Confined spaces, unique bone morphology, and tissues requiring continuous retraction can make it difficult for standard instruments to provide adequate field of vision and access. Custom instruments reorganize space for specific procedures by altering contact, support, and tool paths.
This section includes guiding tools and traction systems, with the evaluation focusing on cutting control, exposure range, stability, and image compatibility.
How do manufacturing and sterilization affect custom instrument use?

Between removal from the printer and entry into the surgical environment, instruments typically undergo support removal, washing, curing, packaging, storage and sterilization. Each step can alter dimensions, residues and mechanical behavior.
The research focuses on the entire manufacturing and handling chain, particularly whether custom geometry alters the outcome of standard material flow.

Customization can target patient-contact surfaces or task-specific channels, handles, retraction ranges and assembly sequences. Patient matching determines where an instrument sits; task matching determines how it enables an action. Combining them turns complex anatomy into operations that are easier to check and execute.

The three research questions focus on orthopedic positioning and cutting, manipulation of complex sites, and final manufacturing processes, respectively. They share a common logic from requirements to geometry, from geometry to load, and from load to usage results. The research should first clarify the degrees of freedom constraints and workspace of the instrument, and then select materials and manufacturing methods to ensure that each design has corresponding validation.

Custom instruments also have different delivery schedules. Elective orthopedics allow for repeated discussions and fittings, while acute trauma requires faster preparation; short-term guidance and prolonged retraction also have different material requirements. Product solutions should incorporate these time constraints into the initial requirements, rather than adjusting the surgical procedure after the design is completed.
N1 | Semi-automated instrument design (2018–2019)

The radial orthopedic study, published online in 2018 and published in 2019, compared semi-automatic and conventional design methods using plans from 5 patients. The semi-automatic method reduced guide and implant design time by organizing repetitive procedures into parametric steps. This improved design time, providing a methodological basis for subsequent batch services. [R01]

The core of the semi-automatic design is to organize repetitive geometric operations into steps with clearly defined inputs and constraints. The patient surface is still determined by imaging and clinical goals, while the software is responsible for generating the corresponding contact surfaces, guide structures, and matching morphologies. With the reduced design time, the study also needs to confirm whether critical dimensions, modifiable ranges, and human review points remain clear.

This allows for the separate timing of the initial design and subsequent modifications of a case, enabling repeated completion by designers with varying levels of experience. If the time gains come from reducing irrelevant operations while clinical decisions are still fully expressed, the process is easier to scale. Furthermore, it allows for the statistical analysis of reasons for modifications and types of design failures, identifying which patients' geometries are suitable for parameterization and which require a redesign of the structural approach.
N2 | Fragment reduction and instrument use (2021)

The 2021 series of intra-articular radial fracture studies utilized patient-specific instruments for assisted reduction and fixation, resulting in improved articular surface geometry postoperatively. However, the authors argued that the gains were insufficient to offset the additional work required. The practical handling of complex fragments, soft tissue relationships, and case preparation may diminish the advantages observed solely from numerical planning. [R02]

In the fracture fragments, the digital model shows clear boundaries, but actual surgery is also constrained by soft tissue connections, bone quality, and exposure. Patient-specific instruments need to be placed, reduced, and fixed in a permissible sequence, and the design must consider whether each preceding action alters the contact basis of the subsequent instrument. Preoperative morphological matching is only the starting point of the entire operative chain.

This node is suitable for evaluating the coupling of instrument design and clinical workflow. Evaluations can record whether each fragment moved as planned, which steps required manual intervention, and whether the instrument occupied necessary workspace. For acute fractures, manufacturing time is also a design constraint; for elective orthotics, more planning and fitting can be allocated. The most suitable automation and delivery methods should be determined for each type of application.
N3 | Sequencing multiplanar osteotomy (2023)

The 2023 foot deformity study used patient-specific guides for osteotomies related to triple arthrodesis, observing a reduction in operation time and the number of imaging examinations. The design here plays a role in pre-planning tissue cutting angles and locations. [R03]

Multiplanar osteotomy requires simultaneous maintenance of resection volume, bone segment relationships, and fixation space. Custom-designed guides can encode these relationships into different cutting slots, but the number of guides and switching frequency increases preparation work. The design should start from the complete operation sequence, clearly defining when each instrument contacts which bone surface, under what conditions it is removed, and how to check the correction results afterward.

The instrument sequence can be compared through simulated surgery to observe whether repeated measurements and temporary adjustments can be reduced while maintaining the necessary direct field of vision. For clinical outcomes, surgical time, imaging examinations, and functional recovery should be recorded separately. This allows for the identification of procedural benefits and assessment of whether structural improvements truly achieve the treatment goals.
N4 | Comparing instruments under the same plan (2024)

The 2024 randomized trial of total knee replacement compared patient-specific instruments with conventional instruments in two groups that used artificial intelligence for preoperative planning. Improvements in partial osteotomy and alignment parameters were observed, but the operation time increased, indicating that the impact of planning quality and execution tools can be studied separately. [R04]

Shared digital planning provides a clear comparison for the instruments used in the study. Patient-specific structures fix the planned section onto the physical tool, while conventional instruments achieve the same goal through intraoperative positioning. The coexistence of improvements in some geometric parameters and increases in operation time indicates that the functional and procedural burdens of customized instruments need to be designed simultaneously.

Product development can break down time-consuming steps for analysis: is it due to difficulties in identifying the contact surface, cumbersome fixed operations, or the fact that necessary checks themselves require more time? The former two can be addressed through structural and interaction improvements, while the latter requires clarifying its relationship with accuracy gains. Repeated measurements, accumulated with the team's experience, can differentiate between the learning process and the inherent burden of the equipment.
N5 | Prospective comparison of osteotomy workflows (2025)

A 2025 study on high tibial osteotomy found that surgical guides reduced operating time and radiographic exposure, but corrective and functional outcomes were similar. The benefits of patient-specific instruments may lie in both operative procedures and geometric control, and need to be evaluated on a procedural basis. [R05]

The prospective comparative study of high tibial osteotomy places the value of the instrument within an observable process. Predetermined cut sections and correction relationships reduce on-site spatial judgment, but patient recovery also depends on bone healing, soft tissue regeneration, and rehabilitation. Therefore, the design objectives can simultaneously include stable execution and resource conservation, with independent endpoints set for each objective.

Further research could break down instrument preparation, osteotomy, opening, fixation, and image confirmation into segments for timing, comparing the benefits across different case complexities. If the tool primarily reduces a single repetitive operation, that interface should be optimized first; if efficiency improvements are distributed across multiple stages, the instrument pack and usage sequence should be treated as a whole product. Ultimately, it should be verified whether these benefits can be replicated across different teams.
N6 | Guiding nasal dorsal osteotomes (2018)

The 2018 Rhinoplasty Technical Report linked CT data with the predetermined nasal dorsum resection morphology, fabricated a guide chisel, and sterilized and used it during surgery. The study demonstrates the workflow from target morphology to instrument constraint; further evaluation should compare resection deviations with actual procedural burden. [R09]

The nasal dorsum bone chisel guide translates aesthetic and morphological goals into local tool movement constraints. The design challenge lies in the correspondence between the target contour, contact position, and chisel movement. The tool must both limit dangerous directions and preserve access and observation space. Given the small local dimensions, even minor changes in contact or fixation can alter the final resection shape.

The technical report provides an implementation chain from imaging to intraoperative tools. The next step involves measuring resection depth, contour deviation, and tool contact force on models with different nasal bone morphologies, and then comparing the actual operation time and number of examinations required. Correlating the target surfaces before and after instrument use allows for the connection between subjective morphological planning and quantifiable geometric results.
N7 | Hand retraction and operative space (2021)

The 2021 PolliRS hand-retraction system was designed from preoperative patient imaging dimensions, printed and sterilized, and used in one index-finger pollicization procedure. Radiolucency and repositionability helped maintain exposure and adjust the surgeon’s operating posture. This pathway focuses on surgical workspace rather than cutting trajectories. [R11]

The retractor's role is to maintain a stable workspace, not to prescribe a cutting trajectory. Patient-fitting dimensions allow for support and clamping positions tailored to local anatomy, while interchangeable positions cater to different stages of the procedure. Evaluation therefore needs to focus on continuous load, contact pressure, slippage, and the surgeon's accessibility to the exposed area.

The single-case application reveals specific needs, and subsequent comparisons of different hand sizes and retraction directions can be made in bench tests and simulated surgery. The design should clearly define which parts bear weight, which parts are for adjustment, and whether re-fixation is required during adjustment. If the instrument reduces the need for assistants to maintain posture continuously, team movements and steps that can be performed independently should also be recorded to directly measure workspace benefits.
N8 | Imaging-compatible oral retraction (2024)

The 2024 oral retraction system study used a polymer structure to validate CT/MRI compatibility, robotic maneuverability, and sustained retraction stability under bench and cadaver conditions. It connects the instrument's function with image-guided navigation requirements, reducing potential image interference from metal structures. [R12]

The imaging-compatible retraction system integrates mechanical, imaging, and robotic channels into a single design. The polymer structure provides an imaging interface distinct from metal instruments, while maintaining its shape during sustained retraction. Sufficient workspace, minimal image artifacts, and structural stability address different validation tasks, and any one of these could become a system bottleneck.

This study can evaluate the discernibility of key anatomical structures under actual scanning settings, and then test the robot's reachability under the same retraction posture. During continuous loading, the displacement of the tongue plate and support connections should be tracked, and the changes in tissue stress over time should be observed. Overlaying this data onto the same geometric model helps identify design trade-offs between increasing space, improving stiffness, and improving imaging.
N9 | Load bearing after processing (2022)

2022 surgical guide Material Research: Comparison of Mechanical Performance and surgical guide Dimensions under Different Treatment Conditions. The effect of heat treatment on materials means that "sufficient strength during printing" does not directly represent "meeting requirements after treatment." Stress and shape should be checked under conditions close to use. [R14]

Custom-made instruments undergo processing before entering surgery, and their load-bearing capacity should be defined under these conditions. Standard specimens help compare material changes, while complete instruments show how thin walls, connections, and channels are magnified. For short-term guidance and continuous retraction, the loading method and time differ, requiring separate selection of validation conditions.

By listing strength, stiffness, and permanent deformation before and after heat treatment side-by-side, can distinguish between changes in material condition and structural instability. For adjustable or modular instruments, connection loosening, friction, and locking performance should also be checked. If material treatment needs to be changed, key geometry and function should be confirmed simultaneously to ensure that local material optimization is consistent with the overall instrument performance.
N10 | Validating final-processing combinations (2025)

The 2025 material extrusion guide study tested various materials and combinations of cleaning, disinfection, steam, and hydrogen peroxide treatments. The results emphasize the interrelationship between material selection and treatment conditions. The dimensional performance of one combination does not automatically extend to another material or more complex structures. [R16]

The hospital process determines the chemical, temperature, and humidity conditions the material experiences during use. Freeform surfaces, pinholes, and weak connections in the actual guide geometry exhibit varying sensitivities to these conditions. The material's initial print precision can serve as a starting point, but the final selection should be based on its functional performance after complete processing.

The validation of custom-designed instruments establishes parameter ranges: specifying permissible span, wall thickness, contact area, and channel dimensions, then selecting the most unfavorable combination for treatment and loading. New cases within the validated range can be delivered through explicit geometric checks; those outside the range require supplementary validation targeting the changed critical functions. This transforms individual case designs into a repeatable product process.

These two instrument paths share a development principle: describing the structures requiring stability separately from the areas allowing for patient-specific adjustments. Guided instruments prioritize maintaining the tool axis, while distracted instruments prioritize maintaining contact and workspace; both verify that parameter changes remain within usable limits through post-processing functional loading and update this range based on operational feedback.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: How do patient-specific instruments assist orthopedic positioning and cutting?

Materialise's osteotomy and knee joint services connect physician-approved plans with guide delivery; VISIONAIRE relies on imaging, physician, and engineering workflows to generate patient-matched devices. [R06] [R07] [R08]

The value of extends from single-piece customization to design communication, modification speed, and delivery reliability. Semi-automated studies provide methodologies for improving design efficiency, while clinical comparisons help determine which devices deserve continuous standardization.
How can custom instruments support procedures in complex anatomy?

Materialise's osteotomy guide service provides a mature organizational approach from patient imaging to protocol confirmation to customized delivery, serving as a workflow reference for the development of specialized instruments. Formlabs' guide materials and manufacturing process embodies the system requirements of printing, cleaning, and post-curing. [R06] [R13]

The PolliRS and imaging-compatible oral retraction systems originated from specific research projects. Their connections with existing companies mainly lie in design services, manufacturing equipment, and material capabilities. Productization still requires establishing performance and processing validation for the corresponding instruments.
How do manufacturing and sterilization affect custom instrument use?
Formlabs provides printing, washing and post-curing workflows for guide materials; Materialise organizes instrument processing and use conditions through instructions for use.[R13] [R17]

The FDA's additive manufacturing Medical Device Technical Guidance links manufacturing characteristics with finished product evaluation, providing a framework for companies to establish validation systems. [R18]
The competitiveness of enterprises therefore includes not only printing speed, but also the depth of validation and delivery record of the material-equipment-geometry-process combination.

The semi-automatic design research conducted by in 2018-2019 extended the bottleneck of customized medical devices from printing to design time; PolliRS in 2021 demonstrated a small-batch patient-matching retraction tool; and the imaging-compatible retraction research in 2024 further integrates devices into robotics and imaging systems. On the industry side, Materialise planning and device services, and Formlabs material workflows correspond to the design delivery and manufacturing processing interfaces, respectively. [R01][R11][R12][R06][R13]

For enterprises to establish stable services, managing parameter changes is necessary. For the same product family, load-bearing structures and tool interfaces can be retained, with only adjustments made to the patient contact area or dimensions; the scope of each change should correspond to the validation criteria. For multifunctional devices, compatibility information for imaging, robotics, and sterilization equipment must also be maintained so that design changes can be identified by relevant processes.

sections.title: Specific Connections Between Academia and Enterprise

blocks.text: How do patient-specific instruments assist orthopedic positioning and cutting?

In academic research, parametric design can correspond to engineering time and rework rates in enterprises; while location, cutting, and clinical outcome studies correspond to product validation. The most direct connection between the two is to transform clinical failure patterns into checkable design rules and to confirm the effectiveness of these rules in subsequent cases.
How can custom instruments support procedures in complex anatomy?

Academics have identified operational needs that standard devices struggle to meet, while companies can provide reproducible manufacturing, materials, and delivery systems. A scalable product roadmap involves extracting stable functional structures and then allowing contact dimensions and local morphology to be adjusted according to the patient.

For example, the load-bearing frame of the retractor can be standardized, while the tissue contact and fixation interfaces can be customized; this preserves individual value and establishes clear boundaries for quality verification.
How do manufacturing and sterilization affect custom instrument use?

Academic research identifies deformation and performance changes caused by processing. Enterprises translate these findings into process scope, inspection items, and user manuals. Effective cross-referencing involves mapping specific structural failures to manufacturing steps and then verifying whether modifications improve the final function.

For continuous load-bearing traction devices and short-term guiding tools, performance indicators suitable for the task should be established separately to avoid using the same material name to replace the evaluation of the device.

sections.title: Key Issues and Validation Methods for translation

blocks.text: How do patient-specific instruments assist orthopedic positioning and cutting?

The academic pathway has formed two interconnected directions: reducing engineering input through semi-automated design, and identifying which cases truly benefit through clinical comparison. The former improves manufacturing scalability, while the latter determines the scope of application.

The future technological maturity will be more reflected in whether the design results can be checked, whether the reusable process can be recorded, and whether different hospitals can achieve consistent performance.
How can custom instruments support procedures in complex anatomy?

The research scope is expanding from surgical guides to a wider range of operational support devices, and the validation methods are also extending from morphological demonstrations to functional testing under continuous load, imaging compatibility, and human anatomical conditions.

The depth of this direction stems from an understanding of specific surgical bottlenecks. Whether the research findings can be generalized depends on whether case studies can be adapted into a series of adjustable yet verifiable instruments.
How do manufacturing and sterilization affect custom instrument use?

Research has moved from showing that prototypes can be sterilized toward joint assessment of dimensions, fit and mechanical properties after processing. As custom instrument geometry becomes more complex, standard test bars alone cannot represent local thin walls, guide holes and load-bearing connections.

The next key step is to establish the relationship between representative structural prototypes and actual finished products, so that materials research can support the verification of specific instruments.

The validation should be organized using a functional matrix. The positioning guide checks contact uniqueness, guidance direction, and drilling load; the retractor checks continuous displacement, slippage, and contact pressure; and the imaging-compatible instrument checks artifacts and target visibility under specific scanning conditions. A common geometric scan can serve as a foundation, but each function still requires dedicated experimental support.

Parametric design should record key inputs and outputs, such as patient contact area, tool diameter, operating direction, wall thickness, and support spacing. Designers should be able to see which functions might be affected when modifying parameters. Evaluation of automatically generated structures can include statistics on manual modification rate, error types, and review time to determine whether automation makes the design more reliable and easier to deliver.

Manufacturing validation should use a fully processed representative part. Printing orientation, support removal, surface treatment, and sterilization can all alter subtle features; for assembled instruments, fitting tolerances and locking performance must also be checked. Mapping changes before and after processing to specific actions directly determines the necessity of rework or redesign and establishes reusable testing ranges for subsequent cases.
How do patient-specific instruments assist orthopedic positioning and cutting?
Near term: Repetitive design steps will be further automated. The value of automation needs to be validated by the amount of manual modifications and design time.

Mid-term: Medical device services will be more stratified by complex and routine cases. Highly complex cases will emphasize geometric customization, while routine cases will emphasize process and cost.
Observation indicators: design time, number of modifications, delivery cycle, placement consistency, cutting deviation, intraoperative conversion and patient outcome.
How can custom instruments support procedures in complex anatomy?
Near term: Small-scale specialty devices will continue to be driven by clinical teams. Tools with clear needs and specific operational procedures are easier to develop into verifiable prototypes.
Mid-term: Modular and adjustable series may improve marketability. This is contingent on demonstrating consistent stress, cleaning, and performance across a range of structural variations.
Observation indicators: operating space, exposure stability, contact damage, continuous stress, imaging artifacts, design modification range, and repeat manufacturing success rate.
How do manufacturing and sterilization affect custom instrument use?
Near term: Post-processing inspection will become an important part of design verification. Contact surfaces, guide holes, and load-bearing connections need to be considered separately.

Mid-term: Validated process portfolios will become bespoke service assets. When expanding to new materials or geometries, it is necessary to confirm that existing validations still cover critical functionality.

Observation indicators: dimensions before and after treatment, repeatability, continuous load, residue and cleaning performance, batch-to-batch differences, manufacturing traceability and usage feedback.

A realistic advancement for by 2027 is the establishment of a limited family of instruments centered around clearly defined surgical tasks, enabling common dimensional variations to be handled through parameters, while maintaining consistency in key load-bearing capacities and interfaces. This is contingent upon the clinical team clearly defining operational requirements and continuously providing feedback on design changes. Key performance indicators (KPIs) include design time, number of reviews, actual usage rate, and intraoperative modification rate.

In 2028-2029, imaging compatibility, robotic accessibility, and adjustable structures are likely to be important directions for instruments targeting complex locations. Their value depends on whether multiple functions can be achieved simultaneously under the same usage conditions. Postural stability during sustained retraction, visibility of key structures, and tool workspace should be observed, and it should be examined whether similar performance can be maintained under different patient morphologies.

sections.title: Priority Research Tasks and Product Development Judgments

blocks.text: The first task is to develop a clear description of the procedures. The surgery is broken down into placement, fixation, manipulation, adjustment, and removal, with each step clearly indicating the constraints imposed by the instruments and the degrees of freedom the surgeon needs to retain. The sequence is validated using a simulated surgery, recording any locations where interference occurs or temporary modifications are required, ensuring the design goals directly correspond to the actual procedure.

The second task is to establish the patient variation range. Models with different sizes, curvatures, and exposure conditions are selected to examine the contact, load, and workspace of the parameterized structure throughout the range. Focusing on boundary cases as validation priorities allows for the early detection of geometric failures in the automated generation process and the identification of situations requiring manual design.

The third task is to connect the processing and load. Set up operating conditions for short-term guidance, repeated adjustments, and continuous traction, and measure the functionality after cleaning, curing, sterilization, and storage. If the processing causes localized deformation, determine whether it changes the contact or tool orientation; if it primarily changes stiffness, observe the displacement under actual load.

The fourth task is to evaluate the actual delivery. Design time, physician confirmation, printing, processing, and clinical preparation should all be documented and linked to the usage results. Even if the design software reduces operation time, it should be checked whether additional reviews or rework are needed; similarly, even if the material flow is simplified, it should be confirmed that the final functionality remains consistent.

The fifth task is to incorporate instrument and team interaction into the study. This involves observing whether it reduces prolonged holding, repeated adjustments, and visual obstruction; whether it makes critical steps easier to check; and whether recovery is rapid after anomalies occur. For retraction and complex-channel instruments, these indicators are often closer to practical value than single surface deviations.

Product development priorities should revolve around the quality of task completion: more stable key actions, clearer reachability, quantifiable operational burden, and repeatable delivery across different cases. Feeding these results back to parameter ranges, structure, and processing procedures allows customized devices to develop a continuously evolving engineering methodology.

P5-01.title: Personal Protective Equipment
P5-01.subtitle: Performance Evaluation from Printed Components to Complete Wearable Systems
P5-01.thesis: The value of printed protective equipment depends on the combined performance of facial edges, filter interfaces, material structure, and service life; custom frames, face shields, and respirators should be evaluated at their respective endpoints, and manufacturing consistency and care burden should be incorporated into delivery.
