blocks.text: Personal protective equipment (PPE) comprises devices that perform different tasks. Respirators require evaluation of filtration and fit around inhaled particles; transparent face shields need to protect against splashes, maintain visibility, and coexist with other equipment; printed frames and adapters alter the way existing equipment is secured or its interfaces. The common focus of the research is the complete wearing system, with specific endpoints varying depending on the device's function.

The four research questions can be explored along the usage cycle. Mask fit, protection, and breathing resistance are related to the airflow path; the mask experience involves visibility, stability, and extended use; materials and disinfection determine whether geometry and surfaces remain intact after reprocessing; and custom accessories translate facial shape differences into design variables for contact boundaries. Scanning accuracy, filter material properties, and printed surfaces are all meaningful and need to be tested in the same assembled state.

This paper comprises ten original studies forming two parallel tracks. The fit track moves from whole-device particle testing to comparisons of face molds, frames, and healthcare personnel; the reusability track moves from community production to physical compatibility, microbial challenges, and user surveys. The two tracks ultimately converge on care procedures, continuous wear, and batch consistency, providing clear research objectives for transitioning from emergency manufacturing to routine products.
N1 | Whole-device particle testing: identifying entry paths beyond the filter medium

The 2021 study compared respirators with different printing processes, materials, and designs, measuring particle transport under test conditions assuming a completely sealed face. Most samples showed filtration efficiency of less than 60% for particles between 100 and 300 nanometers; cleaning the surface, sealing the structure, or improving the filter cap seal could alter the results. [R01]

This method temporarily fixes the face edges, making the housing and connection points observable. For printed materials, air can flow along material defects, seams, and around the filter element, so the nominal efficiency of the filter material itself cannot independently describe the performance after assembly. Design evaluation requires first drawing possible flow paths, then changing the housing, interface, and filter element individually to pinpoint which component dominates penetration.

Subsequent tests can compare housing manufacturing processes using identical filter media and effective filtration areas, while recording assembly force and interface dimensions. If reinforcing the filter cover reduces particle penetration, repeated assembly should test whether the effect is reproducible and how much it depends on handling. This node calls for measuring particles and pressure drop on the same test rig: once an easy bypass is closed, more air must pass through the filter, changing system resistance.
N2 | Population-based and individual face shapes: treating fit as a geometry problem

A 2021 study used scanning to generate rigid test face molds, set up breathing simulation tubing, and compared personalized printed masks, statistically shaped masks, and commercially available products. The personalized approach had lower overall air leakage, while the statistically shaped approach provided an alternative sizing method for the test face molds. [R02]

The value of the rigid face mold lies in its fixed geometric boundaries, allowing for repeated changes in mask shape and observation of leaks. Actual wearing also involves soft tissue deformation, headband tension, and speaking movements; therefore, the face mold results are suitable for screening contact contours, which are then verified through human testing. In the design, the curvature of the bridge of the nose, cheekbones, and jawline needs to be addressed separately, and local gaps may determine the airflow channel more directly than overall shape errors.

Individualized designs and population-based sizing can use a common comparison framework. First identify facial shape combinations prone to poor fit, then compare the design and service resources needed to add another standard size with those needed to scan each wearer individually. The contact contour can then be adjusted together with compliant padding and frame elasticity. This expresses customization benefits for specific groups with poor fit and identifies which manufacturing parameters require personal data and which can remain standardized.
N3 | Scan-based frames improve peripheral fit (2021)

In 2021, a dental team compared the quantitative fit performance of medical masks before and after adding a custom-designed scanning frame in ten participants. The average overall fit factor of the two types of masks improved from three and seven to 145 and 109, respectively; the test used a counting pattern and prescribed movements for peripheral fit. [R03]

The frame works by altering edge stress and wrinkle shape. Medical masks are inherently soft; localized compression can reduce warping and may also shift gaps to another location. Therefore, research needs to simultaneously record the frame outline, compression method, and contact changes during movement; it cannot rely solely on still photographs. Average improvement also needs to be supplemented with individual distribution data to identify still-mismatched individuals and areas.

This node provides a clear starting point for customized accessories: existing filter media provide filtration, while the printed structure constrains shape. Each function can be measured separately before evaluating the combination. Future studies can compare individualized frames, population-sized frames and adjusted standard fastening on the same mask over repeated donning cycles. This separates geometric benefits from familiarity with donning and tests whether better sealing also increases local pressure.
N4 | Adjustable frames for different respirators (2021)

A 2021 study used printed side frames, bendable metal connectors and elastic headbands to test several respirator types and headband-failure scenarios in 45 volunteers. Qualitative fit testing showed that some previously poor-fitting combinations passed, with results varying by respirator model and initial condition. [R04]

The adjustable structure delegates part of the form-fitting process to the wearer, reducing individual design steps but introducing issues of adjustment consistency. Research can record the initial adjustment time, required assistance, changes in position after re-wearing, and test results. With more degrees of freedom in adjustment, users may find a more suitable state, or it may be difficult to restore the fit after disassembly; therefore, clear positioning and inspection methods are needed.

Compared to custom scanning frames, adjustable frames are better suited for comparing service paths: which types of mismatches are suitable for on-site adjustments, and which require regenerating contact profiles. Using the respirator model as a stratification factor helps avoid generalizing improvements on one model to all combinations. Headband condition, material usage time, and filter performance are recorded separately, ensuring that structural fixation effects correspond to the remaining performance of the entire product.
N5 | Joint bench measurements of leakage and pressure drop (2023)

A 2023 bench study compared four printed mask designs, two types of filter media combinations, and different head molds, measuring particle entry and respiratory pressure differential. Filter media, effective area, foam sealing, and thermoforming all affected the results; improving edge sealing may increase the flow rate through the filter media, thereby increasing pressure requirements. [R05]

Particle penetration and pressure drop must be interpreted at the same flow rate and assembly state. A low pressure drop can reflect adequate filter area or a bypass around the filter. A higher pressure drop after leakage is reduced indicates a changed airflow path. Studies should therefore report leakage, filtration and resistance together, specifying flow direction, flow rate and headform contact conditions so that numerical advantages can be traced to their causes.

The design optimization can begin by fixing the sealed state and studying the filter media area and support structure; then, fixing the filter media assembly and studying the edges and interfaces. Finally, the two sets of parameters are combined to find an acceptable range between particle control, respiratory burden, volume, and weight. When connecting with the aforementioned human frame studies, it is also necessary to evaluate whether speaking and head movements reopen the bypass, so that the performance obtained from the bench can be maintained during dynamic wear.
N6 | Crossover trial in healthcare workers: from geometric hypotheses to wearer outcomes

A 2023 prospective crossover study enrolled 66 healthcare workers and compared a respirator alone with the same respirator fitted with a smartphone-scan-based printed frame and silicone surface treatment. The number passing quantitative fit testing rose from 27 to 62, and comfort questionnaire scores also improved. [R06]

The pairing comparison makes the facial structure of the same person a relatively stable condition, suitable for examining immediate changes after the frame is added. The results should also be analyzed based on whether the initial test was passed: for those who have already achieved a fit, the focus is on whether the added structure causes pressure or operational burden; for those who were initially misfitted, the focus is on which shapes and contact points have improved. These two groups correspond to different product needs and service benefits.

Further research could add repeated donning, longer work periods and repeated cleaning to the crossover design, counterbalancing the order to assess learning effects. Time from scan to delivery is also a service outcome: a successful fit must translate into timely access to usable equipment. Feedback therefore returns to facial design, using persistent leakage locations, comfort scores and adjustment records to refine contact contours rather than optimizing only the mean result of a single test.
N7｜Community face shield Production: Converting Geometric Files into Deliverable Components

The 2020 community production study organized face shield manufacturing around the printing headband, transparent sheet, and fasteners, combining daytime single-piece and nighttime stacking scheduling, and arranging collection, quality inspection, processing, and assembly. The study presents how distributed devices enter the shared delivery process. [R07]

The face shield manufacturing unit is a component system. Headband printing time, transparent sheet cutting, punching, and assembly need to be coordinated; adding printing equipment does not necessarily increase the number of finished products. Research can record the reasons for waiting, rework, and defects at each stage, identifying resources that limit delivery. Differences in shape and hole placement of the same model on different machines also require comparable results through standardized part or assembly inspections.

Production scheduling optimization also impacts post-processing quality. While stacking methods may save manpower, they alter splitting and edge finishing tasks; therefore, capacity should be measured in inspected complete units. As this node extends to reuse studies, product records should retain material, process, and batch information to facilitate returning subsequent warping, cracking, or cleaning issues to manufacturing conditions. Distributed manufacturing thus forms a learning production network, rather than simply a remote copy of documents.
N8 | Physical changes after repeated processing (2020–2021)

A 2020 online study compared the appearance of different printed headbands and transparent sheets after repeated treatments. Under the tested chemical treatment conditions, no significant physical damage was observed after multiple cycles; some materials showed shrinkage, warping, or cracking after high-temperature treatment. The direct endpoint of this study was physical appearance compatibility. [R08]

Visual inspection is one layer of reusability evaluation and needs to be integrated with dimensions, connection strength, light transmission, and wearing stability. Minor deformations may not yet form obvious cracks, but they can alter the position of the transparent lens or the tension of the headband; surface fine lines can also affect vision. Studies can continuously track the same product and use untreated samples as time controls to describe the path of performance changes with the number of cycles.

The material name needs to be recorded along with the specific printing and assembly conditions. Different polymers of the same type may exhibit different performance during processing due to variations in structural thickness, interlayer bonding, and residual stress. The next step incorporates microbial challenge into the evaluation, establishing "physically still usable" and "processing to the preset cleaning target" as two independent criteria. The final reuse window is determined by both criteria and aligned with the actual care procedures.
N9 | Microbial challenge: comparing the reprocessability of material–structure combinations

The 2021 study investigated E. coli contamination, treatment, and subsequent culture of printed materials and structural combinations. Among the compared schemes, the culture results of the single-walled polypropylene combination were superior to several other combinations, indicating that the wall structure and treatment accessibility warrant further investigation. [R09]

Microbial residues can be influenced by surface roughness, interconnected gaps, cavities, and wetting conditions. When both material and wall design vary, the results describe a combined performance; to identify their individual roles, polymer type and geometry need to be considered as independent factors. Controls should also include contamination load, drying time, and post-treatment recovery efficiency to avoid interpreting sampling difficulties as adequate removal.

By integrating with physical compatibility research, a continuous cyclical joint scheme can be established: at each stage, microbial recovery, size retention, connectivity, and wearing status are measured to observe whether any performance degradation occurs initially. For practical devices, interfaces and shielding areas also need to be covered to ensure that the patterns obtained from simple samples are applied to complex components. The research focus shifts from whether a single treatment is effective to whether materials, structures, and processes consistently meet common evaluation objectives throughout a usage cycle.
N10 | Frontline surveys locate wearing-experience differences (2021)

A 2021 Canadian survey obtained 63 responses from frontline workers and compared experiences with printed face shields in clinical-contact and community settings. Ratings differed by job role and patient volume, with assembly and visibility also receiving different evaluations. Practicality therefore needs to be analyzed by task. [R10]

The wearing experience of the face shield is influenced by work pace, viewing distance, communication frequency, and other factors. Overall satisfaction is suitable for describing the general level of acceptance, while specific issues help identify areas for improvement. Studies can record fogging, glare, slippage, collisions, and adjustments in conjunction with specific actions, linking subjective ratings to modifiable geometric or material parameters.

This node shares a user-centered evaluation approach with the frame crossover trial, but needs to retain its respective functional endpoints. The visibility and coverage of the face shield, the fit and breathing burden of the mask can be measured separately within the same workflow, and then it can be observed whether there are any conflicts when wearing them together. When feedback is given to the production end, in addition to changing the structure, the assembly method, size selection, and component replacement can also be adjusted to ensure that the experience improvements can be stably replicated in mass production.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: Prusa's 2020 face shield project uses an open design to connect desktop printing equipment with transparent protective sheets, forming corresponding components and assembly data. Its technical role is to combine rapidly printable headbands with existing sheets, reducing the reliance on a single molding process for the entire product. This forms a parallel route with community production research: both require coordinating the delivery of printed and non-printed parts. [R11][R07]

In June 2020, Prusa documented its face-shield certification process, covering fused-deposition printing and injection-molding routes. Product documentation included materials, process parameters, transparent sheets, assembly and quality records. Mechanical performance, optical properties, field of view and splash protection were assessed, showing how commercialization fixes manufacturing conditions together with the final assembly. [R12]

The shift from printing to injection molding can be understood as a process choice driven by changes in demand and batch size. Printing is suitable for early modifications and multi-point supply; once recurring demand stabilizes, producers can compare mold investment, unit time, and material utilization. Whether the two approaches can share evaluation results depends on the comparability of the final geometry, materials, and assembly state; the process change also provides an opportunity to test the robustness of the design.

In 2020, Formlabs demonstrated a printed adapter connecting a diving mask to a medical breathing-circuit filter. The official project page lists validation tasks concerning sealing, breathing performance, fogging and communication, illustrating rapid prototyping with existing components during an emergency. [R13]

The adapter route focuses its research on interfaces and complete gas paths. Fitting dimensions can be quickly modified via printing, but the filter element, face shield valve, dead space, and wearing method all require joint testing. Compared to the Prusa face shield route, it involves different functional endpoints and validation resources; therefore, enterprise development should be described on a per-device mission basis. Observable changes in industry progress are the maturity of processes, materials, interfaces, and testing systems, rather than the number of devices or the amount of open-source documentation available for download.

sections.title: Connecting Academic Research with Corporate Practice

blocks.text: There are three clear connections between academic evidence and business activities. In dental frame research, facial scanning and printed frames enter the same experimental process, forming a connection between specific design tools and testing; the Prusa and community face shield projects share modular manufacturing issues, belonging to parallel practices in similar scenarios; Formlabs' adapter solution and whole-machine particle research meet on the interface sealing issue, but their respective test objects and implementation teams need to be identified separately. [R03][R07][R11][R13]

The facial customization approach can form a closed loop from failed testing to design modifications. Fit testing provides information on which person, which action, and which combination exhibits leakage; scan data provides adjustable boundaries; and printing provides low-volume production capabilities. When used together, the product value can be expressed by mismatch resolution, re-wear stability, and delivery time. Improving the model's geometric accuracy in isolation requires explaining how it alters these final metrics.

The face shield route is better suited for linking user feedback to component changes. If the issue focuses on visibility, sheet curvature, distance, and surface condition can be compared; if the issue focuses on stability, headband flexibility, weight distribution, and fastening methods can be compared. Unified version management in distributed production allows these modifications to reach every manufacturing point, with subsequent investigations verifying whether the changes improve the target task.

Collaborative research between enterprises and hospitals should also clearly define the service chain. Scanning, design, manufacturing, cleaning, delivery, and field testing may be performed by different personnel, and each handover affects wait times and consistency. Research can use real-case pathways to record workload, using successfully worn complete units as the unit of outcome. This can explain how a product that performs well in a trial can be reliably obtained with affordable service resources.

Comparative testing of complete face masks should adopt a phased design. First, evaluate the shell and interface under uniform filter material and sealing conditions. Then, compare the filter material area and pressure differential under uniform flow rate. Finally, proceed to repeated wearing and dynamic movement tests. Each phase should retain a clear failure classification, allowing particle entry to be traced back to the filter media, edge leakage, or assembly location, rather than all being categorized into a single overall score.

For facial accessories, both stress and sensation need to be evaluated simultaneously. When frames improve fit, localized pressure may redistribute; therefore, studies can compare contact points, wearing time, and comfort components. For combinations such as glasses, goggles, and face shields, it's also possible to observe whether there is an increase in the frequency of adjustments or face touching. For individuals with different face shapes and work tasks, individual results and failure scenarios should be reported to support appropriate size and service selection.

Reuse studies need to make the processing cycle resemble routine procedures. After establishing a method in a single experiment, storage, transportation, reassembly, and wearing actions can be added, continuously recording appearance, transparency, connection strength, microbial recovery, and fit. Time series of different indicators on the same item helps determine which changes occur first and facilitates the formation of observable replacement criteria.

Manufacturing consistency can be achieved by sampling from key features. Features such as filter element holder dimensions, contact edge continuity, and headband orifice positions are directly related to function and are suitable for batch inspection. Different equipment, material batches, and operators form stratified samples; by including the number of qualified finished products, rework, and assembly failures in the efficiency calculation, production optimization can be linked to actual deliverable performance.

Clinical application studies can be conducted with a longer observation period based on clearly defined roles, taking into account usage frequency, continuous wear, and nursing workload. The primary endpoint should be determined by the device's function, while secondary endpoints should interpret acceptability and resource consumption. When mismatch, fatigue, or visual field issues discovered during the trial are incorporated into the next design, the affected version should be retained so that subsequent evaluations can identify which modification was effective.

If, by around 2027, mobile scanning and parametric design can consistently shorten delivery times, custom frames are more likely to serve individuals experiencing repeated misfits in standard sizes. Observable metrics include the first-time fit test pass rate, the rate of improvement among misfits, consistency with repeated wear, and the time from scanning to a usable product. Product expansion requires these metrics to remain repeatable across different institutions.

If the 2027-2028 research incorporates continuous wear, combination products, and reprocessing into the same approach, the optimization objective for protective accessories will shift from single-use fit to lifecycle performance. Observable changes are reported geometric, microbiological, and wear data corresponding to the number of treatments, and the ability to trace failure causes back to materials and structure. Such evidence is helpful in comparing the resource requirements of reusable components versus replacement components.

If, by 2028-2029, the distributed manufacturing network establishes a shareable bill of materials, process records, and final inspection methods, face shield products may have more stable multi-point delivery capabilities. It is necessary to observe the yield and rework differences between different manufacturing points, the distribution of delivery times, and whether performance improves synchronously after version updates. High output at a single production point needs to be evaluated in conjunction with consistency across the network.

Another scenario is that after standardized mass production resumes, the demand for emergency whole-part printing decreases, while printing remains in the individual parts, test fixtures, and rapid revision stages. Research can compare the total delivery cost and service response of the two paths to determine which individual differences are sufficient to support customization. This scenario allocates printing capacity to areas requiring change while allowing stable parts to continue using manufacturing methods appropriate to their scale.

sections.title: Observation Indicators and Priority Research Tasks

blocks.text: One of the priority tasks is to establish a joint data structure for facial sealing and whole-device filtration. The same sample should have a geometric version, material process, filter media area, interface status, test flow rate, and particle results; for the human body stage, the actions and wearing sequence should be added. Such records can explain differences between different experiments as variations in specific design or methodology and support the reproducibility of experiments.

The second task is to evaluate the incremental value of customization. For wearers whose equipment initially fits poorly, compare adjustable frames, population-based sizes and individual frames under standardized test conditions, accounting for scanning, design, manufacture, modification and on-site assistance. Outcomes should include the number of wearers passing the fit test and the adjustments and time needed to maintain that fit, linking product selection to service capacity.

The third task is to establish an interactive material-structure-treatment experiment. Keeping other conditions constant, vary the wall design, surface condition, and treatment cycles, and jointly observe the physical and microbiological endpoints. Interfaces and shielded areas in complex components should be independent sampling locations to identify the sources of variation between simple samples and actual products.

The fourth task is to translate the wearer's experience into repeatable design metrics. Vision, fogging, slippage, pressure sensation, and communication impact can be correlated with specific job actions, forming a combination of short-term, controllable testing and longer-term observation. Feedback is then incorporated into the next version of the design, and the same tasks are repeated for testing, gradually accumulating the correlation between product modifications and user benefits.

When jointly reporting results, items can be organized into four states: "first assembly, first wear, repeated wear, and reuse after treatment." Each state retains the identifier of the same sample, listing performance changes and required operations separately. If an item is only successfully assembled on the first attempt, the study can pinpoint assembly/disassembly consistency; if changes occur after treatment, the materials and connection status can be traced. Longitudinal recording is more suitable for identifying the failure sequence than averaging samples from different stages.

The resource assessment can also simultaneously record equipment occupancy and personnel contact time. Printing wait times, assembly operations, and field adaptations are different resources; improving one of them may not necessarily shorten the overall delivery time. Using complete products that have passed the target test as the unit of calculation, it is possible to compare three organizational methods: local manufacturing, centralized manufacturing, and hybrid supply, and also to retain an actionable capacity basis for the next demand change.

P5-02.title: Sampling Devices
P5-02.subtitle: Connecting collection, release, detection and mechanical safety in a complete performance chain
P5-02.thesis: Research on printed swabs has moved from supply substitution to structural and fluid function design; the true unit of performance is the effective target quantity that is ultimately sent into the detection system after a complete sample, while simultaneously satisfying the consistency of pathway adaptation, expected fracture location, and post-manufacturing state.

questions.question: How can the sampling and testing performance of the printed nasopharyngeal swab be guaranteed?
questions.focus: Distinguishing collection, release, concentration and clinical test agreement

questions.question: How do the structure and materials of sampling supplies meet mechanical safety requirements?
questions.focus: Assessing safety through anatomy, combined bending–torsion–tension loads and the final manufactured state

blocks.text: The sampling device transfers target material from the human body surface to a detection system, studying a continuous material transport chain. The swab first contacts the target site via anatomical pathways, then collects mucus and cells, subsequently retaining sufficient effective target quantity during transport, release, and pretreatment. Printing allows for adjustments to shape, pore size, and microchannels, and also enables the creation of anatomical models to test these designs.

The first issue concerns the sampling and detection performance of the printed nasopharyngeal swabs, requiring separate measurements of the collection volume, release volume, release concentration, and final test results. The second issue concerns mechanical safety, requiring differentiation between head contact, narrow neck bending, handle force transmission, and predetermined breakage after use. These two issues are closely related: structures that easily access the pathway still need to obtain sufficient samples, while increasing surface area or porosity alters strength, cleaning, and material residue conditions.

Ten nodes extend from emergency design and clinical comparisons in 2020 to anatomical testing platforms in 2025. The structural branch examines adaptation to individual anatomical passages, the fluidic branch examines losses during sample transfer, and the clinical branch tests the complete sampling procedure. Arrows connect these research tasks, while the industry section relates studied products and later academic prototypes to their manufacturing routes.
N1 | Hospitals establish swab manufacturing workflows (2020)

A 2020 technical report from USF Health and Northwell describes the development and hospital manufacturing process of an integrated printed swab. The research focuses on design modifications to the head, neck, handle, and break-off area, and integrates cleaning, curing, packaging, and handling into the delivery of the testing kit. [R01]

The one-piece molding simplifies part assembly, but each area still performs a different function. The head needs to contact and retain the sample, the narrow neck needs to adapt to the passage, the handle needs to transmit direction and rotation, and the break-off area needs to fit with the container after sampling. During optimization, the dimensions and stress targets of these areas can be defined separately, and then it can be observed whether new stress concentrations are generated at the joints, so that the structural partitioning is consistent with the overall operation.

The manufacturing process itself is also a design variable. Printing direction affects the forming of slender rods, cleaning determines the smoothness of complex surfaces, and curing and subsequent treatments alter the material state. Comparative studies should use the final delivery state as the starting point for testing, while retaining records of each process. This way, subsequent bending, embrittlement, or inspection interference can be traced back to the specific process, and the design documents, along with the necessary manufacturing conditions, can form a reproducible research object.
N2 | Open prototypes undergo paired validation (2020)

The 2020 open collaboration project progressively screened designs submitted from multiple parties and compared four prototypes with a reference swab in 276 symptomatic outpatient participants. The κ values for paired RT-PCR results ranged from 0.85 to 0.89, demonstrating the feasibility of a shared validation process across multiple designs. [R02]

The common workflow enables different prototypes to be evaluated around the same clinical task, and screening indicators can be extended from mechanical and procedural performance to test results. Paired sampling reduces some of the differences in individual disease states, but it is still necessary to record the sampling order, the interval between two operations, and the operator. These factors are particularly important for samples close to the detection limit, because small changes in the target amount can alter the positive and negative classifications.

The next organizational step is to retain the reasons prototypes are rejected. One design may fail consistency checks during printing, while another may be limited during sampling or sample recovery; each requires a different modification. Recording screening alongside clinical results can identify which bench measurements predict performance. Collaboration then produces comparable knowledge about iteration and provides a basis for validating specific products and platforms.
N3 | Pediatric imaging constrains access-path design (2020)

A 2020 study established a nasopharyngeal pathway model using CT scans of five children aged 11 to 34 months, comparing three printed designs with two commercially available thin swabs. The elliptical cross-section and head shape jointly affected transit time and resistance, and the study used these factors to select the appropriate design; initial cell recovery testing was also performed in two adults. [R03]

The elliptical cross-section exhibits different bending responses in different directions, thus expanding the fitting problem from overall shape reduction to the direction of motion and pathway curvature. The model can control the anatomical environment, allowing the same prototype to repeatedly traverse different pathways and locating areas most prone to contact and deflection. Scale information provided by imaging can also be used to determine the relationship between the neck length, head size, and handle transition.

Subsequent evaluation should cover anatomical variation within the target age group and define model friction, soft-tissue compliance and operating conditions together. Clinical studies in appropriate pediatric populations can separately record sampling completion, experience and test results. These participants must be distinguished from the adults involved in the initial cell-recovery tests. This node asks whether, beyond reducing cross-section, the swab head can be designed to deform in a more favorable direction under pressure.
N4 | Mechanical and functional testing: measuring strength, absorption and sample recovery separately

The 2021 study compared the tensile, torsional, bending, and sampling capabilities of various printed and conventional swabs using a common device. The overall mechanical performance of printed samples was comparable or better, while differences in liquid absorption did not directly translate into similar differences in RNA recovery; processing and short-term aging also altered the strength of some designs. [R04]

Mechanical measurements must be interpreted with failure modes. A higher fracture load indicates greater resistance to pull-off, while a higher bending reaction force can affect contact during insertion through an anatomical passage. Tests should record fracture location, permanent deformation and the head–neck junction so that strength and flexibility can be optimized together. The planned break point requires separate testing to distinguish behavior during sampling from break-off into the collection tube.

Functional testing shows that absorbed volume, retention and release efficiency describe different stages. A structure may absorb less but release more completely, yielding a similar final amount for analysis. Future studies can establish a mass balance for the same sample by measuring the initial amount, collected amount, released amount and residual amount, then relate these to amplification results. This sets design targets for microchannels and open-pore structures and explains why swabs with similar clinical agreement can perform differently on the bench.
N5 | Clinical comparison of two commercial designs (2020–2021)

A prospective study published online in 2020 and in a 2021 journal issue enrolled 70 adults and compared Lattice Swab and Origin KXG with a flocked reference swab. Agreement κ values were 0.90 and 0.84, respectively. For some positive patients, the interval between sampling procedures was as long as 24 hours. [R05]

This study places specific products into a fixed testing platform, thus enabling it to answer questions about the clinical manifestations of corresponding combinations. Comparisons also involve transport media, sampling sequence, and patient status; these conditions should be preserved during analysis. Especially in samples with inconsistent results, tracing the original amplification value and sampling interval is more helpful in explaining where the variation in the target quantity originated than simply recording the overall concordance rate.

Product iterations can be evaluated with paired sampling, counterbalanced sampling order, standardized transport conditions and blinded testing, with a prespecified analysis of low-analyte samples. Sample size should be chosen for the desired precision of agreement estimates, and differences expressed with intervals. Multicenter studies then extend the question from whether one product works to whether its performance relationships persist across institutions, operators and assay platforms.
N6 | Multicenter evaluation across three testing platforms (2020–2021)

A USF-associated study published online in 2020 and in a 2021 journal issue enrolled 291 symptomatic patients at three clinical sites. It compared printed and flocked swabs using three RT-PCR platforms. Overall diagnostic agreement was 95.88%, and κ was 0.901. [R06]

The multiplatform design broadens observation of the complete testing chain. Differences in sample input can be attenuated or amplified by each platform’s preparation and amplification steps. Within-platform results should therefore be retained before interpreting pooled performance. Staffing and logistics at clinical sites can also reveal service-process effects, connecting product validation with actual hospital testing pathways.

The next phase could involve organizing cross-institutional studies into a unified core process with clearly documented local components. Samples from the same batch would be tested on different platforms to observe methodological differences; different manufacturing batches would be tested on the same platform to observe product differences. For samples approaching detection limits, attention should be paid to paired variations and repeatability. The resulting feedback could be returned to a common bench to examine whether a particular release or material specification truly explains changes in clinical outcomes.
N7 | Auxetic structures regulate axial compression (2020–2021)

A study published online in 2020 and in a 2021 journal issue used finite-element analysis and surrogate models to screen swab heads with a negative Poisson’s ratio, then tested printed specimens against the mechanical model. The goal was lateral contraction under axial compression while controlling structural stress. This was a mechanism-based prototype study. [R07]

The flexibility of traditional solid configurations is mainly determined by materials and cross-sections, while structured heads add degrees of freedom such as unit shape, connection angles, and rod diameters. Lateral contraction provides a testable design assumption: when in contact with the path, can the head width change with the load and reduce lateral resistance? This assumption needs to be observed in a model with curvature and friction, and correspond to the calculated response under pure axial compression conditions.

Mechanical optimization must preserve sampling function. More open space can change sample retention, while slender struts and junctions can affect surface treatment and residue removal. Subsequent comparisons can measure insertion resistance, shape recovery and analyte recovery together, weighing deformation benefits against sampling losses. The shared question for microlattice designs is how geometry can tune several functions and how experiments can separate structural from material effects.
N8 | Fluidic swabs integrate flushing and recovery (2023)

The 2023 fluid swab connects the sampling head, microchannel, and syringe, optimizing the inlet using fluid simulation. Spiked samples and eight retained patient samples were used in a printed nasal mold to compare recovery and testing performance; twenty-eight volunteers participated in a separate comfort survey, showing an overall preference for the fluid protocol. [R08]

The fluid-assisted sampling technology revolutionizes the way swabs acquire samples. Traditional surface structures rely on contact, adhesion, and subsequent elution, while channel structures collect target analytes through localized liquid exchange. Comparisons require fixing the initial sample volume and the final total volume, and observing collection efficiency, channel residue, and dilution levels separately. Otherwise, changes in the detection signal may arise simultaneously from increased recovery and changes in liquid ratio, making it difficult to pinpoint the specific mechanism.

When advancing from models to in-vivo evaluation, paired diagnostic sampling and comfort assessment can be combined in one workflow, recording completion and events such as abnormal backflow. Model experiments can vary viscosity, target location and inlet shape to identify conditions favoring fluid-assisted sampling. The next node addresses concentration after transfer: can dilution during release be reduced while keeping output volume controlled?
N9 | Open-cell microlattices enable controlled release (2024)

In 2024, research was conducted on printing three types of perforated microlattice swabs, adjusting sample release through geometric parameters and centrifugation. Dye and honey mucus models demonstrated high recovery and concentration retention. Furthermore, rapid IgG detection and concentration measurement demonstrated the impact of release mode on the detection signal. [R09]

The key to 's research is the integration of release methods into the instrument system. An open space accommodates the liquid, and centrifugation forces it away from the structure, allowing for sample collection with minimal introduction of additional diluent. When comparing different approaches, it's necessary to report both release volume and concentration, and calculate the total amount of the target analyte. Increased concentration may be advantageous for detecting low abundance, while total amount and matrix composition still determine the adequacy of subsequent pretreatment.

The flexibility, liquid storage space, and cleanup accessibility of the microlattice can be altered using the same set of geometric parameters, making it suitable for multi-objective optimization. Studies can fix the material and post-treatment, adjust the pore size and rod diameter separately, and measure residues and mechanical recovery at different viscosities. In the actual testing phase, the release liquid is connected to the target platform to observe whether high-concentration matrix alters the reaction. The anatomical test model thus becomes a subsequent screening tool, helping to verify whether the advantages of the experimental vessel can be maintained in real-world pathways.
N10 | Anatomy and mucus jointly form a test bench (2025)

A 2025 study printed a dual-material nasopharyngeal model with a mucus-mimicking hydrogel and compared injection-molded Heicon swabs with nylon-flocked swabs. Relative to a simple tubular model, the anatomical model changed collection amount, release fraction and RT-qPCR results, demonstrating the effect of the sampling environment on performance assessment. [R10]

The printed object here is a test platform that allows pathway geometry, soft and hard boundaries, and mucus properties to be considered together in experiments. Simple immersion primarily examines material-liquid contact, while the anatomical environment incorporates accessibility, local contact, and operator movement; therefore, the two methods answer different questions. Research can first decompose the simplified environment mechanism and then use the anatomical platform to verify the combined results, avoiding treating model complexity itself as a substitute for realism.

The continued value of the platform depends on its reproducibility and relevance to clinical tasks. Pathway size, surface friction, hydrogel thickness, and rheological properties need to be designed to provide reproducible conditions, and the operation process should be able to record speed, contact path, and completion. By incorporating different age and morphological models for comparison, the location of performance degradation can be traced back to the head and narrow neck design. This provides a common intermediate evaluation environment for the structure, fluid, and detection branches.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: In March 2020, Formlabs, USF Health, Northwell Health, and Tampa General Hospital announced a collaboration to develop printed nasal swabs. The project combined the hospitals' design and validation capabilities with printing equipment, processable resins, and manufacturing support, utilizing existing hospital printing infrastructure for emergency supply. [R11]

The technological shift in this collaboration involves moving from single-piece prototypes to batch manufacturing and testing kits. Hospital technical reports link design, cleaning, curing, and delivery, while subsequent multi-center papers place the same process into specific clinical platforms for comparison. Company materials and equipment constitute the manufacturing conditions, while clinical studies provide the results of the entire sampling and testing combination; these two types of evidence can be mutually interpreted when the product and process are clearly correlated. [R01][R06]

On April 8, 2020, Resolution Medical launched Lattice Swab, using Carbon Digital Light Synthesis and Keystone’s KeySplint Soft Clear material. Its hollow lattice head uses geometric design freedom to provide flexibility and space for sample retention, offering a different route from surface-nodule designs. [R12]

In May of the same year, Carbon's technical exchange focused on the product's design, mechanical testing, clinical evaluation, and manufacturing, and introduced the development plan for pre-sterilized products. This change suggests that the supply model itself also needs to be studied: hospitals receiving unprocessed parts and receiving pre-packaged supplies place different demands on on-site resources and delivery time. [R13]

In 2021, Carbon expanded the user availability of its Design Engine software and listed Lattice Swab as an existing production case for its lattice design technology. The changes at this stage primarily occurred with general-purpose design tools and manufacturing platforms; further research could examine how these tools support dimensional consistency, aperture manufacturability, and rapid iteration. [R14]

This leads to two organizational models for enterprise routes: hospitals collaborate with equipment companies to complete local production, while device manufacturers utilize platforms and supply networks to organize centralized or multi-point delivery. Both require capacity to be measured by qualified, complete supplies usable in the target detection process. Later papers on fluids and microlattices expanded the functional targets, requiring specific materials, release methods, and validation objects to be evaluated individually on their respective prototypes.

sections.title: Direct Links Between Research and Industry

blocks.text: There is a clear link between the USF/Northwell design, the Formlabs collaboration announcement, and the multicenter clinical paper, indicating a clear collaboration and product roadmap. Lattice Swab, however, enters independent product comparison after its corporate release, forming a "commercial product being studied" connection. These two relationships provide different information: joint development explains how the design was formed, while independent comparison explains the performance of a specific product within the selected process. [R01][R05][R06][R11][R12]

The microlattice and fluid swab share geometric degrees of freedom with existing grid products, but their research questions further involve the release process and output concentration. Academic analysis can compare how these schemes arrange pores, liquid movement, and pretreatment, while technology transfer requires establishing corresponding material, manufacturing, and testing platforms one by one. Similar shapes are suitable for proposing mechanistic comparison questions, while whether the performance is the same is determined by joint experiments.

The intersection of enterprise manufacturing and academic testing indicators should run throughout the sample path. The effective target quantity per unit operation can be decomposed into the initial accessible quantity, collection ratio, release ratio, and volume delivered to the reaction, and then the operation completion rate can be recorded. This allows for a clear identification of the effects of increasing sampling surface area, expanding pores, or reducing elution volume, and also facilitates determining whether an improvement simply shifts the loss to the next stage.

The manufacturing platform can also provide batch structures for research. Samples of the same model are formed under different equipment and post-processing conditions, and then tested for dimensions, mechanical properties, and recovery using a unified platform, establishing a link between key process parameters and functionality. The clinical platform provides real-world failure scenarios, allowing design optimization to focus on the features necessary to complete sampling, maintain structure, and ensure stable testing.

sections.title: Key Issues in Transformation and Comparative Study Design

blocks.text: For sampling performance studies, it is advisable to first establish a mass balance. Place a known starting amount in a defined environment and measure the environmental residue, swab release, and internal swab residue after collection. Suitable surrogates or detection markers can be selected according to the research stage, and then incorporated into the real sample. Simultaneous recording of volume and target concentration can explain whether the signal advantage of a particular design stems from increased recovery, decreased dilution, or a combination of both.

Mechanical safety studies need to cover the sequence of operations. Different loads are generated through bending paths, rotational contact, withdrawal, and in-tube breakage; a single tensile test cannot fully describe this sequence. Forces and locations can be recorded on a anatomical model, and the most unfavorable combination can be tested on a repeatable bench. Observational indicators include unintended fracture, surface damage, irreversible deformation, and changes in the head-neck connection, and these should be correlated with design dimensions and manufacturing defects.

Material evaluation can be arranged around the final delivery state. Newly printed, post-cured, finished, and stored samples should undergo the same mechanical and testing compatibility tests to identify changes in state. Complex pores and microchannels also require checking cleanability and patency. If process improvements increase the factory pass rate, it should also be observed whether they affect flexibility or target adsorption, avoiding judging the finished quality solely by appearance.

Paired clinical studies should counterbalance sampling order and record the interval between procedures. Participants and analyte levels should reflect the intended use, particularly near the detection limit. Overall agreement, positive agreement, negative agreement, differences in amplification values and user experience provide distinct information. Stratification by platform, batch and operator helps identify conditions under which results generalize.

Products for children or other narrow anatomical passages should begin with a stratified geometric description and representative models. Passage width, curvature direction and contact location can enter parametric design separately to explain size selection. Clinical evaluation addresses completed sampling and comfort, while models locate mechanical and structural causes. Shared version records allow the two forms of evaluation to inform each other.

The interface between the swab and container also deserves to be considered as an independent comparison. Whether the head can completely enter the target liquid, whether the remaining length after breakage affects the capping, and whether liquid residue remains on the tube wall during release all affect the state of the sample entering subsequent processes. Studies can keep the swab unchanged while changing the container, or keep the container unchanged while adjusting the breakage area, measuring the volume and target amount after complete transfer. For centrifugation or microchannel solutions, the additional operations required for adapting the external connector to the container can also be recorded, directly correlating structural performance with laboratory workflow.

If, by around 2027, the common evaluation method for collection and release is reproduced in different laboratories, swab optimization will more likely focus on the effective target amount. Observable metrics include reporting the initial amount, collection amount, release amount, residue, and final detection signal simultaneously, and specifying the total liquid volume. This allows performance differences between different structures to be explained by comparable mass transfer processes.

If studies in 2027-2028 confirm that fluid or controlled-release protocols remain advantageous in paired sampling, these devices may be further integrated with pre-test processing. Patient consistency, low target volume performance, operational completion, and comfort changes need to be observed, as well as any increase in required steps. The benefits of functional integration should be assessed based on the complete workflow, including sample transfer, container interfaces, and resources required for test preparation.

If, by 2028-2029, printed anatomical models exhibit reproducible dimensions, friction, and mucus conditions across laboratories, they could become a common screening tool before new sampling materials enter clinical comparison. Observable metrics include ordination stability of the same design across different laboratories and whether model failure scenarios can predict practical operational problems. The model library can also support systematic comparisons of pediatric size and directional flexibility.

Another scenario is where traditional supply capacity meets regular demand, while printing focuses more on new structure development, special population sizes, and contingency reserves. In this case, the product roadmap should compare manufacturing costs, turnaround time, and the speed of design changes to identify which uses require continued printing. The arrangement between demand recovery and equipment idleness can also be verified through regular batch drills and clear manufacturing records.

sections.title: Observation Indicators and Priority Research Tasks

blocks.text: The primary task is to standardize the reporting units for collection and release. Liquid volume, total target amount, and concentration are listed separately, with the amount of release solution used further explained in the test results. For complex viscous environments, the properties of the recovered matrix can be added to observe whether concentration simultaneously alters the detection reaction. This data structure helps connect geometric, fluid, and detection studies to the same performance chain.

The second task is to establish a correspondence between manufacturing variations and failure locations. Dimensional and surface inspections are performed on the neck, grid nodes, neck transition, and fracture zone, and then correlated with combined tensile, torsional, and bending tests. Samples are organized by manufacturing batch, equipment, and material condition to identify the areas most requiring stable control. The yield rate and finished product quantity are reported together to support a comparison between hospital production and supplier deliveries.

The third task is to involve users and operators early in design. Participant experience can be related to contact and force in anatomical models, while operator feedback informs grip, orientation and handling into the collection tube. Sampling interruptions, repositioning and repeat attempts can be recorded to assess their effect on recovered analyte. Repeating the same tasks after each structural revision creates traceable evidence of iteration.

The fourth task is to verify how contingency capabilities are maintained. This involves creating a reusable manufacturing log that includes design versions, material sourcing, printing and post-processing conditions, sampling inspections, and testing compatibility, and periodically verifying its implementation with small batches. Observing the time required to resume production and the percentage of qualified deliveries allows for the conversion of potential equipment capacity into concrete service capacity and facilitates resource allocation between regular production and short-term incremental demand.

P5-03.title: Emergency Supply and Manufacturing
P5-03.subtitle: From rapid prototypes and functional validation to restartable regional supply
P5-03.thesis: Emergency additive manufacturing has value when qualified supplies reach users during shortage windows. Face-shield parameter experiments, paired clinical swab evaluations and respiratory-device failure studies show that product function determines validation needs. Hospital demand records and printing-to-injection-molding cases further show that manufacturing, testing and network scheduling must be coordinated to turn one mobilization into a supply capability that can be restarted.
