blocks.text: The core of emergency supply and manufacturing research is to transform modifiable digital designs into qualified supplies that arrive at the point of use on time when demand suddenly surges and regular supply is disrupted. Face shields, sampling swabs, connectors, and breathing apparatus have different functional chains: some rely on geometric coverage, some affect test results, and some continuously withstand cyclic loads. Corresponding manufacturing capabilities should be measured by the ability to deliver these functions. Production volume, validation cycle, and usage conditions collectively determine the value of a technology during a shortage window.
What medical supplies can distributed printing produce when supply is scarce?

Product selection can consider two dimensions: structures achievable with local manufacturing processes and intended-use validation available to hospitals. Face shields combine standard sheets with printed supports; swabs connect structural integrity with sample testing; respiratory-system components connect manufacturing precision with airflow and continuous operation. Studies spanning community supply, paired clinical tests and experimental ventilators create a progression from external protection to diagnostic consumables and complex systems. [R01][R02][R03] This progression can organize a project portfolio: products with established validation tasks can fill early gaps, complex devices follow dedicated test pathways, and actual shortages determine priorities.
How can the quality and clinical suitability of emergency manufacturing be verified?

Quality involves three connected questions: design function, manufacturing repeatability and field performance. Different printers can change internal surfaces and effective dimensions even with the same digital file; different resins can change mechanical and reprocessing behavior despite identical shape. Validation must therefore preserve traceability across product, material, machine and post-processing. Paired swab tests and comparisons between physical flow restrictors and computational models show how test outcomes and manufacturing deviations become observable endpoints. [R02][R06] Wearability and component compatibility belong alongside capacity assessment for protective equipment, while durability and environmental treatment belong in system testing for continuously operating devices.
How do the costs, production capacity, and supply chain performance of emergency printing compare?

The denominator of contingency costs should be the number of items delivered on time and available for the designated task. Beyond material costs, personnel coordination, cleanup, packaging, inspection, rework, and distribution all consume the shortage window. Printing facilitates initial initiation and design modifications, while injection molding facilitates scaling up repetitive production after the design is finalized; the two processes can take turns within the same project. Hospital networks and hybrid production case studies provide a real-world scenario for observing this takeover. [R04][R05] Explanatory comparisons should align demand duration, available manpower, and alternative sources before calculating delivery speeds and total costs for different routes.
How to conduct design and performance verification for the emergency respiratory support device?

Respiratory Support extends the research scale of emergency manufacturing from individual components to complete systems. Material heating, gear cyclic stress, airway resistance, monitoring interfaces, and operator understanding all contribute to its operation. Design validation can sequentially connect computation and bench testing, continuous operation, physiological evaluation in healthy animals, and task assessment with clinical personnel involvement. Each stage answers different questions: bench testing characterizes controllable loads, animal studies observe physiological coupling, and clinical involvement clarifies the working scenario. Therefore, the research framework requires iteratively connecting engineering trials with user requirements to form interpretable design iterations. [R03][R07][R08]
N1 | 2021: testing manufacturing parameters for face-shield capacity

Studders and colleagues varied infill fraction, shell thickness, extrusion width and layer height, assessing face-shield headbands with tensile tests, finite-element analysis and print-time measurements. Increasing layer height and extrusion width reduced printing time by approximately 50% and 39%, respectively. Layer-height changes did not significantly alter strength, while thicker shells and greater infill strengthened specimens. [R01] This separates faster production into parameter changes with different mechanical consequences and provides testable manufacturing settings for community equipment.

The methodology juxtaposes the mechanical results of the specimen with the headband structural analysis, linking material load-bearing capacity with the actual structural stress. Shell thickness, internal filling, and layer height are not equivalent time-saving tools: they respectively alter the load-bearing path, material distribution, and interlayer quantity. Emergency projects thus arrive at a more precise question: under the functional constraints of the target structure, which time can be saved, and which materials must be retained? When reproducing across equipment, this question should be transformed into a remeasured response relationship, forming an acceptable production window for each piece of equipment.

The node shares with swabs and pneumatic components the commonality of treating manufacturing parameters as part of functionality. The difference lies in that headbands can be screened using mechanical parameters, swabs ultimately connect to test results, and pneumatic components connect to flow rate and pressure. From this point, the research chain branches into three paths: face shields move towards large-scale process selection, sampling supplies towards clinical paired evaluation, and respiratory devices towards system load testing. These three paths ultimately converge again based on qualified delivery capabilities.
N2 | 2020: connecting open development with paired clinical swab evaluation

Callahan et al. screened 160 designs and 48 materials, comparing four prototypes with conventional swabs in 276 suspected infection outpatient participants. The κ value for the consistency of detection among the prototypes was 0.85–0.89, and it took 22 days from identifying the shortage to completing the validation of the first prototype; the staff as a whole still preferred conventional swabs. [R02] This case simultaneously retained three dimensions: diagnostic performance, user experience, and development time.

The value of paired design lies in comparing sampling results from the same individual, reducing the interference of pathogen load differences between populations on device evaluation. Materials and structures are screened before entering clinical testing, allowing a large number of candidate solutions to share a common problem definition. Observing consistent testing but different user preferences indicates that result reliability and user experience each have their own areas for improvement. Structural development can iterate separately around sample acquisition, integrity, and acceptability, rather than trying to encompass all functions with a single endpoint.

From a supply organization perspective, multiple prototypes completing the same validation path allows for alternative sourcing options. It's worth extending this to the sharing of evaluation methods: participants can compare the same metrics and then choose a route based on their manufacturing capabilities. The next step in network research should therefore track the replication of validated versions, batch releases, and order allocation, observing how new manufacturers affect delivery times and consistency, and bringing user feedback back to the candidate design selection process.
N3 | 2020: animal studies reveal material failures in cyclic mechanisms

A 2020 rapid-prototype ventilator study combined bench testing with experiments in anesthetized healthy pigs. Early PLA and ABS components failed, prompting redesigned heat-resistant nylon gears. The revised system completed 72 hours of bench operation and maintained stable physiological measurements in crossover comparisons in healthy pigs. [R03] Material and manufacturing-route changes thus turned observed failures directly into engineering revisions.

The analytical value of animal experiments stems from the simultaneous presence of continuous mechanical operation and realistic physiological load. The test bench facilitates input control, while the physiological model links gas exchange, time accumulation, and equipment status. With these two complementing each other, the question shifts from "can a single respiratory waveform be generated?" to "can the required output be maintained under cyclic conditions?" This approach suggests that the time required to manufacture a device and the operating conditions the device will endure during use should be considered in the same design evaluation.

Compared to the face-shield parameter experiment, the failure here is amplified by the overall machine function; compared to the swab pairing comparison, the time dimension becomes the key variable. Further research should bring the failure modes caused by heat, wear, and load variations back into the part design and select suitable processing methods for each part. The convenience of printing in rapid prototyping can be combined with the material and load-bearing advantages of processes such as cutting to form hybrid manufacturing driven by performance requirements.
N4 | Capacity handoff from printing to injection molding (2021)

A case report from the Drexel AJFlex project documented printed-headband production alongside injection molding. The team delivered approximately 33,000 face shields to more than 100 organizations in the region. Clinicians, engineers, manufacturers, distribution teams and volunteers participated, with industrial partners supporting capacity expansion. [R04] Project operations and delivery records show how manufacturing organization changed.

The process relay addresses the issue of misalignment between demand and design status. In the early stages, when quantities are unclear and designs are still being adjusted, digital manufacturing can handle small-batch trial production. Subsequently, as demand becomes concentrated and the structure stabilizes, fixed mold costs can be spread across more products. Running two processes in parallel also preserves a channel for rapid modifications, separating standard batch production from specific localized needs. The actual switchover conditions therefore include remaining orders, mold delivery time, design freeze level, and assembly capacity.

The case extends the single-machine time-saving problem of N1 to the production network: as machine output increases, sheet supply, assembly stations, and last-mile delivery may become bottlenecks. When evaluating a project, waiting times can be recorded by process step to pinpoint where the capacity increase occurs. Subsequent hospital network research further links production capacity with daily consumption, refining process changeover criteria from total order volume to sustainable replenishment needs.
N5 | 2021: hospital networks establish the scale of real deliveries

A single-center observational study documented emergency production from March 14 to May 10, 2020, delivering a total of 17,276 items, of which 57.3% were manufactured by individuals; the study hospital served as a central node connecting 10 other hospitals, receiving daily requests and coordinating production both inside and outside the hospital. [R05] Products cover protective equipment, ventilation support, and diagnostic consumables.

Such records connect distributed manufacturing with specific uses. The central hospital observes demand, while external makers contribute flexible equipment and staffing; orders and deliveries close the loop. Shifting the unit of analysis from an individual item to a replenishment task allows delivery proportion, response time, product gaps and stock-recovery speed to be studied together. Equal output quantities can alleviate shortages to very different degrees, depending on when demand occurs and what clinical task each item serves.

Expanding a network also creates consistency challenges: more equipment, operators and post-processing conditions increase the acceptance-testing workload. Manufacturing-deviation experiments at N6 provide a physical explanation, while version and process records at N9 provide an information-management response. Research on hospital hubs therefore extends from mobilizing resources to allocating validation capacity, matching manufacturing tasks with the receiving department’s inspection capabilities.
N6 | Flow-resistance checks reveal manufacturing deviations (2022)

Duke et al. measured the flow resistance of 30 printed throttling device designs and compared them with computational fluid dynamics models based on actual ventilator flow data. Significant differences were observed between different devices and materials, with internal surface roughness and a reduction in the actual average pore size explaining the deviation of the actual devices from the ideal model. [R06] The study covered fused deposition and photopolymerization equipment, incorporating manufacturing differences into the functional evaluation.

Choosing flow resistance as the connection metric allows geometric errors to be converted into perceptible performance differences within the system. The model describes the ideal shape, while actual measurements reflect the effective channels after forming; subtracting the two reveals the impact of the manufacturing process. For narrow cavities, even with consistent external dimensions, changes in internal pathways may still occur. Therefore, when a distributed network replicates a file, it must also replicate its functional measurement methods and establish a correspondence between the allowable range of variation and the production results.

This node directly explains why N5 requires acceptance testing by source, and also extends the material durability issues of N3 to gas path performance. Computational models are suitable for helping select test conditions and identify sensitive structures, while physical data, in turn, corrects the models and design margins. Research feedback should focus on performance distribution across equipment: by manufacturing at multiple locations with the same geometry, identify which differences can be mitigated by process control and which require structural redesign to reduce sensitivity.
N7 | Durability evaluation after device processing (2022)

The CRISIS study tested a sintered printed device after a 1.83 m drop and autoclaving, and evaluated an extrusion-printed version with a variable-compliance model. Sustained ventilation was generally maintained; the extrusion version delivered minute ventilation of 4.1–12.2 L/min, with respiratory rate inversely related to tidal volume. [R07] Validation addressed treated devices and system output under simulated loads.

Adding transport and reprocessing events before testing covers part of the real path from supply to use, rather than evaluating only newly made prototypes. Variable compliance introduces changing loads and reveals coupling between output variables. The key is test order: expose the device to events that may alter materials or assembly, then measure function. Storage, handling, treatment and operation can therefore form a continuous emergency-device study, with performance recorded separately at each stage.

N3 focuses on failures exposed during operation, while N7 focuses on performance retention after treatment; together, they form durability evidence. Next, N8 needs to be integrated for clinical task analysis, because the device's output range can only be translated into design requirements when it corresponds to a clearly defined use case. Engineering research can then be used to assign tasks such as alarm identification, interface understanding, and continuous monitoring, enabling manufacturability, maintainability, and operator usability to form a unified product evaluation.
N8 | Clinical co-design defines use requirements (2022)

The origami-bag ventilator project held three focus groups with frontline clinicians. Audio transcription and inductive thematic analysis identified needs and collaboration lessons concerning user analysis, use-context understanding, early sustained involvement, prototype communication and educational support. [R08] The findings identified development priorities and human–device interaction issues.

The qualitative approach is suitable for answering product tasks that are not yet clearly defined. Prototyping allows different professionals to communicate around a common, visible object; clinicians can specify the usage environment, patient interaction, and workload, while engineers explain the structure and controllability. Once these two approaches converge, the abstract concept of an "emergency ventilator" can be broken down into specific functional requirements and usage steps. The process of requirements formation itself is also worth documenting, as it explains why a particular parameter becomes a priority design objective.

This path provides an application context for the technical measurements of N6 and N7, and also forms a demand feedback loop back to N3. For supply research, frontline involvement also plays a role: identifying projects where actual needs have changed as early as possible, and reallocating scarce development and testing resources. Requirements, prototypes, and validation results need to be documented in the same version; N9 organizes these relationships into a traceable development process across multiple hardware trials.
N9 | Lifecycle records connect evidence (2021)

Vallatos and colleagues investigated anesthesia-equipment components, leak ports, plastic diagnostic consumables and syringe-pump lockboxes. They found that reproducing shape did not necessarily reproduce function, and developed an Aras Innovator lifecycle workflow from project experience. The paper records replicas that fitted but still leaked; the hardware and system remained under development and evaluation. [R09] Unsuccessful specimens thus became part of the manufacturing knowledge base.

The value of process documentation lies in preserving the causal relationship between design choices and test results. If only the final document is stored, the next manufacturer cannot know whether a certain dimension originated from assembly requirements or machining compensation, nor can they explain which tests should be repeated after a material change. Linking requirements, design versions, manufacturing sources, and acceptance results allows for evidence-based handover in emergency collaborations. Technological changes thus progress from replicating the external form to replicating a set of manufacturing tasks whose applicable conditions are already clearly defined.

The node integrates clinical co-creation, hospital networks, and cross-device testing, feeding back to early product screening. Historical failures help determine more quickly which components are suitable for direct resumption of production during the next shortage, and which require re-validation or process switching. The relationships in the diagram are organized sequentially by problem. Although the lifecycle study was published in 2021, its documentation methods can be used to integrate subsequent flow resistance, durability, and user studies, forming a knowledge loop for the next emergency.
2020: From Open Design to Organized Production Tasks

On March 18, 2020, Prusa Research announced the launch of face shield manufacturing and distribution. The project page disclosed that nearly 200,000 units had been printed and donated, and described the final Prusa PRO Face Shield as meeting EN 166:2001's Class 3 design for droplet and splash protection. [R10] From open documentation to clearly defined uses and product versions, this approach brings broadly participating organizations together for collaborative design. Its industrial value lies in lowering the barrier to entry and reducing redevelopment work at each location through shared versions.

Formlabs' swab project,, was initially designed by USF Health, with Northwell Health collaborating with the company to develop prototypes and conduct testing; project documentation also documents a production network involving hospitals, local medical device manufacturers, and government. [R11] This approach combines equipment, materials, and hospital evaluations into replicable manufacturing capabilities. For industry services, deliverables can include design versions and quality processes, enabling a new location to clearly identify its manufacturing conditions and validation tasks.
April 2020: lattice swabs enter a specialist manufacturing network

On April 8, 2020, Resolution Medical announced Lattice Swab, made using Carbon DLS and Keystone’s KeySplint Soft Clear material. The announcement identified Resolution Medical as the manufacturer and described the product as a Class I, 510(k)-exempt in-vitro diagnostic device. [R12] In this partnership, the manufacturer implements the product, while platform and material partners support structural development around that specific device.

These three enterprise case studies correspond to different organizational scales: Prusa connects the open community, Formlabs connects hospitals and manufacturing resources, and Carbon and its partners connect specialized medical device manufacturers. A common technological shift is expanding geometric files into information packages containing materials, manufacturing processes, and intended uses. Enterprises can then develop different services based on this: the community side emphasizes version communication and component compatibility, the hospital side emphasizes seamless manufacturing processes, and the specialized manufacturing side emphasizes stable batches and supply commitments. Together, they address the issue of replication consistency raised by academic research.

sections.title: How can academia and industry connect?

blocks.text: The most concrete connections between academia and industry occur within the same product development and evaluation task. Formlabs project documentation explicitly lists collaboration with clinical institutions, while Carbon announcements clearly define the roles of manufacturers, platforms, and materials; these relationships can be used to explain how the product is formed. [R11][R12] On the other hand, the manufacturing parameters of N1, the flow resistance of N6, and the durability studies of N7 provide cross-product discussion of methodological questions: which parameters affect functionality, how to measure processing deviations, and how to maintain performance before and after processing. Companies can embed these questions into their own product validation.

Open development and specialized manufacturing each have different information needs. Open participants need to understand task boundaries, component matching, and acceptance requirements; specialized manufacturers need to maintain complete records of batches and changes; hospitals need to know what the product can do and whether replenishment is timely. N2, N5, and N9 together suggest that this information can be linked around the product version. In this way, when research results enter production, they can indicate which structure and process they correspond to, and when field feedback is returned to R&D, specific changes can be located.

The most worthwhile endpoint for studying industry collaboration is whether such connections reduce repeated trial and error and delivery wait times. Two manufacturing networks can be compared: one sharing only geometry files, and the other sharing testing methodologies, version history, and acceptance requirements. Under the same demand scenarios, first-time acceptance pass rates, cross-location variance, and production recovery time can be observed. Such comparisons can translate the value of collaboration models into measurable evidence, explaining which organizational arrangements are suitable for products of varying complexity.

sections.title: Key Transformation Issue: Turning Resource Mobilization into Stable Delivery

blocks.text: Identifying the Real Bottleneck with Qualified Output

Capacity accounting can be recorded sequentially as printing, post-processing, inspection, assembly, and delivery, and standardized using the final deliverable quantity. If a machine's cycle time is shortened, and inspection or component supply becomes a new bottleneck, the total network output may change only slightly. Therefore, scheduling studies should simultaneously arrange equipment and support processes, combining the manufacturing window of N1 with the demand records of N5 to observe how delays propagate along the supply chain. Maintenance personnel, material batches, and packaging capacity can also be included as constraints in the same model.

Economic comparisons also need to incorporate the time structure of shortages into the analysis. Brief disruptions emphasize initial arrival times, while sustained high demand emphasizes stable unit costs and supply volumes; when demand declines rapidly, prematurely increasing fixed capacity will leave idle capacity. N4's process relay is suitable for developing into scenario models: testing the switching conditions for printing, injection molding, and parallel production with different durations and demand fluctuations, and then validating the model's predictions with real order records.
Turning manufacturing deviations into allocable validation tasks

Products can be divided into modules with clear validation tasks: mechanical testing for load-bearing structures, functional-output testing for critical internal passages, assay compatibility for sampling devices, and continuous-operation and human-factors testing for complete systems. The network can then decide which tests require a central laboratory and which can be repeated locally. This preserves common standards as the network expands while assigning tasks appropriate to each site’s equipment.

For emergency networks that require repeated restarts, personnel changes and material modifications should be considered research variables. A successful production run can be documented as a record of version, process, and result; subsequent resumptions should be monitored through sampling to observe whether capability is maintained. The requirements updates for N8 and the process records for N9 connect here: changes in clinical tasks trigger design reviews, changes in manufacturing conditions trigger corresponding tests, and historical data helps determine which validations should be prioritized.

sections.title: 2027-2029: From Incident Response to Routine Preparedness

blocks.text: As of November 3, 2026, an FDA official page announced that the relevant COVID-19 device EUA declaration would terminate on December 26, 2026; affected authorizations and transition arrangements determine the scope. [R13] This timeline makes it important to define product pathways, routine operating capacity and activation conditions for future emergencies separately. Each company’s device category and market-access pathway should correspond to its actual product and be retained in the product record.
2027: Establishing a Recoverable Manufacturing Catalog

A valuable early outcome is a supplies catalog that enables production to be restored through drills. The conditions for its establishment include clearly defined requirements, contactable manufacturing locations, available materials and components, and repeatable testing methods. The observation metric can be set as the time from simulated stockout notification to the first qualified delivery, breaking down delays into requirements confirmation, material preparation, production, and release. Catalog maintenance thus becomes an ongoing task: periodically checking versions, alternative sources, and personnel capabilities.
2028: Validation of cross-site replication and process switchover

If the catalog and records are stable, the next stage can involve multi-site blind sample comparisons, allowing different manufacturers to submit products under a common task, followed by standardized measurement of key performance indicators. Areas with significant research value are expected to identify structures insensitive to equipment differences and to reliably determine functional indicators with fewer tests. For high-demand products, a print-to-injection molding transition can be simultaneously practiced to observe how mold preparation, design freeze, and inventory changes collectively affect the switchover timing.
2029: Joint evaluation of clinical missions and supply restoration

More mature research can embed manufacturing networks into regional emergency drills, pre-setting supply consumption and delivery disruptions, and then measuring replenishment recovery, task completion, and resource usage. This scenario is valid only if cross-agency data is consistent and product tracking is possible. Complex systems such as respiratory devices are driven by clearly defined use cases for engineering and clinical evaluation, utilizing continuous operation, human factors analysis, and manufacturing records to interpret product performance, forming an evidence path distinct from that of ordinary consumables.

The primary priority is to establish a functional database linked to application. Face shield studies retain strength, wearability, and component compatibility metrics; swab studies retain sampling and testing data and user experience; and gas path components retain measured performance and manufacturing conditions. Each result corresponds to a specific version and batch, enabling researchers to differentiate between design variations, manufacturing variations, and usage differences. The value of this shared database lies in supporting cross-site comparisons and providing an interpretable basis for selecting future tasks.

The second priority is to measure the supply recovery process. It is recommended to report the first qualified delivery time, the on-time demand fulfillment rate, the first-pass yield, rework time, and waiting time at each stage. Cost statistics should include coordination, processing, inspection, and distribution, and be grouped by product complexity and demand duration. This combination of metrics can explain why a network is performing well and identify whether adding more printers or strengthening inspection and distribution is more valuable.

The third priority task is design and manufacturing change experiments. Under unified functional requirements, various materials, equipment, or structures are compared, and processing and continuous operating conditions are set up to examine how changes propagate to final performance. Breathing devices are particularly suitable for juxtaposing fluid modeling, durability, and human-machine interface tasks; each experiment is linked through traceable versions, allowing improvements obtained from the experiments to be reintroduced into production. The research can thus progressively establish acceptable ranges of change and evidence-based validation rules.

Finally, the sustainability of the network is studied. This can be observed through repeated drills to assess the initial pass rate after personnel rotation, the speed of resumption of production after a period of inactivity, and whether partners continue to maintain records after supply is restored. The long-term value of emergency manufacturing is reflected in its repeatable startup capability: when demand arises, appropriate products can be selected, corresponding processes can be allocated, necessary verifications can be completed, and the results can be stored again for the next round of preparation.

P6-01.title: Preoperative Planning Models
P6-01.subtitle: From displaying anatomy to traceable models that change decisions
P6-01.thesis: The value of a preoperative model is determined by the specific questions it addresses. Geometric accuracy, spatial representation, material response, and timely delivery constitute a continuous chain of evidence; physical, screen, and virtual reality models support different tasks, and in the future, the appropriate model will need to be selected based on the correspondence between changes in the treatment plan and actual operations.

blocks.text: Preoperative planning models derive value from the unresolved decisions they help address. The research pathway starts with image conversion and geometric reliability, examines changes in plans for complex anatomy, and extends to multiformat clinical services, randomized comparisons and dynamic device rehearsal. Spatial identification, design revision and contact simulation require different combinations of physical, screen-based and virtual-reality models.
How can personalized physical models help with complex surgical planning?

Complex surgical planning requires understanding lesions, vessels, lumens and adjacent anatomy, and anticipating how instruments or reconstruction structures will reach the target. Physical models make these relationships available for rotation, touch and, in some cases, manipulation.

The value of the model should be defined by the decision-making task: clarifying the anatomy, selecting the approach, determining the instruments, or practicing in advance, each of which requires different structures and materials.
How can the cardiovascular and craniofacial model demonstrate complex anatomy?

Relationships among intracardiac channels, vascular branches and craniofacial bone segments can be difficult to understand from a single image slice. Physical models expose internal anatomy through cutaway sections, separable layers or transparent structures, enabling a team to discuss the same object.

The cardiovascular system involves flow and instrument passage, while the craniofacial system often involves cutting, bone block placement, and reconstruction. Therefore, the functions of the models need to be designed separately.
What tasks are physical models, screens, and VR models suitable for?

The screen model is suitable for quick viewing, measurement, and sharing; virtual or mixed reality provides immersive space and overlaid information; and physical models allow for grasping and manipulation of real instruments. The choice depends on what needs to be understood, what needs to be changed, and what needs to be practiced.
The comparison should be based on the same cases and tasks, and the learning, decision-making, actions and resource input should be recorded.

The three original problems correspond to decision-making, expression, and media selection, respectively. Complex planning first requires listing the relationships to be confirmed, such as the adjacency of lesions and important structures, or whether the proposed path can maintain necessary connectivity. Cardiovascular and craniofacial models then determine how to make these relationships visible; the former often involves internal connectivity, while the latter often involves bone block location and reconstructed morphology. Media comparison examines whether the same information is more easily understood through different interaction methods. The three tasks are interconnected, but observable outcomes should be defined separately for each.

A case can be studied by progressively adding information: first record the plan and remaining questions from routine imaging, then review a digital 3D model, and use a physical model when tactile or contact information is needed. Record which questions are resolved and which plans change at each step. This measures incremental model value and identifies cases that need no further fabrication, aligning personalized services with available resources.
N1 | The image-to-object error chain (2017)

Bücking et al. (2017) implemented image segmentation, mesh trimming, and FDM printing processes using rib, liver, and lung models, and evaluated the results by comparing digital and physical dimensions. The use of different segmentation methods for different tissues indicates that the quality of the anatomical model primarily depends on the matching of the image to the object. [R11]

The significance of selecting multiple organ examples lies in revealing the different difficulties within the same process. The visibility of high-contrast bone boundaries differs from that of soft tissue boundaries; hole repair and smoothing can also alter the contours of narrowing, bifurcation, or lesions. A final solid size approaching the digital mesh only indicates good print transfer, not that the mesh itself accurately represents the image. Errors should be located along the transformation chain; otherwise, improved manufacturing precision may mask earlier segmentation deviations.

Further planning and research requires translating "accuracy" into task-oriented language. When determining instrument size, the key is specifying the cross-section and boundaries; when discussing the approach, the key is occlusion and adjacency relationships; when conducting cutting simulations, material response is also required. This node therefore branches into the clinical decision-making branch and the manufacturing resource branch, respectively entering N2 and N4. The common starting point is to retain records of every step of modification, so that changes in the protocol can be traced back to patient images, rather than just to a perfectly finished product.
N2 | Multicenter decisions in congenital heart disease (2017)

In 2017, Valverde and colleagues studied 40 complex congenital-heart-disease cases across 10 centers, comparing decisions based on routine imaging, decisions after viewing a physical model and intraoperative findings. Surgical decisions changed in 19 cases. The design assessed both model dimensions and decision impact, rather than relying solely on satisfaction to establish clinical utility. [R09]

Within-case before-and-after comparison uses each complex anatomy as its own reference and directly records plan changes after additional spatial information. Model review also occurs later and gives the team more time to think, so changes cannot all be attributed specifically to touch or the physical medium. The most informative records identify which anatomical judgment changed, why existing views were insufficient and whether operative findings supported the revision.

The results also imply that model benefits depend on case selection. For cases where the original plan remained unchanged, further distinctions can be made between cases confirming existing protocols, cases where risks were identified but the strategy remained the same, and cases with no new information. This decomposition is more effective in guiding resource allocation than a uniform calculation of the "helpful percentage." It connects to the construction of N5 clinical services: if unresolved issues can be clearly identified at the time of application, options such as print, screen, or virtual reality can be chosen, and whether the model answers the question can be used as the endpoint of service quality.
N3 | From craniofacial abnormalities to operative steps (2018)

The 2018 Craniofacial Resident Study used patient CT scans to create models, combining abnormal bone morphology with preoperative step-by-step exercises and recording changes in skill milestones. The study focused on case-related learning processes, with the model serving as the medium for translating three-dimensional abnormalities into operational understanding. [R02]

The difference between craniofacial planning and intracardiac access lies in the fact that the observation plane and the boundaries of the bone blocks to be altered are often directly related. A physical model allows the operator to compare the positions after cutting at the same scale, but if the model doesn't indicate which parts are from the imaging and which are design additions, it's easy to misinterpret the proposed reconstruction as the original structure. Choosing a patient-specific bone model is to provide spatial reference for surgical steps, not to prove that the more realistic the appearance, the better the skill.

Educational changes can highlight the value of information expression, while clinical planning still needs to be verified against actual procedures. Subsequent comparisons should separate morphological identification, step sequence, and cutting location to observe whether progress occurs within the expected task. It, along with N6's aortic teaching, forms a branch of expression methods: local physical operations can be performed by physical entities, while hidden structures and dynamic interpretations can be handled by digital overlays; both share cases but do not undertake the same cognitive tasks.
N4 | Estimating fabrication time and material use (2021)

In 2021, Chen et al. placed seven orthopedic anatomical models on slicing software of six different printers, comparing the effects of orientation, layer height, and infill on estimated printing time and material costs. The study observed significant differences between equipment and settings, with the measured objects representing manufacturing resources estimated by the software. [R10]

The resource differences in the same geometry across different processes illustrate that costs cannot be estimated solely based on model volume. Supports, orientation, and required surface quality all influence the process. While slicing comparisons can control geometric input and make equipment variations an auditable factor, the labor involved in model review, segmentation, and rework is not automatically factored into cost estimates. Therefore, when used for hospital decision-making, these processes should be accumulated as distinct resource items.

This study raises practical questions for the N8 hepatobiliary and pancreatic pilot project: The worth of creating complex models must be evaluated along with the decisions they can alter. Low material costs may be accompanied by long wait times, while high automation may save manpower but increase fixed costs. A reasonable unit of comparison is cases delivered on time and fulfilling predetermined planned tasks, rather than per gram of material. Resource analysis also provides feedback to N1: clearly defining the anatomical information that must be retained can reduce the manufacturing burden caused by irrelevant details.
N5 | Multiformat clinical modeling services (2022)

Ghosh et al. reported in 2022 112 modeling cases from a pediatric cardiology center between 2018 and 2020, 96 of which served clinical planning. The team combined printed models, flat screens, virtual reality, and digital restoration design to demonstrate a practical way of organizing interdisciplinary services. [R01]

The methodological advancement here is moving the model from a single-instance technical demonstration to a continuous service. Different display formats share segmentation results, allowing problems to be modified in a digital environment before deciding whether to create an entity. It's necessary to differentiate between service utilization, case difficulty, and outcome: highly complex cases are more likely to be transferred to modeling, thus directly comparing surgical outcomes between users and non-users can introduce choice differences. Recording the reasons for application and decision points is more interpretive than simply accumulating usage counts.

The multi-format platform also changes quality responsibility. Those responsible for segmentation need to know the surgical issues, those responsible for planning need to understand the boundaries of image visibility, and those responsible for manufacturing need to know which areas are most important. The next step in clinical research should centralize the confirmation of these three aspects in traceable case versions to reduce the asynchrony between digital and physical maps. This organizational condition is a prerequisite for N7 randomized studies and N9 dynamic simulations to enter the routine process.
N6 | Comparing mixed aortic representations (2023)

The 2023 Aortic Teaching Study divided 51 resident physicians into two groups to compare traditional teaching methods with those using a mixed reality-based printed model. The experimental group had higher overall scores and higher scores in anatomy and pathophysiology, while no similar differences were observed in differential diagnosis and treatment. [R03]

The separate score components clarify the mechanism: spatial presentation directly supports structural understanding, whereas diagnosis and treatment also depend on pathology, risk assessment and experience. A combined-media comparison evaluates an entire teaching approach but cannot assign effects separately to physical and mixed-reality components. To isolate the medium, content, exposure time and feedback must be held constant across display conditions. To study an actual service, evaluate the combined workflow as a whole.

For preoperative planning, the implication is to define the task before choosing the medium. Screens facilitate measurement and iterative modification; virtual reality supports inspection of internal spaces; physical models support shared pointing and contact manipulation. The same case can be evaluated for relationship identification, plan agreement and device passage to test whether advantages vary by task. This leads to N9: when the question shifts from “where is it?” to “how can the device pass?”, contact-related evidence is needed.
N7 | Randomized pilot study in endometriosis (2026)

Cooke and colleagues’ 2026 randomized pilot included 5 model-group cases and 8 controls. MRI-derived models of deep endometriosis were used, and clinicians repeatedly estimated difficulty, allocated time and blood loss. Actual operating time differed between groups, and estimates changed before versus after model review. [R04]

The design, with its repeated measurements, makes intermediate steps that the model might affect visible. Early identification of difficulties may increase planning time but reduces intraoperative adjustments; therefore, "increased expected time" and "reduced actual time" are not contradictory. Interpretation should separate planning quality from surgical speed and examine whether changes correspond to a specific anatomical relationship, rather than attributing any positive postoperative outcome to the model.

The focus of small-scale randomized studies is to identify measurable mechanisms and subsequent trial endpoints. Patient and physician responses are not presented in the same statistical units, and multiple judgments from the same case may be correlated; case severity and surgical procedure also affect the time distribution. The next step could be to establish a more stable outcome chain around planning deviations, intraoperative changes, and resource preparation for key steps, and to examine whether the model's benefits differ for physicians with varying experience, thus connecting it to the N5 selection rule.
N8 | Costs in complex hepatobiliary and pancreatic cases (2026)

The 2026 Hepatobiliary and Pancreatic Study analyzed the anatomical features, clinical use, and resource costs of image-derived printed models in three complex cases, combined with a systematic review. The original pilot section examined patient selection and production burden within the same framework. [R05]

In these cases, the key information is often the spatial relationship among tumor, vessels and the organ to be preserved, rather than the complete appearance of every tissue. Case pilots reveal fabrication bottlenecks and the information surgeons actually use. A transparent shell that obstructs the view or ineffective color coding can hinder the task despite accurate dimensions; visual presentation therefore deserves its own quality assessment.

Cost assessment can be extended along the manufacturing resources of N4 to include image processing, expert review, post-processing, and delivery. The time savings brought by the model occur across different departments; if the costs are borne solely by the manufacturing department while the benefits occur in the operating room, the service may be unsustainable. Future research should employ resource accounting along the same case pathway and match costs with the key questions being answered. This makes economic assessment a tool for selecting appropriate model complexity, rather than applying the same price threshold to all cases.
N9 | Static and dynamic aortic models (2026)

The 2026 Complex Aorta Study included a retrospective comparison of 46 cases, combining rigid anatomical models and compliance models of the connecting pulsatile flow system. Dynamic models provided information on instrument passage and deployment; the assisted planning group had shorter operation times and less contrast agent usage, with no similar differences observed in one-year outcomes. [R06]

The value of a dynamic model lies not in adding another component, but in its ability to answer contact questions that static models cannot. Material compliance, wall thickness, and boundary fixation all affect device path, and realistic flow appearance does not guarantee accurate mechanical response. Therefore, dynamic simulations should first verify task-related deformations and drag before interpreting difficulties discovered during pre-simulation; otherwise, the model may misinterpret manufacturing material properties as patient risks.

This node converges three branches: geometry, display, and resources. Complex bending and contact problems require dynamic information; simply identifying the branch might be handled by a simpler model. Reviewing intergroup comparisons also requires understanding case selection and time phases. In the future, it's possible to predefine what unresolved issues trigger dynamic modeling and examine whether new information alters key decisions. When feeding back to N1, the model quality definition will shift from average geometric error to "the range of geometric and mechanical errors sufficient to support this decision."

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: In academic research, the 2017 study on image conversion and multi-center planning primarily addressed whether the model could accurately represent and alter decisions; the 2021 cost comparison incorporated manufacturing choices into the design; and the 2022 clinical service study further organized multiple manifestations into a single case workflow. The corresponding industry development can be understood through two product routes: one enhancing data services from image to design, and the other enhancing the operability of patient-specific entities.

Axial3D’s current AXCEL platform combines image acquisition, automated segmentation, device-related landmarks, measurement, planning and surgeon confirmation in a configurable workflow. Its official page emphasizes cloud deployment and integration across different device portfolios. [R07]

The product form expands the deliverables from a single model to structured 3D data available for subsequent applications. For hospitals and medical device companies, the key change is the ability to reuse the same case information and save confirmation points within the workflow. Platform competition therefore involves task adaptation, handling of unusual cases, and version management. If automated segmentation reduces processing time for routine cases, the saved professional time can be redirected to reviewing difficult cases; evaluation should simultaneously document automated coverage and the burden of manual revisions.

Lazarus 3D’s Pre-Sure produces patient-specific soft-tissue rehearsal models from CT or MRI. Its official product page describes cutting, suturing and clamping applications, together with image upload, digital-anatomy review and physical-model delivery. [R08]

This route concentrates value on rehearsal using patient-specific geometry. Material response and manipulable critical regions become design inputs, while case geometry and delivery deadlines distinguish it from a generic trainer. The two industry routes can meet at their data interface: one supplies confirmed anatomical structures, the other converts selected structures into manipulable materials. Academic research then explains which decisions gain useful information from that conversion.

The observable product evolution from 2027 to 2029 is not about increasingly complex model appearances, but rather about increasingly clear delivery boundaries: recording problems at the time of application, recording anatomy at the time of confirmation, recording changes in the treatment plan during use, and recording the correspondence between postoperative records and actual situations. Services with this record chain are more likely to form a verifiable case database and select appropriate manufacturing complexity for different tasks.
How can personalized physical models help with complex surgical planning?

The academic side raises anatomical or procedural questions requiring clarification, while the enterprise side provides the ability to repeatedly translate and deliver the solutions. The most direct connection is to write the model's intended use as a verifiable task and then document whether it alters the clinical plan.
Simply increasing the realism of a model does not necessarily increase its value; only when new features help answer previously unsolvable questions does it constitute a clear improvement.
How can the cardiovascular and craniofacial model demonstrate complex anatomy?

Academic research helps define which structures must be retained, which information is suitable for layered display, and which deformations or flows are meaningful for training. Enterprises translate this into design and delivery specifications.
Different models of the same case should maintain a consistent spatial benchmark so that static understanding and operational simulation can be cross-checked.
What tasks are physical models, screens, and VR models suitable for?

Academic task comparisons can help companies determine when printing is necessary and when digital presentation is sufficient. Enterprise platforms, on the other hand, maintain consistency in segmentation, schemes, and model versions, providing a stable foundation for comparative studies.
The clear cross-path is: shared 3D data → digital discussion and modification → key tasks requiring tactile feedback → physical simulation → results back to the plan.

Direct links can be organized around transferable research outputs. Segmentation studies supply critical structures and their uncertainty; manufacturing studies supply dimensional and material-response ranges; clinical studies identify situations in which a model changes a decision. Companies can incorporate these into request forms, review interfaces and delivery reports to define use-specific quality requirements. Research methods transfer through these concrete interfaces, and corresponding measurements can evaluate the collaboration.

Joint development is better suited to focusing on a clearly defined bottleneck, such as how much manual correction is needed for complex lumen segmentation, or whether a certain type of tissue contact can be reproduced using a material model. Comparing methods first on the same input, and then expanding the case range, can avoid the difficulty in interpreting changes made to multiple aspects during product iteration. For multi-center services, unified task definitions and modification records can also support independent review, allowing local usage habits to coexist with a common evidence framework.
How can personalized physical models help with complex surgical planning?

Research has moved from geometric representations to workflow and decision evaluation. A new trend is to combine different model formats and select rigid, soft-structure, or dynamic representations depending on the problem.

Clinical service cases demonstrate the feasibility of implementation, while prospective studies begin to examine decision-making and surgical procedures. These two chains of evidence jointly determine the conditions for widespread adoption.
How can the cardiovascular and craniofacial model demonstrate complex anatomy?

Research is shifting from reproducing overall external shape to representing task-relevant internal anatomy and incorporating dynamic function. Teaching and planning studies show that useful information depends on separable layers, cutaways and interaction, alongside printing accuracy.
Explainable progress should be manifested in the fact that a particular relationship is easier to understand, or that a particular operation can be evaluated in advance.
What tasks are physical models, screens, and VR models suitable for?

The trend is shifting from simple tool substitution to task specialization. Digital platforms improve the efficiency of information adjustment and dissemination, physical models provide specific touch and operational experiences, and dynamic models further expand verification capabilities.
Future research should focus on reporting which tasks participants benefited from, rather than simply asking participants which format they preferred.

The first translational issue is decision-relevant error. Average surface distance can be dominated by broad flat regions, while a surgeon may need a branch opening or a thin anatomical partition. Quality assessment should mark critical regions first and report boundary stability, connectivity and dimensional deviations there. Global measurements check scale; local measurements check risk-relevant information. Together they determine suitability for the intended task.

The second issue is how the model is used by the team. The model provides a shared reference during preoperative meetings and may highlight certain structures due to color, windowing, or transparency choices. Studies allow different professionals to independently propose solutions, then examine whether discussions reduce disagreement and map convergence to specific structures. Improved protocol consistency is only meaningful when linked to correct anatomy and actual operation; therefore, "greater consensus" and "more accurate judgment" should be measured separately.

The third issue is model freshness. Digital models can be updated immediately after modifications, but physical entities need to be recreated; patient status, imaging time, and proposed protocols may also change. The service should connect imaging versions, segmentation versions, planning versions, and physical entity versions, and specify which changes trigger a re-review. Such a workflow design directly affects clinical usability and determines whether cross-center studies can compare model interventions of the same significance.
How can personalized physical models help with complex surgical planning?

Near term: Task-oriented models for complex cases have greater potential for development. When key anatomical and procedural requirements are clear, models are more likely to generate measurable benefits.
Interim Phase: Static, soft tissue, and dynamic models will be grouped by task. Quality control and delivery time are required to support clinical scheduling.
Observation indicators: type of protocol change, intraoperative planning compliance, problems identified in advance, preparation and delivery cycle, temporary adjustments, and total case input.
How can the cardiovascular and craniofacial model demonstrate complex anatomy?
Near term: Models of decomposable and observable internal structures will continue to be refined. They directly correspond to the understanding of complex anatomy.
Mid-term: Dynamic and multi-material capabilities will be used for specific interactive tasks. Demonstration is needed to show that the new features improve practical judgment or operation.
Observation indicators: key structure identification, internal pathway understanding, planning consistency, geometric error, dynamic repeatability, and model making burden.
What tasks are physical models, screens, and VR models suitable for?
Near term: Hybrid workflows will become more common than single tools. Different formats will be combined by case and task.
Mid-term: Cross-form version consistency and outcome documentation are more critical. They determine whether the model can continue to be used in real-world decision-making.
Observation indicators: task accuracy, plan modification, operational performance, cognitive burden, production waiting time, sharing efficiency, and resource input for each task.

The baseline scenario for 2027-2029 selects tools based on unresolved issues. If digital reconstruction adequately addresses spatial relationships, resources are focused on expert review and team sharing; if issues remain regarding instrument contact, cutting, or post-reconstruction morphology, physical simulations are added. Indicators supporting this scenario include application-to-confirmation time, number of critical structural revisions, changes to predefined solutions due to the model, and on-time delivery rate.

Rapidly advancing scenarios require prospective studies to connect intermediate decisions with the clinical process. Pre-defined key steps, intraoperative modifications, and resource preparation more closely approximate the model's mechanisms of action and can be evaluated in conjunction with operative time and patient outcomes. If these indicators remain consistent across different centers, services can expect to develop stable case selection rules; if benefits are concentrated only in a few anatomical types, specialization should be expanded around those types.

Research priorities should shift from "whether to use a model" to "which question requires which model." We can first develop task classifications and minimum quality sets, then compare the incremental value of digital, rigid physical and dynamic physical models, and finally evaluate the resource benefits of the entire path. Sample selection, operator experience, and intervention time need to be documented together to place results from different centers within the same interpretive framework.

P6-02.title: Simulation and Training
P6-02.subtitle: From Realistic Touch to Explainable Skill Learning
P6-02.thesis: The printed training model needs to simultaneously and stably provide task cues, distinguish operational quality, and support comparable repeated practice. Material calibration, action feedback, curriculum scheduling, and consumable lifespan are mutually constrained; its future value depends on whether training gains can be maintained and transferred to new scenarios.
