blocks.text: The simulation training model needs to correlate anatomy, tissue response, and imaging performance with teaching objectives. Realistic tactile feedback addresses what cues the operator receives; training effectiveness addresses how these cues alter abilities; and repeated practice addresses whether the model and curriculum can remain comparable across multiple rounds of use. Eight original studies form three mutually reinforcing lines of evidence: materials, tasks, and learning.
How can the printed training model reproduce the feel of tissue?

Tactile sensation encompasses hardness, elasticity, viscosity, friction, and fracture behavior. Models with similar shapes only answer the question of "does it look like this?"; the change in resistance during manipulation determines the practice experience.
This problem uses specific surgical procedures as the unit of material evaluation, examining how printing, casting, and composite structures work together to form a model.
Can training models improve procedural skills and learning curves?

The training model should help learners perform more accurate, stable, and independent operations. Evaluation can be divided into whether the model resembles the real task, whether it can differentiate between experience levels, whether there is improvement after practice, and whether the improvement can be retained and transferred.
These types of evidence progressively deepen, with satisfaction and short-term performance each providing a portion of the information.
How can specialty-specific procedural simulators support repeated practice?

Repeated practice not only requires the model to still be usable, but also requires the next practice session to face a similar level of difficulty. Needle marks, cuts, material fatigue, and changes in component position all affect performance comparisons.
This question focuses on how to break down specialized tasks into resetting, replaceable, and gradeable practice units.

Tactile questions differ by action: palpation involves surface-to-deep-anatomy relationships; puncture involves resistance during entry and breakthrough; cutting involves advancement and fracture; and suturing involves needle tracks and tissue pull-out. Learning-curve questions place these actions over time: how much effective practice produces stable performance, how much is retained after a delay and whether skill transfers to new anatomy. Specialty simulators should address both groups of questions.

The evaluation can be organized sequentially along the lines of "model conditions—action process—task result—capability maintenance." Material testing verifies the input, instrument movement and sensor recording verify the process, target location or resection quality verifies the result, and delayed and new case testing verifies capability. The connections between these layers allow for the interpretation of any performance improvement and help the course determine whether to increase practice, improve feedback, or revise the model itself.
N1 | Action-specific validation of anesthesia models (2018)

A 2018 neuraxial-anesthesia model study invited 22 anesthesiologists, of whom 21 completed comparison with a commercial model. The printed approach scored better for loss-of-resistance, puncture and ultrasound-related tasks, but worse for surface palpation. Realism therefore needs to be assessed by procedural task. [R01]

This method shifts model evaluation from an overall impression to specific sensory cues. The operator palpates the relationship between the surface and deep bone, the needle senses changes in material resistance, and ultrasound observes the acoustic interface; these three require different physical properties. Using a commercial model as a comparison helps identify the relative advantages of the new approach and also reveals task limitations caused by softer or more fragile materials. Design optimization should first determine the most important instructional actions, then allocate material and structural requirements.

The inconsistent scores across different tasks is a useful finding because it demonstrates the potential for task modularization. Localization training preserves a stable surface, the puncture zone can be used as a consumable replacement, and the ultrasound zone needs to maintain scattering and contrast. Future research should document the stages at which errors occur in each task, rather than just the completion time. This node connects the learning performance of N2 with the modular structure of N3: the former answers what changes practice brings, and the latter answers how this practice can be repeated on the model.

Material selection can also be optimized step-by-step through comparison: fixing the bony geometry to compare the surface coverage, then fixing the coverage to compare the deeper resistance layer. This breakdown allows each change to correspond to a specific sensory cue, and also allows determining whether one improvement impairs another task. The research yields transferable design principles, which the course uses to select modules, rather than relying on a single overall score to determine all applications.
N2 | Repeated learning in lumbosacral needle procedures (2018)

A 2018 study by Li et al. embedded a printed lumbosacral spine into a tissue-based simulation medium and compared CT-guided procedures under different training regimens. After additional training, the number of needle adjustments required for trainees to reach their target decreased; confidence improved in both groups, demonstrating that skill and self-assessment can vary. [R09]

The reason why the number of adjustments is closer to the training objective than simply assessing satisfaction is because it involves both spatial planning and action correction based on image feedback. Fewer adjustments may indicate that the trainee has developed more accurate path judgment, or it may indicate familiarity with the location of the same model. To distinguish between the two, the case structure should be changed after practice, while maintaining a similar level of target difficulty. This design transforms the test of "doing repetition faster" into a test of "being able to make effective judgments on new spatial relationships."

Learning curves should include several timescales: consecutive trials measure immediate familiarization, delayed retesting measures retention and new anatomy tests transfer. Instructor prompts and the number of imaging observations should also be recorded, since additional assistance can improve performance. Linking these records with N1’s task decomposition identifies improvements in localization, trajectory planning or needle-tip control and guides subsequent teaching beyond simply adding practice time.
N3 | Replaceable pediatric difficult airways (2020)

A 2020 Scientific Reports study established a replaceable difficult airway model for young children, comparing the size, material rigidity, and expert evaluation of the printed structure based on patient-specific anatomy. The study incorporated the functional coordination of the oral cavity, tongue, and airway into the simulator design. [R10]

Replaceability has value beyond maintenance. Changing the internal airway while retaining the external frame controls positioning and the instrument environment while deliberately varying task difficulty, creating a platform for studying skill transfer. Geometry and materials must be assessed together: the same narrowing feels different at different compliance levels, and a single hardness value cannot describe the deformation of a complex thin-walled structure.

Expert judgment provides the first layer of information on whether the model corresponds to the target scenario. Subsequently, the judgment should be broken down into measurable actions, such as visible space, tissue displacement, and instrument contact, and it should be observed whether beginners use these cues to improve. Interfaces between modules also affect the task: seams that create additional resistance may become erroneous learning cues. Therefore, functional consistency before and after replacement should be considered part of course quality and managed separately from changes in case difficulty. This approach is further applied to abrasion records in N8 neonatal puncture.
N4 | Experience-stratified robotic nephrectomy training (2023–2024)

The study of the robotic partial nephrectomy model was published online in 2023 and in the journal in 2024. Thirty-six participants completed a simulated nephrectomy in experience-based groups, and tissue preservation, resection margins, time, and GEARS scores were evaluated. Performance differences existed between experience groups, and the trend of score improvement with repeated attempts was not statistically significant. [R02]

The importance of multi-endpoint evaluation lies in preventing speed from being equated with overall skill. Faster resection accompanied by excessive loss of normal tissue does not align with the task objective; longer operation times may also stem from more cautious boundary control. Experience stratification provides construct validation clues: if the model allows existing experience to translate into better task quality, it is suitable for partial skill evaluation. The next step should be to examine whether this difference is stable across different case structures and material batches.

Repeated-attempt results must be interpreted in relation to each tumor’s difficulty. A harder later task can obscure improvement, while material wear can make a task easier and create apparent progress. Learning curves should therefore model the learner, task and simulator condition together. This node joins N2 in describing learning through quality-constrained efficiency, delayed retention and transfer to new cases, rather than extending a single expert rating into a conclusion about training effectiveness.

Consistency in scoring is equally important. Resection margins and tissue preservation can serve as indicators that closely approximate task outcomes, and the performance scale needs to clearly define the rules for rater training and repetition scoring. Pairing error events in the video with the final resection result can identify which actions deserve priority teaching and also facilitates the reuse of the same competency definition across different training centers.
N5 | Post-processing calibration of vascular materials (2025)

The 2025 research on vascular model materials utilizes UV treatment and hydrolysis to alter the mechanics of printed polymers, making them approximate the mechanical properties of target atherosclerotic tissue. Material post-processing becomes a designable variable, expanding the research focus from shape reproduction to the target tissue response. [R03]

The advantage of using materials testing for calibration is that it allows for the determination of the response range before introducing complex anatomy. If the material is too easily stretched or deformed, even with a realistic shape, erroneous feedback may be obtained during instrument delivery and expansion tasks. However, uniaxial parameters only describe one loading mode; vascular instrumentation tasks also involve bending, contact, friction, and local instability. Research should select necessary material tests based on the task, rather than pursuing a uniform "tissue-like" metric.

Post-processing also makes time part of the model specification. Storage, repeated wetting and light exposure can continue to change performance, so factory calibration must be connected to the condition during teaching. Batch witness specimens and periodic functional checks can track change and inform replacement. This complements N6: material calibration stabilizes the stimulus, while sensors measure the operator’s response. If the model drifts, the educational meaning of the sensor data changes.
N6 | Force feedback for arachnoid manipulation (2025)

The 2025 transsphenoidal surgery training model combines a printed structure, a thin film, and a liquid system. It uses pressure sensing to indirectly estimate and simulate the forces acting on the arachnoid membrane, and was tested by 11 experienced surgeons. Different instrument operations produced different force distributions, and the study established a preliminary feedback range. [R04]

Indirect sensing requires first explaining the measurement chain: the instrument contacts the membrane, the membrane responds to the liquid, and the sensor records the pressure. Loading location, contact area, and boundary conditions can affect the same reading; therefore, calibration determines what the feedback represents. Expert data is suitable for describing the operational distribution in a specific model; further instruction should focus on which signals effectively prompt action corrections and whether those corrections improve task quality.

The form of feedback also constitutes an instructional intervention. Continuous display of force values may help control peak values, but it makes learners dependent on the display; intermittent feedback is closer to autonomous completion, but initial error identification is slower. Learning under both arrangements and retesting without feedback can be compared, linking sensor signals, motion videos, and results. This node outputs a new capability to N7 curriculum organization: teachers can not only say "the movement is too heavy," but also point out when and where the deviation occurred, and check and adjust in the next practice session.

After the sensor is incorporated into the model, the reset process also requires checking the zero point and sensitivity. Thin-film replacement may alter the mechanical coupling, causing the same action to produce different signals. Incorporating each round of functional calibration into the training log helps distinguish between trainee progress and changes in the measurement system, and preserves an interpretable data foundation for future use of automated scoring.
N7 | Structured head-and-neck reconstruction curricula (2025)

A 2025 head-and-neck reconstruction workshop enrolled 30 residents who practiced osteotomy and flap placement using printed models and customized artificial fibulas. Independent blinded assessment used the Zwisch scale alongside pre- and post-course questionnaires. Self-assessment and measures of technical independence improved after the course. [R06]

The research value of the workshop lies in placing materials within a clear teaching sequence. There is a planning dependency between osteotomy and placement; deviations in one step accumulate in subsequent matching. Therefore, a complete task helps observe whether participants can organize local movements into a holistic plan. Independent assessment reduces the confounding effect of teacher-led instruction, while questionnaires supplement the learning outcomes based on what participants found most helpful. Both types of results can be interpreted concurrently, but they address different issues.

The next step in the course comparison can record the final geometric deviation, number of reworks, and teacher intervention, using a new defect structure during delayed retesting. This allows it to determine whether trainees have learned a fixed cutting sequence or the ability to organize steps according to the target morphology. Compared to N4, the robotic kidney model emphasizes tissue quality and boundaries, while the reconstruction model emphasizes the geometric accumulation of multiple actions; both suggest that specialist simulators should be tied to clear competency objectives before selecting appropriate materials and evaluation tools.
N8 | Tracking neonatal needle-model lifespan (2026)

A 2026 neonatal vascular-access study used a small-scale model for ultrasound-guided puncture, recording repeated punctures, covering-layer replacement and minor leakage. Ultrasound images were relatively little affected by reuse. All participants identified the vessels, and some completed the puncture and guidewire tasks. [R05]

This node transforms model lifetime from an abstract durability into an observable process. Puncture paths, surface damage, and leakage progressively alter the conditions for the next practice session; if different trainees reach different stages of wear and tear, their performance may be affected by the model's condition. Recording surface coverage and deep vessels separately allows identification of which component is experiencing functional decline, enabling the development of replacement rules while preserving usable components.

Small-scale manipulation also requires both image and tactile reliability. Clear images can reduce positioning difficulty, while soft surfaces can alter needle insertion stability. Therefore, training evaluation needs to observe the continuous process of needle tip visibility, path correction, and final task quality. It integrates N3 module replacement, N5 material stability, and N6 feedback measurement, and provides feedback N1: the model should be re-validated by task after the course. The basic unit of future training systems should be a round of well-defined, effective, and traceable practice, rather than just a reusable entity.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: The research pathway progressed from task validation for anesthesia and image-guided puncture in 2018 to replaceable airways in 2020, experience-stratified robotic-resection assessment in 2023–2024, and material calibration, force sensing and structured workshops in 2025. A 2026 neonatal model study further recorded wear during use. Training tools thus developed from realistic shapes toward systems that repeatedly provide comparable practice conditions.

The Lazarus 3D offers Skill-Sure, providing customized training models, and Pre-Sure, offering preoperative simulations based on patient images. The official page highlights soft tissue response and realistic instrument manipulation as key product capabilities; the two services are organized around training courses and specific case studies, respectively. [R07][R08]

The differences between the two product lines directly impact manufacturing organization. The course model emphasizes multiple learners facing comparable difficulty, consumable replenishment, and repetitive supply, while patient rehearsals focus on responses to specific geometries and critical areas, as well as pre-operative delivery. Shared material capabilities can be reused, but specification management needs to be established separately around course objectives and case-related issues.

From a product evolution perspective, the next valuable incremental step is to incorporate component replacement, reset time, model lifespan, and scoring interfaces into the delivery. Replaceable parts reduce the scrapping of entire units and also support preset difficulty levels; standardized records allow training centers to compare different course rounds. For medical device companies, the model can also provide training on the use of new devices, but device familiarity and clinical competence should be treated as different learning objectives.

Industry collaborations can revolve around real-world usage burdens. If instructors spend a significant amount of time fixing models each time, even low material costs make it difficult to achieve high-frequency training; consumables that can be quickly replaced and maintain functionality will increase the available time for learners. Therefore, the economics of model services depend on the total cost of a single effective practice run, including instructor preparation, equipment usage, maintenance, and disposal, not just the physical selling price.
How can the printed training model reproduce the feel of tissue?

Materials research provides adjustable parameters, training research provides the task endpoint, and enterprises are responsible for manufacturing consistency and delivery. These three should be connected around the same operational principle: does a certain mechanical change improve the realism of the exercise, can it help differentiate experience levels, and does it remain stable after repeated use?
Can training models improve procedural skills and learning curves?

The most direct link between academia and industry is to transform research tasks and scores into training products: the same operation, similar material performance, clear errors, and comparable results.

If companies can maintain a consistent level of difficulty across different batches of models, the research results are more likely to be reproduced in multi-center courses; the research can also help determine when the next stage of training requirements are met.
How can specialty-specific procedural simulators support repeated practice?

The academic side provides specific metrics for acceptance testing: the anesthesia model focuses on resistance and ultrasound; the resection model focuses on resection margins and tissue preservation; the endoscopic model focuses on operative force; and the puncture model focuses on imaging, leakage, and catheter placement completion. The enterprise side's replaceable components and multi-organ platform provide a product organization method for continuous practice. [R08]

The connection begins with task design and reusable structures. Procurement and course evaluation can ask suppliers to demonstrate replacement-part consistency, reset procedures and cost per effective practice session, while independent skill tests assess learning. Manufacturing consistency is a delivery objective to be verified through those measurements.

The most direct connection between academia and industry is measurable task specifications. Research can provide the relationship between certain puncture feedback, cutting quality, or image contrast and learning objectives, which companies can then translate into material acceptance and batch quality ranges. When instrument operation methods change, specifications should also be redefined according to the task. This kind of collaboration, centered on clear inputs and results, enables the determination of which training conditions have been improved by product iteration.

Another connection is data structures. Academic research rating scales, sensor signals, and action events can be converted into course records, but a single attempt, success, and effective feedback need to be defined collectively. If companies simultaneously record model numbers, component usage counts, and material conditions, they can link product maintenance with learning analytics. Instructors can then assign the next exercise based on the error type, without having to guess the cause from the overall score.
How can the printed training model reproduce the feel of tissue?

Tactile research has shifted from overall satisfaction to task-based functional evaluation. Material conditioning and sensing structures enable the recording of resistance, contact, and damage, further supporting objective training.

Printing and casting processes are often used together. Technological advancements should be interpreted according to the actual function of the model, rather than requiring all tissues to be printed directly.
Can training models improve procedural skills and learning curves?

Research is shifting from satisfaction levels to process indicators and structured scoring. Experience stratification, blinded evaluation, and sensor feedback are gradually supplementing subjective evaluation, enabling the model to serve training and assessment.
The next phase will focus on continuous training, skill retention and transfer, forming a complete chain of model-course-ability outcomes.
How can specialty-specific procedural simulators support repeated practice?

The research pathway shows an expanding evaluation scope: 2018 studies focused on task-specific tactile cues and comparison with commercial training models; robotic-nephrectomy research added experience groups and objective procedural measures; 2025 workshops and sensor-equipped models linked learning feedback to action data; and a 2026 neonatal model study directly documented usability after repeated punctures.

Currently, it is clear that the evaluation dimensions have become more abundant. Maintaining long-term skills, ensuring consistency in difficulty between different batches of replacement parts, and evaluating real-world performance after training are the three key areas for further developing the repetitive training platform.

Research and transformation first requires separating learning from model familiarization. Fixed geometry facilitates comparison of consecutive trials, while new geometry is used to test transfer; fixed feedback facilitates comparison of teaching methods, while retesting without feedback is used to test independent operation. Courses can systematically alternate these conditions, giving each stage of the learning curve a clear meaning. Learners' prior experience, teacher prompts, and task difficulty should be recorded simultaneously to avoid directly merging individuals with different backgrounds onto a single average curve.

The second key issue is the non-stationarity caused by wear and tear. A puncture trajectory may make subsequent needle insertion easier, cutting edges may reduce usable tissue, and repeated compression may alter springback. Model lifespan should be defined by functional degradation, not by whether it remains aesthetically intact. A brief, task-related check before each round can separate malfunctions from teaching difficulties and provide a verifiable basis for replacement rules.

The third issue is the connection between training costs and learning benefits. When comparing courses, the effective number of practice sessions and teacher time required to reach a preset skill level can be calculated, along with material replacement and equipment usage. High-fidelity models that only provide necessary information in the last few rounds can adopt a course organization from simple to complex; if key feedback is required from the first round, this function should be retained from the beginning. Cost optimization therefore comes from task allocation, rather than uniformly reducing material quality.
How can the printed training model reproduce the feel of tissue?
Near term: Mission-specific material combinations are superior to pursuing a single, universal soft material. Different organs and operations require different feedback.
Mid-term: Mechanical calibration and sensing may be incorporated into training products. Repeatable measurements and clear skill assessment criteria are required.
Observation indicators: puncture and cutting force, suture pull-out, expert evaluation, batch-to-batch variation, storage stability, replacement cycle and training performance.
Can training models improve procedural skills and learning curves?
Near term: structured tasks and feedback will become important parts of training models. Learners need to know where errors occur.
Mid-term: Course validation and skills transfer will determine product value. Delayed retesting and comparisons closer to real-world work are needed.
Observation indicators: task success, tissue damage, operation time, independence, number of practice sessions, delayed performance, and performance in new scenarios.
How can specialty-specific procedural simulators support repeated practice?
Near term: Replaceable task modules will continue to become more widespread. They reduce the burden of repeatedly creating complete models.
Mid-term: Module and digital evaluation may be combined. Consistency between materials, location, and sensing results needs to be maintained.
Observation metrics: reset time, number of times each module is available, difficulty difference after replacement, task performance, damage record, and overall cost of each training session.

The baseline scenario for 2027–2029 is the development of specialty simulators into replaceable modules and standardized practice units. This requires consistent geometry, tactile response and imaging appearance after replacement, repeatable scoring across instructors, and records of wear alongside learning across courses. Indicators include reset time, the proportion of effective practice attempts, material-batch differences and practice needed to reach the task standard.

A more advanced scenario is the stable integration of sensor feedback and structured curriculum. This requires signals that represent critical errors, feedback that helps learners improve, and improvements that are retained in tests without feedback and with new cases. If these conditions are met, the model will support more refined, individualized training arrangements; if gains are only seen in immediate results, the curriculum should focus on adjusting the timing and difficulty progression of feedback, rather than continuing to increase the types of sensors.

Research priorities can begin by establishing cross-model task endpoints, followed by controlled practice exercises, and finally, studying the transfer of skills to clinical or higher-fidelity scenarios. The most valuable aspects to continuously observe are changes in error types, movement stability, tissue protection, delayed retention, and responses from learners with different experience levels. Pairing these results with each model state is crucial to creating an evidence base that both explains learning and guides product maintenance.

Cross-center comparisons can utilize common key tasks while preserving authentic equipment and processes across specialties. A unified endpoint enables comparisons between model versions, and recording local instructional schedules explains why the same product produces different learning trajectories. This research design helps transform successful courses into replicable training conditions.

Future focus will be on organizing reliable data, diverse expressions, and audience-relevant outcomes into a continuous service.

blocks.text: The teaching and communication model transforms spatial relationships that cannot be directly observed into commonly identifiable objects. Professional teaching focuses on structural concepts and reasoning, patient communication focuses on understanding one's own illness, choices, and subsequent processes, and extension issues focus on all resources used effectively each time. These three types of issues are connected through information design, interactive activities, and outcome evaluation, forming a complete research chain from creation to understanding.
How can physical models improve anatomy teaching?

Anatomy teaching includes not only structural identification but also orientation, hierarchy, adjacency relationships, and functional connections. Different learning tasks require different models: normal morphology is suitable for basic identification, while lesions and separable structures are suitable for comparison and reasoning.

The effectiveness of the model should be evaluated through specific learning objectives, and a distinction should be made between immediate post-class performance, delayed memory, and practical operation.
Can the model help patients understand surgery and disease?

Patients need to connect medical terminology with their own situation to understand their illness. Physical models allow doctors to point out lesions and the scope of treatment, and also allow patients to raise questions, creating a shared space for discussion.
Evaluation focuses on understanding, communication and decision quality; the model is an explanatory tool rather than a treatment.
How do model fabrication time and cost affect educational adoption?

The total investment in the teaching model includes data processing, engineering design, equipment usage, materials, post-processing, inspection, and maintenance. Printing wait times can be paralleled with other tasks, but human workload often directly limits the service scale.
Comparisons should use a completed teaching or training task as the unit and account for both reuse and learning outcomes.

The rational mechanism by which physical models improve teaching is to reduce the mental transition from two-dimensional images to three-dimensional relationships and allow learners to actively test their understanding through rotation, combination, and pointing. To test this mechanism, research should compare the correctness of relational interpretations, error types, and transfer performance. If only the presentation time is increased, the model may primarily provide repetitive exposure; if questions and feedback are set around the model, it is closer to a clearly describable teaching intervention.

Patient communication and classroom teaching also have different rhythms. Classrooms can include standardized tests and repetitive lessons, while outpatient consultations require explanations tailored to individual problems. The model should help patients ask questions, confirm understanding, and express preferences, while doctors can identify misunderstandings through patient identification and repetition. The production cost and time must ultimately be measured within this practical usage path: only when the model arrives on time, is properly explained, and is effectively used does it constitute an evaluable resource output.
N1 | Open imaging-to-model workflows (2017)

The 2017 PLOS ONE study divided image-to-solid transformation into segmentation, mesh trimming, and printing, demonstrating the feasible process using examples of ribs, liver, and lungs. Its contribution is transforming individual anatomy from implicit information in images into identifiable and manipulable objects. [R01]

Teaching and patient communication need different presentations. Students identify anatomy, establish spatial relationships and connect mechanisms; patients need the parts relevant to their illness and choices. Model generation must therefore be followed by information selection: which structures to retain, where to add cutaways and whether colors or separable components are helpful. Each choice directs attention, so presentation should follow the learning question rather than reproduce every visible tissue.

The key connection at this node is linking the manufacturing process to the understanding process. Even if the model is accurate, if the focus is unclear, users may still only see complex shapes; a model that is appropriately simplified and has clear relationships has the potential to reduce the burden of spatial transformation. Research allows users to explain structural relationships, rather than just saying whether the model looks good, and then feedback on incorrect answers is used to design colors, windowing, and labeling. Subsequent N2 and N5 developments follow professional learning and patient understanding respectively, while N4 evaluates how many resources these designs require.
N2 | Teaching with patient craniofacial cases (2018)

The 2018 craniofacial education study used patient-specific CT-printed models to combine abnormal anatomy with preoperative procedural learning and to record milestone changes in resident physician competence. Case models provided a bridge from knowledge of normal structures to interpretation of specific lesions. [R02]

The teaching value of selecting real cases lies in enabling students to process structural variations rather than simply memorizing standard forms. Complex spatial relationships need to be linked to proposed operations; handheld and rotating models can provide shared references for this connection. If teaching simultaneously increases instructor explanation and practice time, the effect should be understood as the result of the complete course; further comparisons can maintain consistency between content and time, investigating which cognitive step the physical interaction specifically facilitated.

Compared to routine anatomical recognition, case-based learning should evaluate whether students can explain why a particular step was chosen and how structural changes affect subsequent steps. This reasoning can be tested for transferability using unseen abnormal morphologies, rather than simply repeating the teacher's sequence on the same model. This research line has found a more explicit structural design in N8 fracture teaching: deconstructibility and reconstructibility not only provide tactile feedback but also organize classification, relationships, and treatment choices into actionable learning tasks.
N3 | Comparing low-cost task models (2018)

The 2018 low-cost spinal anesthesia model study combined printed structures with simulated tissues, and anesthesiologists evaluated them against commercial models. Performance varied across different actions; puncture and imaging tasks were performed well, while surface palpation was weaker. [R03]

For teaching and promotion, this result is more enlightening than a single cost figure: savings can occur in parts that do not carry core information, while key clues need to be preserved. Palpation lessons and needle-tip observation lessons have different requirements for the same model; courses should define the task first, then choose the complexity of the materials. Otherwise, low cost may weaken the most critical information, while high cost may be invested in appearances that have little effect on the target ability.

Resource comparison therefore requires functional integration. It can calculate the materials, preparation, and reset time required to complete a specific task, and then observe whether students reach the same ability standards. Reusable bony structures and consumable surfaces have different lifespans; managing them separately helps expand curriculum coverage. This issue connects the equipment selection for N4 and the ongoing service for N6: economics comes from the arrangement of the entire instructional path, as well as the model's ability to maintain information consistency across multiple rounds of use.
N4 | Resource comparisons across six machines (2021)

The 2021 six-device study used seven orthopedic models to compare printing time and material costs estimated by slicing software under different devices, orientations, layer heights, and infill levels. The results show that geometry and manufacturing settings jointly determine resource requirements, providing a controllable comparison when selecting devices. [R04]

The cost structure of the teaching model depends on how it is used. A basic model can be used repeatedly by multiple classes, while a patient-specific model may only serve one consultation; detachable parts facilitate replacement but also increase assembly management. Equipment comparisons should be conducted under the same functional objectives; otherwise, evaluating courses requiring multi-color display based on printing speed, or evaluating courses requiring only overall relationships based on surface refinement, may deviate from the true needs.

This research is suitable for establishing a basic estimate of manufacturing resources. A complete evaluation and promotion process also requires connecting image processing, content design, teacher preparation, and rework. Costs can be divided into three parts: fixed development, unit manufacturing, and per-use, and then amortized according to the expected number of users. If the model design reduces unnecessary materials while maintaining the recognizability of key relationships, it can unify academic expression with economic efficiency. This relationship is reflected in the N5 grid-based thyroid model as a joint design of information visibility and lightweight structure.
N5 | Randomized thyroid informed-communication trial (2021)

In 2021, Seok et al. conducted a randomized study of 53 patients undergoing thyroid surgery, using deep learning-assisted segmentation and a grid-based model to represent the relationship between tumors and glands. The model group showed improved performance in categories related to knowledge, surgical benefit-risk understanding, and satisfaction. [R05]

The choice of the mesh structure follows a clear informational logic: external organs provide locational references while allowing internal lesions to be visible. Entities here serve as interpretive tools; the crucial outcome is whether the patient understands the location of their lesion and related surgical information. Random grouping helps compare communication approaches, but it's also important to record the time doctors spend explaining, opportunities to ask questions, and the users' existing knowledge to understand the mechanisms by which the model exerts its influence.

Individualization may enhance attention and a sense of connection, but it may also make lesions appear more prominent, triggering new anxieties. Therefore, future evaluations should separately observe knowledge, emotions, and the choice process. Having patients describe key relationships in their own words and then reiterate them after a period of time can test whether understanding has been retained. This step leads to research on the N9 communication scale: how spatial objects alter physician explanations, patient questioning, and shared confirmation is closer to the communication process that can be improved than overall satisfaction.
N6 | Shared data for clinical care and teaching (2022)

2022 Pediatric Cardiac Center Modeling Service Report: 112 cases, 16 for educational purposes, the remainder for clinical planning; the service combined print, screen, virtual reality, and digital design. This example demonstrates that the same data foundation can support multiple expressions and usage scenarios. [R06]

Sharing data can reduce redundant segmentation, but shared representations need to be tailored to the audience. Surgical teams focus on pathways and structural boundaries, students need relationships and mechanisms, and patients need concise information relevant to their own problems. Establishing a clear view for each use is more feasible than requiring a single complex model to handle all interpretations simultaneously. Case repositories can also organize comparisons of differences between similar lesions, expanding learning from single instances to patterns of variation.

The academic challenge of continuous service lies in the link between stable delivery and stable learning. Scheduling, quality review, and version consistency determine whether a model can be incorporated into a course or consultation at the appropriate time. Research can record content preparation time, the actual structure used in instruction, and changes in knowledge after use, identifying which steps involve the most repetitive work. The service evidence obtained in this way can help companies design interfaces and schools decide which foundational models are worth focusing on developing and which cases are suitable for on-demand production.
N7 | Domain-specific outcomes of mixed aortic teaching (2023)

The 2023 aortic education comparison study included 51 residents. The mixed reality combined with printing group showed better overall performance and scores in anatomy and pathophysiology, while there were no equal differences in diagnosis and treatment. The study provides an example of interpreting effects by knowledge type. [R07]

This breakdown supports a mechanism hypothesis: the model primarily helps organize existing facts into spatial relationships, while complete diagnostic reasoning requires additional knowledge and decision-making practice. Instructional design can use this to identify entities for relationship recognition, and then connect risk and treatment options through case discussions. The research object of the combined media is the entire course; subsequent analysis can determine the incremental effects of entities, digital overlays, and teacher feedback by breaking down the conditions.

When assessing, it's important to observe whether students can maintain their interpretive abilities in new perspectives and cases. If they only remember the color positions on a model, their scores may decline as the display method changes; if they form a structural concept, they should be able to restate it from another perspective. This, along with the decomposable model of N8, creates two active learning approaches: one that changes the viewpoint, and one that changes the structural composition. Comparisons should focus on the learning task, rather than prioritizing media technology levels as a measure of teaching effectiveness.
N8 | Randomized teaching with combinable fracture models (2024)

A preliminary randomized study of fracture education in 2024 ultimately analyzed 104 medical students, 52 in each group, comparing combinatorial detachable printed models with traditional solid models. Improvements were observed in some aspects of anatomy, fracture classification, injury mechanisms, and treatment options; however, no significant differences were found in response time. [R08]

The core innovation of the model is that it transforms structural changes into actionable problems. Students can observe the relationships between the bone blocks by disassembling and combining them, and then explain why they belong to a certain form and how this form affects subsequent judgments. Physical actions serve as the cognitive step, rather than adding entertainment. Using a solid model helps evaluate the incremental changes in interaction design, but further recording of the actual operation time and teacher prompts for both sets should ensure that knowledge improvement is connected to specific activities.

Benefits differed across fracture topics, indicating a need to match model design to content. Evaluation can progress from identification to explanation and treatment selection in new cases, showing where benefits persist. Delayed tests distinguish short-term recall from durable concepts. This node joins N2’s patient cases, N4’s resource design and N7’s spatial knowledge: greater fabrication effort has a clear educational purpose when model functions are linked to learning activities.
N9 | Randomized orthopedic clinician–patient communication evaluation (2024)

A 2024 randomized orthopedic-outpatient study compared explanations with and without model support in 46 patients, measuring changes in disease knowledge and using the Communication Assessment Tool (CAT). The model group scored better on several communication dimensions. This moved evaluation beyond general preference toward specific features of the interaction. [R09]

Once entities provide a common referent, doctors can confirm which part of the body the patient is talking about, and patients are more likely to ask specific questions. Communication scales can help capture this change in interaction, but understanding, feeling listened to, and participation in decision-making remain distinct outcomes. Research should link model usage, explanation content, and patient questioning to observe which type of change best predicts the retention of key knowledge.

The next step can be to use a retelling task to record whether information has been correctly reconstructed, a delayed test to record memory, and decision conflict and reasoning to record the participation process. Different health literacy levels, visual abilities, and language backgrounds will change the tool requirements, and the model's colors and text need to be designed accordingly. This node feeds back to N1: the best communication model should start with the questions the audience needs to answer, and then decide how much detail to present, so that individualization is reflected in the information relationship and communication style, rather than just the appearance of the patient's organs.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: The evolution of capabilities presented in this study began with open image production and case teaching, followed by lightweight grid-based patient models, equipment resource comparison, and continuous clinical services. Recent randomized studies have further broken down the results into different knowledge and communication dimensions. Therefore, industry development can be divided into two routes: data supply and teaching scenarios. The former reduces the burden of creating individual models, while the latter ensures that models are integrated into specific activities.

Axial3D’s current AXCEL platform combines imaging, automated segmentation, measurement, planning and physician confirmation in a configurable cloud-based workflow for structured 3D data. [R10] Such services could support teaching and communication by reusing confirmed patient anatomy in several formats and concentrating staff time on difficult cases and presentation design.

The product value of the data platform needs to be observed through downstream tasks. If automated processing reduces waiting time, but teachers still have to redesign colors and structures one by one, the course cost may simply be a change in location. A more valuable interface is one that preserves anatomical labels, versions, and key areas, allowing the teaching view and clinical view to share a reliable foundation, while allowing for selection of complexity based on different audiences.

The Skill-Sure official page for Lazarus 3D provides models for structured skills development, instrument training, and custom applications, and describes replaceable anatomical components and iterative design capabilities. Its product logic connects entities to training objectives, supporting reuse within the same course and adaptability of structures for different purposes. [R11]

For anatomy classes, products can be developed into a series based on reusable basic models, case variations, and modular components; for patient consultations, products require image confirmation, concise presentation, and pre-appointment delivery. These two types needs have different procurement and usage cadences. By designing production services, explanatory materials, and usage records together, companies can transform models from one-off displays into stable teaching resources.

From 2027 to 2029, a noteworthy industry shift is whether products offer verifiable learning activities and maintenance rules. Expanding the model catalog means more optional structures, but its actual value depends on course coverage, effective usage frequency, and ease of content updates. A case library and accompanying activities built around clearly defined tasks accumulate more evidence of sustained use than simply adding model details.
How can physical models improve anatomy teaching?

Academic research defines learning objectives and evaluation methods, while enterprise manufacturing stabilizes model structures and materials. Effective connection means assigning a specific model characteristic to a specific teaching activity; for example, a disassembleable structure corresponds to fracture relationships and treatment choices, rather than simply comparing "with a model" and "without a model."
Can the model help patients understand surgery and disease?

Academic research helps define communication effectiveness, while corporate capabilities provide stable and timely models. The connection between the two ends should be determined by the consulting task: whether it is location, size, surgical path, or reconstruction result that needs to be explained.
Image data can be shared for different purposes, but the model's colors, windowing, and annotations should be designed for the corresponding users.
How do model fabrication time and cost affect educational adoption?

Academic studies supply task-specific cost and outcome information, while companies supply sustained delivery capacity. Their connection can identify the dominant adoption bottleneck: improve data workflows if segmentation time is limiting, introduce replaceable structures if consumables are limiting, or standardize tasks and reuse models if course organization is limiting.

Academics and businesses can collaborate on specific cognitive problems. For example, when identifying the location of internal lesions, research can compare meshes, transparent shells, and fenestrations; when understanding fracture relationships, research can compare fixed morphologies and combinable structures; when patients are interpreting information, research can compare pointing and repetition activities. Businesses translate the results into manufacturable structures and accompanying instructions, while schools or hospitals continue to record usage performance from different audiences. This task-based collaboration helps both parties identify which product changes are worth developing.

Data reuse also supports continuous course updates. After a reviewed case segmentation is completed, simplified views suitable for beginners, complex relationship views suitable for advanced learners, and personalized interpretation views suitable for individual patients can be created. Each view should retain common structural identifiers and versioning to allow for the interpretation of differences in expression. Academic work is responsible for verifying that these levels meet learning needs, while enterprise work is responsible for ensuring consistency in generation, delivery, and updating.
How can physical models improve anatomy teaching?

Research has progressed from satisfaction and structure identification to pathological explanation and case-based reasoning. Separable, patient-specific and mixed-media models are expanding curriculum design.
The next step is to connect specific model features with learning tasks and measure delayed outcomes, identifying which students and topics benefit most.
Can the model help patients understand surgery and disease?

Research has progressed from creating individual models to randomized comparative and communication scales. More granular assessments can differentiate between anatomical understanding, surgical understanding, and communication experience.
Further work should identify which patients and questions benefit from models, test whether understanding persists and examine changes in questioning and participation in decisions.
How do model fabrication time and cost affect educational adoption?

Research has expanded from material prices and print time to complete workflows and service organization. Open tools reduce initial barriers, while quality checks and staff capabilities determine whether services scale consistently.
The key to promoting teaching is to select a complexity commensurate with the task and to make digital design, models and courses repeatable.

The first transformation question is about the comparison conditions. The model group and the traditional group need clear records of the content, teachers, instruction time, and practice activities. If the model group receives more interaction, the study answers whether the reinforcement curriculum is effective; if we want to estimate the role of the entities themselves, the interaction between the two groups needs to be kept similar. Once the comparison objects are clearly defined, positive results can be used for appropriate curriculum decisions and can also explain why different studies show different results.

The second issue is the level of the outcome. Multiple-choice tests assess factual recognition; localization and explanation tasks assess spatial relationships; new cases test reasoning; and observation of questions and teach-back assesses communication. Satisfaction measures acceptance, whereas curriculum deployment requires evidence of improved capabilities. Combining immediate, delayed and transfer outcomes distinguishes brief attention effects from durable conceptual learning and informs how often lessons should recur.

The third issue is accessibility and information overload. Too many colors, labels, or internal structures can make it difficult for users with limited knowledge to find the key points; oversimplification may miss crucial relationships. Research can stratify users based on their existing knowledge and spatial abilities to examine who benefits most from physical interaction. For patients, it is also necessary to examine whether verbal expression, visual recognition, and hand manipulation affect use, and to select alternative modes of expression that support the same core interpretation.
How can physical models improve anatomy teaching?
Near term: Task-oriented and case-oriented models will continue to be added. They are easier to align with course objectives.

Mid-term: The model, digital content, and assessment question bank may be delivered together. Evidence is needed to demonstrate that the instructional combination is helpful for delayed comprehension and reasoning in new cases.
Observation indicators: structural identification, spatial relationship interpretation, case reasoning, delayed performance, learning time, model reuse, and effective learning cost per student.
Can the model help patients understand surgery and disease?
Near term: models with clear tasks are particularly relevant to complex spatial explanations and major-surgery consultations. The decision to fabricate should follow the patient’s questions.
Mid-term: The model may be combined with digital explanatory materials and shared decision-making tools. Delayed understanding and decision-making participation need to be evaluated.
Observation indicators: correct paraphrasing, questioning quality, decision conflict, anxiety changes, consultation time, delayed memory and patient's actual use of the model.
How do model fabrication time and cost affect educational adoption?
Near term: Reusable design and task adaptation will help expand usage. Complexity should be determined by the course objectives.
Mid-term: Model services may shift from unit purchases to course or periodic supply. This is contingent on relatively stable usage frequency and maintenance requirements.
Observation indicators: man-hours, equipment occupancy, rework rate, delivery cycle, number of available times, maintenance costs, and cost per effective learning session.

The baseline scenario for 2027–2029 is joint design of models and learning activities. Products that connect what to observe, what to do and what to explain can support established teaching and consultation pathways. Indicators include key-knowledge accuracy, delayed retention, reasoning about new cases, completeness of patient teach-back and clinician or teacher time per effective use.

In scenarios with ample resources, digital case libraries can support the generation of multiple expressions based on the audience, with entity models concentrated on parts requiring common identification or manipulation. This scenario is valid only if data review and version management are reliable, generated views retain key relationships, and production processes are compatible with the curriculum. When resources are limited, prioritizing the establishment of reusable base models and representative variations, and comparing the return on investment using the same learning task, can also create a sustainable path.

Research priorities should begin by identifying effective endpoints for different learning objectives, followed by a comparison of content and time fit, and then an evaluation of long-term use and cost-effectiveness. Cost statistics should include design, manufacturing, review, explanation, and maintenance, and be amortized according to the number of effective users. If the increased explanation time of the model can be exchanged for better retention and less misunderstanding, this investment needs to be evaluated throughout the learning or consulting process; if long-term benefits are concentrated in a specific group, then evidence-based targeted usage rules can be developed.

The promotion of the course should also observe the differences in results among teachers. If the same model performs significantly differently in the hands of different teachers, it indicates that the accompanying questions and feedback methods deserve standardization; if the differences mainly stem from students' prior knowledge, then tiered activities can be adopted. Adding this information to a case database allows the model iteration to focus on real learning difficulties.
